en: The Third Uddyota.

The Third Uddyota—thus, having demonstrated the nature of *dhvani* along with its varieties by way of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), it is now elucidated again by way of the suggester (*vyañjaka*). Locana: The Third Uddyota. I remember [the Lord] who is distinguished by his skill in the playful destruction of Smara (Kāma).
The Supreme Goddess, who forcibly takes half of Śambhu’s body.
In order to establish the connection with the subsequent section, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) says "evam" and so forth.
In that regard, first of all, the varieties such as *avivakṣitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is not intended) are presented by way of the expressed meaning (*vācya*);
and although the expressed meaning itself is indeed the suggester (*vyañjaka*).

As it has been said: "Wherein the meaning or the word [is predominant]. And thus, although the distinction was stated by way of the manifestor (vyañjaka), nevertheless that expressed meaning (vācya-artha) is distinguished precisely by way of the manifested (vyaṅgya).

For thus, that which is not intended to be expressed (avivakṣita) is subordinated by the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), while that which is intended but where the primary meaning is other than the literal (vivakṣitānyapara) is said to be directed solely toward the suggested sense; in this way, within the two fundamental divisions themselves, along with their respective intermediate subdivisions, there exists the nature of the suggester (vyañjaka). [Now begins the commentary on the third chapter (udyota): Now, I shall [expound] the third, the mature chapter, according to my understanding.
I shall explain something; may the wise be gracious toward me in this matter.
"I remember.
For Smara, that is, Kāma, the very act of destruction is his sport; he is one who possesses skill—that is, the capacity—in that regard.

By the phrase "forcibly seizing half of Śambhu’s body," the superior agility of the Supreme Goddess (Parameśvarī) is illuminated, even when compared to the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) who possesses such [power].
"Uddyota" means another illumination; "udyotāntara" refers to the third illumination.
The meaning is that he intends to establish a connection with him in the form of an association, together with a second light.
By the statement "shown by way of the suggested," it is understood that it is not shown by way of the suggester.
Having raised the objection that this is untenable, he introduces [the following] by showing the intended meaning of that statement, beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*) and so forth;
it should be connected with the passage beginning "Even though" (*yadyapi*).
In that context, "in that" (*tatra*) refers to *dhvani*.
"By way of the expressed," and so forth.

The meaning is that the various divisions of *dhvani*, such as "that whose expressed meaning is unintended" (*avivakṣitavācya*), are possible only by relying upon the "distinguishing factor" (the expressed meaning) as qualified by being "unintended" and so on.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And the expressed," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "as it has been stated":
the meaning is that it has been stated that the expressed [meaning] possesses the capacity to suggest.
To the question, "What follows from this?", he says: "And therefore," and so forth.
"Sa" means the manifestor;
"rendered subordinate by the manifested" means [the manifestor].

The sense is that by stating that the expressed meaning is not intended [as primary], it is established that it has been rendered subordinate by the suggested meaning. "Inclined toward the suggested meaning" means dependent upon the suggested meaning. He concludes with the words "Thus," and so forth.

"In the two primary divisions" means in the cases of *avivakṣitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is not intended) and *vivakṣitānyaparavācya* (where the expressed meaning is intended but has another purpose).
"By way of the suggested meaning," and so forth.
The meaning is: "precisely by virtue of its dependence on the suggested sense.
For this very reason—that is, for the reason already stated—[he says] "moreover" (kiñca).
The manifestation of that type of suggestion where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣita-vācya*) occurs through words and sentences;
likewise, the same applies to the other type of *dhvani*, which consists of a suggested meaning in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya*). (DhvK 3.1)
The manifestation of that type of dhvani in which the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary occurs through both words and sentences;
this applies as well to the other type of dhvani, in which the suggested meaning takes the form of a resonance (anuraṇana).

Regarding the type where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*) and the literal sense is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*), its manifestation through individual words (*padaprakāśatā*) is seen, for example, in the great seer Vyāsa: "These seven are the fuel-sticks of prosperity," or in Kālidāsa: "Who, when you are ready [for battle], would neglect his wife distressed by separation? or again: "For what indeed is not an ornament for beautiful forms?"
In these examples, the words "samidhaḥ" (the fuel-sticks), "sannaddhaḥ" (armed), and "madhurāṇām" (of the sweet things) have been employed solely with the intention of being suggestors (*vyañjaka*).
The *Locana* states: "That meaning attains its distinction precisely by being dependent on looking toward the suggestible (*vyaṅgya*);
for this very reason, he says: 'by way of the suggestible.'"
Furthermore, although the object (artha) is indeed a suggester (vyañjaka), it is also capable of being the suggested (vyaṅgya);
the word (śabda), however, is never the suggested, but is always only the suggester.
Thus he says: "by way of the suggester."

Nor is it the case that the distinction of the expressed meaning (vācya) from its unintended forms and so forth has not been revealed in every respect; rather, although it was revealed previously, it is now revealed once more by way of the pure suggester (śuddhavyañjaka).

To explain: apart from looking toward the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), there is a distinction among the suggesters based on their very nature—namely, whether they are a word, a sentence, phonemes, a portion of a word, a composition (saṅghaṭanā), or a great sentence (mahāvākya).

And since these [suggesters] can never themselves become the suggested meaning in the same way that the "meaning" (artha) can, the intended sense is that the distinction is revealed by way of that specific nature which is restricted solely to being a suggester.
As for the one who explains, "by way of the suggested objects, figures, and sentiments," he should be asked this: first of all, this threefold division was not made by the author of the *kārikās*;
rather, it was shown by the author of the commentary (*vṛtti*).

The meaning is that the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) does not now proceed to reveal the distinction [between the two types of *arthavāda*], because there is another intended purpose for the statement "it has been shown by the *Bālapriyā*.
He states this with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*), etc.
"Meaning" (*arthaḥ*) refers to the expressed sense (*vācya*).
"Vyaṅgya," and so forth;
the meaning is that it sometimes also becomes the suggested (vyaṅgya). He says this [to explain].
The meaning is: "He says this because of that intention. [Objection:
But if it is thus, then in the passage "again by way of the manifestor," the meaning is "it occurs"; so why does he say "he says this"?
[Response: The meaning is: "He says this because of that intention."

[Objection: But in that case, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) in the phrase "again by way of the manifestor" (*punar-vyañjaka-mukhena*) is inappropriate; therefore, he explains the intended meaning with the words beginning with "na ca.
"Therein" (*tatra*) means:
in the denoted object as qualified by distinctions such as being unintended (*avivakṣitatva*), and so forth.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the distinction] does not fail to exist because of its being a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

Alternatively, if the reading is *vyañjakamukhatvam*, the meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "of the expressed" (*vācyasya*) and so forth, there is a distinction based on the reason—which consists in the nature of the expressed being unintended (*avivakṣita*) and so on; this refers to a specific sub-division of *dhvani* within that distinction of *dhvani*.
He explains the very meaning already stated—that it is not non-existent—by means of the phrase "even through the medium of the manifester" (*vyañjakamukhenāpi*), and so forth.
Furthermore, he states the resultant meaning of the phrase "through the medium of the manifester" with the words "pure," and so forth;
the sense is "solely through the medium of the manifester."
"Of these" means "of words and so forth. "Is possible" [means:]...
The reading is also "sambhāvyate.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
[The *Locana* states: "In that case, if there is a difference in agents—such as 'this was done' and 'this is being done'—what connection (*saṅgati*) could there be?"

Nor, however, has the consistency with all the preceding texts been thereby established, since other varieties such as those where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*) have also been shown; so enough of this dispute with those who share the lineage of my own venerable teachers.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the verse is for the purpose of dispelling any suspicion regarding a correspondence based on numerical order (*yathāsaṅkhya*).
Therefore, that [type of suggestion] whose expressed meaning is unintended (avivakṣitavācya), though having two divisions, is further twofold as being manifested by a word or by a sentence.

As for the other type—whose denoted meaning is intended (vivakṣitābhidheya)—its subdivision called "successively indicated" (kramadyotya), together with its own internal subdivisions, is likewise each twofold. The meaning is: that which has a suggested sense (vyaṅgya) whose form consists of a "resonance" (anuraṇana), that is, a similarity through such representation.
By the phrase "of the great seer" (maharṣeḥ), he refers back to what was previously stated,
namely that [these qualities] are observed in literary works such as the *Rāmāyaṇa* and the *Mahābhārata*.
Fortitude, forgiveness, compassion, purity, kindness, and speech that is not harsh;
Not betraying friends and the sevenfold fuel of prosperity are the sources of glory.
In this context, the meaning of the word *sami* is entirely set aside because it is impossible [for it to apply here].

Furthermore, by the word *sami*, the suggested meaning—the capacity of the seven [qualities] to serve as an illuminator (*uddīpana*) of splendor (*lakṣmī*) that is independent of anything else—is intimated by the poet’s intention (*vaktr-abhipreta*). This is what is meant by "dhvani."

Although this meaning is also indicated by examples such as "like a mirror blinded by breath," nevertheless, other examples have been stated here in order to demonstrate, by way of occasion, their extensive application to various instances of usage.
And in these cases, there is a complete sublation of the literal meaning, following what was previously stated; such is the nature [of this figure].
The meaning is that [the word] has the nature of being the beginning of a line (*padādi*).
Regarding the phrase "what is the connection when there is a difference in agents?":
the meaning is that when there is a difference in agents, the state of being logically connected (*saṅgatatva*) is not possible for this [word].

By the statement, "When this has been shown by way of the suggested (vyaṅgya), it is then illuminated by way of the suggester (vyañjaka)," it is naturally understood that the acts of showing and illuminating have a single agent; [the point is] that such [a claim] would be inconsistent.
The connection is: "What is the consistency? It should be asked thus."
He states another fault, beginning with "na ca" and so forth,
and "cakāra" and so forth.
In the absence of the word "ca," there would be the manifestation of a literal meaning that was not intended to be expressed.

The intention is that, otherwise, there would be a confusion regarding the meaning due to the sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) between "that" and "the manifestation of the sentence by another.
The phrase "by that" means "by the particle *ca*, which has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*)."

With the intention that the phrase "of something other than that" (*tadanyasya*) is a non-co-referential qualifier (*vyadhikaraṇaviśeṣaṇa*), he explains it with the words beginning "the intended" (*vivakṣita*).
The explanation of the passage beginning "in resonance" (*anuraṇane*) is given by the words beginning "succession" (*krama*).
The explanation of the word "form" (*rūpa*) is given by the word "manifestation" (*rūpaṇā*).
He states the result: "similarity," etc.; the connection is with the phrase "that which was stated previously."
Of the meaning of the word *samit*, which is qualified by being fuel (*idhma*); "by the word *samit*"—
the remainder [of the sense] is that its status as an indicator (*uddīpakatva*) is what is to be defined (*lakṣya*).

In this context, the word *sāmiccha* indicates by way of a mode (*prakāra*) that is common to both the expressed (*vācya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*), namely, its nature as an excitant (*uddīpaka*).

Similarly, in the phrase "indicating the state of being prepared" (*udyatatvam lakṣayati*), it should be understood that it indicates by way of a property (*dharma*) common to both [the expressed and the indicated], such as the state of being prepared (*udyatatva*).

Immediately after the words "and by the word," [the example] for that very same case of "transferred expression" (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) should be connected: "By Rāma, whose life was dear, the eye was sacrificed"—what need is there for further elaboration?

Here, by the word *sannaddha* ("armed" or "prepared"), which indicates preparedness (*udyatatva*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because its primary sense is impossible [in this context], there are suggested (*dhvanyante*) the speaker’s intended meanings such as mercilessness, the state of being beyond remedy, and acting without foresight.

Similarly, by the word *madhura* ("sweet"), which indicates qualities such as being pleasing to all objects and satisfying, there is suggested the speaker’s intended meaning that it is not surprising for this [object] to be the object of excessive longing.
[The phrase] "of that very [person]"...
The meaning is: "of that which is the second variety of [suggestion] where the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary.
For example: "An appropriate act was done by you toward the cruel Rākṣasa who grew angry at being rebuffed; and you endured it in such a way that respectable people now hold their heads high.
Now, carrying this bow in vain as a witness to your own misfortunes..."

Since he is cruel by the very nature of a *rakṣas*, and since he is blinded by anger when forcibly repulsed due to his arrogance and his refusal to obey commands, this act of cutting off the head is indeed consistent with the disposition of his own mind; for even though he is worthy of respect, [this is what follows from his character].
(The reading "mānyo 'pi bālapriya" is seen as containing a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya-artha*); if that were the case, the term "dhvanitam" would mean "made known" or "indicated.")
Regarding the phrase "asambhavatsvārthena": *svārtha* means "armored. Amara states: "'Asannaddha' [unarmed] and 'varmita' [armored]."
"They resound" (*dhvanyante*):
the word "of the cloud," which is the referent of your term, is to be supplied.
"By the sweet sound" (*madhura-śabdena*).
The meaning is: "expressing that which is distinguished by the flavor of sweetness.
Regarding the word "all" (*sarva*):
it means "one among the various qualities," such as its power to delight all objects of perception or its capacity to satisfy.
Regarding this:
"in the forms" (ākṛtiṣu) is the meaning.
"In the rejection" (pratyākhyāne) refers to these words spoken by Śrī Rāmacandra with reference to his queen Sītā.
He explains [the passage] beginning with "rakṣa" and so forth.
"Rāvaṇa" refers to the one who is Rāvaṇa.
The explanation of the term "obstructed by the refusal" (pratyākhyānaruḍ) extends from "not having transcended" up to "blinded by anger."

The teaching of which [the Buddha] cannot be transgressed in its true nature—that very state of being intoxicated with pride, namely the false conceit "I am one whose teaching cannot be transgressed," serves as the cause for being blinded by anger. Being rejected means being refuted by you.
The connection is: "This performance is appropriate to the disposition of your own mind."
He explains this [point] as follows: "That which is called 'decapitation' is not appropriate for one who loves his beloved.

Here, the word *rāmeṇa* (by Rāma) is the suggester (*vyañjaka*), its literal meaning being transferred through suggestion (*vyaṅgyābhisaṅkramitavācya*) due to its singular essence of daring (*sāhasaikarasatva*).
[The Locana says: "Someone might transgress my command."
The meaning is that even though it was such [an offense], it was not taken into account by her;

furthermore, it was endured in that manner—without any change of state—with the thought that it was a festival, as evidenced by the dilation of the eyes, the serenity of the face, and other such signs.

"In such a way" (*yathā*) means by whatever manner; "a person of good family" (*kulajana*) refers to anyone, even one who is like a commoner, who is designated by the term "wife of a noble family" (*kulavadhū*).
She held her head high, thinking, "Indeed, we are noble women of such a lineage.

Yet, at the time of having her hair cut, she endured it and held her head so high that even other women of noble family would hold their heads high; thus, by the very fact that they did not do so, Rāvaṇa’s and your own propriety of action was brought to fulfillment.
For me, however, everything has turned out to be entirely inappropriate.

For instance, although my engagement with the bow was rendered impossible by my exile from the kingdom and other such events, that bow which once existed for the sole purpose of protecting my wife— now that she is no longer to be protected and is even in peril— I nevertheless continue to carry it.
Therefore, it is certainly conceivable that the sole purpose for him is the protection of his own life;
yet this is not proper, as it is said:
"O beautiful women!"
The meaning is that [the hero] is transformed by other suggested qualities such as incomparable daring, heroism, truthfulness, faithfulness to one's word, and acting appropriately.

As for the explanation given—that "the inclusion of qualities such as those of a base person (kāpuruṣa) is due to the word 'etcetera' (ādi)"—that is incorrect; for indeed, these very qualities would be appropriate for a base person.

The word "dear" has now become a mere sound; even that which is called "love," the very ground for the application of the word "dear," is stained by impropriety—this is because Rāvaṇa, before Śrī Rāma, performed the decapitation of the illusory Sītā. This is the sense.
The meaning is "by means of this understanding.
The word *te* (they) is connected with both *pratyākhyāna* (rejection) and *kṛtam* (done).
He states the meaning of the passage: "Just as," and so forth.
Even though he was such [a person], distinguished by unsurpassed sovereignty and other qualities, he was *gaṇitaḥ*, that is, respected.
Even that, namely, the cutting off of his head.
The qualification of the word "buddhyā" (by means of cognition) is "netra" and so forth.
"Visphāratā" means expansion;
"soḍham" means experienced.
The connection is: "he holds his head high. The meaning is that by such conceit, he makes his head erect.
He explains it otherwise as well, beginning with "And yet," and so forth.
The explanation of the word *tat* (that) is "at the moment of decapitation.
Likewise, the commentary on the word *soḍham* (endured) is "thus loudly," and so forth.
The meaning is that when a certain lover, blinded by anger due to the rejection of his request, prepares to cut off the head, saying "He holds up his head high," [the woman] raises her head.
"By way of being eternally active" is an explanation of the meaning of the present tense suffix (*laṭ*).
Intending to explain the second half of the verse, he says "In this way," and so forth.
"Again" (*punar*) is an explanation of the word "but" (*tu*).
The explanation of "vyartham" and so forth begins with "rājya" and so on.
The explanation of "priyajīvitena" begins with "tannūnam" and so on.
And [the explanation] of "asya" [is as follows].
The meaning is "of the wielding of the bow.
"This" refers to the wielding of the bow for the purpose of protecting one's own life.
He explains the commentary passage beginning with "By Rāma" (*rāmeṇa*) and so forth—namely, the words "By Rāma" and so on.
The explanation of the phrase "having daring as its sole essence" (*sāhasaikarasatva*) is "without meeting [the enemy]" (*asametya*) and so forth.
The statement of the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is "truthful" (*satya*) and so forth.

In this regard, the author of the Pradīpa holds that the delimitor of the indicated sense (lakṣyatāvacchedaka) of the word "Rāma" is cowardice; Cakravartin holds it to be feigned affection; and Bhaṭṭa Gopāla holds it to be a turning away from manly effort.
Or as it is said:
"In this way, people compare her cheek to the orb of the moon; yet in the investigation of ultimate reality, the wretched moon is merely like the moon."
Here, the second occurrence of the word "moon" (*candra*) is one in which the expressed meaning is transferred to another sense (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*).

An example of the type of "sentence-revelation" (*vākyaprakāśatā*) belonging to the sub-variety of "the expressed meaning being entirely set aside" (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*) within the category of "the expressed meaning not intended" (*avivakṣitavācya*) is as follows: "That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man keeps watch;
that wherein all beings keep watch is night for the sage who sees."
"Because of the presence of the objective and the excitatory determinants (*ālambana* and *uddīpana-vibhāva*) of grief, the rasa of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*) is made manifest in Rāma.
"Emea" means:
in this very way, people offer the orb of the moon as a comparison for her cheek.
But when the ultimate truth is investigated, the moon is as wretched as the moon [itself]—so it is said.
"In this very way" means by one's own blindness due to a lack of discernment;
"the people" refers to those who rely solely on following the path established by worldly convention.

Regarding her— she whose form is of great value due to its multitude of extraordinary qualities— in the matter of providing a comparison for her cheek, the lunar orb, which ought to have been something superior to that [cheek], instead becomes vastly inferior; for the moon’s disc is rendered dim under the pretext of a dark spot, even though it is intended as a comparison for the surface of the cheek, which resides in the midst of her face and constitutes the very essence of all natural beauty.
Thus, although the world has fallen into the current of a torrential flood,

nevertheless, if investigators were to examine it, that wretched thing known as "the moon"— which is merely a vessel for pity— is in fact nothing but an object that has undergone a transition into other properties such as perishability, the absence of brilliance, and impurity.
And here, just as there is a transference of other suggested properties (*vyaṅgyadharmāntara*), so too should what was stated previously be kept in mind;
the same applies to what follows.

Having thus illustrated both varieties of the first division by way of their manifestation through words (*padaprakāśakatva*), he illustrates them by way of their manifestation through sentences (*vākyaprakāśakatva*) with the verse beginning "yā niśā... (That which is night...).

Regarding the phrase "what is intended to be said": for by that which has been so stated, no instruction toward one who is to be instructed is accomplished. [The commentary] begins with "bālapriyā śoka" and so forth.
The beloved’s death being contemplated is the objective determinant (*ālambana-vibhāva*);
the recollection of the beloved’s extraordinary deeds and so forth connected with her is the excitant determinant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).
He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "in this very way" (*evameva*) as follows: "by himself" (*svayam*), and so on.
"Tadadhikam" means "superior to the cheek"; the grammatical connection is that it should be employed in the simile (*upamā*).
The meaning is that it should be stated as a point of comparison. "From there" means from the cheek.
The commentary on the word *śaśipada* (the moon's foot) begins with "the pretext of a spot" (*kalaṅka*) and so forth.
It means "made dim," that is, made turbid, by the hare which serves as the pretext for the spot.
With the intention of explaining that the particle *via* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), he says: "only the moon" (*candra eva*).

In this context, the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the term "second moon" should be understood as occurring either by way of its being denotable by the word "moon" or by way of its being devoid of [actual] qualities (*guṇaśūnyatva*).
He states the properties of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyadharma*) beginning with "perishability," etc.,
[and] "the meaning which has been transferred."
The meaning is "the referent of the word 'moon'";
"here" means "in the two examples mentioned."
"Previously stated" means that which was stated at the beginning of the second chapter (udyota). "By that which has been stated" refers to that very [statement].

The meaning is: "by the object denoted by the word *niśā* (night) and so forth," that is, by the referent such as "night" and so on. For by this sentence, neither the meaning of "night" nor any meaning of "waking" is intended to be expressed. What then? It is the sage's state of being intent upon the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and his turning away from what is unreal (*atattva*) that is established. Thus, this [sentence] functions as a suggestor (*vyañjaka*) through the process of the literal sense being set aside (*tiraskṛtavācya*).

An example of that same type of suggestion where the expressed meaning is transmuted (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) and is manifested by the sentence as a whole is as follows: "For some it is composed of unevenness; for some it is fashioned from restlessness; for some it consists of weariness; and for some it is free from weariness—such is Time."
For some, Time acts as poison; for others, it proceeds as the creation of nectar.
For some, it consists of both poison and nectar; for others, it is neither poison nor nectar.
[Thus is the shadow. What is the point of saying that one must stay awake during the night and otherwise behave as if it were day?

Therefore, this sentence—whose literal meaning is sublated—suggests through the sign of the world-transcending nature of the self-restrained (saṃyamin) an attentiveness toward the vision of reality and an aversion toward false views. Furthermore, since the meaning of every word is established through relativity, one should not assume that an implied meaning is necessitated by the impossibility of the literal sense of the word "all" (*sarva*).

For all beings—of the fourteen classes beginning with Brahmā and ending with the stationary—the night is that vision of reality which produces delusion; in that [vision], the self-controlled one remains awake, [thinking] "How might this [state] be attained? (Bālapriyā: "No one" means that no instruction whatsoever is effective.)
The sense is that it is necessary for this [verse] from the Bhagavadgītā to be devoted to instruction.
To the question "Why is it not established [as such]?", he says: "In the night," and so forth;
"elsewhere, as in the case of night."
"By day and by night" means at all times. "Sublated" means sublated by its lack of utility.
"Statement" (vākya) means a collection of words such as "The night is awake," and so forth;
the intended meanings indicated by each of those respective words will be demonstrated.
"Supramundane," and so forth;
the meaning is "by reason of being supramundane.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the word *niśā* (night), which denotes the time of sleep, is connected with all beings as it encompasses all entities, does it not follow that even the practitioner (*saṃyamin*) is included within that connection?

And since the phrase "he is awake" is logically inconsistent with that intended meaning, he dispels the doubt that—because the suggested sense has been made explicit by this [statement]—it cannot be considered *dhvani*, by saying "of every word and meaning," and so forth.
Regarding the term "relatively":
here the word "all" (*sarva*) denotes everything except for that which is being restrained; therefore, the meaning is "in relation to something."
"Regarding the phrase *sarvaśabdārtha*":
it means "the concomitance with all word-meanings.
This meaning refers to the previously mentioned suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).
"Projected" means manifested.
He explains the verse beginning with "of all," etc.:
"even of the fourteen elements."

The meaning is: for all embodied beings (dehin) of fourteen kinds—namely, the eightfold divine (*daiva*) divided into *brahma*, *prājāpatya*, *aindra*, *pitrya*, *gāndharva*, *yākṣa*, *rākṣasa*, and *paiśāca*; the single-fold human (*mānuṣa*); and the fivefold animal (*tairyagyona*) divided into beasts, birds, snakes, insects, and stationary beings (*sthāvara*).
As it is stated in the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*: "The divine is of eight varieties," and so forth.

The phrase "producing delusion" explains the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) of the word "night. To the question "What is it?", he says: "That very [night]. He states the indicated meaning of the word "is awake" with the words beginning with "How," and so forth.
The meaning is that one is not a self-restrained ascetic (*saṃyamī*) merely by the avoidance of sense objects;
rather, one is so when one remains awake during the night of all beings—that is, during the deluding [ignorance]—and considers how this [delusion] is to be abandoned.
On the other hand, that false view in which all beings remain awake, being in a state of extreme wakefulness, is his "night," for it is a domain of non-awakening.
For he is not awakened to that activity;
in the very same way, one established in supramundane conduct sees and reflects.
For him, the functioning of the internal and external faculties has already fulfilled its purpose.

But another [person] neither sees nor reflects; the intended meaning is that one should be intent upon the vision of reality (*tattva*). Thus, even the expressions "one who sees" and "of the Sage" are not merely deluded regarding their own self-interest.
Rather, it comes to rest solely in the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Since the words "yat" and "tat" do not possess independent meanings, this entire collection of words, accompanied by the verb, is directed toward the suggested meaning.
Thus he says: "For by this sentence..."
"It is being presented" means it is being suggested (*dhvanyate*). "Rendered uneven" means having attained a state of unevenness;
[this refers] to certain evildoers or to those who are excessively discerning.
For some who possess only good deeds or are utterly lacking in discernment, it consists of the creation of nectar;
for others whose karma is mixed or who possess both discernment and lack of discernment, it consists of that which is composed of both poison and nectar.

The connection [of the verse] is that for some who are mostly deluded, or for those who have ascended to the stages of yoga (*yogabhūmikā*) attained through the flow [of practice], time passes as if it were composed of poison and nectar.

Furthermore, the terms "poison" (*viṣa*) and "nectar" (*amṛta*) function here to denote the means of pleasure and pain through conventional metaphorical usage (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), similar to words such as "saltiness" (*lāvaṇya*);
for example, as in the expressions "the neem tree is poison" (*viṣaṃ nimbaḥ*) and "the wood-apple is nectar" (*amṛtaṃ kapittham*).
And in this case, pleasure and pain do not rest merely in their means of accomplishment;
rather, they culminate in the pleasure and pain that constitute one's own task.
Nor are those means entirely dear to the ignorant; rather, with the thought "How might this [pleasure] be attained?", one practices the means for its attainment—this is the meaning.
He states the intended meaning with the words "But not," and so forth.
"The self-controlled one" (saṃyamī) refers to one who is denoted by the term *saṃyamī*.
Since it is not well-known that the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*) produces delusion, he explains it otherwise with the words "Or if," and so forth.
"In delusion" (mohinyām) means "in ignorance" (avidyāyām).
"In false view" (mithyādṛṣṭau) [is the meaning].
The meaning is: "in ignorance" or "in its effect, the manifold world of duality.
Regarding the word "his":
it means "of the practitioner who has restrained his senses."
The following is an elaboration on the phrase "the object of non-awakening": "For of that," and so forth.
"Asau" (this one) means the practitioner of restraint (*saṃyamī*).

"Establishment in supramundane conduct" is the statement of the intended meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) of the term "restrained one" (*saṃyamin*). Regarding the explanation of "the Sage who sees," it is said: "he sees and he reflects.

Here, the word "sees" indicates [the Sage] by way of the functioning of the external senses having fulfilled their purpose, and the word "reflects" indicates him by way of the functioning of the internal organ having fulfilled its purpose; thus he says, "of that very [Sage]," and so forth.
By this, he states the meaning to be understood: "other," and so forth.
He states the resultant suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*): "in reality," and "only the suggested."
The meaning is: "only in the primary suggested sense (mukhyavyaṅgya) previously mentioned. Regarding the phrase "he says that":
the meaning is "he says it because of the aforementioned intention."
The explanation of the phrase "of some" (*keṣām api*) and so forth is "of certain ones" (*keṣāñcit*) and so forth.

The word "goes" (*prayāti*) means "transcends. With the intention of following the reading of the verse as *amiaṇimmāo*, he provides the shadow-translation (Sanskrit equivalent): "consisting of nectar" (*amṛtanirmāṇa*).
The meaning is: he whose creation is like that of nectar.

Intending to establish what was stated in the commentary—that the words *viṣa* (poison) and *amṛta* (nectar) have their literal meanings transferred to denote suffering and happiness respectively—the author says: "the words *viṣa* and *amṛta*, etc.
The mention of *sukha-duḥkha* (happiness-suffering) in reverse order means [the objects] which are the causes of suffering and happiness.
Or there may be such a reading; in this way, it should be understood for what follows as well.
Here he states an illustration, beginning with "just as," and so forth.
The meaning of "iti" is "in such cases as 'iti' and so forth.
He states the specific distinction regarding the example under discussion with the words beginning with "na ca," etc.
Regarding the word "atra":
The meaning is "in the case of the example under discussion.
"Tanmātra" means "merely the means for pleasure and pain."

In this sentence, because the words "poison" (*viṣa*) and "nectar" (*amṛta*) have their literal meanings transferred to the forms of suffering and pleasure respectively, there is a linguistic usage based on those transferred meanings; thus, the function of suggestion belongs to that type where the literal meaning is transferred to another sense (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*).

Regarding the variety arising from the power of the word (*śabdaśaktyudbhava*) where the intended denotation is a suggestion in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇanarūpa-vyaṅgya*), its manifestation through the word (*padaprakāśatā*) is as follows—[according to] the *Locana*: [it is] not [manifested] by the intended [meaning], because those two [meanings] would be impossible without a means of proof.
Thus he says: "by means of the two [types of suggestion] where the expressed meaning is transferred (*saṅkramitavācya*).
The term "of some" (*keṣāñcit*) refers to its transfer to a specific [object], while for the verb "does not transfer" (*atakrāmati*), there is a transfer of the action alone.

And regarding the term "time" (kāla), there is a transition into all conventional usage; however, for the sake of illustration, the author of the commentary explained it as merely the transition of [the notions of] poison and nectar. Thus he says: "in the sentence."

Having thus illustrated the four modes characterized by the first half of the verse, he now illustrates in sequence the other six modes adopted in the second half of the verse, beginning with "of the intended subject matter" (*vivakṣitābhidheyasya*) and so forth;
[the word] "to obtain" (*prātuṃ*) means "to fulfill.
The plural number in "with riches" (*dhanaiḥ*) is for the purpose of indicating that "whatever one desires, that very thing [is given]."
For this very reason, the word "wealth" (artha) is included; for the world is generally intent upon wealth, rather than being intent upon benefiting others through virtues.
"By fate" (daivataḥ) means "by that which cannot be questioned"; it is to be connected with the phrase "and for the pleasure of the ignorant" (bālapriyā).
The word "intended" (*vivakṣite*) is drawn back [from the previous context].
"To its own task" (*svakartavya*) means "to its own probandum" (*svasādhya*).
The term "svapada" (one's own position) refers to the means of proof (*sādhana*).
And it is not that [the reason] is absent where it is intended; rather, it is indeed present where it is intended.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because it is devoid of a means of proof," and so forth.
"He says this" means that, according to the stated intention, he asserts that the denotable meaning has been transferred to the forms of pleasure and pain.

In expressions such as "The neem is poison; the wood-apple is nectar," what is intended by the conventional (nirūḍha) secondary function (lakṣaṇā) is precisely the sense that the neem is a cause of suffering and the wood-apple is a cause of happiness.

In the present context, however, since the intended meaning is that time passes for some as consisting of suffering and for others as consisting of happiness, there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *viṣa* (poison) toward a suffering produced by some means, and of the word *amṛta* (nectar) toward a happiness produced by some means; the distinction between suffering and happiness is thus suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

Furthermore, because poison and nectar appear as the means [to those respective states], there is a case of the literal meaning being transferred to another sense (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācyatā*); such is the underlying idea.

The meaning is that there is a transfer (*saṅkrānti*) of the word "of some" (*keṣāñcit*) to a specific [referent]; and likewise, there is a transfer of the word "of some" (*keṣām api*), which denotes those delimited by qualities whose specific nature is unknown, to the specific referent already stated, namely "of the evildoers" (*duṣkṛtinām*) and so forth.
The fact that the evildoers and others are unknown and so on is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
When the meaning is "in mere action," it means "in all conventional usage"; that is to say, in the totality of things that constitute the sphere of conventional usage.
Regarding the phrase "the second":
the meaning is that which was accepted—that is, what was stated—in the second half-verse.
Regarding the word "to obtain" (*prātuṃ*): [it refers to the attainment of the goal].

The indeclinable ‘asmī’ is used in the sense of ‘I’. ‘If indeed by fate I were not created to satisfy the desire of those seeking wealth through riches’—this is an admission; the word ‘then’ (tarhi) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

"I am dull-witted; why was I not made by fate, or rather, why was I not created as a pond with clear waters on the path, or even a well?"— the pond is mentioned first because it is superior to the well.
"Locane" means "one who seeks after an object"— that is to say, a person who is desirous of some wealth, such as cattle, gold, or the like, from among various things.
"Therefore" (ata eva) refers to this very fact.
The meaning is: "precisely because of the intention already stated.
The explanation of the sense is: "it is impossible," and so forth; the underlying idea is that fate (daiva) is invisible.

"I was not created to satisfy the desires of supplicants with wealth; if indeed I was not created by fate [for that purpose], then why have I been made so dull as a pond or a well on a path where the clouds are pouring rain? (1)

For here, the word "jaḍa" (dull/stupid), employed by the despondent speaker as being in grammatical apposition with his own self, attains through its own power an apposition with the well (*kūpa*) by way of resonance (*anuraṇana*). This is precisely what constitutes the manifestation of a sentence: as in the lion-roars in the *Harṣacarita*: "Now that this great dissolution has occurred, you alone remain as the serpent Śeṣa to support the earth.
For this sentence clearly manifests another meaning through the power of the word itself by means of resonance.
"I am the eye"—
this is the sense of detachment (*nirveda*), for while someone else has certainly been created, "I" have not.
It holds water that is clear and beneficial to the world.
"Or a well" means not even being noticed by people.
"By way of being in grammatical apposition with the self" means...

"Insentient" (*jaḍaḥ*) means bewildered as to what ought to be done; furthermore, a well is "insentient" in the sense that it lacks the capacity for discrimination regarding whose request is of what kind.
For this very reason, it is "insentient"—that is, cool and devoid of the fever of world-weariness (*nirveda*).
Likewise, "jaḍa" (dull/inert) is capable of benefiting others due to its connection with cold water.
With this third meaning, he says "the state of being in grammatical apposition with 'well' (kūpa)," intending that this word "jaḍa" connects with a redundant meaning in the sense of a pond (taṭāka).
By the phrase "by its own power," he applies the quality of arising from the power of the word itself.
Regarding the term *mahāpralaya*:

it refers to that which is a cause of sorrow where there is a complete dissolution (*pralaya*) of the great festival (*maha*). When such a state has occurred, you alone remain as Śeṣa for the purpose of sustaining the burden of the earth—that is, the sovereignty—so that she may find comfort. Since the meaning of the sentence is thus complete, [the author] states the implied sense through the words "O Beloved of Children" (*bālapriya*) by saying "for another indeed," and so forth.
"Useful to the world" refers to the phrase "by the world," and so forth; it is an explanation of the implied meaning.

The phrase "as being co-located with the self" (*ātmasamānādhikaraṇatayā*) is taken as a pratīka at the beginning in order to indicate that an insentient object (*jaḍapadārtha*), which is connected to the sense of "we" (*asmadartha*), will be explained.
He states that meaning [with the words] "confused as to what ought to be done" (*kiṅkartavyatāmūḍha*).
He states the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) connected to the word "well" (*kūpa*) with the words "and yet," and so forth.
Regarding this, he states another point: "For this very reason," and so forth.
"For this very reason" means precisely because of the absence of distinction (*viveka*). "Cool" [is the term used].
“*Śiśira* means *jaḍa* (dull/frozen),” according to Amara. By this, he states the implied meaning: "through despondency" (*nirveda*).
Since there is no distinction between the letters *la* and *ḍa*, he explains that the word *jaḍa* also signifies "consisting of water," as indicated by the phrase beginning with "likewise" (*tathā*).

In the commentary, by the phrase "it attains coreferentiality with the word *kūpa*," it is stated that the word *jaḍa* has coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) only with the word *kūpa*, and not even with the word *taṭāka*.
Anticipating the doubt as to why this is so, he introduces the relevant passage, beginning with "by this" and so forth; [the phrase] "by this, in the sense of the third case" means:
By this, in the sense of the third case (instrumental), [it is shown].
The meaning is: by means of the third reason stated among the things connected with the well—namely, "by virtue of carrying cold water," and so forth.
"By the purpose of the pond" (taṭākārthena) means: together with that [purpose].
Regarding the term "tautology" (*punarukta*): the meaning is that by stating the very purpose of the qualifier "clear clouds" (*prasannāmbudhara*), there would be a connection to a redundant meaning.
To exclude any other possible interpretation regarding the phrase "by its own power" (*svaśaktyā*), he says "sound," and so forth.
He states the literal meaning with the words "in the festival" (*maha-sya*), etc.
The explanation of the word "in this" (*asmin*) is given by "in grief," etc.
[The phrase] *vṛtte jāte* means "when it has occurred."
He demonstrates another suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) with the verse beginning "kalpa" and so forth.

This very [suggested meaning], whose body is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, attains the status of a "manifestation of the power of the sense" (*arthaśaktyudbhava*) within its specific variety, as in the *Harivijaya*:
"With sprouts on its shoulders, fragrant for a moment, and possessing a delightful scent of wine..."
The face of the Goddess of the Month of Madhu was seized by the God of the Flower-Arrows, even though it was not desired by her.

For here, although it was not bestowed by the Flower-Arrowed One (Kusumaśara), the face was seized by the splendor of the spring season; thus, the phrase "although not bestowed," which denotes this particular state, reveals through the power of its meaning (arthaśakti) the forceful compulsion of the Flower-Arrowed One.

Within this very same variety, the manifestation through a sentence (vākyaprakāśyatā) is as previously illustrated by the example beginning with "Prepare yourself for the spring month" (sajjehi surahimāso).

In this context, the sentence-meaning—"The fragrant month is preparing [itself], yet it does not yet discharge its arrows at the bodiless god"—has its body produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet; it indicates the state of the spring season being tormented by the agitation of the god of love.
As for the *Locana*: "Even though the serpent-king has dissolved even within the elephants of the quarters," etc., is another meaning (*arthāntara*).
It possesses mango-sprout ear-ornaments and the momentary, spreading, highly precious, and captivating fragrance of wine;
that is, where there is the exhilaration—the aesthetic wonder—of the god of love, Manmatha, during the highly precious expansion of the festival.
Here, the word *mahārgha* is placed at the end [of the compound].
Because there are no fixed rules in Prakrit,
*chaṇa* means a festival.
Even though it was not offered, the face of the Fortune of the month of Madhu was seized by the god whose arrows are flowers.
"Mukham" means both the beginning and the mouth;
and that [mouth] becomes filled with the fragrance of wine.
The meaning "At the beginning of honey [wine], desire seizes the mind" has been rendered here as a suggestion of another meaning through the bold poetic assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*) of the poet.

In this context, two examples for the manifestation of meaning through the power of the body of the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a character invented by the poet—occurring within the scope of what is manifested by words and sentences—have not been provided. This is with the intention that the previous verse, "The body [of the suggestion] may be produced solely by bold assertion, or it may be possible by itself," would suffice as an illustration. Among these, an example of manifestation by a word is as follows: "Truly, desires are enchanting; truly, riches are delightful."
But life is indeed as fickle as the flickering side-glances of a beautiful woman.
The *Bālapriyā* provides the following explanations: "the great dissolution" (*mahāpralaya*) is glossed as "the end of the kalpa";
"for the support of the earth" (*dharaṇīdhāraṇāya*) is glossed as "the burden of the earth," and so forth;
and "Śeṣa" is glossed as "the king of the Nāgas."
"Digdantī" and so forth:
this is the explanation of the meaning of the state of being (*bhāvārtha*).
Here, the simile (*upamā*) is to be understood as suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
By perceiving the Fortune of the month of Madhu as the heroine (nāyikā), he states a meaning consistent with that [perception]—namely, "and the face.
*Surā* means liquor (*madya*).
The phrase "suggestive of another meaning" (*arthāntaravyañjaka*) refers to this.
A different meaning has been stated in the commentary regarding the passage beginning with "here," and so forth; the connection is that [the objection] was not raised with this intention.
"It is true.
This verse has also been cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.

Regarding the variety [of suggestion] arising from the power of the meaning of a body [of words] that is inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavi*), its manifestation through individual words (*pada*) is as follows:
O merchant, where are elephant tusks, and where is the reputation for wealth among us,
as long as the young woman with disheveled locks wanders about the house?

In this context, the phrase "her face with disheveled locks" suggests the hunter-woman’s attachment to the play of sexual union through the power of the meaning inherent in her own body; this, in turn, reveals the constant exhaustion of her husband from incessant sexual intercourse. In the word *locana*, the poet has composed a detached speaker; through his bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*), the word "life" (*jīvita*)—by virtue of its power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*)—suggests this: that all these desires and worldly prosperities [are but fleeting].
For in its absence, even those things considered "existent" by the wise are realized to be of the nature of non-existence;

and that very life, because it consists of the maintenance of breaths and because the function of the vital breaths is fickle, is a ground for lack of reliance. Thus, what is the use of the base act of proclaiming faults in these wretched sense-objects? One should rather reproach one's own life, which is likewise naturally fickle and therefore not at fault. It is by this much alone that profound dispassion (*vairāgya*) arises.
Manifestation through sentence (vākyaprakāśatā) is as in the verse beginning with "śikhariṇi":
"O merchant, where are our elephant tusks and tiger skins?
As long as the daughter-in-law with her face framed by disheveled locks embraces me at home."
Thus is the shadow.
He paces about with graceful movements.

Here, the word "lulita" (tossed) serves as a qualifier by its mere form; and since it is possible to imagine the seizing of elephant tusks and the like through such a state of being overwhelmed, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the meaning of the sentence at that point.
Desires are those things, such as women and the like, that are craved by the foolish. "In their absence" means in the absence of life; the connection is that life is a state of no concern [for them].
The reason for this is stated in the passage beginning with "prāṇa," and so forth.
The word *iti* here indicates a reason;
"because it is naturally fickle" means for the reason that it is by nature fickle.
The meaning is that the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is unavoidable.
Regarding the term "vāṇijaka":
how could there be [such things] in our house?
The meaning is that they do not exist.
Here, showing that being occupied with another task is the reason, he says "yāvat" and so forth;
"yāvat" means "because."
"Lulita" means "disheveled";
she is one whose face has locks of hair (*alakā*) scattered here and there in such a manner. "Snuṣā" means a son's wife.
"Because we have been embraced [by you]," the sense is: "therefore, we are intent upon protecting that [you].
Regarding the words "by ourselves," etc.:
"In the world," [it is] "naturally possible" (svatas-sambhāvitam), meaning that which is considered possible due to propriety; "of such a person" means by the power or capacity for such a matter.
The commentary on the word "embraced" (*pariṣvakta*) in the *Locana* is: "she wanders about with graceful movement.
He dispels the doubt that the suggested sense might be merely a subordinate factor in establishing the expressed meaning, beginning with the words "here," etc.
"Rolling about," and so forth— this is the meaning of "and so on.
"Its own nature," and so forth.
The meaning is "the statement of one's own nature.
"By way of arrogance" means by way of the conceit of being wealthy and so forth.
The particle *ca* serves to include other possible causes as far as they exist;
for example, "an elephant," and so forth.
Or rather, it indicates that this very [cause] is what makes the sentence manifest, as follows:
Adorned with earrings of peacock feathers, the haughty wife of the hunter wanders amidst her co-wives,
who are decorated with ornaments fashioned from pearls.

By this statement as well, the extraordinary good fortune of a certain newly married woman— a hunter’s wife whose ears are adorned with peacock feathers— is revealed; for by making known the fact that her husband has become capable of killing nothing more than a peacock, being solely intent on enjoying her company, the extreme misfortune of other women who have been married for a long time and whose ornaments are set with pearls is proclaimed.
This is because it reveals the meaning that at the time of their union, that very hunter was capable of the act of slaying a noble elephant.
Now, it has been stated that *dhvani* is a specific type of poetry; how then can it be manifested by a single word?
For a specific type of poetry is a particular arrangement of words (*śabdasandarbhaviśeṣa*) which serves as the cause for the comprehension of a distinguished meaning (*viśiṣṭārthapratipattihetu*).
And that state [of being a sentence] is not possible if it consists of words,
because words are merely reminders and are not expressive.
It is said in reply:
This fault might arise [in the verse] "the eye is like a peacock's feather";
however, the verse was already applied previously.
Is it not so?
This objection applies to the position that sound (*dhvani*) is nothing other than the aggregate [of phonemes]. "Its existence" means its status as a specific kind of poetry (*kāvyaviśeṣatva*).

Regarding what was stated—"because it is non-expressive"—he first demonstrates by means of a quibble (*chala*) that this reason is "unproving" (*aprayojaka*), saying: "This might be a fault. Having thus refuted [the objection] by means of a quibble, [the reading is]: "the non-taking away (*anāharaṇa*) of the elephant's tusks and so forth," or alternatively, "the non-taking away of the tusks and so forth" (with *dantādyanāharaṇam* as the reading). The word "of the son-in-law's husband" (*snuṣābhartuḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Collection" (samudāya) means a collection of the signifier, the signified, the suggested meaning, and so forth. "In this position" (ity atra pakṣe) refers to this [point].

The intention is that in the verse beginning with "avavakṣitavācyasya," since it is the *samudāya* (the whole) alone that is asserted as the referent of the term *dhvani*, it is only within this very position (*pakṣa*) that the objection is appropriate.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the words "But then... (*nanu*) and so forth, and "thus it has been said" (*ity uktam*).
The intention is [as expressed] by the passage beginning with "wherein the meaning or the word... "That" means for that reason.
He establishes the objection with the passage beginning with "for it is a specific kind of poetry... and so forth.

‘Distinct’ (viśiṣṭa): the meaning is that it is the cause for the comprehension of that distinct object which is twofold, by way of the distinction between the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya). ‘In the word,’ and so forth.
The meaning is: a specific combination of words;
that is to say, a specific sentence that conveys a distinguished meaning.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And its existence," and so forth.
"In being manifested by words" means while it is being manifested by words; "is not tenable" means it does not cohere.
The meaning is that its existence is contradictory with being manifested by words.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the words," and so forth.
"Because they are non-expressive" means because they lack the capacity for direct denotation (*anubhāvaka*).
By that [capacity], those respective meanings are recalled (*smāryante*).

In the view that those [words] remembered, when conjoined with the desire to know and the capacity [of the listener], bring about the experience of the sentence-meaning, the quality of being "illuminated by words"—which consists in being remembered by words—resides only in those respective meanings.

Since the nature of *dhvani* (suggestion), which is a specific type of poetry, does not reside therein, it follows that *dhvani* is not illuminated by words, but rather its illumination is possible only through sentences; this is the intended meaning.

Intending to show that by this passage the meaning is established—that words do not reveal *dhvani* because they are non-expressive (*avācaka*)—the *Locana* introduces the section on the resolution beginning with "this objection might arise" (*syādeṣa doṣa*), stating: "because they are non-expressive," etc., up to "it is irrelevant" (*aprayojaka*).
[This would be so] if expressiveness (*vācakatva*) were the determining factor in the conventional usage of *dhvani*.
But this is not the case; for that [the word-meaning] is established as being a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

Furthermore, just as in the case of the bodies of poems, the perception of beauty—which is accomplished by a collection delimited by specific configurations—is attributed to the individual parts through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); thus, the application of the term "suggestion" (*dhvani*) as established by way of the manifestor-status of words is not contradictory.
The *Locana* also refutes this by way of the actual state of things with the words "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*).

"Even though she disregarded her elders, she nevertheless looked at me with longing, yet with a gaze slowed by anger, dejection, and pride"—

through such a recollection, the intensification (*uddīpana*) of the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) characterized by the departure of life-breaths, which is mutually causal, appears clearly in the proximity of the word "tribhāga.
And thus, it takes the form of a sentence (*vākya*).
The intention behind this non-distinctive presentation in the first exposition is as follows:
even while phonemes, words, and their constituent parts exist, the suggestion (vyaṅgya) of imperceptible sequence, though manifesting, appears as something that pervades the entire poem,
because its life-force consists in the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva) and other elements.

Therefore, while phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth possess merely the status of being causes (*nimitta*), the sentence (*vākya*), however, does not assist the suggestion of *dhvani* whose sequence is imperceptible merely by being a cause like the phonemes; rather, because it is occupied with the non-apprehension of the complete determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, it manifests as consisting of rasa and the like. Thus, in this verse beginning with "the sentence" (*vākya*), the word itself is what is primary here.
This is the state [of the emotion].
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), another example beginning with "ajhaṭiti kanake" has been interpolated; for this very reason, it was not explained in the *Locana*.
Someone reflects upon the manner of looking by a young woman (*prayā*) who, having seen herself about to depart on a journey in the presence of her elders:
Or rather, she says to her lover: "Because of the absence of grain" (vījāyogāt).
[She refers to] the elders, such as her father and others.
[She describes him as one] by whom a trembling has been produced and fixed upon her jar-like breasts.
Even when his departure was obstructed, he felt indignation—the anger born from that effort;
why was it not said to me, "Stay"?
It was indeed said, for she shed tears, beautiful like the eyes of a startled doe.
Alternatively: "The third part" (tribhāgaḥ) means one-third of that eye which is captivating to a startled doe (*cakitahariṇīhārī*).
Or, *cakitahariṇīhārī* may be treated as a separate word serving as a secondary qualifier (*āsañjana-krayāvaśeṣaṇa*) for the eye.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "attached to me" (*mayi āsakta*), meaning "clinging" (*āsañjin*).
He explains the suggestive power (*vyañjakatva*) of the word "tribhāga" with the passage beginning "gurujanaṃ... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "full of longing" (*sābhilāṣā*):
the meaning is that emotional states (*bhāva*) such as longing are manifested through the eyes.
"By means of recollection" means that it is to be understood through mere recollection. "The state of being mutual causes" means...
The meaning is: "because it has as its cause the bond of mutual reliance.
Regarding the word "first":
the meaning is by means of the nominative case ending in the expression "sound in the form of a sentence."

The "instruction of non-exclusion" (avyatireka-nirdeśa) is the communication of non-difference; this will be explained later with the words "this sentence, however," and so forth. The connection is: "[appearing] only when [the causes] exist."
The meaning is: although it appears as something not actually employed [as a linguistic unit] such as a phoneme or a word, nevertheless...
"By that" means:
because it appears as having its life-force (*prāṇa*) consisting in the conjunction of the *vibhāvas* and so forth.
"Like color and so forth" is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*). "Complete" means that it conveys the complete set of conditions, such as the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
That is the statement;
"iti" indicates the reason;
"vākya" and so forth [begin the explanation].
The meaning of the word *vākya* (sentence) as it occurs in the *kārikā* is this:
it refers to a *śloka*.
For this sentence, by demonstrating a mutual affection that has reached full development, reveals the supreme essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) from every perspective.
An example of [a figure] mixed with another ornament is the verse beginning with "carried away by the fresh flood of the river of love" (*smaranavanadīpūreṇoḍhāḥ*).

In the *Locana*, it is stated that [the locative case in the word *rikāyām*] is not merely the locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), but rather has the sense of being restricted to that alone (*ananyatra-bhāva-viṣaya*).
"Pure" means unmixed with any other poetic figure (artha-alaṅkāra).

O beloved, that hard-hearted lover of yours—who, though supported by his mother out of affection even as she went to the forest, weeping with feigned anger and looking upon her with piteous glances—now gazes at the quarters of the sky darkened by fresh rain-clouds without you, yet continues to live; [This verse is an example of the figure *Śuddha* (the Pure), being unmixed with any other figure.]

In this context, the phrase "even though the mother was thus supported by them in various ways" indicates that you have transgressed the word of your elders due to being overcome by passion (*anurāga*).
By the words "O beloved, O beloved," the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love—consisting of the mutual conceit of each other being one's very life and all-in-all—is expressed.

By the phrase "navajaladhara" (fresh rain-cloud), the sight of the first monsoon clouds, which was previously unbearable, is stated to be an excitant (*uddīpanavibhāva*) for the state of separation (*vipralambha*).
The phrase "he indeed lives" expresses a state of dependence; the particle *eva* (indeed) is used to exclude any room for compassion.
The term "from all [sides]" (*sarvata eva*) means that no single word here possesses a greater capacity than the others for manifesting the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Regarding the phrase "the essence of rasa":
it is the very nature of the erotic sentiment in separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*).

Even though they have been swept away by the fresh flood of the river of memory, they remain at a distance with their desires unfulfilled, held back once more by the great embankments [of social restraint].
Even so, with limbs resembling paintings, those beloved women drink the nectar brought by the stalks of their lotus-eyes as they gaze intently at one another.
In the passage beginning with "bālapriyā na," the meaning of the locative case in "tat" is merely a cause (nimitta); that is to say, it means "not [in the sense of] elsewhere.
Regarding "ananyatra":
"Non-existence elsewhere" means the absence of occurrence in anything other than that;
[the compound] refers to that whose object has such a nature.
The meaning is that the locative sense of the word "in the sentence" (vākye) is the object.
Regarding the word *kṛtakā*: it is construed with *dhṛtāt* (having been maintained), which ends in the third case. *Yasya prītyā* means "by whose affection," that is, by love for me.
"Held" means obstructed.
He explains this with the words "here," and so forth;
[the phrase] "it is done" refers to the following.
The word "is manifested" (*vyajyate*) is to be supplied [as the verb]. Regarding the phrase "to the beloved, as the beloved":
this means "by these two."
"Expressed" means manifested; that is, by this [verse], "The fresh rain-cloud," and so forth. This is the meaning.

The connection [of the words] is that by the particle *eva* in the phrase "he indeed lives," the state of being dependent is expressed. Regarding the word *smara*, there is also the reading: "they remain held apart from afar, incomplete."
*Prāvṛṣeṇyaḥ* means "born in the rainy season.
Regarding the superimposition of being a current (*pravāha*), he states the common property (*sādharmya*) that is to be understood through the words beginning with *sarabhasa*.
By the word *ūḍhāḥ* ("carried"), he expresses what is intended here through the words beginning with *paraspara*.

The phrase "immediately following" (*anantaram*) is an explanation of the word "again" (*punar*). By the term "guru," another meaning is also implied here; for in this poetic figure (*rūpaka*), which conforms to the aforementioned characteristics of the suggestor (*vyañjaka*), the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—established as having its suggestible content of imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*)—is manifested all the more clearly. It has been stated that "suggestion (*dhvani*) shines forth in the composition (*saṅghaṭanā*)," and therein, the very nature of composition is first being defined: [The verse: "O friend, you have become one whose face is like a lotus, whose eyes are like bees, and whose body is like a tree. In this [verse], the *rūpaka* (poetic identification) is established by means of the word "like" (*iva*), which possesses the aforementioned characteristics of a suggestor. Here, the *rasa* is manifested even more intensely. Regarding the statement that "suggestion with imperceptible sequence shines forth in composition," the nature of that composition itself is now being examined.
Composition is declared to be threefold: that which is without compounds, adorned with middle-length compounds, and likewise that which consists of long compounds. (Dhvanyāloka 3.5)
Composed without compounds, adorned with middle-length compounds, and likewise with long compounds—thus composition is said to be threefold. (5)
According to some, [the phrase] "by means of a metaphor" refers to the *Locana*:
"Smara himself is a fresh river-flood, a monsoon torrent; because it has increased with such impetuosity, they have been carried away—led into mutual confrontation quite unintentionally."
Immediately thereafter, the elders, beginning with the mother-in-law, are indeed the embankments,
because they obstruct the expansion of desire;
therefore, the elders are not to be transgressed, for by them the embankments are maintained and desires are restrained.
For this very reason, they remain with their desires unfulfilled.

Nevertheless, through the mutual orientation characterized by their reciprocal identity, they suppress all other functions within their own bodies; thus, with limbs as if painted still, they savor the essence brought forth by their very eyes—which serve as lotus stalks—by means of the technique of blending the flashes of their glances, which consist of mutual longing.
"They pass the time.
Now, one might object: "Is not the metaphor (rūpaka) here left unfulfilled, since the pair of lovers has not been represented in the form of swans, ruddy geese, and so forth?

For those swans and others are appropriate for such things as playing in the water drawn from a single lotus stalk,"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "by the aforementioned suggestors" (yathoktavyañjaka).

For it was stated previously—in the passage beginning with "by being intent on the desire to speak" and ending with "no excessive desire for elaboration"—that [the rasa] is established. "Established" means that even the rasa is established by way of the ornaments of the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth. // 3.4 //
In the word *saṅghaṭanāyām*, the suffix *vati* is applied [in the sense of "like"]; the locative case ending is used in the sense of a mere cause, as in the case of [the rule] *varṇādiṣu ca*.
It has been stated [thus].
In the *kārikā*,
"is examined" (*nirūpyate*) means that it is investigated as being distinct from the qualities (*guṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "rasān," the author states what is intended by saying "atha ca" and so forth.
The explanation of "tadapi" is "tathāpi.
He states that "parasparam unmukhāḥ" serves as the justification for the expression "likhitaprakhyaiḥ" by saying "paraspara" and so forth.
He shows the similarity with the accessible [example]— beginning with "one's own body" and so forth. "Vṛtti" means activity (ceṣṭā).
The instrumental case in "with the limbs" (*aṅgaiḥ*) is used in a figurative sense (*upalakṣaṇe*).
Regarding "the rasa," etc.,
the meaning is that it is water in the form of mutual longing.
He states the intended meaning with the words "paraspara... (mutual).
The meaning is: by means of the logical application—that is, the blending—of the glances, which consist of mutual longing and manifest that mutual longing.
In the word *priyāḥ* (beloved ones), as well as in *haṃsacakravākāḥ* (swans and ruddy geese), a collective singular (*ekaśeṣa*) should be understood.

"Because it is formless" (arūpitatvāt) means "because it does not undergo transformation" (arūpaṇāt). He states the reasoning for its being so transformed with the words beginning "for then," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "How can rasa be adorned by a metaphor (rūpaka) in this case? To this, he says: "The excitants (vibhāva), etc. [3.4].
"In the sense of 'state' (bhāva),
the suffix -ya" means that the suffix *yuc* is applied when the meaning is of the nature of a state (*bhāvarūpa*). "The locative case" [refers to the rule governing its application].
In the phrase "in the conjunction" (saṅghaṭanāyām), the locative case is intended.
Having merely referred to that [conjunction], this is stated:
"Residing by depending upon the qualities, it manifests sweetness and the other [qualities]."
The aesthetic flavors (rasas) ... [Dhvanyāloka 3.6a]

"Abiding by depending upon the qualities (guṇas), it manifests the sentiments (rasas) such as sweetness and so forth"— that is, that *saṅghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) manifests the *rasas* and so forth while abiding by depending upon the qualities.
And in this regard, one must consider whether there is identity or distinction between the qualities and the structural arrangement.
Even if they are distinct, there are two possible ways:
either the composition is based on the qualities, or the qualities are based on the composition.

In that regard, concerning the view of identity and the view of *saṅghaṭanā* (structure) as a quality (*guṇa*) residing [in the word], the term "locanam"—the first word of the second half of the *kārikā*—refers to the half-verse: "The cause for the restriction of those [flavors] is the appropriateness (*aucitya*) of the speaker and the expressed. This [term] stands by relying on the flavors (*rasas*), which are not identical with it and are not to be grasped [as its essence].
He shows that the meaning of "and so forth" (*ādi*) is included by means of the plural number, stating: "rasādīn" (flavors, etc.
and "atra ca" (and here).
This refers to this very half-verse of the *kārikā*.
This collection of objects can be conceptualized and explained through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). To the question "What is that?", he says: "Of the qualities" (*guṇānām*).
Those three positions which are conceivable can be explained.
To the question "How so?", he says: "In that regard, the position of unity" (*tatraikyapakṣe*).
"Identical with the self" (*ātmabhūta*) means that,

for the purpose of demonstrating the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) through conceptualization, the linguistic expression "residing in its own substratum" is seen to be applied to the indicated entity, as in "the state of being a tree resides in the *śiṃśapā*.
"Existing as the contained" (*ādheyabhūta*) means...

Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa and others maintain that the qualities (guṇas) are the properties (dharmas) of the composition (saṅghaṭanā), and that properties must reside in a substratum (dharmin). To the question "Where was this stated?", he says: "In the kārikā.
He supplies the agentive word "by some" (kaiścit) in the commentary for the phrase "is said to be [the result] of the composition."
The commentary (*Locana*) shows that the portion beginning with "tām" and ending with "rasāni" is the reading of the verse (*kārikā*), stating: "rasān ityādi";
the meaning is "rasa and the other [aesthetic sentiments]."
To explain how [this] is obtained, he says "many," and so forth.
By the plural form "rasān" (tastes), the plural is intended. The explanation of the word "atra" (here) is "asmin" (in this), and so forth.
He explains the term "vikalpyam" (to be conceptualized) in accordance with the context of the present discussion, beginning with "vikalpena" (by means of conceptualization), and so forth.
This refers to what is about to be stated.
[The word] "śakyam" (possible/capable) [is used].

The intention is that the analysis of the term *vikalpyam* is "that which is to be conceptualized by means of conceptualization" (*vikalpena kalpyam*). He states the meaning [of the verse] with the words "the three," etc.,
and in the commentary with the words "or exclusion" (*vyatireko vā*).
"Or distinction" means "or difference.
"'A twofold course' means 'a state of duality.'"
To explain how there is a twofold division, he says "āśraya of the qualities" (guṇāśraya), and so forth.
This is connected with the phrase "the meaning of the two words ending in the locative case.
[He further explains] "become the self" (ātmabhūtāni).
"Not distinct from itself" means not eternal.
"Existing as that which is supported" means residing in itself.
"‘Thus is the meaning’"— the word "of the verse" (*kārikāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

In the view that the quality (*guṇa*) and the composition (*saṅghaṭanā*) are identical, [the author] demonstrates in the *Locana*— starting with "of the nature" (*svabhāvasya*), etc.— the justification for the designation of a relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) in the statement, "They abide by depending on the qualities."

For the purpose of demonstrating intrinsic nature—that is, to demonstrate the intrinsic nature of a real entity—there is that [conceptualization] wherein a distinction is shown by means of conceptual construction.
The meaning is: having imagined a distinction of the entity from itself, even though it is not distinct from itself.
"Having its own substratum" (svāśraya) means that it is described by way of having its own substratum.
He provides an example— beginning with "the śiṃśapā tree"— in accordance with the view that the universal and the individual are one.
The term "iti" means "and so forth. The meaning is that [the word] manifests rasa and the other [aesthetic elements].

But when the position of plurality is held—that is, the position that there is a conjunction of the qualities (*guṇas*) as their substratum—then [the substance] exists depending upon the qualities, having a nature that is dependent on the qualities, and not being of the very nature of the qualities themselves; this is the meaning.
What, then, is the purpose of such a conceptual distinction?
It is stated: if the qualities and the conjunction were one and the same reality, or if the qualities were merely the substrata of the conjunction...

In that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that *guṇas* (qualities), like *saṅghaṭanā* (structure), would have indeterminate objects; for the excellence of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and clarity (*prasāda*) belongs only to the objects of the pathetic (*karuṇa*), the erotic-in-separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*), and the erotic-in-enjoyment (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*),
whereas *ojas* (force) belongs to the objects of the furious (*raudra*), the marvelous (*adbhuta*), and so forth.

The *Locana* states that sweetness (*mādhurya*) and clarity (*prasāda*) have as their objects only rasa, bhāva, and their semblances (*tadābhāsa*); this is the well-known path regarding the restriction of their scope.
As for the phrase "dependent on the qualities" (*guṇaparatantreti*), here the meaning of "substratum" (*āśraya*) does not refer to a relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*).
For it is not the case that the *saṅghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) resides within the *guṇas* (qualities).

Therefore, just as in the expression "the group of subjects has the king as its support," the meaning is that the subjects, such as the ministers, are so called by virtue of their dependence on the king;
in the same way, the meaning obtained here is that the *saṅghaṭanā* is dependent in nature upon the *guṇas*, reliant on them, and looking toward them for its direction. This is the intended sense.
