The phrase "as if of a composite" means that, according to the first position, [the relation] is one of identity (*tādātmya*) because they share the same security and destiny (*samānayogakṣema*), whereas in the other case, it is by way of being a property (*dharmatva*).
Having raised the doubt, "Let it be that its object is not restricted," he says: "For of the qualities... (*guṇānāṃ hi*).
The word *hi* has the sense of the word *tu*;
however, it is not thus logically tenable,
but rather it follows by the force of reasoning— this is the meaning.
The connection is with the phrase "she is seen as dear to children.

The point is that just as, despite the identity of "treeness" and "śiṃśapā-ness," one speaks of the śiṃśapā being the locus of treeness by means of a conceptualized distinction, so it is in the present case as well.
He states the support for [the fact that] impermanence is that which is to be contained (ādheya) in the words beginning with "of the composition" (*saṅghaṭanāyāḥ*).
He provides the seed for the explanation that its intrinsic nature is dependent upon qualities (*guṇa*) in the words beginning with "here" (*atra*).
The meaning of "substratum" (*āśraya*) is the referent of the word "substratum."
Regarding this, he states the reason: "For not," and so forth.
"By that" means by the sublation of the primary meaning of the term "substratum."
The word "is obtained" (*labhyate*) is connected with this [term].
"By way of the propriety of being a refuge for a king" means: for the sake of making the meaning of the term "refuge for a king" suitable for logical connection (*anvaya*).
The third case ending is used in the sense of a cause that is the result (*phalarūpahetu*).
Immediately after this, one should read: “the constituent elements such as the ministers are dependent upon the king”;
if the reading “dependent upon the king” (*rājaparatantrā*) is absent, that word must be supplied.

"Evam" means "tathā" (in that manner). "Dependent upon the qualities" (*guṇeṣu paratantrā*) and so forth is the very explanation of that [term]: "dependent on them" (*tad-āyattā*). In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the objection beginning with "What... (*kim*) and so forth is raised.
The reply begins with "is designated" (*abhidhīyate*) and so forth:
"one reality" (*ekaṃ tattvam*).
The meaning is "a single ontological category" (*ekaḥ padārthaḥ*).
In the *Locana*, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "as if of a composition" (*saṅghaṭanāyā iva*) as follows: "In the first alternative," etc.;
that is, in the first alternative, namely the position that there is a single reality (*ekaṃ tattvam*).
The words "of the qualities and the composition" (*guṇasaṅghaṭanayoḥ*) are to be supplied [as the object of comparison].

Because they share the same security and well-being, and because they possess an identical nature; in the alternative position that qualities depend upon conjunction, [it is] by way of their nature as phenomena— that is, by way of their nature as being conjoined.
The phrase "because they share the same security and risk" (*tulyayogakṣematvāt*) is to be supplied as a continuation.
He explains the consequence that [the cognition] would have an indefinite object by saying "but not so," and so forth.
"In this way" (*evam*) means:

The meaning is that [the senses] have an indefinite object; however, it is not the case that [this] "occurs," because the fixedness of the objects of the qualities (guṇas) is established— this is the intended sense.

"It entails" means "it follows [as a logical consequence]. Having raised this doubt, he says [the following]; the meaning is that he prevents the acceptance of such an undesired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).
The word "tu" has the sense of restriction;
it is fixed [in its meaning],
whereas that [connection] is dissolved by the arrangement.
For instance, even in the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiment, long compounds are observed, while in the furious (*raudra*) and other sentiments, there are no compounds.
In that regard, an example of a long compound in the erotic is: "Her locks were turned golden-brown by the pollen of mandāra flowers.
Or, for example: "Your [face], whose decorative leaf-designs have been washed away by the incessant falling of drops of tears from the eyes..."
O powerless one, whom does this face resting in the palm of your hand not cause to burn?
In such cases as these,
and likewise in the Furious (raudra) and other rasas, the absence of compounds is observed;
for example, in "Whosoever bears a weapon, his own arm being heavy with its weight," and so forth.
Therefore, the qualities do not have the nature of the composition, nor are they the substratum of the composition.
Now, if the composition is not the substratum of the qualities, upon what basis are these [qualities] imagined?
It is said:
their objective support has indeed already been explained;
it is the "eye."
This rule regarding qualities which has been stated is the purpose [of the definition].
To show that this is indeed the case, he states the observation of the object of definition as the reason, beginning with "for thus" (*tathā hi*).
Having said "it is seen," he introduces an example for the locus of that observation, beginning with "therein" (*tatra*).

Anticipating the objection that there is no element of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) here, he provides a second example, saying "or as follows" (*yathā vā*). For this is the speech of a hero addressed to appease his beloved who is angry due to a misunderstanding.
Therefore... [he says].

The meaning is that these two explanations are not appropriate for the *kārikā*. The point is that the ancient masters have stated: "If [these figures] have words and their meanings as their objective support (*ālambana*), what distinction is there between them and the ornaments of those [words and meanings]? This is the intended sense.
"It has indeed been explained" means by our own author of the root-text (*mūlagranthakṛt*).
Regarding the phrase "that [bond] is severed," he explains the word *tat* (that) with the words "this which... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the rule has been stated":

the meaning is that there is a rule that the composition (saṅghaṭanā) in [rasas] such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) should consist of compounds only, whereas in [rasas] such as the furious (raudra), it should consist of long compounds only.
The phrase "vighaṭate" means "it deviates.
The phrase "tathātve" means "in the case of the disruption of the rule."
He indicates and demonstrates;
he introduces another example with the words "not here," etc.
The sense is: because the emotional state (*anubhāva*) and so forth are not perceived.
"Anavaratā" means:
that in which the decorative leaf-patterns (*patralekhā*) have been completely robbed away—that is, stripped away—by the incessant falling of drops of tears from the eyes;
[this refers] to "your" (*te*).
The connection is that "this is the face.
He states the [opponent's] position with the words "not this," and so forth.
He states the intention behind the objection "on what basis? with the words "sound," and so forth.
The word "of the qualities" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
"What distinction?
means that there would be no distinction.
Regarding the phrase "in the root text":
it means in the *kārikā*.
He explains the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "na caiṣām" by stating "na hi," and so forth.
"Unity" (aikya); the words "of two things" (vastunoḥ) are to be supplied [as the object of the genitive],
meaning "of the quality and the ornament" (guṇālaṅkārayoḥ).
Those qualities which support that primary object are known as *guṇas* (excellences);
however, those dependent on the subordinate parts should be considered *alaṅkāras* (ornaments), like bracelets and the like.
Thus [it is said].
Alternatively, let the qualities (guṇas) indeed reside only in words; yet they do not possess the same nature as alliteration (anuprāsa) and the like.
For alliteration and the like have been explained as properties of words alone, regardless of their meaning;
whereas the *guṇas* (qualities) are indeed properties of words capable of conveying a denoted meaning that manifests a specific suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).
And although these [qualities] reside elsewhere, they possess the status of being properties of words just as heroism and other such traits reside in the body.
Now, if the qualities (*guṇas*) have sound as their substratum, then it follows that they must either consist of the arrangement of those sounds or have them as their substratum.

For unarranged sounds cannot serve as the substratum for qualities that depend on rasa and so forth—which are conveyed by specific meanings—since [unarranged sounds] lack the capacity to express [meaning].
[This is stated in the *Locana*: "Or else..."]
For unity does not follow merely from having a single substratum, as that would entail the absurdity of color and conjunction being one and the same.

If it is argued that in the case of conjunction there must be a second correlate, we reply that here too there is indeed a dependence upon the manifestor, the benefactor, and the signified; thus the situation is the same.
Nor is this my own position;
rather, let it be that even according to the view of these undiscriminating people, qualities such as bravery are properties of sound, just as they are properties of the body.
For an undiscriminating person is incapable of distinguishing between what is metaphorical and what is literal.
Nevertheless, he says this— "the state of being a property of sound"— to show that even so, there is no fault;
for the phrase "even though it has another locus" means "even though it resides in the self."
Regarding the phrase "residing in words":

if, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), these qualities belong to words, then this is the intended meaning: the very capacity of a word to convey a denoted meaning that manifests aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) is its sweetness (*mādhurya*).
And that [sweetness], residing in the word, is obtained only through a specific arrangement [of sounds].

Now, conjunction (*saṅghaṭanā*) is not something distinct; rather, it is simply that which is conjoined, because otherwise it would entail [the absurdity of] being a single entity. The intended meaning is that it is based upon a single substance, such as a jar, and so forth.
He refutes the consequence of identity with the words "conjunction," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the second is required":
since the effect in the form of conjunction arises from both [entities], that which has a conjunction produced within itself stands in need of that [second entity]; this is the meaning.
The meaning is that since form arises in only one [atom], there is no dependence on a second; he states "here," etc., to show that the manner of the rebuttal is the same—
here too, even in the case of qualities.
Regarding the word "vyaṅgya" (suggested):
by this, the passage beginning with "the qualities, however, [reside] in the suggested" is explained.
He introduces the passage beginning with "and the state of being a property of words" with the words "na ca" (nor is it), and so forth.
The construction is: "this position of mine is not [correct].
Regarding the word "eṣām" (of these), it means "of the qualities" (guṇānām).
"Let it be the nature of sound"— this is the connection [to the previous statement].
"The distinction of being figurative" means the difference between the figurative and the primary.
"To discern" means to know.
This is what was stated by the words "Or rather," and so forth.
"This [is] that" refers to this very point.
The meaning is "it has been stated.
Regarding the phrase "even though it is grounded in the self" (*ātmaniṣṭhatve 'pi*): by the word *ātman*, both *rasa* and the individual soul (*jīvātman*) are to be understood.

He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the passage beginning with "If [the cognition] were based on words" and ending with "is already attained"—namely, "by way of metaphor" (*upacāreṇa*), and so forth.
The explanation for the section ending with "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) is as follows: "by way of metaphor," and so forth.
"This" refers to...
It is not so according to the *Anupada*;
for it has been established that rasa and the like are manifested by words, phonemes, and phrases. [The *Locana* says: "Words..."
The intended meaning is that by saying "its capacity is dependent on that," it is stated that [the capacity] is indeed dependent on the *saṅghaṭanā* (structure).
Now, one might object: "Let it be that [the capacity] is a property of the word or identical in essence with the word itself;
why this intermediate intervention of the *saṅghaṭanā*? Anticipating this doubt, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) himself says: "For not... and so forth.

The meaning is this: the suggested elements—namely, rasa, bhāva, their semblances (tadābhāsa), and their subsidence (tatpraśama)—are not to be conveyed by specific meanings that are mere word-referents independent of other words, such as universals (sāmānya). These [suggested elements] are primarily based on and grounded in the qualities (guṇas) which reside therein; therefore, words that are not so combined do not serve as their substratum, even figuratively.
The reason for this is "because they are non-expressive" (*avācakatvāt*).
The meaning is that unconnected [words] do not convey a denoted meaning (*vācya*) that is suitable for suggestion (*vyaṅgya*) and free from expectancy.
He refutes this with "not so."

For as long as it has been stated that rasa is manifested by the phonemes (varṇa), so long is it clearly observed that even a word which is not directly expressive possesses, through its own inherent excellence perceivable by mere hearing, the quality of being a cause for the manifestation of rasa—just like the phonemes themselves. Therefore, since that very quality constitutes sweetness (mādhurya) and the rest, what is the need for syntactic arrangement (saṅghaṭanā)? Likewise, as long as it has been stated that dhvani is manifested by words (pada), so long does even a pure word, by virtue of its capacity to evoke its own meaning, possess the quality of manifesting an object capable of evoking rasa; this alone constitutes sweetness and the rest in that case as well.
What is the purpose of this composition?
The meaning is that it is for the delight of the ignorant, as will be explained; and that [delight] resides in the words.
The capacity based on words is of two kinds: that which consists of the expressed capacity and that which is implied.
Regarding the term "distinct" (*viśiṣṭā*):
the meaning is that it is obtained precisely through a particular arrangement of other words.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Now," and so forth.
"Now" (atha) means "and furthermore. [The word] is not distinct, meaning it is not different from the sound.
"Dependent upon that" means dependent upon the word "saṅghaṭita" (assembled). "That" refers to what was previously stated.
"Iti" is used in the sense of a reason.
"Dependent on a composition" means that its nature as a composition is also to be understood in the manner previously stated.
[The word] "nanu" [is used to introduce an objection].
The word "of qualities" (guṇānām) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The word "only so far" (tāvatā) means "by way of metaphorical designation" (upacāreṇa).
By the phrase "he himself says," this meaning is conveyed through the passage beginning with: "And that [distinction] resides in the word only through a specific arrangement."
"It is manifested by itself" means it is made manifest.
"By specific meanings" (arthaviśeṣaiḥ) means by the forms of the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth, which are conveyed by a collection of words that stand in mutual expectancy.
By this, he states what is to be refuted: "But not," and so forth.
Regarding the term "by universals" (*sāmānyaiḥ*):
it was stated previously that objects in the form of universals are the denotata of words.
Intending that "because of being non-expressive" (avācakatvāt) means "because of not causing [the object] to be experienced" (ananubhāvakatvāt), he explains: "For not," and so forth.
The word "words" (śabdāḥ) is to be supplied as the subject.
"They express the denotable" (vācyam āhuḥ) means they cause the sentence-meaning to be experienced.
He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "varṇa" and so forth: "vama-vyaṅgyo hi" and so on.
The word "yāvat" means "since.
It has been stated—that is, demonstrated—by the passage beginning with "yastvalakṣyakramavyaṅgyaḥ" and so forth.
In that case, from that [word]:
even of a word— which is a collection of phonemes— that is non-expressive, that is, which does not cause the recollection of its own meaning.
"Just as with color" means "just like color";
the sense is that it is obtained quite clearly by way of the principle of *kaimutya* (a fortiori).
"And thus" (tathāca) means:
once it is established that even a word which does not recall its own primary meaning can be a cause for the manifestation of rasa;
"even of the pure" (śuddhasya api) [means...]

The meaning is: "even of that which is not combined. Or, if it is accepted that rasa and the like are suggested by the sentence (*vākya*), then no fixed *saṅghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) can be established as their substratum; thus, words with unfixed *saṅghaṭanās* are the substrata for the qualities (*guṇas*) as they follow upon specific suggestibles (*vyaṅgya*).
Now, if it is indeed said thus regarding sweetness (*mādhurya*), let it be so; but as for vigor (*ojas*), how can it have as its basis words with unrestricted composition?
For a composition that is devoid of compounds never attains the status of being a basis for vigor.
It is said:
If the mind were not corrupted by a mere grasping at conventional renown, then we would not deny this point either; for how could a composition lacking compounds not be the locus of *ojas* (vigor)?
For it was previously established that *ojas* (vigorousness) is the brilliance of poetry when it manifests qualities such as the *raudra* (fierce) sentiment;

and if that *ojas* were present even in a composition (*saṅghaṭanā*) that lacks compounds, what fault would there be? [Objection: But surely, in the case of *dhvani* where the meaning is suggested by the sentence, one must necessarily enter into the question of whether the beauty belongs to the composition itself or to the expressed meaning (*vācya*). *Locana*: Indeed, in *dhvani* where the meaning is suggested by the sentence, one must necessarily enter into the question of whether the beauty belongs to the composition itself or to the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
Anticipating the objection, "How can that be without her?", he says: "is accepted.
The word *vā* has the sense of *api*;
it should be construed with the phrase "even though it is suggested by the sentence" (*vākyavyaṅgyatve 'pi*).

This is what is meant: enter into that [context of] composition (*saṅghaṭanā*); for we do not deny its presence there. However, the sweetness [of poetry] does not have a fixed composition, nor a fixed substratum, nor a fixed nature; for even without it, there is the manifestation (*vyaṅgya*) of phonemes (*varṇa*) and words (*pada*).

Since sweetness and other qualities exist in rasa and so forth by virtue of being emotional states (bhāva), and since a sentence can manifest that rasa even while abandoning such a specific structural arrangement (saṅghaṭanā)—because the sentence itself possesses the power to manifest that rasa—the structural arrangement, though present, is not a necessary factor for the manifestation of rasa.
Therefore, he concludes that even if they are used figuratively, the *guṇas* reside only in the words, stating: "the words themselves."
Regarding the word "nanu" (surely):
some hold that this should be understood with the intention of referring to *dhvani* as manifested by the sentence (*vākya-vyaṅgya-dhvani*).
This refers to the passage beginning with "nanu".
"By composition" means by a particular arrangement;
"one's own" means the beauty of the sentence.
In the commentary, "of them" means "of the qualities.
"Followed by specific manifestations" [is the meaning].
The meaning is "that which manifests a specific suggested sense.
Regarding the passage beginning with "accepted" (*abhyupagata*), the *Locana* explains its intent with the words "this," etc.,
[and] "of Mādhurya," etc.

The meaning is "of sweetness and so forth. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that fixed composition is neither the locus nor the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of sweetness. He states the reason for this with the words beginning "by that" (*tayā*).
"Because of the existence of sweetness and so forth" means "because of the presence of sweetness and so forth.
By the word "existence" (bhāvāt), the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) is demonstrated.
For this very reason, he says "vākya" and so forth;
the phrase "in rasa and the like" is to be supplied.
This means even apart from *saṅghaṭanā* (poetic structure), that is, even without the assistance of *saṅghaṭanā*.
Because it manifests those respective rasas— that is, because it is possible for it to manifest those various rasas—
it is *aprayojikā*, meaning useless.
This refers to the passage in the *Vṛtti* beginning with "But [it is] not," and so forth.
‘Thus’ (evam) means being based on words whose arrangement is not fixed; ‘let it be stated at that time’ means let it be stated in such a manner.
The word "again" (*punar*) indicates a specific distinction.
"In this case too, we do not say 'no'" means that even regarding this objection, we certainly provide a reply.
"Locane"— this refers to the passage beginning with "suggested by the sentence" (*vākyavyaṅgya*). "This" means the objection (*codya*).
It should be considered that the sense is: because the connection [of words] is possible only within a sentence.
Furthermore, there is a lack of aesthetic charm (acārutva) which is to be experienced by the hearts of connoisseurs.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that the *guṇas* (poetic qualities) serve as the basis for compositions with unrestricted structures.
However, their own essential nature—which is restricted to its respective object, just like the eyes and other sense organs—never deviates from it.
Consequently, the *guṇas* are one thing, and the *saṅghaṭanā* (composition/structure) is another.
Nor is it one view that qualities depend upon the arrangement;
rather, qualities are themselves of the nature of the arrangement.
As for what was said—"it follows that, like the arrangement, qualities would also have unrestricted objects"—[that is not so].
"Because deviation is observed in the object of inference.
To this, it is said:
In that case, let it be simply the nature of that very object where there is a deviation regarding the imagined subject.
If it is asked, "How is it that suchness does not appear as unlovely to the sensitive readers (sahṛdayas) with respect to such an object?
[the answer is: because it is concealed by the power of the poet.
For defect is of two kinds: that caused by the poet’s lack of proficiency and that caused by his incapacity.
Among these, a defect caused by lack of proficiency is sometimes not perceived because it is eclipsed by [the poet's] power;
however, as for the defect caused by incapacity—
It is perceived instantaneously.
And there is a verse by another author on this point: "The defect caused by a lack of proficiency in a poet is concealed by his power;
however, that which is caused by a lack of skill manifests itself instantly."

Regarding this, we say: even in the case of *ojaḥ* (vigorousness), which has the nature of the Furious (*raudra*) and other sentiments and is suggested by phonemes and words, such beauty does not manifest in the phonemes and words alone until they are fashioned as marked by *saṅghaṭanā* (structural arrangement). Thus, this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) applies generally.
In the phrase "prakāśayataḥ," the suffix *śatṛ* is used according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*.
The meaning is that *ojas* (vigor) is characterized by the manifestation of the Furious (*raudra*) and other [rasas].
As for "and not" (*na ca*),
the word *ca* indicates a reason.
The meaning is: because no lack of aesthetic charm (anācārutva) manifests in such instances as "yoyaḥ śastram" and so forth;
"of those" refers to the qualities (guṇas);
"according to their respective [nature]" means...

Furthermore, by the statement beginning with "The erotic sentiment alone is the supreme rasa that gladdens the mind," the restriction of the subject matter has indeed been stated. Alternatively, [the phrase] "bālapriyā varṇa... etc. [is used].

The meaning is: even though *ojas* (vigor) is suggested by both phonemes and words; [it exists] in the nature of the Furious (*raudra*) and other sentiments, which are the attributes of the Furious and other aesthetic moods (*rasa*); "of such a kind" means possessing excellence.
The connection is that "those two do not yet open.
"Those" means the phonemes and words.
"Marked by a combination" means distinguished by a particular arrangement;
"by the general [arrangement] alone."
The meaning is: "precisely with reference to the general category of dhvani manifested by words, parts of words, and sentences.
Regarding the phrase "of the Furious and so forth":
the meaning is that which is being observed—that is, inferred—through the manifestation of the Furious and other rasas.
"Nor is there unloveliness":
the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that "unloveliness does not appear. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "of them" (*teṣām*) [is used].
The meaning is "of the qualities.
This connects with the term "of the essential nature" (*svarūpasya*).

For instance, even in the works of great poets, such things as the depiction of erotic love (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*) toward a supreme deity—which is otherwise considered improper—does not appear as vulgar (*grāmya*), because it is set aside by their poetic power (*śakti*).

Just as in the *Kumārasambhava* there is the description of the union with the Goddess, and in other such instances, the point is that there is no abandonment of propriety; so too, in the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), this alone is the capacity of words: namely, their being arranged in such and such a manner.
"Power" (*śakti*) is creative intuition (*pratibhāna*), characterized by a novel portrayal of the subject matter to be described.
"Vyutpatti" (erudition) is the skill in reflecting upon the sequence of all matters useful for that [poetry].
"Tasya" means of the poet. "Anaucityam" (inappropriateness).
For those who relish [the aesthetic experience], that very non-obstruction of wonder (*camatkāra*) is the essence of *rasa*, because it is dependent upon such relishing.

Furthermore, in the contemplation of the enjoyment of a supreme deity, what opportunity for wonder could there be, given the presence of shame, fear, and so forth—as occurs in the case of the enjoyment of one's own father?
This is because [such a state] is obscured by [ordinary] power (*śakti*).

For even this *saṃbhoga* (the erotic sentiment) has been described by the eloquent poet in such a way that the heart comes to rest therein and refuses to investigate the sequence of what precedes and follows; just as when a man of genuine prowess fights even against an opponent who is not his equal, at that very moment he receives acclaim for his valor, but none once the sequence of events has been scrutinized.
Regarding the phrase "not within the range":
the objects of the eyes and other senses are visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, whereas for the [taste-]qualities, they are tastes (*rasa*).
Regarding the term "vision" (*darśana*): [it refers to the visual faculty].
This is the intended meaning.
Alternatively, he states the purport of the passage beginning with "athavā" in the *Locana*: "rasa... and so forth.
"In such and such a manner" (*tathā tathā*).
The meaning is "in accordance with each respective rasa.
As for the phrase "this is the sense":
sweetness (*mādhurya*) and other qualities inherent in the word are nothing other than the capacity to manifest those respective rasas, such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
And that [beauty] arises from such-and-such a configuration;
therefore, the qualities are indeed of the nature of configuration—this is the meaning of the intended sense (*bhāvārtha*).
In the commentary, the passage beginning with "But as for... (*yattu*) and so forth [is stated].
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "that which was stated" refers to [the passage] beginning with "wherein, in the object of definition (*lakṣya*)" and "unceasingly," etc.
The meaning is: "and in cases such as *yo yaśśastram*";

"in the case of what is imagined" (*parikalpite*) means that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the subject matter stated in the passage beginning with "in the absence of a compound" (*asamāse*).
In the section on the mastery of power (*śakti-vyutpatti*), he explains in the *Locana*: "Power," and so forth.
"Tadupayogi" means skill or capacity in the sequential consideration of those objects which are useful for that subject matter being described.
He explains the impropriety (*anaucitya*) of composing erotic poetry concerning the enjoyment of a supreme deity with the words "he who," and so forth.
"Non-obstruction of aesthetic wonder" (*camatkārāvidhātaḥ*) means the absence of anything that obstructs aesthetic wonder.
"Enjoyment with one's father" (*pitṛsambhoga*)—[is an example of such an obstruction].

The meaning is that there is an attachment to the enjoyment of the mother and father. He explains the passage beginning with "because it is obscured by incapacity" and so forth with the words "enjoyment also," etc.
[He refers to] "this."
The meaning is that it concerns the sphere of the supreme deity;
it is described as being within that very enjoyment (sambhoga).
The heart is the agent.
He does not give himself [to anyone],
with the understanding that "to one who possesses a heart" is the ellipsis; or alternatively, "he" is the ellipsis.
The enjoyment has thus been described; now follows the heart-mantra and its function,
even in regard to that which is not its proper object.
The meaning is: "even in the case of children, elders, and so forth. At that occasion, during the time of battle, it is bestowed—that is, given—by those who look on.
In the *Vṛtti*, it says: "Non-abandonment of propriety" (*yathaucityātyāga*).

This means that in whatever manner (*yathā*) or by whatever means (*yena prakāreṇa*) there is description, there is non-abandonment of propriety, which is the absence of impropriety (*anaucityābhāva*).
‘Shown’ means demonstrated by the collection of passages beginning with ‘vibhāvabhāva’.
‘In front’ means subsequently.
One might object: "In that case, one should say 'it will be shown,' not 'it has been shown. To this he says in the *Locana*: "It has indeed been shown immediately below.
Furthermore, the fact that [the emotion] is suppressed by its capacity is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
For instance, when a poet devoid of creative power composes a depiction of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) in such a context, it clearly appears as a defect.
Now, one might ask: in this view, what is unpleasing about such examples as "Whosoever bears a weapon"?
We simply do not perceive any such thing [as being unpleasing].
Therefore, it is said that whether *saṅghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) is distinct from the *guṇas* (poetic qualities) or identical to them, some other restrictive cause must be stated.
The reason for that restriction is the appropriateness of both the speaker and the subject matter.
The reason for that restriction is the appropriateness of both the speaker and the subject matter. (6)
In that regard, the speaker is either the poet himself or one fashioned by the poet;
and the one fashioned by the poet may be devoid of rasa and bhāva, or endowed with rasa and bhāva.
Furthermore, the rasa may have as its locus either the protagonist of the narrative or his adversary.

The protagonist of the narrative is divided into types such as the *dhīrodātta* (noble and firm) and so forth, with the options being either the previously mentioned type or one following that; and the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is a limb of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which is the soul of suggestion (*dhvani*)—this is the sense here, just as in the case of the *locana*.
This has indeed already been demonstrated.
The suffix *-ta* in *kārikākāreṇa* denotes a past action;
for it will be stated later: "There is no cause for the disruption of rasa other than impropriety," and so forth.
[The phrase] *apratīyamānam eva* means "only that which is not being perceived."
The meaning is: "even by those possessing the discernment that reflects upon what precedes and follows. Regarding the phrase "as being distinct from the qualities":

for if they are distinct, there is no cause whatsoever for the restriction of the composition; and even on the view that they are one, it must be stated that something other than rasa is the cause of the restriction.

The remainder of the verse is "tanniyamaḥ" (the restriction thereof). One who leads the discussion (*kathā*) toward its constituent parts that are to be performed by oneself is the protagonist of the discussion (*kathā-nāyaka*), who partakes in the fruit at the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*).
[This refers to] the *dhīrodātta* and other types of heroes.

There are four types of heroes (nāyaka), each characterized by a predominance of specific qualities and corresponding dramatic styles (vṛtti): the *dhīrodātta*, who is primarily a hero of righteous combat (*dharmayuddhavīra*); the *dhīroddhata*, who is primarily a hero of valor and ferocity (*vīraraudravīra*);
the *dhīralalita*, who is primarily a hero of valor and erotic passion (*vīraśṛṅgāravīra*);

and the *dhīrapraśānta*, who is primarily a hero of generosity, righteousness, valor, and tranquility (*dānadharma-vīra-śāntavīra*). These four are respectively dominated by the *sāttvatī*, *ārabhaṭī*, *kaiśikī*, and *bhāratī* dramatic styles.
The first is the protagonist of the narrative, and the one following that is the secondary protagonist (*upanāyaka*).
"Varieties" (*vikalpāḥ*) means differences among the speakers.
"It should be stated" means "by the author of the kārikās. The sense is that since the statement in the kārikā has already been established, the use of the past tense (bhūta-nirdeśa) is appropriate.
"For it will be stated" means that the phrase "and by the author of the Vṛtti" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In the Vṛtti, the passage beginning with "nanu" [is intended].
"In this view" means the position that the qualities (*guṇas*) consist solely of the form of structural arrangement (*saṅghaṭanā*). "What is the lack of beauty? is the objection.

The answer to that is: "not being perceived," and so forth. The term "ugliness" (*acārutva*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. To the question "by whom is it not perceived? he says in the *Locana*: "by those who have previously," and so forth.
He explains this with the words "For in the case of mutual exclusion," and so forth.

"It does not exist" means that while the restriction of the objects of the *guṇas* has indeed been stated, no cause for the restriction regarding their arrangement (*saṅghaṭanā*) has been mentioned at all.
The meaning is that rasa is not the cause of restriction, because it deviates in the case of the objects of definition (lakṣya). In the commentary, it says: "it is thus stated."
The meaning is that for this reason, the restrictive cause (niyamahetu) is now demonstrated. Regarding the phrase "the remainder of the verse" (kārikāvaśeṣa),
the intention is that it has not been supplied by the author of the commentary (vṛttikṛt).
He explains the term "the status of the protagonist of the narrative" with the words "the narrative," and so forth.
"One's own duty" means that which is to be accomplished by oneself.
The term *svapada* refers to that which possesses the fruit (*phalabhāgin*).
Regarding the word *dharma*: it means one for whom the heroism of dharma (*dharmavīra*) and the heroism of battle (*yuddhavīra*) are preeminent.

Although the *dhīrodātta* and other types of heroes are respectively dominated by the *raudra*, *śṛṅgāra*, and *śānta* sentiments, since energy (*utsāha*) is necessarily present in them as well, he says "heroic," etc.,
and "sāttvatī," etc.;
or else, it may have the semblance of a sentiment (*rasābhāsa*) as its constituent part.

It is of many kinds: whether intended for dramatic performance (*abhineyārtha*) or not intended for performance (*anabhineyārtha*), and whether based on characters of the highest nature (*uttamaprakṛti*) or other types.

In that regard, when the poet is a speaker whose own emotional state (*rasabhāva*) has departed [from the work], then the "eye" (*locana*) of the composition is the "suggestor" (*vyañjaka*)—meaning it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that rasa which constitutes the essence of *dhvani*.

That which is to be represented (*abhineya*) is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) whose object is to be led toward a state resembling direct perception through speech, gesture, spirit, and costume; this object, being of the nature of suggestion (*dhvani*), takes the form of the implied (*vyaṅgya*).
For that alone is called the "meaning of poetry" (*kāvyārtha*), and it is precisely with that [implied meaning] that representation is connected.
As the Sage has stated in various places: "They bring to life the meanings of poetry through speech, gesture, and spirit," and so forth.

However, since the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is necessarily involved in the enactment of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), or takes the form of its determinants (*vibhāva*) and so on, it is that which is enacted; thus, the expression "the expressed meaning is the object to be enacted" (*abhineyārtha*) is the most logical formulation.
One should not, however, explain this here by applying the principle of "as if possessing a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).
"As with others" means that it is other than those; "the remaining one" means that which relies on a middling basis and that which relies on an inferior nature.

Having thus described the differences among speakers and the differences among the expressed meanings, he states the principle of propriety (*aucitya*) that governs them, beginning with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
Regarding the phrase "of the composition" (*racanāyāḥ*), it means of the structural arrangement (*saṅghaṭanā*).
Even if an ascetic or similar figure—devoid of rasa or bhāva, unanimated, and indifferent—is a subordinate element of the plot, he nevertheless follows the primary rasa.
Nevertheless, the definitions of the *sātvatī* and other *vṛttis* should be sought elsewhere.
He explains the word "varieties" (*vikalpāḥ*) in accordance with the context as "differences among speakers.
The meaning is: the internal differences among the speakers mentioned in the phrase "of the speaker and the expressed" (*vaktṛ-vācyayoḥ*).
He explains the statement "the expressed meaning is that which is to be enacted" with the words beginning "to be enacted," etc.,
and "speech," etc.;
the meaning is "by means of the fourfold [modes]."
This is an elaboration of the phrase "in the form of the suggested" (*vyaṅgyarūpa*): namely, "having the nature of resonance" (*dhvanisvabhāva*).
The meaning is "having resonance as its essence" (*dhvanyātmā*).
He establishes what has been stated with the words beginning "that very [thing]," and so forth.
That very thing is the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) itself.
"Connection through gesture" (abhinayena yogaḥ) means the state of being acted out (abhinetavyatva).
The etymological explanation of the term *bhāva* is given by the phrase ending with "they bring [it] into being" (*bhāvayanti*) regarding speech, body, and so forth.
The connection is that [the author] has stated such things in various places.

The meaning is that, by the etymological derivation *kāvyena arthyate* ("that which is sought through poetry"), the term *kāvyārtha* (poetic meaning) refers to the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "In that case, is there no representation (*abhinaya*) of the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*)? To this, he says: "representation of aesthetic flavor," and so on.
He concludes the explanation with the words "iti" and so forth.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "This very mode of expression (*vācoyukti*) is the most logical."
The meaning is that the aforementioned explanation alone is endowed with excellence.
However, as for the phrase "but not," etc.:
if it were the case that only the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is what is to be represented (*abhineya*), [then the following would apply].
Regarding the statement "then the denoted meaning is that which is to be enacted" (*tadā vācyam abhineyārtham*), the analysis is *abhineyaḥ arthaḥ yasya* ("that whose object is to be enacted").

Because the referent of the word *yat* (the denoted) and the referent of the word *artha* (the object) are identical, the genitive case is explained as being used through the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as if it were distinct from itself) to express a distinction, just as in the expression "the head of Rāhu" (*rāhoḥ śiraḥ*).
This is the implied sense.

Having demonstrated the meaning of the statement that "the speaker composed by the poet is devoid of rasa and bhāva," he raises an objection regarding its logical inconsistency and resolves it with the words beginning "devoid of rasa and bhāva.
The explanation of the phrase "devoid of rasa and bhāva" is "unpossessed" (anāviṣṭa); the meaning is "lacking the immersion (*āveśa*) in rasa and so forth."
Regarding the question "Who is he?", he says: "The ascetic and so forth," and so on.
The word "api" (also) is used for conjunction.
[He is] "one who follows the primary aesthetic flavor (rasa)" and so forth.

And thus, through his immersion in those various mental states (*cittavṛtti*), he has freedom of action (*kāmacāra*). Even when the speaker is one fashioned by a poet and devoid of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) or emotion (*bhāva*), it is still the same;

but when the poet or the speaker fashioned by the poet is endowed with *rasa* and *bhāva*, and since *rasa*—being dependent on the primary element—is the very soul of suggestion (*dhvani*), then there must necessarily be only non-compounded or middle-compounded words therein.
Regarding composition (*saṅghaṭanā*):
in the cases of the erotic sentiments of compassion (*karuṇa*) and separation (*vipralambha*), the composition must indeed be non-compound (*asamāsa*).
If one asks why this is so, it is said:

When rasa is predominant—as in the *Priyadarśikā* and other such works—then, in the apprehension of that rasa, all obstructing and contradictory elements must be entirely avoided. Thus, because long compounds, loose composition (*asaṅghaṭanā*), and the absence of compounds can, through various possible combinations, sometimes obstruct the perception of rasa, one should not be excessively attached to them. It has been stated [in the *Locana*] that [the work] is "devoid of rasa and so forth. The phrase "that very [work]" is used according to one's preference.
Having thus considered the propriety of the speaker's purity of mouth, he states that very point along with the propriety of speech, beginning with "But when...
Although it is appropriate for the poet to be a speaker who is indeed permeated by rasa,
otherwise— according to the principle that "if he himself were devoid of passion"— the poetry would be entirely devoid of rasa.
Nevertheless, when this [speaker] is primarily intent upon displaying poetic figures such as *yamaka* (paronomasia) and the like,
he is then said to be "devoid of rasa and so forth.
A speaker is invariably endowed with *rasa* and *bhāva*, and is never in any way a mere bystander.
And the *rasa* is indeed the very soul of the *dhvani*, and not merely a figure of speech such as *rasavat*.
Therefore, it should be understood that it occurs both in compounds and non-compounds when they are properly joined; otherwise, however, it may also occur even in long compounds.
Therefore, one need not suspect a redundancy in the word *niyama* or in the two occurrences of the particle *eva*.
If it is asked "How so?", the intention is this: is this the statement of a Dharmasūtra author?
"It is said" means by way of logical justification. "In the cognition of that" [means as follows].
The meaning is that those which are obstructive to the relish of that [taste], being of the nature of impediments to relish and non-conducive to it, consist of a relish contrary to it.
Regarding the phrase "by way of possibility" (*sambhāvanayā*):

the sense is that while many varieties are possible, it is the *saṅghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) that is the operative factor in such possibility; this is what should be understood by the term *bhāvya*.
"Tāvatī" means "in oneself. Thus it has been said.
By the phrase "devoid of rasa and bhāva," the intended meaning is that its absence is innate (*naisargika*).
Regarding "pure" (*śuddha*): the meaning is that it is pure, being unmixed with anything else, which constitutes the propriety (*aucitya*) of the speaker.

However, by the verse beginning with "When the poet," it is understood that at times a poet may be devoid of rasa and bhāva; having raised an objection regarding the inconsistency of what was previously stated, he refutes it with the words "Even though the poet," and so forth.
"He himself" refers to...
This verse will be demonstrated.

Regarding the phrase "then necessarily only in a compound," he explains it by commenting on the word "necessarily" (*niyamena*) and the two occurrences of the particle "only" (*eva*), applying them respectively and showing their respective excluded meanings— beginning with "necessarily," etc., up to "by that."
The meaning is "by the reasoning already stated.
As for the passage beginning with "What dharma," the intention is that the words of the authors of the *Dharmasūtras* are to be respected even if they are devoid of logical justification.
Regarding the phrase "having the nature of obstacles to relish":
obstacles to relish (*āsvādana-vighna*) such as doubt (*saṃśaya*) and so forth have been demonstrated in the *Abhinavabhārati* and other works.
Regarding the phrase "opposed to that": [it refers to those qualities which are the opposite of such obstacles].
The meaning is "contrary to the primary rasa.
Regarding the term *sambhāvanayā*, he says—starting with "aneka" and so forth—that it is derived from the causative form (*ṇijanta*) of the root *bhū* with the suffix *ṇac*.
[He further explains that] it is "conceived" (*sambhāvyate*).
The word "by the practitioners" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "The agent" (prayoktrī) means the instigating agent (prayojaka-kartṛ).
In the commentary, the words "especially" (*viśeṣataḥ*) and so forth are used;
they are to be supplied with the phrase beginning with "in that" (*tasyām*).
In a poetic work intended for dramatic performance (*abhineyārtha*), an excessive attachment (*atyantābhiniveśa*) to that [verbal expression] is especially not fitting.
This applies especially to poetry intended for dramatic performance,

and even more so elsewhere to the *karuṇa* (pathetic) and *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation) sentiments; for these two, owing to their extreme delicacy, cannot endure even the slightest lack of clarity in either word or meaning.
The comprehension [of the meaning] becomes sluggish.

However, when another rasa such as the Furious (raudra) is to be conveyed, a composition with moderate compounds—or even one with long compounds—is not defective, provided it relies on the activity associated with a hero who is bold and haughty, or is considered appropriate in view of the expressed content (vācya) which is invariably connected with and suggestive of that [rasa]. Thus, that too [is permissible].
It is not to be entirely avoided;
furthermore, in all compositions, the quality known as clarity (prasāda) is pervasive.
[The word] *locanam* contains two causative suffixes (*ṇic*).
"Especially regarding the meaning intended for dramatic representation (*abhineyārtha*):
first of all, it is impossible to perform the dramatic representation of the condensed meaning (*samāsārtha*) without the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*),
[as well as] intonation (*kāku*) and so forth, and internal clarity, singing, and so on."
In that case, a practice characterized by difficult application and an extensive proliferation of doubt would not be appropriate for drama;
the point is that such practice possesses the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And "elsewhere" means...
Even regarding an object that is not to be led away [from attachment],
it becomes sluggish;
the meaning is that the relish is obstructed because it is impeded.

The requirement for that long compound construction— which cannot exist without the suggestion (ākṣepa) that serves as the manifestor of the suggested meaning— is the cause of its non-deficiency, provided that such a denoted meaning, being appropriate to the rasa and employed for the purpose of manifesting that rasa, is present.
As for the explanation that the "operation" (vyāpāra) is the "introduction" (ākṣepa) of the hero, that does not seem quite fitting; so, enough of that.
Regarding the term "pervasive" (vyāpī):
whatever composition there may be, it should be executed in such a manner.
That is to say, just as there is an immediate comprehension of the expressed meaning;
this is what is meant by "it has been stated," beginning with the words:
"As for that which constitutes the capacity of poetry to convey [the suggested sense]," and so forth.
The phrase "it does not manifest" is to be construed with "it shines," meaning "it appears beautiful.
To dispel the inquiry as to why this is so, he states the underlying intention: "by that which is unbroken," and so forth.

The word "therein" (tatra) should be applied to each sentence; its meaning is "when there exists a composition characterized by long compounds. In this case, it cannot be accomplished by means of an uninterrupted suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).
However, the sense is that one must indeed perform the destruction of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) first.
He states other defects as well, beginning with "intonation and so forth" (*kākādya*).
Regarding the word "in between" (*antareti*):

The term "in between" (*antare*) means in the middle; those [activities] such as singing which are for the sake of pleasing are "difficult to employ" (*duṣprayojāḥ*), meaning they are to be employed with difficulty.
In that case, there would be a practice characterized by the proliferation of much doubt, and that [practice] is not suitable for drama (*nāṭya*). This is the construction [of the sentence].
He states the reason for this with the words "perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*):
the meaning is that it consists of a direct realization free from obstacles such as doubt and the like.
[The phrase] "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) refers to that [knowledge].
The meaning is "because of the cognition of drama.
It is stated in the *Abhinavabhārati* that what is called "drama" (*nāṭya*) consists of a cognition whose nature is the relishing of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says: "there and elsewhere."
It should be understood that the phrase beginning with "in that" (*tasyām*) is to be supplied here as well.
Regarding the word "locane," he states the meaning of the abstract noun (*bhāva*) in the passage beginning with "taste" (*āsvāda*).
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), he says "another rasa" (*rasāntara*), and so forth.

Furthermore, when the *raudra* (furious) rasa and others are to be expressed, neither a composition with moderate compounds nor even a composition with long compounds ever becomes defective; this is the connection [of the text].
The reason for the non-defectiveness of the long-compound composition is "its suggestion" (*tad-ākṣepa*) and so forth. He explains this passage starting with "of that" (*tasyāḥ*).
In the phrase "of the composition" (*saṅghaṭanāyāḥ*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karma*).
"Implication" (*ākṣepa*) means the drawing in (*ākarṣa*) into the collection of words that express [the meaning] itself; that is to say, its application (*yojana*).
He states "by that," etc., to explain that this is an adjective qualifying the "denotable" (*vācya*) as being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvī*) with it.
For it has been stated that this [quality of clarity] is common to all rasas and common to all compositions (*saṅghaṭanā*).
Indeed, even a composition free of compounds (*asamāsa*) does not manifest the *karuṇa*, *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*, or *śṛṅgāra* rasas if it exceeds [the degree of] clarity.
And when that [clarity] is not abandoned, even a composition with moderate compounds (*madhyama-samāsa*) does not fail to reveal them.
Therefore, clarity (*prasāda*) must be pursued everywhere.

For this very reason, in such instances as "Whoever bears a weapon," if the presence of vigor (*ojas*) is not desired, then the quality present is indeed called clarity and not sweetness (*mādhurya*);
nor is there any lack of beauty.

Because it reveals the intended rasa, whether the *saṅghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) is non-different from the *guṇas* (qualities) or different from them, there is a restriction of its scope based on the aforementioned propriety (*aucitya*). Thus, it too possesses the capacity to manifest *rasa*.

Furthermore, since this very cause of restriction—which was just mentioned—is the factor that determines the specific domain of the *guṇas* as the means for the manifestation of *rasa*, their establishment upon the basis of the *guṇas* is likewise not contradictory.
The meaning is that the *locana* does not convey its own expressed meaning as a suggester.
Regarding the word "that" (*tad*):

since it is desired that clarity (*prasāda*) should not be abandoned, the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) have been stated here by the author's own voice regarding this matter.

"Not sweetness" means that since it has been previously established that *ojas* (vigour) and *mādhurya* (sweetness) consist in mutual exclusion, their commingling is utterly contrary to the sacred scriptures (*śruti*); this is the intended sense. "Abhipreta" (intended).
The meaning is that by grace alone that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is manifested; it is not the case that it is not manifested.
Therefore:
even if the qualities (*guṇas*) are of the same nature as the structural arrangement (*saṅghaṭanā*), the restriction of the qualities is itself the restriction of the structural arrangement.

The same applies even to the view that the composition is dependent upon the qualities (guṇas). Even in the view that the qualities reside in the composition, since the composition acts as the regulator, the suitability of the speaker and the expressed meaning is such that the expressed meanings become manifestors [of the suggested sense] only when the words expressing their respective meanings are marked by a composition characterized by long compounds; this is the intended sense. *Bālapriyā*: The connection is that whatever expressed meaning does not become a manifestor of the suggested sense [is not so]. The point is that the expressed meanings become manifestors only when the words denoting them are indeed marked by a composition consisting of long compounds.
He states "she," etc., to show that the word *apekṣayā* (in view of) is connected with the phrase "it does not become defective.
Having presented an alternative interpretation for the term *tadākṣepa* (its implication), he refutes it with the words "of the hero," etc.,
[stating] that "it does not coalesce."
The meaning is that [the quality] exists in accordance with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
He explains that the quality called *prasāda* (clarity) is pervasive by saying "yā" and so forth;
"whatever arrangement (*saṅghaṭanā*) there may be" means that.
The meaning is that "composition" refers to a form consisting of long meters and so forth.
"Because it is desired" means because following [the style of] *prasāda* is intended.
The word "uktāv" (in what has been said) is connected with this [word "arthe"].
Regarding the phrase "atrārthe":
the meaning is that in all cases, serenity (*prasāda*) is to be followed.
The phrase "with his own throat," and so forth,

means that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is stated by the words "if he does not abandon that, he does not reveal [the truth]," while the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is stated by the words "transgression of his favor," and so forth. This is the intended meaning.
He states the [underlying] nature: "Ojas [is the opposite] of Mādhurya," and so forth.
Regarding the word "mutually" (anyonya):
the meaning is that Ojas consists in the absence of Mādhurya, and Mādhurya consists in the absence of Ojas.
"Confusion" (*saṅkara*) means the coexistence of *ojas* in the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other rasas, and of *mādhurya* in the furious (*raudra*) and other rasas.
"Extraneous to the scriptures" (*śrutibāhya*) means...
The meaning is "unheard.
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Therefore" and ending with "is not contradictory" by means of the words "If [there were] qualities," and so forth. (5–6)
Another propriety, which has as its basis the subject matter (*viṣaya*), also governs that [poetic suggestion];
for it exists in various forms, depending on the specific divisions of poetry. (Dhvanyāloka 3.7)
Another propriety, which depends on the subject matter, also regulates that [poetic sentiment];
for it exists in various forms, established according to the different divisions of poetry. (7)
Even when there is propriety pertaining to the speaker and the subject matter, another kind of propriety based on the specific context governs the composition (*saṅghaṭanā*).
For the varieties of poetry include the *muktaka* (single verse), as well as those composed in Sanskrit, Prākṛta, and Apabhraṃśa;
and the *sandānitaka*, *viśeṣaka*, *kalāpaka*, and *kulaka*.

Paryāyabandha, parikathā, khaṇḍakathā, sakalakathā, sargabandha, abhineyārtha, ākhyāyikā, kathā, and so forth—based on these [categories], the *Locana* has stated that [the *Kāvyaprakāśa*] is the cause; thus, even in all three positions, there is no contradiction regarding the fact that it is the cause for determining their qualities. This is the intended meaning. // 5, 6 //
He states that there is yet another regulator: "based on the subject matter" (*viṣayāśrayam*).
By the word "subject matter," a specific type of composition (*saṅghāta*) is meant.

For just as a person situated within a composite whole such as an army remains compliant with its requirements even if he is timid, so too does a poetic sentence, when situated within a specific composition such as a *sandānitaka* or the like, [attains its proper effect].
In that case, it functions according to propriety (*aucitya*).

However, as for what was stated by the word "object" (*viṣaya*) regarding the *muktaka* (isolated verse), that is intended merely to demonstrate independence due to the absence of a composition, just as [one says] "space established in itself.

By the word "also" (*api*), he says this: even when there is propriety between the speaker and the subject matter, the propriety of the object (*viṣaya-aucitya*) is pervaded solely by the distinction of degrees of intensity.
But it is not the case that the propriety of the speaker and the expressed meaning is precluded by the propriety of the subject matter.
"Mukta" means not embraced by another; the suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of its name (*sañjñā*).

Therefore, even though it possesses an independently complete meaning that leaves no further expectation for supplementation, a work situated in the middle of a larger composition is not called *muktaka* (detached).
He explains the nature of the *muktaka* itself with an illustration, beginning with "Just as," etc.,
[saying] "by him" (*senā*).
That which is a collection or aggregate consisting of an army and so forth— [the term] "niveśin" means one who is situated or established therein.
"Even a coward" (kātara) means even one who is lacking in fortitude (adhīra).
The reading is also "kātarādirapi" (even the timid and so forth). "In accordance with that" means in accordance with the army and so forth.
"By way of being undaunted" means up to that point.
"A poetic sentence" (kāvyavākya) means a sentence in the form of poetry.

Now, one might ask: since a *muktaka*—being a single verse—lacks the nature of a composite (*saṅghāta*), for what purpose is it described as a variety of poetry (*kāvyaprabheda*) in the commentary? To this, he says: "But the *muktaka*," and so forth.
That [is] that statement; "by the absence of a composite" means by the absence of having the nature of a composite.
Regarding the term "svātantrye" (in independence):

the meaning is that even the *muktaka* (isolated verse) has been mentioned as a variety of poetry merely to demonstrate that it possesses independence (*svātantrya*) in its structural arrangement (*saṅghaṭanā*), because it too flows with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
To provide an illustration for this, he says "sva... and so forth.
When it has been stated that the four elements beginning with earth are established in space, the question arises as to where space itself is established;
in response to this, the statement "this space is established in its own space" means that, just as Brahman is established in Brahman, space is established in space alone and nowhere else.
The meaning is: "just as" this statement merely demonstrates the independence of space;
"even though" means "precisely because."
"Regarding 'gradation' (tāratamya)":
the meaning is that it is the sole determinant of the distinction of gradation.
"Unembraced by anything else" means:
The meaning is "not depending on anything other than itself" for the sake of a cognition free from further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*). Regarding the suffix *-kan* in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*),
by this [suffix], it becomes possessed of a specific composition (*saṅghaṭanā*).
In that regard, for a poet who is intent on the binding of sentiments (*rasa*) within liberated characters, there is propriety (*aucitya*) based on those characters;
and this has already been demonstrated.
Elsewhere, however, there is freedom of action.
The term *locana* is an adjective, beginning with *saṃskṛta* and so forth;
it is designated in that very order because [the qualities] arise sequentially.
When an action is completed by means of two [verses], it is a *sandānitaka*.
A *viśeṣaka* consists of three [verses];
a *kalāpaka*, four;
and a *kulaka*, five or more.

Thus, the varieties produced by the completion of an action have been indicated by way of a copulative compound (*dvandva*). Furthermore, even when there is the completion of intermediate actions, a *paryāyabandha* (successive composition) is one that proceeds with the description of spring as its intended subject to be heard.

A *parikathā* (circumstantial story) is a mode of describing infinite narratives through various diversities of style, directed toward a single human goal such as *dharma* and so forth. A *khaṇḍakathā* (fragmentary story) is the description of a single portion [of a narrative].
The description of the entire narrative, including the final result, constitutes the *sakalakathā* (complete story).
Both types are designated by a copulative compound (*dvandva*) because they are both well-known in the vernacular (*prākṛta*).
However, for the former types, such as the *muktaka* (detached verses) and others, there is no restriction regarding the language used.

The *mahākāvya* (great poem) is a composition in the form of a continuous narrative (*sargabandha*) consisting of descriptions of all manner of subjects, which yields the fruits of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*) and is composed exclusively in Sanskrit.

The *daśarūpaka* (the ten types of drama), intended for performance, consists of various sub-varieties such as the *nāṭikā*, *troṭaka*, *rāsaka*, and *prakaraṇikā*, and is characterized by a mixture of many languages.
It is further joined with features such as the *ucchvāsa* (chapter divisions) of the *ākhyāyikā* and metrical forms like the *vaktra* and *aparavaktra*.
*Kathā* is that which is devoid of those [ornaments]. Both are designated by way of a pair (*dvandva*) because they both consist in the form of prose composition (*gadyabandha*).
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), *campū* is also included.
As Daṇḍin said: "The *campū* consists of both prose and verse. "Elsewhere" refers to cases where there is no intent toward the composition of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
The conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) dear to the ignorant has been shown.
By the word "by that" (*tena*), the meaning is: by the existence of even that conventional usage.

"It is not called 'isolated' (muktaka)"—the sense is that it is accepted as being established only when included within a continuous composition (prabandha). Because it is specified with a singular ending as "composed in Saṃskṛta, Prākṛta, and Apabhraṃśa," he says: "of the isolated [verse] alone," and so forth.
Regarding the term "viśeṣaṇam" (qualification):
the ellipsis [to be supplied] is "because it is stated in the singular number.
The intention is that the word [viśeṣaṇam] should be construed with the words "sandānitaka" and so forth by changing its grammatical form [to the plural].
By this, there is no inconsistency with what will be stated later—that for the *muktaka* and other forms of poetry by earlier authors, there is no restriction regarding the language used.
Hemacandra has also stated this: "These [forms] may be composed in all languages.
The defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of Sanskrit and the other languages have been explained in works such as the *Kāvyādarśa*.
"Because they arise in succession" means that the *saṃskṛta* arose first, from which the *prākṛta* arose, and from that, the *apabhraṃśa* arose; such is the meaning.
"In that very same way" refers to the sequence beginning with *saṃskṛta*.

In the passage beginning with "by three," the meaning is that because there is equal primacy due to the distinction created by the non-completion of the purchase, it is expressed by a *dvandva* compound; [the term] "sandānitaka" and so forth refers to what has been set in motion or composed.
"One [is] from dharma and so forth" means that among the human goals (puruṣārtha) such as dharma and the rest, it is one [of them]. "A portion" means...
The meaning is "a portion of a well-known historical narrative.
Regarding the phrase "in the form of a mahākāvya," the definitions of mahākāvyas and other such genres are stated in works such as the *Kāvyādarśa*.
"By means of a dvandva compound" means by means of the dvandva compound "ākhyāyikā" and so forth.
"Under some pretext" means having acted out the pretense of not hearing, as expressed by the phrase "having done so somehow" and so on.
"In the void, devoid of companions.
This verse is explained in the *Kāvyālaṅkārasaṅgrahavyākhyā*:
"Poets devoted to the composition of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) are seen in *muktaka* verses—whether with medium or long compounds—just as they are in extended compositions (*prabandha*)."
For it is well known that the detached verses (*muktaka*) of the poet Amaruka, which overflow with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), function as a continuous composition.
In the case of *sandānitaka* and similar forms, however, because of the propriety of grand composition, the arrangement should consist of middle-length compounds or long compounds.
Regarding compositions based on a larger work (*prabandha*), one must follow the propriety of the specific type of work as described above.

Furthermore, in the *paryāyabandha* (poetic composition using synonyms), the *saṃghaṭanā* (diction) should consist of either no compounds or only middle-sized compounds. Occasionally, even when the *saṃghaṭanā* involves long compounds based on the propriety of the meaning, the *vṛtti* (style) must avoid being harsh or vulgar. In the *parikathā* (narrative prose), there is freedom of choice.
In that regard, because there is no excessive adherence to the composition of rasa through the mere presentation of past events (*itivṛtta*),

there is no contradiction even in the presence of long compounds in *khaṇḍakathā* and *sakalakathā*, which are well-known as the subjects [of these genres] and involve an abundance of compositions such as *kulaka*s and the like.
However, the propriety of style (*vṛttyaucitya*) should be followed in accordance with the specific rasa.

One might raise the objection: "Surely the *locana* [is intended] for a formal composition (*sargabandha*), but how can there be a combination of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth in a detached verse (*muktaka*), since aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) depends upon them? Anticipating this, he says: "In detached verses...
and "Of Amaruka... [The verse:
"When her lover had somehow regained her favor, yet faltered in his reply, she—emaciated by separation—feigned that she had not heard him under some pretext."
Fearing that her friend had reached her ears, she turned her eyes about with agitation; then, in the empty house, she heaved a deep sigh.
For in this verse, the perception of a deficiency in the *vibhāvas* (determinants) is indeed manifest.

Regarding the word "vikaṭā" (awkward): in a composition that lacks compound words (*asamāsa*), the perception is sluggish; being expectant, it pursues the verb which lies far off, and having come to rest only upon the perception of the literal meaning (*vācya*), it is unfit for the savoring of the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
The sense is "it might be so.

Regarding the phrase "in those based on a continuous series," he provides the justification for what was stated as "only for the delight of children" by saying "in the case of the non-compound," and so forth.
"In the case of conjunction" means "when it exists"— this is the ellipsis.
"In a sluggish form" means:
The meaning is that they become feeble.
"Expectant" (sākāṅkṣā) means accompanied by an expectation for an action and so forth.
The sense is that [the function] rests solely upon the cognition of the expressed meaning,
because the cognition of the expressed meaning arises only after a long delay. "It would not be so" means...
Thus, the sense is that for the sake of avoiding sluggishness in the comprehension of the expressed meaning (*vācya*), the composition (*saṅghaṭanā*) should be of medium or long compounds.

In the phrase "in those based on a continuous work" (*prabandhāśrayeṣu*), only the term *sandānitaka* and so forth is to be understood as the subject of the ellipsis, and not the term *muktaka* as well; for while a *muktaka*—defined by the previously mentioned characteristics—is appropriate according to the specific sentiment (*rasa*) when its primary intent is rasa, otherwise there would be a violation of propriety.

In both types of composition, the focus on rasa is more effective for those who employ the structural arrangement of a *sargabandha*. However, in the case of dramatic performance (*abhineya*), one must by all means apply oneself to the construction of rasa.

As for the *ākhyāyikā* and the *kathā*, because they consist largely of prose compositions, and because prose follows a different method from verse composition, even a slight deviation from the established rule is here tolerated, though it has not been done before.
This aforementioned propriety alone is the regulator of that [ornament] everywhere, even in prose composition which is devoid of metrical constraints. (Dhvanyāloka 3.8)
This aforementioned propriety alone is the regulator of that [rhythm] everywhere, even in prose composition which is devoid of metrical constraints. (8)

That which was stated as the "propriety" (*aucitya*) residing in the speaker and the expressed content, serving as the regulator of composition, is itself the cause of restriction even in prose (*gadya*), despite its lack of metrical constraints, depending upon the subject matter.
For instance, in this case as well, when the poet or the speaker composed by the poet is devoid of *rasa* and *bhāva*, there is freedom of choice;
however, when the speaker is endowed with *rasa* and *bhāva*, one must follow exactly what was stated previously.
And even there, it is simply a matter of suitability regarding the subject matter:
in the case of an *ākhyāyikā*, in the *locana*, in *sandānitaka* and other such forms, or at the end of a *kulaka*;
or alternatively, let there be the presence of the *muktaka* even within a larger composition (*prabandha*).
For that by which the savoring of rasa (*rasacarvaṇā*) is performed, even without regard for what precedes or follows it, is precisely the *muktaka* (isolated verse).
For example, the verse beginning with "Having painted you as angry in love" (*tvām ālikhya praṇayakupitām*). The phrase "at times" refers to cases such as the *raudra* (furious) sentiment and others.
The connection [of the phrase] "not excessively" (*nātyantam*) is as follows: it refers to that lack of excessive attachment which exists regarding the composition of poetic sentiments (*rasa*).
Furthermore, [the phrase] "and the modes of expression" (*vṛttayaśca*) [is connected with] "not excessively."

The propriety of the styles (vṛtti)— the harsh, the refined (upanāgarikā), and the vulgar— depends on the specific composition and the sentiment (rasa). "Otherwise" means that when the intent is merely narrative (kathāmātra), there is freedom of choice regarding the styles as well.
"In both cases" refers to the locative case.

When the primary aim is narrative, it is a "composition in the form of a story," such as Bhaṭṭa Jayanta’s *Kādambarīkathāsāra*. When the primary aim is aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), it is [a poem], such as the *Raghuvamśa* and others.
Others, however, explain [the verse] as referring to "both the embellished and the natural.
But in that case, regarding what was stated—that the focus on rasa (aesthetic flavor) is superior—how could that be understood unless it were taken in a figurative sense (neyārtha)? // 7 //
He states that [it is] because it is impossible in compositions such as the *sandānitaka* and so forth, saying "in the *sandānitaka* and so forth.
He states another alternative, saying "or if," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: what then is the definition of a *muktaka*? To this he says: "the preceding," and so forth.
The phrase beginning with "not excessively" (*nātyantam*) constitutes a single compound.

"Devotion to the composition of rasa" (*rasabandhābhiniveśaḥ*) means attachment to the composition of rasa; the absence of that which is excessive devotion to the composition of rasa is "non-excessive devotion to the composition of rasa. With this intention, he explains the meaning as "because of that non-excessive devotion to the composition of rasa," and so forth.
The reading in the commentary (*vṛtti*) is "atyantaṃ rasabandhānabhiniveśāt" (due to the absolute lack of attachment to the bonds of aesthetic flavor).
The word "dvayor api mārgayoḥ" (in both paths) ends in the locative case;
the word "tātparyasya" (of the intended meaning) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He states that the meaning is "of the purport of the narrative and the purport of the aesthetic flavor (rasa)" with the words beginning "of the two" (*dvayoḥ*).
He provides another explanation for the phrase "of both paths" (*dvayor api mārgayoḥ*) with the words beginning "the other" (*anyaḥ*).
He refutes that [explanation] with the words beginning "in that case" (*tatra*). // 7 //
However, for the most part, composition occurs primarily through middle and long compounds;
for prose possesses a certain luster by relying on complex structures (*vikaṭabandha*),
and it is in such compositions that this [luster] reaches its highest excellence.
In a narrative (kathā), however, even when there is an abundance of complex compounds, one must follow the propriety prescribed for the composition of aesthetic flavor (rasa).

"The propriety taught for the composition of rasa shines everywhere as that which is relied upon; yet, that stylistic arrangement (racanā) possesses some variation depending on the subject matter. (Dhvanyāloka 3.9)

The propriety described in the context of *rasabandha* (the composition of aesthetic flavor) shines forth as being applicable everywhere; however, that stylistic arrangement (*racanā*) varies slightly depending on the subject matter.

Alternatively, just as in verse, even in prose composition, the arrangement must everywhere rely upon the propriety described for the expression of rasa; for the *Locana* states that [propriety] is dependent on the subject matter (*viṣaya*). Thus, it should be understood that the specific varieties of prose composition themselves constitute the subject matter. // 8 //
He shows the established position with the words "as stated in the *Rasabandha*.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "or" (*vā*) indicates the stability of this very position.
For example: "Women, kings, fire, and poison, when utilized with skill..."
Whether for one's own sake, or solely for the accumulation of suffering.
Thus [ends the previous point].
"Composition" (*racanā*) means structural arrangement.

To the objection that in that case the suitability of the subject matter (*viṣayaucitya*) would be entirely abandoned, he replies: "Therefore, that very suitability of aesthetic flavor (*rasaucitya*) depends upon the subject matter as a cooperative factor."
"Whatever slight difference exists"—meaning that which possesses internal variety as something to be accomplished—refers to its being the "object" (*viṣaya*).
That is to say, it means by way of being the referent of the word "object. // 8 //

In the verse beginning with "rasabandhe," the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that the composition everywhere appears to rely upon the propriety (*aucitya*) described in the section on the binding of sentiments (*rasabandha*).
Regarding the commentary (*vṛtti*), he states that the word "atha vā" does not signify an alternative; thus he says, "and the word 'vā' in the commentary.
The particle "ca" is used as an ornament for the sentence.
Regarding the word "vā":
the meaning is that the word "vā" occurs in the phrase "athavā" (or else).
Regarding the word "asya" (of this): [it refers to the aforementioned].
The meaning is: "of that which is about to be stated by [the words] beginning with 'like a verse' (*padyavat*).
"Indicating stability" means indicating a state of being established in the form of certainty.
This means it indicates that [the term] is well-established.
Furthermore, when authors of treatises introduce an alternative position with words such as "or else" (*athavā*), they do so out of a firm conviction.
He shows the usage of a great poet as supporting evidence for the stated meaning with the word "women" (*striyaḥ*).
