The fourfold group beginning with women, when cultivated through skillful means, leads to one's own welfare—that is, to one's own purpose.
Having stated this in accordance with worldly convention, he expresses his own view with the words "or else," and so forth.
If that same fourfold group is cultivated otherwise than through skillful means, it results solely in a mass of suffering—that is, in an excess of suffering alone.
In this context, the phrase "yadi vā" (or rather) indicates the established position (*sthitapakṣa*) that [the world] is indeed for the sake of the accumulation of suffering.

As the Lord of Aruṇācala explains the verse from the *Raghuvaṃśa*, "Poison might sometimes become nectar, or nectar might become poison by the will of the Lord," he comments on the verse beginning with "racanā" (*racanetyādi*), stating: "The word 'vā' indicates that the meaning of the sentence represents the established position."
"Then" (tarhi) means: when it is accepted that composition occurs everywhere by relying on the propriety (*aucitya*) mentioned in the context of the binding of aesthetic flavor (*rasabandha*).
"Thus it has been said" (*ity uktam*) refers to this.
"But has it been abandoned?"—this is the objection.
"No," he says; the meaning is that he replies, "It has not been abandoned."
The explanation of the word "tat" (that) is "tadeva" (that very same).
He states the meaning of that term as "rasaucityam" (propriety of rasa); the sense is the propriety mentioned in the composition of rasa.

The explanation of the phrase "dependent upon an object" (*viṣayāpekṣam*) is as follows: "it is an object," and so forth. That [cognition], however, while dependent upon an object, becomes possessed of some particularity (*viśeṣavat*).
But it is not in every respect;

for even in prose composition, a construction with excessively long compounds does not grace the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation) or *karuṇa* (pathos), nor even in the *ākhyāyikā* (narrative).
Likewise, in drama and similar forms, there should be no compounds at all when describing the *raudra* (fury) or *vīra* (heroism) sentiments.

However, propriety (*aucitya*) with respect to the subject matter (*viṣaya*) is diminished or enhanced by the [choice of] poetic measure (*pramāṇa*). For instance, in a narrative (*ākhyāyikā*), there is no absolute absence of compounds, yet even in its own proper domain such as the drama (*nāṭaka*) and so forth, there are no excessively long compounds; thus, the general direction regarding composition (*saṅghaṭanā*) should be followed.

Now, the suggestion (*dhvani*) whose process is imperceptible (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*), consisting of an entire work (*prabandha*), exists in such texts as the *Rāmāyaṇa* and the *Mahābhārata*. (Locana)
He explains this with the words "tattvi" (in that regard).
"In all its aspects" (*sarvākāram*) is an adverbial modifier.
"Precisely without compounding" (*asamāsaiva*).
The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
For instance, regarding the definition of dramatic dialogue and gesture (*vākya-abhinaya*), the Sage [Bharata] stated: "With clear feet and without powder," and so forth.
Here, he states an exception: "but not," etc.
"In plays and so forth" means that it is connected with "even in its own domain. // 9 //
Thus, it has been established that in a composition (*saṅghaṭanā*), the suggestion of which the sequence is imperceptible (*alaksyakrama*) shines forth.
As for the fact that this [suggestion] shines forth in a literary work (*prabandha*), this point is established beyond dispute; therefore, there is nothing further to be said here.

However, with the intention of defining the procedure for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) within a literary work in order to instruct poets and connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), he says "Now," etc.
The connection [of the text] is as follows: "Now, that collection of types is being explained.
First, regarding the phrase "dāvaditi," those types which serve as manifestors of the narrative (*prabandha*) are useful in their respective order;
for previously, there was the examination of the story (*kathā*).
In this context, "initial sowing" refers to bringing about the culmination of the fruit;
this is the explanation of the phrase "having some slight distinction," namely "kiñcit" and so forth.
The grammatical connection is: "of that which exists as something to be accomplished."
In the passage beginning with "tathā hi," he cites the words of the Sage as authority for the statement that "in all cases it is indeed without compound.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), at the point where it says "na ca" ("and not"), the phrase "asamāsaiva" ("only without compound") is to be supplied as a continuation.
The term "pramāṇataḥ" means "by way of authority."

The meaning is: "from the authority consisting of the appropriateness mentioned in the *Rasabandha*. Regarding the passage beginning with "in the narrative" (*ākhyāyikāyām*) and so forth, and "even in its own domain" (*svaviṣaye 'pi*).
The meaning is: "even in the case of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth, provided there is no absolute compounding.
The word "not" (*na*) is to be construed with the verb "it shines" (*śobhate*).
And the meaning is "not beautiful.
Regarding the phrase "in dramas and so forth," the term "even in its own domain" is to be supplied as a continuation.
The meaning is that a composition characterized by excessively long compounds does not shine.
The verse beginning with "iti kāvyārthe" is not seen in some manuscripts;
for this very reason, it has not been commented upon. // 9 //
He introduces the eyes [of the commentary] with the words "Thus," and so forth.
"The procedure" (itikartavyatā) means the manner in which [it is to be performed].
"Examinable" means worthy of examination.
He shows the connection of the word "now" (*idānīm*) with the referent of the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "that is now being explained" by saying "now," etc.
The words "firstly" (*prathamam tāvat*) are used to introduce the citation (*pratīka*).

He shows the seed of the sequence of instruction beginning with "vibhāvya" and so forth by stating "of the continuum," and so on. "Bringing it to the culmination of the fruit" refers to that which is clearly manifest in the discourse; this is indeed well-known.

Now, its manner of manifestation is explained as follows: The rule for the body of the narrative—whether based on actual events (*vṛtta*) or imagined (*utprekṣita*)—is that it must be beautiful through the propriety (*aucitya*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*bhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*sañcārin*). (Dhvanyāloka 3.10)

Having abandoned a mode of narration that has resulted from the constraints of historical fact and is thus unsuitable, one may even employ creative imagination to construct a narrative appropriate to the intended aesthetic flavor (rasa). (Dhvanyāloka 3.11)
The construction of the junctures and their constituent parts is for the sake of manifesting the aesthetic flavor (rasa),
and not merely with the desire to fulfill the formal requirements of the treatises.

The intensification and pacification [of the sentiment] occur at their appropriate times in between; this constitutes the reconnection of the principal sentiment (aṅgin), which had begun but not yet reached its final rest. (Dhvanyāloka 3.13)

Even when the poetic figures possess the capacity [to suggest], their application in accordance with propriety is the basis for the manifestation of rasa and the other elements within a literary composition. (Dhvanyāloka 3.14)

The arrangement of the body of the narrative—whether based on actual events or imagined—is beautiful through its propriety regarding the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*). (10)
Having abandoned an unsuitable state of affairs that has arrived by the force of past events, one may even imagine a narrative appropriate to the intended rasa within the interval. (11)
The construction of the junctures and their constituent parts should be performed with a view toward the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (rasa),
and not merely with the desire to fulfill the formal requirements of the treatises.

The intensification and pacification [of the rasa], as well as the reconnection of the principal rasa—which has begun but not yet reached its rest—at appropriate intervals, constitute [the function of the excitants]. (13)

Even when the figures of speech possess the capacity [to suggest], their application in accordance with propriety is the basis for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like within a literary composition. (14)

It has been stated that even the plot (*prabandha*) is a suggester (*vyañjaka*) of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth; the basis for its suggestiveness is as follows. First, there is the composition of the body of the narrative (*kathā-śarīra*), which is beautiful through the propriety of the determinants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*bhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*sañcārī*), according to the specific requirements of the *rasa*, *bhāva*, and so on intended to be conveyed. That is to say, whichever [element] is appropriate—whether a determinant, an ensuant, a consequent, or a transitory state—[is employed].
In this regard, the composition of the body of the narrative (*kathāśarīra*), which is beautiful through its propriety (*aucitya*), is one basis for suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*).

According to the *Locana*, it is the awakening toward aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and the propriety of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) consists in the description of the appropriate excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
He explains that sequence through the fivefold [classification] beginning with "vibhāva" and so forth. Regarding "tadaucitya" (propriety for that):

one who desires to describe the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) should resort to such a narrative in which there is the presence of excitants (*vibhāva*) such as the seasons and garlands, and ensuants (*anubhāva*) such as amorous play; this is the remainder [of the definition]. *Bālapriyā*.
Regarding the phrase "that pentad":
it should be understood that the first four [members] are indicated respectively by the first four verses, while the fifth is indicated by half a verse.

He explains the composition of the body of the narrative—which is beautiful due to its propriety regarding the *vibhāvas* and so forth—by taking up a specific *rasa*: "In the description of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), [there is] kissing," and so on;
and in the *Vṛtti*, "the *prakṛti*," and so on.
*Prakṛti* means innate nature (*svabhāva*).
"Divya," and so forth.
The meaning is that it is of many kinds, such as divine (*divyā*), human (*mānuṣī*), both divine and human (*divyamānuṣī*), and belonging to the netherworld (*pātālīyā*).
Among these, the divine nature (*prakṛti*) consists in having exclusively the form of an immortal, as in the case of the illustrious Maheśvara and others.
It should be understood that the human [type] has the singular form of a mortal, as in the case of Mādhava and others;
the divine-human [type] is exemplified by the Pāṇḍavas and others.
Regarding the word "her" (tām):
The meaning is "the fundamental nature" (*prakṛti*).
"Unmixed" (*asaṅkīrṇaḥ*) means not mixed with other stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*). There is also a reading: "partaking of propriety" (*aucityabhāk*).
In some texts, following the word "bhavati," there is the reading "nānyathā.
Regarding the phrase "anyathā" and so forth: "anyathā" means by deviating from the manner previously described.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: the enthusiasm and other qualities of a divine being are depicted solely with reference to a human basis, or the enthusiasm and other qualities of a human being are depicted solely with reference to a divine basis.
The phrase "tathā ca" means "for instance" (*tathā hi*).
"Regarding the eyes"—that is, "having those as their object.
The meaning is: "having the activity [of perception] as its object.
"This" refers to...
The meaning is "the locus of activity.
To the question "Why?", he says: "the permanent," and so forth.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), there are two readings: *bhāntī* and *bhavantī*.
For this very reason, Bharata has presented the requirement that a *nāṭaka* must have a well-known plot and a well-known, noble protagonist as a necessary condition.
By means of this, the poet does not become confused regarding the propriety or impropriety of the protagonist's character.
However, for one who would compose a *nāṭaka* or similar work with an invented plot, there would be a great error in describing the nature of an unknown or unsuitable protagonist.
The meaning of this *Locana* is as follows: that which is to be described is such that no contradiction to the understanding of those to be instructed arises therein.

In that regard, for an ordinary human being, the leaping across seven oceans in a single step is false because it is impossible; thus, it instills in the mind of the listener the notion that even the means to the four goals of life (*caturvarga*) might be unreal.
However, the life-story of Rāma, even if of such a nature, does not appear as untrue, because it is established upon a conviction accumulated through a long succession of prior renown.
For this very reason, when another power of that [cause] is imagined, it must be of exactly that same kind;
one should not describe something that falls outside the realm of possibility.
This is why it says, "by that indeed."
Because its subject matter concerns a well-known and noble hero,
one becomes bewildered, wondering what one might describe;
"he who" refers to the poet.
"It is a great negligence.
Therefore, he raises the objection regarding things that ought to be produced, such as plays and the like, which are dear to children, beginning with the words "But surely," and so forth.
He says, "In the world of the Nāgas," and so on.
And there is also the reading "nākaloke"; as for "tat," it means "therefore."
The word "iti" (thus) is connected with "in the description of these rulers of the earth.
"Kimiti" (why/how? is used in the sense of an inquiry or a negation. [The author] refutes [the objection] with the words beginning with "na etat" (this is not so).
This is not so; this objection does not arise. Why? To this he says: "Not," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: we do not say that the two descriptions of the extraordinary power of kings are improper.
In the *Locana*, he states the essential meaning of the passage beginning with "But distinct" (*vyatiriktaṃ tu*) as follows: "This has been said," and so forth.
Regarding the word "wherein" (*yatra*): the meaning is "in whatever [narrative] being described."
The refutation of cognition is the non-establishment of cognition;
[this applies] to a mere human being—
this is the ellipsis for "as it is being described."
The connection is that [the agent] causes the one who has crossed the seven oceans to settle [there]. "Anutām" means "unreality" (alīkatām).
The meaning is "unreality. He states the distinction with the words "but in the case of Rāma and so forth.
[He explains] "of such a kind" as follows:
The meaning is that it has the form of the roar of the ocean and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "established by prior tradition" (*pūrvaprasiddhi*): it is a *hetugarbha* (a term containing its own reason), meaning "ascended upon" that conviction or trust which has been accumulated through a succession of ancient and long-standing traditions.
Of that too— of Rāma and so forth—
it is "imagined," meaning it is described through conceptual construction;
it would indeed manifest as being just like that, namely, as something unreal.
He states the ultimate purport with the words "But not," and so forth.
"The object of the notion of impossibility" means that which has become the objective domain of the cognition that it is impossible.
He states the form of the confusion with the words beginning "What... and so forth.

Since the Sage did not specify that dramas and the like possess "created subject matter" (*utpādyavastutva*), the literal meaning—that one should create dramas and the like as having created subject matter—is incoherent.
Keeping in mind the interpretation that for anyone who were to treat dramas and the like as possessing created subject matter, it would be a great error, [he says the following].
He clarifies the intended meaning with the words "by that," and so forth: "By that"—meaning by way of the cause, which is the occurrence of the great poet’s negligence.

[The opponent objects: "If it is the case that the Sage [Bharata] somehow performs an examination of the propriety (*aucitya*) of divine, human, and other characters when describing emotions such as *utsāha* (energy) in dramas and the like, then let that be done."
But what is the purpose of that [love-making] at the beginning of love and so forth?
For it is the established rule that even for divine beings, love must be described according to the very same conventions as those appropriate to Bhāratavarṣa.
This is not so; in that case, there is the fault of transgressing propriety regarding wine.

For if one were to compose erotic poetry (*śṛṅgāra*) for a character of superior nature (*uttamaprakṛti*) by means of what is appropriate for an inferior nature (*adhamaprakṛti*), how could it not be ridiculous? If it is argued that while there are three types of propriety regarding the erotic theme even within the land of Bhārata-varṣa, the divine propriety (*divyamaucitya*) is of no use there—[we reply: No, we do not say that there is some other divine propriety pertaining to the erotic theme.

What then? Just as the depiction of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is appropriate among the best leaders—such as kings and others—in the land of Bhārata-varṣa, so too does it shine when based on divine beings.
Furthermore, the depiction of the well-known vulgar erotic sentiment among famous figures like kings is not observed in established works such as dramas;
likewise, that [vulgarity] must be avoided in the case of the gods.

If it is argued that there is no fault in this case because drama and similar works have performance as their purpose, and because the erotic sentiment (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) pertaining to such performance is indecorous, we say: no.

If indecorousness belongs to the performance itself when it concerns such a subject matter, by what means can that same indecorousness be prevented from belonging to the poetry itself when it concerns such a subject matter?

Therefore, whether in a poem intended for performance or one not intended for performance, the description of vulgar sexual union between characters of high status, such as kings, and heroines of high status, is like a description of the sexual union of one's own parents.
It is even more improper [to do so] regarding such objects as supreme deities;
the intended meaning is that one should not act [in this way], since the Sage has already defined the "eye" [of perception].
The word "ādi" (etcetera) denotes a class; its purpose is to include well-known divine narratives such as that of Himavat and others.
The connection [of the commentary] is: "the invented subject matter, being existent, has not been defined."
The word "iti" indicates the reason. "It should not be done" means that a poet should not compose a drama or similar work where the plot consists of invented (utpādya) events.
He explains the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "dramas, etc. (*nāṭakādi*) with the words "in the sense of a type," and so forth.
Here, "type" (*prakāra*) means similarity; and that [similarity] is to be understood as consisting in having a well-known subject matter.
By the phrase "in the *ḍima* and so forth," the *vyāyoga* is to be understood.
The definition of the *ḍima* is: "Its subject matter is a well-known event, and its hero is a well-known and noble person," and so on.

Furthermore, the definition of the *vyāyoga*—namely, "it should be composed by those who know the rules, having a well-known hero as its body," and so forth—is stated in the *Nāṭyaśāstra* and other such works.

Regarding the phrase "nāṭakādī" (drama and so forth), according to the etymology "that of which drama is the first," the term "nāṭakādi" refers to the *prakaraṇa* by means of an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound; therefore, there is no inconsistency with the literal meaning of the word.
He states that view as follows: "But another [says]... and so on.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the erotic sentiment (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) has only one variety, namely that characterized by sexual union (*surata*).
Since other varieties, such as mutual displays of affection and so forth, are also possible, why are they not described in relation to the highest character type?
Therefore, even in the case of the sentiment of energy (*utsāha-vṛtti*), one must follow the propriety of the character type.
The same applies to cases of wonder and so forth.
As for the fact that even great poets are seen in their actual works to act without due deliberation regarding such matters, that is indeed a fault;
however, it has already been stated that because they are overwhelmed by their creative power (*śakti*), it does not appear as such to them.
The propriety of the *anubhāvas* (consequent actions), however, is well known from Bharata and others.
Locana says: "Another [scholar] states that the section on the Bahuvrīhi compound as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) is what is discussed here.
Or, there is the reading "nāṭikādi" (the nāṭikā and so forth).
In this context, the mention of "direction" (dig) indicates a general manner;

therefore, the meaning is that within the definition of the *nāṭikā* as formulated by the Sage, in the rule "the plot is invented and the hero is a king due to its connection with the *prakaraṇa* and *nāṭaka*," one should understand— by way of corresponding order— that the hero is a well-known and noble king.
Anticipating the question, "How then should the poet compose the erotic sentiment of enjoyment (sambhoga-śṛṅgāra)? he says: "Not [otherwise]," and "In that very way.

That is to say, the Sage [Bharata] has, in various places, made the propriety of character (prakṛtyaucitya) itself the primary authority regarding the excitants (vibhāvas), ensuants (anubhāvas), and so forth, as in the passage beginning: "By steadfastness for the high, middle, and low [characters], and by agitation for the base," and so on.
By saying this, [the author] has stated that the *bahuvrīhi* compound mentioned in the *Bālapriyā* is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The meaning is that the *bahuvrīhi* compound in the phrase "nāṭakādī" (drama, etc. indicates other [works] as well.
The word *iti* indicates the reason (*hetau*).
He states it by way of another formulation: "the *nāṭikā* and so forth.
This indicates the category and conveys similarity.

The meaning is that similarity is to be understood as consisting in the nature of a produced subject matter (*utpādyavastutva*), and the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is intended to include context and so forth.
By the phrase "by that," it is meant: by the statement that the *nāṭikā* and other such works possess the nature of a produced subject matter.
The meaning is that it refers to the fact that the object itself is what is to be produced (*utpādya*).
"To be understood" (*boddhavya*) implies that there is no logical concomitance (*anvaya*) of the state of being produced with respect to the hero (*nāyaka*).
In the commentary, [it says] "Now then" (*nanu*) and so forth.
Regarding "divine" (*divya*):
it refers to the examination of that which is appropriate, such as divine or human means of knowledge (*mānasa*) and so on.
If it is to be performed— this is the connection— then "that" [should be done] by means of "that," namely,
the examination of what is appropriate for gods, humans, and so forth.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
it means "in [the context of] passion and so forth.
He raises a further objection with the words "as for that which... (*yattu*), etc.
He refutes this with the words "No," and so forth.
The phrase "even though it has a divine basis" is to be construed with the preceding "the composition of the erotic sentiment."
The syntactical connection is as follows: "And not" means that [the king and so forth] are not well-known in dramas and the like.
Regarding the word "well-known":
The meaning is that it is well known for having entered into an inferior vessel; "that" refers to the composition of vulgar erotic sentiment (*grāmya-śṛṅgāra*).
He raises an objection with the words "of drama and so forth" (*nāṭakādeḥ*).
The word "therein" (*tatra*) means "in drama and so forth."
"Thus, the object is indecorous":
this means that the object of erotic enjoyment is indecorous.
"It" refers to [the aforementioned].
The meaning is "indecorum.
And he introduces the passage beginning with "not [the case] of the erotic sentiment of enjoyment" (*na ca sambhoga-śṛṅgārasya*) in the *Locana* with the words "How then? (*kathaṃ tarhi*).
Regarding the phrase "likewise in [cases of] wonder and so forth," he states the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*) with the words "even by the Sage" (*munināpi*), and so on.
Regarding "stability" (sthairya):

this is what is being stated— a poet, having become one whose mind is focused, while conforming to the established conventions (sthiti) composed by Bharata and others, while thoroughly reflecting upon the works of great poets, and while following his own creative intuition, must avoid any lapse in the propriety of the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth.
A supreme effort must be exerted.

By stating that "the adoption of a plot-structure—whether historical or imagined—that possesses propriety (*aucitya*) is the manifestor [of rasa]," he demonstrates this: even though there exist various narratives in the *itihāsas* and other works that are rich in aesthetic flavor (*rasavat*), one should adopt only that plot-structure which possesses the propriety of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, and nothing else.
Furthermore, one must be especially diligent when conceiving a narrative body that is based on an existing plot;
for in such cases, there is a great risk of the poet’s lack of proficiency if he falters through inadvertence.
And here is a supporting verse: "The narrative body, whose subject matter is to be created, should be fashioned in such and such a manner."
Just as everything appears as consisting of flavor, so it is with that.
Regarding the phrase "locanam ity āttvā":

the summary is that one should follow [the path of] expertise in defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇajñatva*), the thorough study of the objects to be defined (*lakṣya*), and being endowed with one's own creative intuition (*svapratibhā*) arising from the grace of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
In the expression "in the flavorful works" (*rasavatīṣu*), the locative case is used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*).

And the state of being "possessed of rasa" (rasavattva) should be understood as intended by way of the conceit of people who lack discernment; for without the propriety of the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth, what "possession of rasa" could there be? [The word] "of the poet" [is used].
Bālapriyā: "In women and those of base nature, grief arising from calamity is thus;
for the high-minded and the middling, it is countered by fortitude, while for the base, it is expressed through weeping."
Thus is the reading in the *Bhāvādhyāya*.
Here, the word "to be enacted" (*abhineya*) is to be supplied.

He states the meaning obtained from the three instrumental-case words beginning with "by one who follows the established practice composed by Bharata and others"—namely, "knowledge of the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇajñatva*), and so forth.
Regarding "adṛṣṭa":

*adṛṣṭa* means merit (*sukṛta`); *prasāda* means the grace of deities and so forth. The meaning is that it is the state of being endowed with one's own creative intuition (*svapratibhā*) arising from those two.
The locative case here is used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*).

The meaning of the commentary (*vṛtti*) is as follows: even though there exist various flavorful narratives such as those found in the *Itihāsas* and other works, the poet should disregard those narratives and adopt from among them only that body of the story (*kathāśarīra*) which possesses propriety (*aucitya*); he should not adopt any other body of the story that is devoid of the propriety of the *vibhāvas* and so forth, even if it is flavorful.
To the objection, "But how can there be flavor (*rasavatva*) in the absence of the propriety of the *vibhāvas* and so forth?", he replies: "And [regarding] flavor-ness... (*rasavatvañca*).

"Avivecaka" and so forth: the meaning is that this should be understood with reference to the conceit of those people who lack discernment—the conceit that [the work] possesses aesthetic flavor (rasa).
He states the reason for this: "By means of the propriety of the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth," and so on.
He explains what was stated—that there arises a great possibility of misunderstanding—with the words "for not," and so forth.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
it means in a narrative framework conceived by oneself.
"Jātyuttara" means an improper rejoinder; the connection [of the phrase] "therein" is that even a futile rejoinder (jātyuttara) is not possible.
He explains the passage beginning with "they exist" and so forth: "accomplished," etc.
"Tasting":
mere tasting is the means therein, which consists in following the propriety of the correct aesthetic realization (*vibhāva*) and so on.
And that has already been shown.
Furthermore: There exist works such as the *Rāmāyaṇa* and others which are like perfected elixirs;
one should not impose upon them, by way of their narrative content, a personal whim that contradicts the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
For regarding those very foundations of narrative, one's own whim alone should not be employed;

as it has been said: "In the path of narrative, even the slightest transgression [of convention] is not permitted. Even if one’s own whim were to be employed, it should not be employed if it is contrary to the aesthetic flavor (rasa).

This is another basis for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in a literary composition: having abandoned a situation that, though arrived at by the force of the plot (*itivṛtta*), is somehow incompatible with the *rasa*, one should—by means of creative imagination (*utprekṣā*)—construct an intermediate narrative suited to the intended *rasa*. This is seen in the compositions of Kālidāsa, and as in the *Locana* on the work composed by Sarvasena. For there, it cannot even be argued as a sophistical rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) that "I have composed this merely by the force of historical fact."
In that context, "and so forth" refers to the accomplishment of being composed of rasa; "established" means proven.
In those [works] where the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) has been perfected and remains only as a relish— not something yet to be cultivated—
the historical narratives serve as the basis for the stories; one should not, by means of those historical themes, indulge in arbitrary personal whims.
He explains that here the relationship between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) is inherent by means of the locative case in the word "teṣu" (in them).
One's own whim should not be applied to them;
or, if it is applied in some way, it must not be applied in a manner that contradicts the well-known [conventions of] aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

For instance, it would be utterly improper for someone to treat Rāma as the hero of a *nāṭikā* by attributing to him the quality of *dhīralalita* (the "calm and playful" hero), as stated by Yaśovarman in the *Rāmābhyudaya*: "He remained upon his bed... and so forth.
Regarding the name "Kālidāsa":
in the *Raghuvamśa*, the description of the marriages of kings such as Aja and others is not found in the [earlier] Itihāsas;
likewise, in the *Harivijaya*, the abduction of the Pārijāta tree and so forth, described as part of the wooing of the beloved, is something never seen in the Itihāsas.

Similarly, in the *Arjunacarita*, [the phrase] "of which Arjuna’s conquest of Pātāla and so forth are the only remainder" means that those are the only portion left for the aesthetic relish (*sahṛdayāsvāda*) of the simple-minded (*bālapriyā*).
He states what is excluded by the word "only" with the words "but not," and so on. "To be cultivated" (*bhāvanīya*) means to be accomplished through description.
The connection is as follows: those works such as the *Rāmāyaṇa* and others, which are based on narratives (*kathāśraya*), are renowned as "famous perfected elixirs" (*siddharasaprakhyā*).
Regarding that, he explains the term "based on narratives" with the words "of narratives" and so forth;
and he explains the word "by them" with the phrase "by means of these [works] containing laughter and wealth."
With the intention that the passage beginning with "not by them" concludes in two sentences, the commentary explains it as "in those," and so forth;
therein, the meaning of "by them" is "in those.
To show how this is obtained, he introduces the text beginning with "by them," etc.
"In them" (*teṣu*) indicates the locative case. The intention is that this locative denotes a locus in the sense of an object-domain (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*).
"By one's own will" (*svecchayā*).
The meaning is that objects are created according to one's own will. "In them" means in those things which serve as the basis for narratives, resembling the elixir of immortality (siddharasa).
Regarding the phrase "as in the case of Rāma":
the meaning is that his rasa, as well-known from the *Rāmāyaṇa*, is indeed the heroic (*vīra*).
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says: "nor even the slightest transgression."
The meaning is that even a slight transgression should not be committed.
Regarding the passage beginning with "iti vṛtte" and so forth:
in some manner, by whatever means, [he acted] in the *Harivijaya* in a way that was not consistent with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
And as it is stated in my own epic poem, the *Arjunacarita*:
"When a poet composes a work, he must be devoted to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) with his whole being.

If, within that narrative, he should perceive a situation inconsistent with the flavor, then even by breaking that [narrative], he may independently create another story that is consistent with the flavor."
For there is no purpose for a poet in merely concluding a historical narrative, since that is already established through history itself; rather,
this is another primary basis for the composition of a literary work when its aim is the manifestation of rasa and the like.

The "joining" (*ghaṭana*) of the junctures (*sandhi*)—known as the introduction (*mukha*), the complication (*pratimukha*), the development (*garbha*), the pause (*avamarśa*), and the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*)—as well as their constituent parts (*aṅga*) such as the "introduction of a matter" (*upakṣepa*) and so forth, is described as the "eye" (*locana*). This [joining] is what is celebrated as the "plot" (*itivṛtta*).
He states that this alone is appropriate with the words "by the poet" (*kavinā*).
Regarding the phrase "of the junctures" (*sandhīnām*):

In this world, for those who have not been trained in the treatises— such as the Śruti and Smṛti— which are equal to the commands of a sovereign and whose ultimate purpose consists solely of injunctions such as "this must be done," and yet who have acquired proficiency in the Itihāsa-Śāstras— which are equal to the counsel of friends and which reveal the connection between actions and their fruits through logical reasoning, such as "this conduct of his arose from that deed"— and who are, moreover, necessarily to be instructed, being of the nature of princes and endowed with the capacity to accomplish the welfare of the subjects; for them, proficiency in the means to attain the four aims of life (caturvarga) must be instilled by way of entering their hearts.
And the entry into the heart consists precisely of the relishing of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

That flavor, moreover, is brought about by the grace of the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors, which are inseparable from the cultivation of the means for attaining the four aims of human life.

Thus, when the determinants and other factors appropriate to a particular flavor are properly composed, the very state of being overwhelmed by the relishing of that flavor is what serves as the catalyst for a spontaneous cultivation [of the mind].
"Delight alone is the motivator for aesthetic proficiency;
and since rasa is of the nature of delight, our teacher [holds that] that itself is drama, and drama alone is the Veda. Moreover, these two—delight and proficiency—are not distinct in form."
Because both have the same object.
"Vibhāvādyaucityam" means propriety regarding the excitants and so forth; "bālapriyā" means devoid of conformity with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); "utprekṣya" means having reflected upon.
‘Antarā’ means in the middle. ‘Abhīṣṭa’ refers to the unfolding or the joining together of the desired rasa and its appropriate narrative.
He clarifies the very meaning already stated in the verse beginning with "By the poet" (*kavinā*). The readings are "the composition" (*prabandham*) and "the poem" (*kāvyam*).

In the *Locana*, he explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "of the joints" (*sandhīnām*) by means of the passage beginning with "here, from those [works] comparable to a master" (*iha prabhusammitebhyaḥ*).
"This must be done" is an illustration [of the rule]; by implication, this includes "this must not be done.
In the phrase "from the treatises," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
And as for the words "nor even":
The phrase "those who have attained proficiency" is connected with this [term].
The word "of this" (*asya*) is a reference to a particular hero (*nāyaka*).
The phrase "this conduct" (*idaṃ vṛttam*) refers to the following.
The meaning is that this fruit has arisen.
Regarding the term *śāstrī*: *śāstra* refers to the treatises consisting of historical narratives (*itihāsa*); [the suffix -ī] is derived from those historical treatises.
Furthermore, he states the reason why they must necessarily be explained: "for the sake of the subjects" (*prajārtha*).

This means they are "assailed" (*ākāntā*), that is, occupied by, that fitness (*yogyatā*)—consisting in such qualities as being born into a royal lineage—which is required for the accomplishment and protection of the welfare of the subjects.
"Fourfold" (*catur*): [refers to the four aims of human life].

The meaning is: "produced by that conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, which is of such a nature that its incidental and secondary fruit is the proficiency in the means for attaining the four aims of life (*caturvarga*)," and this fruit is obtained through the grace of that [conjunction].
"In this manner" means: in the way already described.
"Only joy" means the bliss of tasting the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). "In distinct forms" means:
The meaning is that they have distinct objects.
We have stated more than once that [this] is the true cause of delight.

The thorough knowledge (*yathāsvarūpavedana*) of the *vibhāvas* and so forth, which are elevated to the state of that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), is called "cultivation" (*vyutpatti*) because it culminates in its fruit.
Furthermore, that which is called a "fruit" arises by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), through the grace of a deity, or from some other cause;
and it cannot be taught, because it is impossible to produce a conceptual cognition (vyutpatti) regarding it through a means (upāya).

Success belongs to one who proceeds by means of the proper method (*upāya*), while ruin belongs to one who proceeds by way of what is not a method; thus, one should understand the attainment of purpose and its opposite through the roles of the protagonist and the antagonist. Furthermore, the method, when employed by the agent, undergoes five stages, namely:
its own essential nature (*svarūpa*),...
A slight swelling from its own nature, the capacity for the accomplishment of an effect, and the state of being apprehended as subject to the onset of obstacles.
When the counter-agent has ceased, [the practice] reaches its culmination in a very firm fruit by means of the sublation of the sublater.
Thus, for those who are capable of enduring hardship, who fear deception, and who act with circumspection, the undertaking of the cause proceeds in this manner.
These are the five stages.

The Sage has stated regarding the nature of the cause: "In the connection with the fruit that is to be accomplished, whatever is the operation of the cause [is what constitutes its causal status]. This is connected with the phrase "the cognition of its own nature" by way of its culminating in the fruit.
The word "that" (tad) means the fruit produced by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth;
"therefore" (*tataḥ*) means by the instruction regarding such a fruit.
"Because of the impossibility of proficiency regarding the means" means because proficiency concerning the objects that are the means to those respective fruits does not arise.
"By that" [refers to this].
The meaning is "by the reason already stated. "Establishment" means "establishment of the result."
Regarding the term "anupāya": by the word *anupāya*, both that which is not a cause and that which is an undesirable cause are intended.
Regarding the term "destruction" (*nāśa*): [it refers to the cessation of the continuum].

The meaning is that there is the non-attainment of the desired result and the attainment of the undesired result. The phrase "by way of being located in the protagonist and the antagonist" is to be connected with the preceding term "benefit and harm."
The meaning is that it is the proficiency regarding the means for achieving those ends and misfortunes pertaining respectively to the protagonist and the antagonist.
"To be accomplished" (kāryā) means that it is to be brought about by the poet.
"By the agent" means by the leader (nāyaka) and so forth.

The connection of the words ending in the accusative case, such as "essential nature" (svarūpa), with the preceding term "five states" (pañcāvasthā) is as follows: [the essential nature and the others constitute the five states].
"Own-nature" (svarūpa) means the nature of the means being put into practice.
"Some slight swelling" (kiñcid-ucchūnatām) means...
The meaning is "some nourishment.
This refers to the second stage: that state [of the seed] which possesses the capacity to accomplish its effect.
Regarding the phrase "obstructing," and so forth:

The meaning is: the state of having the accomplishment of the effect doubted due to the occurrence of an obstacle. Regarding the phrase "when the counter-agent has ceased," the meaning is: when the obstacle has been removed.
This means that its nature as an effect is determined through the removal of obstacles.

In the *Pratāparudrīyavyākhyā*, however, it is stated: "The first stage consists of a slight swelling [of the seed] from its original state, while the second is the capacity for the accomplishment of the effect."
The third [stage], however, is the state in which the effect is suspected due to the occurrence of an obstacle;
the fourth is the certainty of the effect through the removal of the obstacle; and the fifth is the firmness of reaching the final result through the sublation of sublation—so it has been said.
In accordance with that, however, it should be understood that "a slight swelling from its own nature" (svarūpāt kiñciducchūnatām) is to be construed with the word "its own nature" (svarūpam).
Regarding the phrase "of those capable of enduring distress" (ārtisahiṣṇūnām),
the meaning is "of those capable of enduring fatigue" (śramasahiṣṇūnām).
As it has been said: “Even though repeatedly thwarted by obstacles,” and so forth.
“Vipralambha” means the non-attainment of the intended effect.
"Having accomplished" means "of the cause," which signifies the hero and so forth.
The eye of the junctures (saṃdhis), such as the beginning and the opening, should be understood by performers as consisting of five stages in their proper sequence.
The undertaking, the effort, the possibility of attainment,
the certainty of obtaining the fruit, and fifthly, the union with the fruit.

Thus, those stages of the causal action (kāraṇa), and that fivefold division of the plot (itivṛtta) belonging to the author which brings them about— these are the five junctures (saṃdhi), known as the Opening (mukha), the Counter-opening (pratimukha), the Development (garbha), the Pause (avamarśa), and the Conclusion (nirvahaṇa); they are segments of the plot whose names correspond to their actual meaning.
They are called *sandhi*s because they are joined together;
and since those *sandhi*s are likewise seen to follow a sequence toward their own respective conclusions, these constituent parts (*vṛttabhāga*) are further subdivided.
The *sandhyaṅgas* (subdivisions of the junctures) are "the introduction (*upakṣepa*), the preparation (*parikara*), the conclusion (*parinyāsa*), the seduction (*vilobhana*)," and so forth.
The *arthaprakṛtis* (the fundamental factors for accomplishing an objective) are included within these very [categories].
For instance, there are three: the seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), and the effect (*kārya*), which constitute the means for achieving what depends on oneself.

Through the seed, all activities are initiated; through the drop, there is connection; and through the effect, there is completion. Indeed, these three—manifestation, aspiration, and exertion—are the *prakṛtis* (inherent dispositions) of the agent, which are specific modes of nature to be accomplished through the objective.

However, when success depends upon a minister, [the action] is undertaken either for the sake of that [minister], or for his own sake, or even for both; this is expressed by the two terms *prakīrṇa* (scattered) and *patākā* (banner). Thus, the five junctures (*sandhi*) and the presence of all the constituent parts of the junctures (*sandhyaṅga*) must be composed within the primary narrative (*adhikārika-vṛtta*)—extending up to the fulfillment of the intended result—in order to provide instruction to all people.

But regarding the incidental narrative (*prāsaṅgika-itivṛtta*), this rule does not apply, as the Sage [Bharata] stated: "In the incidental [narrative], because it is for the sake of another, this rule need not hold."

This being the case, in the *Ratnāvalī*, since there is no impropriety in the hero’s enjoyment of pleasures that are not contrary to the Dharma— and on the contrary, because it is praiseworthy as it ensures he does not become devoid of happiness— the heroine is sought for the sake of the fruit of obtaining a maiden, which is linked to the great fruit of sovereign rule over the earth;
furthermore, the definitions of the "introductory scenes" (*upakṣepa*) and other elements of the plot should be consulted in works such as the *Daśarūpaka*.
"Self-accomplished" means that the fruit is self-accomplished.
"The essential natures of objects are right here" means:
These are to be understood as having been described as "characterized by the seed (bīja), the drop (bindu), the banner (patākā), the episode (prakarī), and the purpose (kārya).
Regarding the phrase "because of success dependent upon oneself" (svāyattasiddheḥ):
the hero (nāyaka) is of three kinds—success dependent upon oneself, success dependent upon a minister (saciva), and success dependent upon both.
"All activities by means of the seed"—
the word "intended" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The same should be understood for the two subsequent sentences as well.
"Anusandhāna" (reconnection) means the act of reconnecting the primary purpose when it has been interrupted by intermediate matters.
"Sandarśana" (demonstration), and so forth.

Having kept that specific purpose in mind and having prayed for its accomplishment, an effort directed toward that end arises; thus, because they are produced by [the stages of] vision and so forth, seeds and the like are of that same nature—this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "in the object" (arthe) and so on: by this, the etymological analysis of the term *arthaprakṛti* (the source of objects) is demonstrated.
Now, intending to demonstrate the meanings of the terms *prakārī* and *patākā*, he says "the minister," and so forth.
"For that purpose" means for the sake of the hero (*nāyaka*).
The reason for designating them by the terms *prakārī* and *patākā* respectively is their being "scattered" (*prakīrṇatva*) and "well-known" (*prasiddhatva*).
The connection is that "it was thus said by the Sage.
The meaning of the word "iti" is "by him who says thus.
He shows the object of indication with the words beginning with "evam" (thus).
This being the case, the logical connection is that [these matters] are indeed shown in the *Ratnāvalī*.
Regarding the phrase "because of its praiseworthiness":
by this statement, it is meant that the enjoyment of things not contrary to the Dharma is intended with a view toward the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
As in the *Ratnāvalī*;
it is not merely out of a desire to maintain the established conventions of the treatises.

For instance, in the second act of the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, the inclusion of the *vilāsa*—an element of the *pratimukhasandhi* (the secondary juncture)—is arranged solely with the intent of following the doctrine of Bharata, even though it is inconsistent with the prevailing aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the composition.

In the introduction to the *Locana*, all five junctures (*sandhi*), together with the five stages (*avasthā*) and complete with their appropriate constituent parts (*sandhyaṅga*), as well as the dramatic sources (*arthaprakṛti*), have indeed been demonstrated.

Starting from the very seed (*bīja*) in the words, "In this undertaking for the increase of my master," and continuing through such expressions as "whose talk of war has ceased" and "the kingdom with its enemies conquered," [the plot] has been delineated beginning from the "introduction" (*upakṣepa*) in the words, "this is the occasion for enjoyment and service."
However, demonstrating the nature of all the constituent parts of the *sandhyā* together on the back of this text would result in excessive bulk;
yet, if demonstrated individually, it would lead only to confusion due to a lack of connection between what precedes and what follows, and thus it has not been expanded upon.

Since this matter is intended to be grasped with diligent effort, he provides an example of the distinction stated in his own words as "but not by [the mantra] alone," beginning with "na tu" (but not).

The intention of one who employs the terms *kevala* and *icchāśabda* is as follows: the Sage Bharata has stated that the sole purpose of the *sandhy-aṅgas* is the production of excellence in the plot (*itivṛtta*), which serves as a constituent of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
It is not, however, for the accomplishment of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) or the warding off of obstacles (*vighna*), as is the case with the *pūrvaraṅga-aṅgas*.
As it has been said: "The composition of the desired subject matter and the non-diminution of the narrative..."
The attainment of passion and the concealment of secrets through application.
The sixfold purpose of the constituent parts (aṅgas) of the scriptures has been observed as follows: the manifestation of things to be manifested, and their exposition in a manner that is marvelous.
Thus, and therefore: "Effort for the sake of enjoyment and pleasure is proclaimed as *vilāsa* (graceful dalliance)," because it is worthy of praise—this is the meaning. *Bālapriyā*.
"Being shown on the back of that reading" means being shown by citing all the respective sentences located within the string of jewels (*ratnālī*).
"By each one" [means...].
The meaning is that it is merely an illustration, lacking the preceding and following sentences. "Not expanded" means it was not stated in detail, along with examples, in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
"Of this meaning" (asyārthasya) means: of the meaning already stated, namely that "the composition of the joints and their members [of a sentence] depends upon the manifestation of rasa and so forth.
The connection is with the phrase "this which is the distinction" (iti yo vyatirekaḥ).
"But not thus" means by means of the passage beginning with "but not," and so forth.
"Of one who employs [it]" means...
The word "of the author of the *kārikās*" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "This" means that which will be stated by the passage ending with the words "not having understood the meaning."

The phrase "of the sandhyaṅgas" is connected with the word "purpose. "Of the desired" refers to the demonstration of the composition. "Attainment of passion in performance" is the perfection of the passion for dramatic representation (*abhinaya*).
"By the observation of the performance" means the abundance of delight for the audience.
"As if it were a marvel" means that which produces wonder.
"Then" (tataḥ) means "by the reason already stated. This connects with the word "employed" (prayukta).
It brings together.

Furthermore, this is another cause for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in the composition: that there should be an "intermediate glance" (*locana*) at the appropriate moments during the intensification (*uddīpana*) and pacification (*praśamana*). This is stated in the definition of *vilāsa*, a limb of the *pratimukha-sandhi*. The term *ratibhoga* (enjoyment of pleasure) is employed as an indicator for the *vibhāva*s and other factors that manifest the dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), which constitutes the primary aesthetic flavor (*ādhikārikarasa*).
As for the statement "the meaning has not been understood according to reality," it is because the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is the subject under discussion here; thus,
[the verse] serves as an excitant (*uddīpana*).
Excitement (*uddīpana*) occurs through the fulfillment of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth;
for example, Sāgarikā’s [utterance], "This is that King Udayana," and so on.
Allayment (*praśamana*) occurs during the escape from Vāsavadattā.
Furthermore, there is the rekindling [of the aesthetic flavor] through the depiction on a picture-board,
and its pacification upon entering into a harmonious union, and so forth.
For a flavor that has been intensely and incessantly rubbed loses its luster all at once, like a delicate jasmine blossom.

In particular, however, it is the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). As the Sage said: "That state of being intent upon a woman who is difficult to obtain, and from which one is warded off—that is the supreme delight for the lover."
Thus,

even in the case of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) and others, when the desired goal— which is like a sudden, marvelous result— is attained without the need for intensification (*uddīpana*) or pacification (*praśamana*) as the occasion demands, the intended relationship between the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*) would simply not be manifested.
"Punar" (again) [is used here].
"Bālapriyā" refers to the desire or longing that is undertaken on account of past events and which consists mostly of what is being suspected.
"For the sake of the enjoyment of pleasure" means for the purpose of experiencing delight.
The meaning is that it has as its object the experience of sexual union (*surata*).

Alternatively, "for the sake of enjoyment" (*bhogārthā*) means for the sake of the object of enjoyment—such as a young woman—which is experienced by *rati*, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) known as love; thus, it means "for the sake of its [rati's] enjoyment.
It is called "authoritative" (*ādhikārikā*).

The meaning is as follows: regarding the rasa under discussion, which is the subject of authority (*adhikārika*), that which manifests it is the excitant (*vibhāva*) and so forth; this is for the purpose of indicating—that is, for the sake of characterizing—that *sthāyibhāva*.
The sense is that it is not intended merely to convey the previously mentioned literal meaning (*vācyārtha*).
Thus it is "employed" (*prayukta*).
The word "muni" (sage) is to be supplied as the subject.
Regarding the word "yathā" (as): it refers to one for whom the object (*artha*) understood or known according to reality is not [the same] as the object intended by the sage. Thus it is.
However, the sense is that only the literal meaning of that [statement] has been understood;
"by the author of the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*" is the ellipsis to be supplied;
and the word "iti" (thus) is to be construed with the word "āśaya" (intention).
Now, regarding the question of what the dominant sentiment (*rasa*) is in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, he says: "the subject matter at hand" (*prakṛta*).
The implication is that it is not the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). Otherwise, he points out the fault with the words beginning with "gāḍham."
"Constantly crushed" means tasted without interruption;
"mālatī" [in the compound] means "the mālatī flower that has been constantly crushed."
Regarding the word "yat":

it refers to the state of being intent upon what is undesirable, namely, the noble lady's longing for contrary conduct. And from which [cause] and that which is warded off—namely, sexual enjoyment with the noble lady—is the remainder of the sense.

For this reason: that which consists of these three is "supreme delight" (*parā ratiḥ*); the meaning is that for a woman whose sexual enjoyment has been obstructed, sexual union is the cause of supreme joy.
He states "in the heroic [sentiment]" and so forth to show that what has been said regarding the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) should also be understood to apply to other sentiments (*rasa*).
"Having marvelous results" means having results demonstrated by means of magic illusions (*indrajāla*) and the like. "Desired to be made manifest" means desired by the poet to be revealed.
Regarding the word *upāya*:

the meaning is that there is a relationship of cause and effect between the various activities of the leaders and so forth and the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*); the construction [of the sentence] is "it is not at all" (*naiva*).
By the word *ārabdha* (commenced), he states what is intended in the present context: "that which is about to be reached as suspected."
[The state of] being brought near has arisen.
He states the meaning of the term "resting place" (viśrānti-pada) as "interruption" (viccheda).
Thus, wherever an interruption of the dominant aesthetic flavor (rasa) might occur, there [is the need for] the [resting place] of that rasa.
As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*:
"Furthermore, there is no juncture (*sandhi*) for the rasa, which is the primary element, when it rests upon the word.
As, for example, in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*.

Furthermore, this other point must be understood as the cause for the manifestation of rasa in specific compositions such as dramas: that even when figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) possess the capacity [to convey rasa], they should be employed in a manner appropriate [to the sentiment].

For a poet who is capable might sometimes begin a composition focused solely on the construction of figures of speech, neglecting the connection with rasa because he is occupied by them; it is for the purpose of instructing him [on the proper method] that this has been stated.
Indeed, poets are seen to be single-mindedly devoted to the construction of figures of speech in their works, disregarding rasa.
"Locana" [means]: that whose rest (viśrānti) is not interrupted by the arrival of all objects; such is its nature.
"Of rasa" means:
of something that has become a constituent part (aṅga) of rasa. Thus it is said.

In the *Tāpasavatsarāja*, the bond of love directed toward Vāsavadattā—which consists of the pride that regards her as the entirety of one’s life while she is alive—assumes the roles of the *karuṇa* (pathetic) and *vipralambha* (erotic separation) sentiments due to its specific determinants (*vibhāva*) and propriety; pervading the entire plot, it is vitalized by the restoration of the kingdom, which is brought about through the power of the minister’s policy and followed by the recovery of Padmāvatī as its constituent part. Thus, the attainment of Vāsavadattā herself, reaching the state of being the most desirable object, constitutes the fruit therein.

For in the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*), the primary importance of the recovery of the Queen is established by the statement: "The Queen and Bhūtadhātrī have been recovered, and there has once again been a reunion with the spectator.

Within this vast canvas painted with the variety of the plot, the bond of affection for Vāsavadattā serves as the foundational wall; from the commencement of the first counsel until the marriage to Padmāvatī and other events, it is through the operation of that very bond alone [that the drama proceeds].

Therefore, that very bond of love directed toward Vāsavadattā, although its interruption was being feared due to the course of the narrative, was maintained. To explain: in the first [act], the meaning is that such a maintenance must be accomplished there.
Regarding the phrase "of the principal rasa," he states what is intended by the word *rasa*: "of that which has become a constituent (*aṅga*) of the rasa."
"Of someone" means "of [the character] Vibhava and so forth. He explains what was stated as "in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*" with the words beginning "for in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "the bond of love":
the word "directed toward the King of Vatsa" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Regarding the word "entire": [it refers to the totality of his qualities].
The word "pervading conduct" (*vṛttavyāpin*) is connected with this [term].
Regarding "compassion" (*karuṇā*),
the sequence here is to be understood.
He strengthens what was stated with the words beginning "by night" (*rātryā*);
the reason for the word "attained" (*prāpta*) is given as "having the nature of being pursued through the restoration of the kingdom.
There are two qualifiers for the restoration of the kingdom: "by night," and so forth.
He provides the proof for what was stated, beginning with "In the conclusion" (*nirvahaṇe*), etc., and "Attained" (*prāptā*), etc.:
"You have seen [the end]; the enemies have been conquered, and the Goddess and the Earth, the sustainer of beings, have been attained once again."
You even had a connection with the Seer; why then is your suffering now stilled because of him?
This is the complete verse.
He connects what was stated in the passage beginning with "of rasa whose repose has been initiated" by means of the words "to this extent," and so forth.
[He explains] the phrase "variegated by the diversity of the plot."
"On the surface of a painting" means on one where various events are depicted; the syntactical connection is that [the painting] stands in the place of a wall or similar surface.
"From the activity... [is the meaning].
The meaning is "due to activity," that is to say, "because of pervasion," and so forth. [The verse continues:

"Even the night was spent by those who were inspired by the god of love with the offering of their limbs; even now, she casts her eyes upon that path. For that very [lover] was clearly placed in her lap; the day was passed by gazing at the moon of her face, and likewise the evening."

By the passage beginning with "tadgoṣṭhyeva" and ending with "baddhotkaṇṭhamidaṃ manaḥ kimathavā premāsamāptotsavam," and in the second [stanza] as well, by the passage beginning with "dṛṣṭirnāmṛtavarṣiṇī smitamadhuprasyandi vaktraṃ na kim," that very same [mental state], though interrupted, is reconnected.

Even in the third [fire], while all the houses were ablaze and the circle of female attendants was struck with terror, as the Queen fell at every step— her hands flailing and trembling from the gasps of breath— and as that wretched woman was intent on repeatedly crying out "O Lord!", we are still being burned by that fire even today, though it has long since been extinguished.
And so forth.

Even in the fourth [watch], for one whose mind is possessed by the Goddess and who is thus inevitably dreaming, how could this fair-faced woman not cause distress upon my grasping her lineage? Thus, through such constraint, the night has somehow or other been exhausted for me as I remain awake.

This is to be understood from the phrase beginning with "of me who has set out to question Bālapriyā. Regarding the expression "tadvaktrā" (by her mouth): here, the word "tat" (that) refers everywhere to Vāsavadattā; "divasaḥ" means consisting of days.
"Conversation with her" refers to discourse and so forth; "with that conversation.
In the phrase "the night also," the word "passed" (*nītā*) is to be supplied by grammatical modification (*vipariṇāmena*).
[The term] "Manmatha... [is explained as follows].
"By whom? means by those in whom enthusiasm has been created or produced by Manmatha (the God of Love). "Why does it become filled with longing?"—having reflected, he says: "Or rather," and so forth.
"Wherein the festival"—consisting of gazing upon her moon-like face and other such acts—"is not yet concluded."

Alternatively, "that by which the festival is uncompleted" means that by which the celebration has not been brought to a conclusion; this is to be connected with the word "anusaṃhita" (connected) ending with the word "bhavati" (it becomes).
Thus [the term] "dṛṣṭi" (vision).
And there is also the reading *nāmṛtadharmiṇī*.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the following verse is included]: “Your heart is not hot with fever, nor are your limbs moist with sandalwood paste; upon what path have you found yourself that this cruel submarine fire has been wrought upon you?
Surely it is some other fire, made of adamant, whose deed this is.”
This is its summary:
"Is that view not a shower of nectar? means "Is it indeed a shower of nectar?
In the same way, the word *kiṃ* (is it not? should be joined with the negative particles (*nañ*) in the subsequent lines as well.
"Moist above" means characterized by moisture in its upper portion; alternatively, "not moist" (*no vārdram*) is another reading.
By the first half [of the verse], it is shown that because of the presence of obstacles in the limbs such as vision, the fire does not obtain a foothold.

Thus he says: "In what," and so forth; he explains this—namely, "upon which limb was this done?"—with the words "by the cruel," and so forth, connecting it as follows: "that you were drunk [consumed] by the cruel fire, that is, burnt.
Out of the force of being overcome by grief, he says: "Surely," and so forth.
The burner is the fire that consumes you;
the thunderbolt is surely something else entirely—
I truly believe this.
"Everywhere" means:
the connection is that it was thus burnt by that wretched, ill-fated queen.
"The queen" refers to her.
"O Queen," [this is] pregnant with a reason;
"the queen" refers to Vāsavadattā;
"certainly" is used in the sense of a conjecture.
The meaning is: "from the grasping of her limbs as it was being imagined in a dream.
"This one" means:
Padminī.
Thus, by such restraint, that beloved was not attained even in a dream by him, whose heart was overcome by courtesy.

By these words and others, [it is shown that] even in the fifth stage, when my compassion had ceased through the hope of reunion and the sprout of separation had begun, my beloved fell into a state of anger— though her resentment was hidden by effort— at that very speech of the Sage which had brought such offense upon me.
"Be gracious"—thus addressed, she who was certainly not angry replied with sweet words, and with tears welling up in her eyes, she said, "She will stay."
By such passages as these;
and also in the sixth [chapter], by "My life was sustained by my ministers, who were enticed by the prospect of attaining you," and so forth.
The genitive case in *alaṅkṛtīnām* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), depending on its connection with the word *yojanā*.
And they are seen,

as for instance in the drama titled *Svapnavāsavadattā*: "Having opened the door of my eyes— the panels of which are her curved lashes— by the blow of her own beauty, that princess entered the house of my heart."
Thus [ends the section]. 14.
The connection is as follows: "For me, who am awake because of the obstacle to sleep consisting of thoughts of my beloved, the night has passed away.
The meaning is that the night has elapsed without sleep.
Therefore, he says: "O daughter of Dakṣa," and so forth.
In this context, courtesy (*dākṣiṇya*) should be understood as pertaining to the realm of Pajhāvatī;
she is Vāsavadattā.
The connection is with the phrase "sprouted" (*aṅkurita*), etc., [ending] with "followed" (*anusaṃhita*).
"In such a state" (*tathābhūta*): the locative case here denotes the occasion (*nimitta*), namely "in the words of the Sage. It is syntactically connected with the word "will abide" (*sthāsyati*).

"That most beloved one will likewise remain behind me"—this is the reading "punar-paścād api puraḥ" (or "puraḥ" as a variant). The suffix *lṛṭ* is used here in the sense of expectation (*āśaṃsā*). [The phrase] "hidden within my efforts" (*prayatnāntargūḍhām*) means:
The meaning is: "restrained within by efforts.
"In such a way that it was sweet and captivating through its expression," [and] "fully blossomed and blended."

The meaning is "fitting"; [this refers to] the reading *samudbhinnaprītiḥ* with the eyes turned inward and fixed. It means that by which the joy (*prīti*) has become most excellent (*sādhiṣṭha*), being fully manifested (*samudbhinna*, i.e., revealed).
For the flow of tears from the eyes is indeed a consequence of the joy of women who are angry.

"O you [who say] *tvat* (from you), etc."—by the word "etc.," [the verse continues]: "Thinking thus, as he was casting off this body, there was no lack of affection; the time for following you was near, and resolve had arisen, yet at that moment, O cruel one, this heart of yours did not follow you, which is a source of grief."
This is the summary of that [verse]:
"by the ministers who are the instigators, and by me who am the one being instigated";
thus [it is said]. "That" refers to this.
The meaning is "attaining you.
The word division is *atyajataḥ* (he did not abandon). It should be understood that the words ending in the third case (*ityādinā*) are to be construed with the word *anusaṃhitaḥ*.
"With regard to the *yojana*" means with regard to the word "yojana" as a form ending in a *kṛt* suffix. "Svañcitā" [is explained as follows].
This is the speech of Vatsarāja.
"Svantite" means whose two eyelashes—the very door-panels—are well joined together to prevent entry;
"nayanadvāram" means the eye itself is the door.

By "striking with one's own form" (*svarūpatāḍena*): "form" (*rūpa*) means shape; that itself is the "strike" (*tāḍa*), meaning the action of striking, that is to say, the instrument for intense impact.
In the reading *svarūpataḍitā eva*, the meaning is: by the very form acting as lightning (*taḍit*), that is, by the instrument of the flash of lightning.
She is the princess Vāsavadattā.

The point here is that the metaphorical representation as "the gateway for the eyes" alone is beautiful because it accords with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), whereas no other such representation would be so. //14//
Furthermore:
"Moreover, that variety which has been described as being like a nasalized vowel (anusvāra) also appears in certain compositions of this *dhvani*. (DhvK 3.15)
Even that variety which has been described as being like an anusvāra also appears in certain compositions of this sound (dhvani). (15)

The two-fold variety of this *dhvani*—in which the intended meaning is not the primary expressed sense (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*)—and which has been illustrated as having a suggested meaning in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇanarūpavyaṅgya*), also shines forth in certain compositions.

For example, in the *Madhumathanavijaya*, in the utterances of Pāñcajanya; or likewise, in my own work, in the *Kāmadeva-sahacarasamāgama*, in the verse beginning with "locanam. He begins [the next section] in order to show that it is not only through a composition as a whole (*prabandhena*) that the suggested meaning is direct, but also through a succession of parts (*pāramparyeṇa*): "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

The "simile of the nasalization" (anusvānopama)—that variety of *dhvani* which is rooted in both the power of word (*śabdaśaktimūla*) and the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*), and which has been illustrated—exists as the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) when certain compositions serve as the suggestive causes (*nimitta*).
Of this—the suggested *rasa-dhvani* and so forth under discussion—it appears as the suggester (*vyañjaka*); this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The commentary (*vṛtti*) should also be construed in this very manner.

Alternatively, the variety illustrated by the simile of the *anusvāra* which shines forth in literary compositions (*prabandha*) is also connected to the subsequent verse—namely, "In some cases, the *alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya* is what is to be manifested"—through both the *kārikā* and the *vṛtti*.

What is meant is this: sometimes, through a literary composition (*prabandha*), a suggestion (*dhvani*) consisting of a resonant after-effect (*anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya*) is directly manifested, and that [suggestion] ultimately culminates in the suggestion of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-dhvani*) and so forth.

If, however, it were explained quite explicitly, then this section of the text would be inconsistent in the midst of the preceding and following portions dealing with *alakṣyakrama* (unperceived sequence), and the lack of aesthetic flavor (*nīrasatva*) in the statements regarding Pāñcajanya and so forth would have been asserted—enough said.

[The commentator] introduces the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*) with the words "Not only... (*na kevalam...*) etc., with the intention of explaining the meaning that he himself will expound.
"Even by way of succession" means even through the medium of another manifested [sound]. He explains the verse with the words beginning "anusvāna," and so forth.
He shows that the word "of *dhvani*" is connected with the phrase "a variety" by stating, "a variety of *dhvani*.
He completes the sense with the words "among the suggestors," and so forth.
The explanation of the word "of this" is "of the currently under discussion *dhvani* of rasa and the like."
Here too, he completes the sense with the words "by way of being a manifester" (*vyañjakatayā*);
this is to be connected with the word "appears" (*bhāsate*).
He explains it in another manner, beginning with "or rather" (*athavā*) and so forth.
The phrase "that which was mentioned shines forth in certain compositions" is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
The remaining portion, "of this *dhvani* also," connects with the word "suggested" (*dyotya*) found in the subsequent verse.
The intended meaning is that the phrase "of this *dhvani* also" refers to the *dhvani* that is like an echo (*anusvānopama-dhvani*).
He states the meaning obtained through this twofold explanation with the words "this" and so forth.
He states the reason for abandoning the literal meaning with the words "if" and so forth:
"this is the text."
The meaning is that the verse beginning with "anusvānopamā" (resembling an anusvāra) is intended.
He states another fault as well— beginning with "nīrasatvam" (lack of flavor)—
meaning that a lack of aesthetic flavor would be asserted.
The lack of aesthetic flavor (*nīrasatva*) is found in the *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*, as well as in the *Gṛdhragomāyusaṃvāda* and other sections of the *Mahābhārata*. [As for the example of] the eye:
"O noble one, you who possess the splendor of a circle of hair that is firm in its playful grace and pure..."
Upon her body, which is tender like a lotus stalk, [the moon] acts with boldness.
These and other utterances of Pāñcajanya reveal the intention of disclosing Vāsudeva’s inner state, which had been deceived by Rukmiṇī;
once revealed, that intention culminates in the essential nature of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) under discussion.
This occurs upon the meeting with his companions, such as Spring, Youth, and the Malaya breeze.
Though you are unrestrained, devoid of discernment, and lacking self-control,
yet even so, O passionate one, you fall again and again into my power.
These and other such descriptions of youth reveal its various inherent natures, and that nature culminates in the aesthetic flavor (rasa) intended by the context;
as for example: [the following].

In order to deceive the people who had descended upon the cremation ground and were busily engaged in burning the body of his son, the vulture, seeking to consume the corpse during the day, quickly said to them:
"Enough of staying in this cemetery, which is crowded with vultures and jackals, filled with skeletons, terrible, and a source of fear to all living beings!"
The *Bālapriyā* commentary explains it as "play" (*līlā*):

"Today, for you who have effortlessly uprooted the entire circle of the earth with the tip of your playfully curved tusk, even this body, heavy with its own weight, has become a mere slender lotus-stalk ornament."
Such is the reading:
"Why is even this lotus-fiber ornament now a burden upon your body, you who once lifted the entire circle of the earth with the tips of your playful tusks?"
"By him who,
in the form of a boar, lifted up the entire circle of the earth with the tip of his tusk as if in sport"— by this, the absence of effort in carrying an exceedingly heavy object is indicated.
The particle *eva* (only/indeed) serves to highlight the contradiction.
"Even an ornament of lotus stalks"— meaning even an ornament in the form of extremely delicate lotus stalks— "why does it become heavy?"— this is the connection [of the sentence].
By this, the intensity of the Blessed One's state of separation is illuminated.
He demonstrates this point with the words beginning "Rukmiṇī" and so forth.

"Vāsudeva," who was deceived by Rukmiṇī and separated from her—his "intention" (āśaya) is his longing for Rukmiṇī; the "unveiling" (pratibhedana) of that is its manifestation, meaning it is directed toward that purpose.
"Of the primary rasa" means "of the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation).
He explains the phrase "upon reunion with the companion" as follows, beginning with "companions," and so forth.
"Even though I am disregarded,
devoid of self-respect, and even lacking discernment,
I do not forget my longing for you, even in my dreams."
Thus is the reading:
"I may become one who has cast aside all boundaries, unrestrained, and even devoid of discernment;
yet, even in my dreams, I shall never forget my devotion to you again."
Thus ends the shadow [section]. Regarding the phrase "one who has cast aside the lines": the meaning is one who has transgressed the boundaries of propriety.
"Tattannijasvabhāva" means having the nature of following desires and so forth.
"Alam," etc., [is as follows].
These verses are also cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*:
