"By means of the relations between nominal and verbal suffixes, as well as by the powers of the grammatical cases (*kāraka*), and by primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*), that which has an imperceptible sequence [of suggestion] is sometimes manifested. (Dhvanyāloka 3.16)

In some cases, that whose sequence is imperceptible (alakṣyakrama) is to be manifested through the connection of nominal and verbal suffixes and their case-endings, as well as through the powers of the grammatical factors (kāraka), and by means of primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa). // 16 //

"The soul of *dhvani*—that which consists of rasa and so forth—is of imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama*), [manifested] through specific nouns, specific verbs, specific numbers, specific relations, the powers of the case-roles (*kāraka*), specific primary derivatives (*kṛt*), specific secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds. Thus says the *Locana*. "And it is not the case that someone who has been brought to life here has met his end;
this moment is full of obstacles, yet he might perhaps live on."
How can you, free from hesitation, abandon this child of golden hue who has not yet reached youth, merely because of the words of a vulture?
And so forth.
Furthermore, that intention, being manifest, has reached its final consummation as the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of tranquility (śānta) alone. // 15 //

Thus, although no other element remains to be defined regarding the *dhvani* of rasa and the like—wherein the suggestible is of imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama*)—once the entire range of suggestors has been examined from the phonemes (*varṇa*) up to the literary composition (*prabandha*), [the author] nevertheless states the range of suggestors once more by relying on subtle observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in order to provide delight to poets and connoisseurs, beginning with "sup tiṅ... and so forth.
We, however, understand this sentence along with its commentary as follows immediately after this point.

That which shines forth like an *anusvāra* by means of case-endings (*sup*) and so forth, being formless due to the speaker’s intention—of this too, which is manifested by case-endings and resembles an *anusvāra*, the suggested meaning is one where the sequence [of cognition] is imperceptible (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgya*).
The phrase "in some cases" connects with the preceding verse to establish the consistency [of the argument].
For in all instances, it is precisely the case-endings and so forth that manifest the particular intention [of the speaker].
In the example, that manifested intention manifests the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and so forth by means of their respective forms as the determinants (vibhāvas) and the rest;
this is what is meant by "so he says.
The meaning is: "he says with this intention."
"The law of time" means death. "He might even live" means... [the rest of the sentence].
The word "this child" is the ellipsis.
He is called "Kanakavarṇābha" because he shines like the color of gold;
or alternatively, it refers to him whose radiance is like the luster—the beauty—of Kanakavarṇa, such as a golden pitcher or similar object.
There is also the reading "tyakṣyadhvaṃ pitṛpiṇḍadam. The form "tyakṣyadhvam" is an archaic (ārṣa) usage, and it is intended [to convey] that very meaning.
The meaning is either the intention to dismiss the people, or the intention to consume [them]. // 14 //
"Thus," and so forth.
The connection is that when [each part] has been examined, nothing remains to be examined.
Just as the preceding passage beginning with "like an echo" was explained, he now begins to explain the passage beginning with "sub" (the suffix su), starting with "we," and so forth.
Immediately following this, he explains the sequence beginning with *suptiṅvacana* and so forth.

He demonstrates that the words *sub* and so on, ending in the third case, are connected respectively with *bhāsate* from the preceding verse and with *dyotyaḥ* (that which is indicated) from the present verse, as well as with *asya dhvaneḥ* (of this resonance).
He thus elucidates [the meaning] starting with "by *sub* and so on," and establishes what was stated starting with "for everywhere... and so forth.

Furthermore, it is observed that [the rasa] is manifested when employed with particles (*nipāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), time-indicating words (*kāla*), and so forth. For example: "This very fact—that my enemies exist—is indeed an insult to me; and that they are ascetics; and that even he [Rāvaṇa] is here, slaughtering the race of Rākṣasas; and oh, Rāvaṇa still lives! Fie, fie upon Indrajit! What is the use of Kumbhakarṇa having been awakened? Or what is the use of these arms, puffed up in vain for plundering the petty village of heaven? In this passage, the *vīra* (heroic) rasa is manifested through the use of the particle *hi*, the prefix *pra-* in *prabodhitavatā*, and the temporal adverb *aho*. Similarly, the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa is manifested by the particle *api*, the prefix *ni-* in *nihanti*, and the temporal adverb *atraiva*. Likewise, the *raudra* (furious) rasa is manifested by the particle *dhik* used twice, the prefix *vi-* in *viluṇṭhana*, and the temporal adverb *vṛthā*. Thus, the manifestation of rasa occurs through such linguistic elements.

The meaning of this "locana" (the commentary) is as follows: it has been stated that rasa is manifested either directly through the elements beginning with the word (*varṇa*) and ending with the composition (*prabandha*), or else indirectly by means of the presentation of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, or again by means of the manifestation of the determinants and so forth. Among these, the fact that the composition acts as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) through this indirect succession was mentioned at the outset as a secondary point.
But now, it is said that [the rasa] is expressed by means of the letters, words, and so forth. Therefore, even in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "it is seen being manifested" is used;

and in expressions such as "its suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is seen," the remainder of the sentence must be supplied, in the form: "by way of the suggestion of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, through a mediated process."

The phrase "mamāraya" (kill me) expresses the inappropriateness of the connection—that it is not fitting for there to be an enemy toward me—thereby manifesting anger as a determinant emotion (*vibhāva*). The plural form "asya" (of this/these) [implies] that he possesses asceticism (*tapas*); thus, the absence of any mention of worldly stories is manifested by the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) in the word *tāpasa*.
In that context, by the particle *api*—which functions as a collection of indeclinables (*nipāta-samudāya*)—there is expressed an absolute impossibility.
If the act of living were performed by me, then the act of killing would first of all be improper;
and regarding that [act], he is its agent, while by the word *api* it is indicated that he is merely a human being.
Regarding the phrase "right here"—the *Bālapriyā* explains the intended meaning as follows: "This has been stated," and so forth.

The connection is that rasa is manifested either directly by means of the presentation of the *vibhāvas* (excitants) and so on, or indirectly by means of the manifestation of the *vibhāvas* and so on.
The word "at first" [refers to this].
The meaning is "in the preceding verse.

He connects the text of the commentary (*vṛtti*) in accordance with the explained meaning, beginning with "by that" (*tena*), and so forth; the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that such is the form of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "by way of the manifestation of the excitants" (*vyañjanadvāratayā*): the sense is that [the rasa] is seen to be manifested indirectly through the door of manifesting the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, by means of specific qualities such as flavor (*rasa*) and the like; this is the intended meaning.
As for the word "insult" (*nyakkāra*).
This is the speech of Rāvaṇa, filled with anger while Śrī Rāma was engaged in the destruction of the race of Rākṣasas;
his words of self-reproach are: "I have enemies, since this very [Rāma] is an insult," and so forth.
Regarding the word "prabodhitavate": [it means "to him who has been awakened"].
It should be understood that [the form] is derived from the causative (*ṇijanta*) in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), followed by the suffix *kta* and then the possessive suffix *matup*.
"Svargagrāmaṭikā" means a very small village, namely heaven itself.
This verse is also cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
The commentary explains the nature of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) brought about by the verbal function (*vṛtti*), beginning with the words "me" and so forth.

The meaning of the term "plural number" (*bahuvacanam*) is as follows: the plural form in the word "enemies" (*arayaḥ*) manifests the excitant (*vibhāva*) of anger, which consists in the inappropriateness of the relationship—namely, that for me, who possess many enemies, [the state of being] possessed by enemies is unbecoming.
In the commentary, the word "relationship" (*sambandha*) means a relationship in the sense of the genitive case.
"Manifested" refers to the meaning of the word "this" (adaḥ);
this is the remainder [of the sentence].

"Extreme impossibility" means that the enmity residing in the ascetic is revealed as being utterly inconceivable. It should be understood that the word "revealed" (abhivyakta) is to be connected appropriately with what follows as well.
Regarding the phrase "the act of killing": the ellipsis is "even that which has any agent whatsoever. That ascetic is merely human—a contemptible man indeed.
The explanation of the meaning of the prefix *ni-* is given as "without remainder" (*niśeṣeṇa*).
For in this verse, the suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) of almost all these [elements] is clearly observed.
Among them, by the phrase "those who were my enemies," the suggestiveness of words connected with case-endings (*sup*) and relations (*sambandha*) is shown.

In the phrase "tatrāpyasau tāpasaḥ" (even there, that ascetic), this occurs through the *taddhita* suffix and the particle; in "so 'pyatraiva nihanti rākṣasakulaṃ jīvatyaho rāvaṇaḥ" (even he slays the race of Rākṣasas right here; oh, Rāvaṇa lives!), it occurs through the *tiṅ* suffix and the powers of the case-roles (*kārakaśakti*); and in the half-verse beginning with "dhigdhikchakrajitam" (Fie, fie on the conqueror of Indra!), it occurs through the *kṛt* suffix, *taddhita* suffix, compound, and prefix (*upasarga*).
And when such a profusion of suggestors (*vyañjaka*) comes together, the poetic splendor of the composition (*bandhacchāyā*), which surpasses all else, unfolds.

For even in a poem where there is the manifestation of a single word that reveals the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), there is a certain beauty of composition; how much more so where there is a convergence of many such words?
As in the verse just recited.

For here, although the word *rāvam* is adorned by a variety of suggestion (*dhvani*) in which the literal meaning is transmuted into another sense (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*), there nevertheless occurs the manifestation of the various modes of suggestion mentioned immediately above.

Furthermore, such varieties of poetic composition (bandhaprakāra) are frequently observed among great souls endowed with exceptional genius (*pratibhā*). Here, "the eye" (*locana*) is the locus (*deśa*) or substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), and "the Rākṣasa army" is the object (*karman*) of the total destruction being effected; thus, the failure of human effort (*puruṣakāra-asampatti*) is suggested by the fact that this seemingly impossible situation has arrived, as expressed through words denoting the verbal root (*tiṅ*) and the case-roles (*kāraka-śakti*).
Regarding the term *rāvaṇa*, its status as having a literal meaning transferred to another sense (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) has already been explained previously.

As for the particle *dhig-dhig* ("fie, fie!"), when combined with the compound *svargati* and so forth—formed by the addition of the secondary derivative (*upapada-samāsa*) "this is a mere story that he conquered Śakra"—it functions as a suggester (*vyañjaka*) toward the recollection of his own prowess.

Furthermore, the use of the feminine suffix along with the pleonastic secondary derivative (*svārthika-taddhita*) in the word *grāmaṭikā* ("little village") functions as a suggester toward its being an object of disrespect.
In the word *viluṇṭhana* ("plundering"), the prefix *vi-* functions as a suggester (*vyañjaka*) of a merciless assault;
in the particle *vṛthā*, there is a suggestiveness toward the censure of one's own prowess;
and by the plural number in *bhujaiḥ* ("with arms"), on the contrary, it is suggested that this [plundering] is merely a burden.
Therefore, even when this verse is divided into pieces as small as sesame seeds, every single part appears as a manifestor; what else could there be?
He shows the fruit of demonstrating this point with the word "thus" (*evam*).
He provides an example of what was stated regarding "one word" with the phrase "as here" (*yathātra*).
The meaning is that even the name of the race of Rākṣasas, which is dear to the ignorant, will perish; "rākṣasabalam" and "rākṣasakulam" are alternative readings.

He demonstrates what is suggested by the sentence beginning with "so 'pi" (even he) through the passage beginning with "tad idam" (this very thing): "the non-attainment of human effort" means the absence of excellence in one's own personal exertion.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the meaning] is suggested (*dhvanyate*) by words that express both verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the powers of the factors of action (*kārakaśakti*).
These are: the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and those which express the powers of the factors of action.
The "powers of the factors of action" are those [powers] such as locusness (*adhikaraṇatva*), agency (*kartṛtva*), and objectness (*karmatva*).
"It has already been explained" means that the sense of being the one who performed the destruction of Mahendra’s city and so forth is suggested by the word *rāvaṇa*.
Regarding the term "of the particle" (*nipātasya*): [it refers to the rule concerning the substitution of *vā* for *va*].
The word "manifesting" (vyañjakatva) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
"Narrative" (ākhyāyikā) means speech whose subject matter is imagined. "Thus" (iti)—[refers to this].
The meaning is "for this purpose";
"sahakṛtaḥ" (accompanied by) is a genitive-ending word that qualifies the term "nipātasya" (of the particle).
He concludes with the words beginning "tena" (by that), etc.
In this context, the readings are both *vibhajya* and *nirbhajya*.
As it was said by the great seer Vyāsa: "The times when happiness prevailed have passed; dreadful times have arrived.
Day after day the days become more evil; the earth has lost its youth."
For here, by means of primary derivatives (kṛt) and secondary derivatives (taddhita), the suggestion of the imperceptible sequence (alakṣyakramavyaṅgya) is conveyed:

"The earth has passed its youth"; and "those times in which pleasure has transcended the eye and never again resorts to the state of being present"—the meaning is that all times whatsoever, not even the slightest fraction of time, is ever present with respect to pleasure.
"Those in whom harsh sufferings—both those that have arrived as adversaries and those returning, as well as those occurring at a distance yet appearing as if present nearby—are manifest;

all portions of time are thus characterized by the recurrence of suffering in its many forms. By this, the poet expresses weariness with time (*kāla-nirveda*), which serves to manifest the aesthetic sentiment of tranquility (*śānta-rasa*).

He speaks also of the country: "The earth"—that is, a land where day after day, morning after morning, every single day is a sinful day; that is, days belonging to sinners, presided over by most wicked people. By its very nature, that time is already full of suffering; moreover, it is a land whose youth is perishing due to its most wicked rulers, like an old woman whose enjoyment is no longer possible because her youth has passed. For, as each day arrives, [it brings only decay]. *(Note: The term "bālapriyā" at the end appears to be a marginal gloss or a signature of the commentator, meaning "dear to children," and is not part of the main text being translated.)*
In this context, it should be understood that the meanings expressed as suggested (vyaṅgya) serve to manifest the intensity of Rāvaṇa’s anger and world-weariness (nirveda).
He explains the verse beginning with "atikrāntam" and so forth;
he states the meaning to be understood through the suffix -kta denoting a past fact by saying "na tu" and so forth.
The explanation of the meaning of the plural "kālāḥ" is "all indeed. By this, he states what is implied: "but not," and so forth.
The explanation of "pratītya" is "pratīpāni" (opposing).
The meaning is that they are extremely disagreeable.
The connection is that the *vṛttas* (metres) have returned and are present;
the meaning is that even though they have gone, they are perceived as returning.
He explains otherwise as well—beginning with "tathā" and so forth.
He states the very same point clearly, beginning with "duḥkham" and so forth.
[He concludes] with "by this" and so forth.
The meaning is that [the word] functions as a manifestor of the aesthetic sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*) by way of expressing world-weariness (*nirveda*).

With the intention that *pāpīyā* ends in the suffix *cha*, he explains it with "of the wicked" (*pāpānām*), etc. "Belonging to the wicked" is the very elaboration of that [term], namely "most wicked" (*pāpiṣṭha*), etc.
The intention is that the word *pāpa*, ending in the suffix *-ka* (denoting purpose), here signifies a meaning characterized by exceedingly great sin.
He states the purport regarding the three types of sin with the words beginning "by nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*), etc.,
[and concludes with] "most sinful" (*pāpiṣṭhā*).
The meaning is: "due to the wickedness of that region, characterized by the earth, which has as its master the most sinful people.
He states "day after day" (*śvaḥśvaḥ*) and so forth, because this phrase is also connected with "whose youth has passed" (*gatayauvana*).

He demonstrates the primary meaning of "whose youth has passed," the reason for the metaphorical usage (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the sublation of that primary sense in the present context, and the similarity (*sārūpya*) between them, by saying "old" (*vṛddha*) and so forth.

The meaning is that the experience of sexual enjoyment (*sambhoga*) is impossible here because of the mention of her having passed her youth; the implied sense (*vyaṅgya*) is that there is not even the possibility of experiencing pleasure. This is the intended point.

Regarding the word *pāpīyān* (wicked one) in the phrase "one whose youth has passed," he provides an alternative interpretation—wherein the word *pāpīya* contains a causal element and refers to another meaning—by stating "gatā" and so forth.
This is to be applied to the passage beginning with "yadi vā" (or if).
[The word] "gata" means...
By this, the *dhvani* (suggested sense) in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*) is revealed.

Furthermore, the suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) of these elements—beginning with the noun (*su*)—is observed almost invariably in the compositions of great poets, whether individually or in combination.

An example of the suggestiveness of a nominal form (*subanta*) is as follows: "O friend, that blue-throated one (*nīlakaṇṭha*), who dances for me at the close of day to the accompaniment of cymbals made beautiful by the jingling of his wings, now dwells within my heart."
An example of a finite verb: "O Lord,
surely these eyes of mine were created by You at the very moment [of my birth], so that Your heart was not known to me until it was filled merely by the sight of You."

That [eye], in comparison with each preceding one, is more evil because it is inferior. Alternatively, this word ending in *iṣṇu* is used by the Sage [Buddha] as if it were derived from the causative suffix *ṇic*.
"Excessively," etc.
The sense is that even this particular form becomes a constituent part of this very [term].
Regarding the phrase "of the nominal stem" (*subantasya*),
the sense is that an example has been provided for the case where they are combined, whereas it is now being considered when they are separate.

The plural number in "tālaiḥ" (with cymbals) suggests a manifold display of skill, which serves to intensify the passion of the lover's separation (*vipralambha*). "Go away! I have created these eyes only for weeping; do not strike them, O fool!
By these two eyes, maddened by the mere sight of you, your heart was not recognized even in such a state."

For one who is intoxicated knows nothing at all; thus, there is no fault here on the part of anyone, as this was the very manner of creation by fate (*daiva*)—the word "of the earth" (*pṛthivyāḥ*) being understood from the context.
[The opponent asks: "But how is the meaning 'one who is more wicked' obtained from what was stated? To this he says: "ending in *itasun*.
[The opponent objects: "In that case, it should have been *pāpīyo divase*"; to this he replies: "by the Sage," and so forth.
The meaning is that this is an archaic (ārṣa) usage. He states another alternative: "or ending in *ṇic*.
The phrase "employed by the Sage" is to be supplied; thus the meaning is "or employed by the Sage [in a form] ending in *ṇic* and *yasun*.

The intention is that in the sense of "he makes the worlds more wicked," from the word *pāpīyaḥ*, when the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), there is the elision of the feminine marker (*ṭi*) and the suffix *ṇic* itself, resulting in this word *pāpīyaḥ* ending in the vowel *a*.
Just as the verse beginning with *anusvāna* was explained, apply it here [to the present case] starting with "that too" (*so 'pi*) and so forth.
That mode as well is *dhvani* in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*).
"Of the rasa" means "of the tranquil (śānta) [rasa] under discussion. "Given" means...
The meaning is that this has been shown by the verse beginning with "nyakkāra" (disgrace).
The passage beginning with "tālaiḥ" (with cymbals) is from the *Uttara-megha-sandeśa*.
"Vaidagdhyam" means skill or proficiency regarding the art of dancing.
"Go away," and so forth, is the speech of a woman separated from her lover addressed to a rogue.
"My wretched eyes"—this is the shadow [of her state].
"You, go away; depart! [is her command].
To the question "Why?", he says: "In order to weep," and so forth.
Since these two wretched eyes of mine were created and fashioned solely for the purpose of weeping, do not nourish them;
do not cause them to increase.
"Do not cause it to bloom facing you," and so forth; [the root] *puṃs* with the prefix *abhivardhana* belongs to the *cur*-class (*curādi*).
"Your heart is not known from this shadow.
The explanation of that is as follows: "of yours," and so forth;
"of such a form."
The meaning is that he will not be attached to me.
He states the sense of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) as follows: "For one who is mad," and so forth.
Regarding the finite verb (*tiṅanta*), it is as in "depart" (*apasara*).
Do not block the path; go away, you shameless boy!
We are without desire; this empty house must be guarded by us.
As an example of *sambandha* (connection): "O child, you speak of non-attachment; why do you look at me thus?
O, for those who fear their wives, this is indeed a source of torment."
"Locana has been made [his wife]," he says;

"depart, do not exert yourself in vain, for it is impossible to alter the course of destiny"—this is the sense that the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) conveys, as well as the other words supported by it. "Do not block the path! Go away, you child, you immature one! Oh, how shameless you are!"
Since we are dependent on others, my empty house must be protected.

In this context, the verbal form *apehi* (go away) suggests the following: "Since you are not yet mature, you should not proclaim this in the midst of people; however, there is a secret meeting place in an empty house, and you should come there.
"Go elsewhere, O boy! Why do you stare so intently at me while I am bathing, you whose intellect is not yet mature?"

"Bho" is a sarcastic address. For those who are terrified of their wives, even the sound of the word "husband" (tadama) does not exist; here, for those who are cowards before their wives, this place is truly out of reach—this is the meaning of the word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). This is what is called "Bālapriyā."
"Expressive" (vyañjaka) means expressive of envy and so forth. "Immature" (bālaka) is explained as "not fully developed" (aprauḍha).
The commentary on the word *ṇirichāo* is as follows:
"We are dependent" is its literal meaning;
"the empty house is not to be guarded" is its implied sense.
The explanation of this begins with "since," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "you reveal," the word "desire for enjoyment" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

The distinction here is that in this verse the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is of the type of union (*sambhoga*), whereas in the previous verse it was of the type of separation (*vipralambha*). Regarding the commentary: "O you who go elsewhere, go! Why do you gaze at me as I bathe? O, for those who fear their wives, even the riverbank does not exist."
Thus: this is the speech of a woman who, while bathing in a reservoir, feels desire for a certain householder who gazes at her with affection.
It is also observed that the reading "titthaṃ" is found in place of "taḍaṃ."
The shadow of that [word] is *tīrtha*.
Regarding "locane," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses the sense of "belonging to.
The construction is as follows: "This bank does not belong at all to those who are afraid of their wives."
This is an elaboration of what was already stated—namely, "born from [the mother]," and so forth.
The connection is "far removed" (*dūrāpeta*);
the meaning is that a connection consisting of their remaining in this place is far removed for those of such a nature.
"Therefore, go" means "by this connection"; that is to say,
by a connection in the sense of the genitive case.
Regarding the word *īrṣyā* (envy):
in the case of artificial compositions, in Prakrit, and in the domain of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), the capacity to suggest meaning is indeed well-known.
What [is there to say] regarding an excess of contempt?

And regarding the employment of compounds according to the propriety of their function, the suggestiveness of particles (*nipāta*) is as follows: "This sudden separation from my beloved has befallen me all at once, and it is utterly unbearable; moreover, the days are bound to become delightful due to the freedom from heat caused by the rising of fresh rain-clouds."
And here the word "ca" (and) [is used].

Or, for example: "The face of the long-lashed-eyed woman—its lower lip repeatedly covered by her fingers, charming yet faltering with syllables of refusal, and turned toward her shoulder—was somehow raised, but not kissed."
Here, however, the word *tu* (but/however) should be understood as follows:
although the indicative function (*dyotakatva*) of particles is well-known, it is stated here with respect to aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

As for the suggestive power (*vyañjakatva*) of prefixes (*upasarga*), for example: "Wild grains (*nīvāra*) fallen from the openings of hollows containing parrots at the base of young trees; in some places, smooth stones are indicated by the breaking of *iṅgudī* fruits."
The deer, their movements unaltered by the approach of trust, endure the sound; and the paths to the water-reservoirs are marked by lines of sap trickling from the tips of their bark garments.
By the phrase "the eye is the connection," an excess of jealousy is manifested by a concealed mistress.
The inclusion of the suffix *ka* in the word *kṛtaka* is intended as an illustration for secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita*);
that is, those poetic sentences in which the suffix *kapratyaya* has been applied, such as in the example "of those who fear their wives" (*jāyābhīrukāṇām*).

"For who else in the world could be more contemptible than those who, being ignorant of flavors, are dependent on their affection for their lawful wives?"— here the suffix *ka* indicates an excess of contempt.
Regarding the phrase "and of compounds," the connection is that it is made known that [the suffixes] alone possess the power of suggestion (*vyañjakatva*).

The word *ca* (and) is used in the singular to denote the class; two *ca*s thus express this: by the maxim of "the crow and the palm fruit" (*kākatālīya*), like a boil breaking out on top of a tumor, both separation from him and the onset of the rainy season have arrived simultaneously—this is sufficient to take away my life.
For this very reason, the word *ramya* (delightful) expresses its status as an *uddīpana-vibhāva* (an excitant stimulus) all the more clearly.
Regarding the word "tu" (but):
the sense is that, as an indicator of regret, it suggests that one's purpose would be fulfilled even by obtaining such a mere kiss.
Regarding the phrase "even though it is well-known": [it refers to the fact that this is already established].

"Bālapriyā" means jealousy caused by attachment to one's wife. Regarding the statement "the mention of *ka* is for the purpose of indicating *taddhita* suffixes," the meaning is that the mention of the suffix *ka* in the rule concerning "compounds ending in *kṛtaka*" is an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for all *taddhita* suffixes beginning with *ka*.
He explains [the verse] with the words beginning "kṛta" and so forth.
The explanation of the word "kā" is "the suffix -ka. He elucidates the rule "'ka' is used in the sense of an excess of contempt" with the words beginning "ya" and so forth.
In this context, the reading is "prema" (love), though some manuscripts read "kāma" (desire).
The phrase "of those who are alone" is supplied as a complement.
The passage beginning with "this" is from the *Vikramorvaśīya*.
"Two *ca*-words" means that there are two instances of the word *ca*, namely in "and [he] approached" (*upanataśca*) and "it must be so" (*bhavitavyañca*).
In such cases, the employment of two or three prepositions (*upasarga*) within a single word is also faultless only when it conforms to the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
As in: "When the luster of the upper garment has fallen away, having seen Indra, Agni, and the creatures with their coverings removed," and so forth;
or as in: "Behaving according to human conduct," and so forth.

The *Locana* states: "For in the houses of grammarians and others, because there is no prior independence of usage and an absence of actual employment, and because the genitive case and so forth are not heard, and because they lack gender and number, particles (*nipātas*) are indicators (*dyotaka*), distinct from denoters (*vācaka*)."
The sense is that they are indeed being proclaimed thus.
The prefix *pra-* in *prasnigdhāḥ* (exceedingly glossy), by indicating excellence while describing the succulence of the *iṅgudī* fruits, suggests the extreme beauty of the hermitage.
However, the claim that "the excessive longing of the ascetic regarding specific fruits is suggested" is incorrect.
In the *Abhijñānaśākuntala*, this statement belongs to the king and not to the ascetic; enough said on that.
By the phrase "of two or three," he excludes any greater number.
When [the king] gazes properly, intensely, and specifically, the Lord’s extraordinary compassion is made manifest.

O Lord, the ignorant, relying on their own reasoning and drawing inferences based on the commonality of their own intellects, desire to understand You— who conduct Yourself according to human behavior and who are difficult even for the masters of yoga to comprehend— by means of their own fallacious logic.
By the phrase "having made it truly secret, moving everywhere," the supreme Lord’s extraordinary desire to favor the world as he engages in various activities is intimated.
Regarding the words "and the agreement," the word "pair" (*dvayam*) is to be supplied.
The two verses beginning with "muhur" (repeatedly) and so forth are from the *Śākuntala* and have been explained in detail in our commentary on the *Śākuntala*.
He explains the well-known usage with the words "the grammarians, etc. The word "in the houses" is connected with the word "is proclaimed.
He states the fourfold reason for its distinction from the expressive [word] with the words "prior," etc.

"Because of the prior application and the absence of independent application. The reading "prākprayogācca svātantryeṇa prayogābhāvācca tasmāt prākprayogāt" (and because of the prior application and the absence of independent application; therefore, from the prior application) is better as a split compound (*vyasta*). This is because particles such as *pra*, *sākṣāt*, and so forth—which are characterized by the technical designation of "prepositions" (*upasarga*)—are applied only before the verbal root, whereas [other] particles like *eva* and so forth are not.
The meaning is that there is no independent usage [of a word] without a word expressing its counter-positive (pratiyogin) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "because the genitive case and so on are not heard":
for example, in such expressions as "the face is similar to the moon" or "similar by means of the moon," the genitive case and so on are indeed heard.
The meaning is that, for instance, in expressions such as "like the moon," the genitive case ending and so forth are not heard; therefore, [the comparison is established].
Regarding the word "liṅga" (mark), the phrase "of the meaning of the particle" is to be supplied.
He explains the phrase "having gazed intently" with the words beginning "properly," etc.;
[it refers to] the Blessed One, the Sun;
[and] "of a human being."
There is also the reading "kṛtābhimānī. He explains the phrase "samupācarantam" with the words beginning "samyak," etc., [and] "ye jīvanti."
When that virtuous and powerful being was seen, those who lived then felt their lives had become truly excellent;
they could not contain themselves within their bodies out of joy.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "those who, with tears flowing from their eyes and their hair standing on end, used to dance," and so forth.
Regarding the term *sādhuddhiṣaḥ*, it means "enemies of the virtuous" (*asajjanān*).
In the reading *sādhudviṣām*, the genitive case is used because one intends to express the remaining relation (*śeṣatva*) of the object.
‘Puṣyatā’ means ‘nourishing.
However, in the reading ‘ye svavapuṣi,’ even particles (nipātas) function in the same way as in ‘jīvanti’ and so forth;
for example, in such passages as ‘aho batāsi spṛhaṇīyavīryaḥ.’

Or for example: "Those who live and do not find room within [the body], who dance with joy upon seeing a virtuous and powerful man—with tears of delight flowing and their hair standing on end—alas, what a tragedy! Oh, where shall I go for refuge for the sake of those people, who have been led to destruction by cruel Fate, which nourishes the enemies of the righteous?"
In such cases, the repetition of words, when employed occasionally with a view toward suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*), brings about beauty. For example:
"That which the wicked person, intent on his own ends, utters as a feigned speech filled with many flatteries and infused with deceit—"
The virtuous know this in many ways, yet they are unable to render this futile exertion of life purposeful.
In such passages,
the *Locana* states "in the same way";
the meaning is that the employment of even two or three [words] as suggestors of rasa (*rasavyañjaka*) is faultless.

The excellence of praise and the excellence of world-weariness are suggested by the expressions "aho bata" and "hā dhik. In this context, he states that even another kind of repetition, namely *pada-paunaruktyam* (repetition of words), can be suggestive;
the mention of "words" (*pada*) is intended as an illustration that includes sentences (*vākya*) and so forth, as appropriate.

"They know"—this implies that they indeed know everything most thoroughly. Regarding tautology of sentence: for example, after the statement "See [him] even from another continent," the subsequent phrase "What doubt is there? [He is known] even from another continent" suggests through suggestion (*dhvani*) that the attainment of the desired object is entirely unimpeded.
By the words "What, what? Are they well while I am alive?", there is an excess of indignation (*amarṣa*).

By the words "O Lord of all kings, has she been seen, beautiful in every limb?", there is an excess of infatuation (*unmāda*). It should be understood that the suffix *laṭ* (present tense) is used here for the past tense when the action is proximate to the present (*vartamāna-sāmīpye bhūte*).
Regarding "locane"—it is suggested (dhvanyate).
Here, the correspondence [of the elements] should be understood according to their respective order.
As for the phrase "yadvañjane":
It is also cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*,
occurring in the *Ratnāvalī* beginning with "dvīpāditya" and so forth,
[in the verse] starting with "svasthāḥ."
This is from the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*.
Regarding the phrase "due to the excess of indignation," the subject "of the speaker Bhīmasena" is to be supplied.
The phrase beginning with "sarva" and so forth is from the *Vikramorvaśīya*. Regarding the expression "an excess of madness," the word "of the speaker Purūravas" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
An example of time acting as a manifesting agent is as follows:
"Where there is no distinction between level and uneven ground, and where the winds blow very gently on all sides—
such days will soon come that will be difficult to traverse even for one's desires."
Becoming indistinguishable whether level or uneven, and blowing very gently from all sides,
the roads will before long become difficult to traverse even for one's desires.

(Thus the shadow. For here, in the phrase "paths will soon come into being," the suffix in the word *bhaviṣyanti* (will be), which denotes a specific time, shines forth as the cause for the nourishment of the rasa. Indeed, this meaning of the verse becomes possessed of rasa when it is perceived as the *vibhāva* (excitant) of the *pravāsa-vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (the love-in-separation of one away from home). Just as the element of the suffix is manifesting here, in some cases the element of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is also seen to be so.

For example: "That house is bent"—this is a palace that has gained entry from heaven; "that cow is old"—these are herds of elephants; "those are pots"—these are masses of clouds; "that is the sound of a pestle"—this is the soft singing of women; "this is a hungry man"—this is a Brahmin who has been raised by the gods to such a height! What a wonder! *divasād dvijo 'yam iyatīm bhūmim samāropitaḥ* (The original text contains *divasād*, which is likely a scribal error for *divasair*; the translation follows the corrected reading).
Regarding the phrase "the eye of time":

the sense is that one must investigate, with subtle vision, the suggestiveness residing even in individual parts— through positive and negative concomitance— within the collection of meanings associated with a finite verb, which consists of the factors of agency, tense, number, and voice.
Regarding the phrase "rasaparipoṣe" (in the nourishment of rasa):
it is suggested that the rainy season, even when merely imagined, causes trembling; how much more so when it is actually present?
He says "as here" because of the very context of the successive parts [of the illustration].
The phrase "is suggested" (*dhvanyate*) is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
He states the meaning: "of that which has entered into a verbal form," etc.; that is, of that which is understood from a verbal form (*tiṅanta*).
"Kāraka," etc.;
the meaning is "consisting of the fourfold [categories] beginning with the kārakas.

"Upagraha" (the verbal suffix) refers to the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* endings; that which is expressed by them is, in short, the result of the action intended for the agent (*kartrabhiprāya-kriyāphala*), and so forth.

"Bhāgagatam" means that which pertains to time, even though it is a constituent part of the fourfold set beginning with the *kāraka* (participant in action); this is the meaning. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "same" [is used].
"Even and uneven places"—those regions where even and uneven terrains become indistinguishable, assuming a single uniform appearance because they are submerged by the flow of water.
Regarding the phrase "even of our desires":
the meaning of the word "even" (api) is "how much more so for people."
He explains what was stated—that "the cause for the nourishment of rasa is manifested"—with the words beginning "utprekṣyamāṇaḥ" (being imagined), and so forth.
"Utprekṣyamāṇaḥ" means being inferred as something about to occur in the near future. "Kampa" (trembling), etc. [is the term].
The phrase "of those separated from their lovers" (*virahijanānām*) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
This verse is also cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa* as an example of "that house" (*tadgeham*).
"'This much ground' means the limit of prosperity; there is also a reading 'bhūtim' (attainment)."
In this verse, even the nominal stem (*prakṛti*) of the word *divasaiḥ* (by days) is suggestive.
Furthermore, the suggestiveness of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) is as seen in the verse just mentioned;
here, having established in his mind that suggestiveness belongs specifically to pronouns, the poet did not employ words such as *kva* (where).

In this manner, by the word *locanam* (the eye), there is a suggestion (*dhvani*) regarding the utter impossibility of this matter [of seeing the sun] during the daytime; and by the rule "and of pronouns" (*sarvanāmnām ca*),
the meaning is that it applies to the stem portion (*prakṛtyaṃśa*) as well.
Thus, it is stated that the word *tad* is seen to manifest all [other] nouns when accompanied by its radical portion (*prakṛtyaṃśa*); therefore, there is no tautology.
For instance, the word *tad*, aided by the radical portion *natabhitti*, suggests the state of being infested with rats and other such creatures—a repository of all inauspiciousness.
Indeed, if *tad* were uttered alone, even an excellence of high status might be imagined.
Nor are these specific qualities, which indicate being an abode of misfortune, expressed even by the word *natabhitti* (having sunken walls).
This should be applied similarly to expressions such as *sā dhenur* ("that cow") and so forth.
And in such a context, the pronoun *tat* (*sa*) functions to indicate the form of recollection (*smaraṇākāra*).
However, it was stated previously that this is not because of being connected with the word *yat*.

For this very reason, here, by indicating through words such as *tat* and *idam* that memory and direct experience possess entirely contradictory objects, their status as the "aesthetic determinant of wonder" (*āścarya-vibhāva*) is established.
In the absence of words like *tat* and *idam*, however, everything would be incoherent; therefore, the vital importance of the elements *tat* and *idam* alone must be acknowledged.
And this [classification] as "in pairs" (*dviśaḥ*) or "in totality" (*sāmastya*), and "in threes" (*triśaḥ*) or "in totality," is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
By that, an infinite variety is stated according to the principle of the "arrangement of clods" (*loṣṭaprastāranyāya*).
He explains what was said in the passage beginning with "by days" (*divasaiḥ*) with the words "for the meaning of 'day' (*divasa-arthaḥ*)," and so forth.
"Divasārthaḥ" means the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) which is "day.
"Asyārthasya" refers to the meaning consisting of the attainment of fulfillment and prosperity.

Now, one might object: since it has already been stated that the base-component is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), and thus pronouns would also necessarily be indicative, the repeated mention of them is redundant; to this he replies: "And of the base-component... [and so forth].
The intention is that the meaning already stated is obtained by the particle *ca* in the rule *sarvanāmnaś ca*.
Having thus explained what is obtained, he says "by that," and so forth.
He explains the word *tat* as "the word."
In the phrase "that house" (*tadgeha*), the word *tat* means "that.
Regarding the word "resounding" (*dhvanati*),
the word "of the house" (*gehasya*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He establishes the statement that two [factors] act together as manifestors by saying "that," etc. Regarding "is possible": the words "as the manifested" are to be supplied.
"Even by the term 'natabhitti' (curved wall)"—
the word "alone" (*kevalena*) is to be supplied through grammatical modification (*vipariṇāmena*).
"These are the distinctions."
The meaning is that the specific characteristics consist in being infested with mice and so forth;
the connection is "and these have not been stated"; the word "might be" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The meaning is that those two [words] alone would not be capable of manifesting the stated sense.
In the phrase "those eyes," he recalls what was previously stated with the words "of such a kind" and so forth.
"For this very reason" means:
The meaning is: "precisely because those words [such as 'that'] indicate the form of recollection.
Regarding the phrase "of recollection and experience":
it means of the recollection accessible through the word "that" (tat), and of the experience accessible through the words "this" (idam) and "that" (etad).
The term *atyantā* means "by indicating the state of having two objects that are absolutely contradictory.

Here, it should be understood that there is a recollection (*smṛti*) of the house by way of attributes such as its walls being sunken and its being infested with mice and the like, while there is a direct perception (*anubhava*) of the sky by way of the attributes mentioned in the phrase "having found space" and so forth.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that "this very [object] is conjoined with sound and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of these two parts alone," the meaning is: "of the part beginning with 'that' (*tad*) and the part beginning with 'this' (*idam*) alone."
"Being *prāma*" means "the state of producing wonder.
And so forth.

The meaning is that this— namely, that two [factors] together, as well as three together, possess the capacity to manifest— is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). "It has been stated" means it has been demonstrated.
Other specific types of suggestors (*vyañjaka*) should also be inferred by sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) for themselves.

Although all of this has already been understood through the discussion on the manifestation (*dyotana*) of words, sentences, and compositions, it is stated again here with a sense of variety for the sake of further instruction.
Now, it was indeed said that aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and the like are suggested by the power of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*).
And thus, the statement regarding the diversity of the manifesting capacities (*vyañjakatva*) of *sub* and other particles is indeed incoherent.
This has been explained previously on the occasion of discussing the manifesting capacity of words.

Furthermore, even though aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and the like are implied by specific meanings, since those specific meanings are invariably concomitant with the manifesting words, the thorough understanding of the nature of the manifestor—as it has been demonstrated—is useful when analyzed in detail.

Likewise, it should be understood that the aesthetic charm (*cārutva*) of specific words—which has been demonstrated through various classifications both here and elsewhere—is also established solely by virtue of their being suggestors (*vyañjaka*).

Even in cases where that charm does not manifest at present, the very excellence (*sauṣṭhava*) observed in other compositions that act as suggestors remains present in those words when they fall into the stream [of usage]; through practice, that same excellence appears even when the words are extracted from that context.
Thus it should be understood;
as he will say [later]: "others also."
With the intention that the disciple’s intellect might not become overly distracted, he summarizes [the matter] with the words "and this.
He recalls the purpose even though it was explained at length by saying "in its variety.
[The opponent asks] "But surely... [etc.]
Although this has already been determined previously, it is raised here for the sake of avoiding forgetfulness and for the purpose of further elaboration. It was stated therein:
"Expressiveness is not what is required for the application of the term 'dhvani,' such that that which is non-expressive would be incapable of being suggestive"—as was already explained before.

Now, one might object: "Even though it is not like song and so forth, the word certainly does have an operation (*vyāpāra*) in the manifestation of rasa; and that [operation] consists precisely in suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
This point has already been definitively established by us in the first chapter (*uddyota*).
He says, "And of specific words," because this has not been stated by us previously.
"Elsewhere" refers to the commentary on Bhāmaha.
Regarding the phrase "by way of distinction":

words such as *srak* (garland) and *candana* (sandalwood) are beautiful when associated with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) sentiment, but unbeautiful when associated with the loathsome (*bībhatsa*). Thus, the distinction is made solely by the sentiment (*rasa*).
Furthermore, it was stated previously that the function of a word with respect to the sentiment is exclusively that of a suggester (*vyañjaka*).
Regarding the phrase "yatrāpi" (even where):

the connection is that [the author] will state later with the intention of supporting this point by saying, "as others also say," that even though words such as *srak* (garland) and *candana* (sandalwood) lack the capacity to suggest *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) and so forth at that time, they nonetheless possess the power of suggestion (*vyañjakatva-śakti*) in abundance. *Bālapriyā* states here the corroboration for this. The syntactical connection is as follows.
He demonstrates the purpose of the objection beginning with "nanu" by stating "pūrvam" and so forth.
The meaning is that the objection was raised for the sake of mentioning something additional;
that is, the objection was made in order to make known the additional portion that will be explained immediately following in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
In the commentary, the word "ananvita" means "incoherent. He provides the resolution with the words "It has been said," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "it has been stated herein":
the meaning here is "it has been stated in this [context].
He explains this with the words beginning "not denotative-ness," and so forth.

The word "yena" means "by virtue of its being expressive (vācakatva) as applicable to the linguistic usage of 'sound' (dhvani). It does not, however, connect with the phrase "na tu... vyāpāro 'sti" (but there is no operation...).
He states the [intended] meaning: "garlands, sandalwood, and so forth," etc.
He explains the purport of the passage beginning with "even where" and ending with "is to be understood": "of the words 'garland,' 'sandalwood,' and so forth," etc.
Otherwise, if the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of words were equal, what distinction regarding beauty could there be?
If it is argued that this [beauty] is something entirely different, perceivable only by those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*), then what is this so-called "aesthetic sensitivity"?

Is it the state of being conversant with specific conventions (*samaya*) based on poetry while disregarding rasa and bhāva, or is it proficiency in thoroughly understanding the very nature of poetry as consisting of rasa, bhāva, and so forth?
In the first case, there would be no fixed rule regarding the aesthetic charm of specific words established by such connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*),
because it is possible for them to establish them differently at another time through a different convention.
In the second case, however, being a connoisseur consists precisely in the state of knowing aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

Thus, for words, their innate excellence consists precisely in this capacity to impart aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, which is to be experienced by those of sensitive hearts (*sahṛdaya*); therefore, their primary beauty resides solely in their power of suggestion (*vyañjakatva*). However, as for those [words] based on denotation (*vācakatva*), they possess the capacity to convey a meaning that has become beautiful through being permeated by that [flavor], as seen in the *Locana*.

For instance, in the verse "The bank (*taṭī*) languishes intensely," sensitive readers disregard the masculine and neuter genders of the word *taṭa* and adopt only its feminine form, because even the name "woman" (*strī*) is sweet.
Thus it is said;

or as our own preceptor, Bhaṭṭendurāja—the sovereign of learned poets and connoisseurs—has written: "If he were not to bear the luster of a blue lotus, there would be no marks [of beauty]; and if his playful charms, the sole friends of wonder, were not present..."
Granted that it may be so by the power of the transformation of merit, yet how could the moon possess a luster as soft as the surface of her cheek?

For here, words such as *indīvaralakṣma*, *vismaya*, *suhṛd*, *vilāsa*, *nāma*, *pariṇāma*, *komala*, and so forth—whose power to manifest the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) has been observed elsewhere—bring about a supreme beauty in this context.
And this must necessarily be admitted; thus he says, "Otherwise, what [could it be]?
With the intention that it is not logical for this [beauty] to be imperceptible, he says, "by the sensitive reader" (*sahṛdaya*).
Regarding the word "punar" (again):
"tadānīm" (at that time) means at the time of the present application [of the argument].

That is to say, in a context where there is a description other than the erotic (śṛṅgāra) sentiment. Regarding "masculinity and neuter gender": the meaning is that these two [genders] are applicable according to the grammatical rule (anuśāsana) stating, "The word *taṭa* [is used] in all three genders."
"O Indīvarā!
By the power of the transformation of merit, when the moon— possessing the luster of a blue lotus— is no longer perceived,
then his graceful charms shall become the sole companions of wonder.
Nevertheless, the connection is: "What indeed might that be, possessing the soft luster of the surface of a cheek? The word *yadā* means "if" (*yadi*).
Regarding *kapola*:
The meaning is that its delicate luster is like the surface of a beautiful woman’s cheek.
In the reading *kerīkapola*, the word *kerī* should be understood as denoting a particular type of woman.
[He asks: "What indeed could it possibly be?"
The meaning is that it simply would not exist.
"In this case" means: in the speech of a certain connoisseur standing as a neutral observer who has beheld the moon.
He introduces the section of doubt beginning with "anya" (other) with the words "asaṃvedya" (unperceivable), etc.

The word "asau" (this) refers to *prasāda* (clarity) itself; it is the specific quality of those [figures] when there is dependence on meaning (*artha*), whereas when there is no dependence on meaning, it is simply alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and so forth.
Having thus described the nature of the manifestors of rasa and the other elements, this is now undertaken to define their contrary forms:

"Whether in a continuous composition (prabandha) or even in a single detached verse (muktaka), one who desires to bind together rasa and the other elements must exert effort, with a keen intellect, toward the avoidance of their opposites. (Dhvanyāloka 3.17)

Whether in a continuous composition or in detached verses, one who desires to compose with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like must exert effort, being wise, to avoid all that is contradictory. (17)

Whether in a continuous composition or in a detached verse, a poet whose mind is intent upon the evocation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and emotion (*bhāva*) must exert supreme effort in the removal of contradictions; otherwise, not even a single verse consisting of aesthetic flavor can be properly accomplished. For how could a linguistic convention (*samaya*), which depends on the unrestrained will of men, ever be fixed? *Locana*: Indeed, since a convention depends on the unbridled desire of individuals, how could it be restricted?
"And beauty is primary"; the word "distinction" (viśeṣa) is connected with what precedes it.
"In regard to the expectation of meaning" means:
The meaning is "in dependence upon the expressed object.
"Only alliteration and so forth" means that this distinction depends upon the arrangement [of sounds] together with other words.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is a collection of verbal qualities (śabda-guṇa) and ornaments (alaṅkāra).
Therefore, the intended meaning is that only those words which are augmented by composition (racanā), clarity (prasāda), and beauty (cārutva) should be employed in poetry. // 15, 16 //

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having stated the essential nature of that which manifests rasa and the rest—ranging from phonemes and words up to literary compositions—it is commenced. By means of this verse, the purpose for formulating the definitions even of opposing [views] is stated, namely, "the possibility of avoidance."
The meaning is that the definition [of the suggested sense] will be provided by the passage beginning with "connected with a conflicting rasa," and so forth. // 17 //

[Objection: "But surely this will also be understood by way of contrast from what was stated [in the definition], namely: 'The excitants (vibhāva), ensuants (anubhāva), transitory states (sañcārī), and the propriety (aucitya) that is beautiful.
[Response: Not so; for by way of contrast, only the mere absence of those qualities is perceived, and not their opposite.
And the mere absence of those qualities is not as detrimental as their opposite."
The meaning is that the non-employment of wholesome [remedies] does not cause disease in the same way as the aforementioned [faults], which are merely distinctions residing in words.
By the passage beginning with "aniyantritā," the underlying sense of the section beginning with "apunar" has been stated.
He explains the meaning of the term *anuprāsa* with the words beginning with "śabdāntareṇa."
He states the conclusion: "Therefore, by means of composition," and so forth.
"Upabṛṃhitāḥ" means distinguished. // 15, 16 //
He states the purpose: "Even of those that are contradictory," and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the conflicting rasa," this is another cause for the disruption of rasa: the detailed description of some other matter, even if it is somehow connected, when it is undertaken in preference to the rasa that is the subject at hand.

He expresses this state through the eyes in the passage beginning with *yatra*.
The "bond of the station of rest" (*viśrāntipadabandha*) is the foundation for the resting of cognition; "therein" means in such a place. "Of this" refers to death.

In the *Kāvyānuśāsana* it is likewise stated: "Regarding the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), however, there is no fault when the determination to die is intended, provided that the sentiment [of death] has been firmly established; for when the members of a conflicting sentiment are described as being subordinated, it is not a defect—as in: 'Where is the improper act of the moon-crested one, and where is my noble lineage? Might she be seen once more? Ah, my learning is for the sake of quelling my faults; even in anger, her face is lovely.'"
What will those sinless ones of perfected intellect say? She is difficult to obtain even in a dream; O heart, attain composure! For what fortunate youth indeed shall drink from her lip?
Accompanied by his beloved Locanā, who was even more clever than her former self, he took delight in pleasure-pavilions once again, as if within the inner groves of Nandana.

In this case, the status of death as a constituent part of love (ratyaṅgatā) is perfectly clear. For this very reason, the skilled poet has not employed a formal poetic composition (*padabandha*) regarding death,
because it is presented merely as something being referred to (*anūdyamānatva*).

If, however, one insists on the placement of this verse [at the end], then grief would arise in every respect, even though the restoration [of the hero] occurs after a very short time; for if it is argued that death is designated as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) because its restoration takes no long time according to the intention of the sensitive audience (*sahṛdaya*), then alas, in the *Tāpasavatsarāja* as well, there would not even be the name "Pathetic" (*karuṇa*), since those whose minds are refined by hearing the path of policy from Yaugandharāyaṇa and others would have no perception at all of Vāsavadattā’s death. Enough of this digression.
Therefore, it should be understood that "long duration" here refers precisely to the attainment of the formal arrangement of words (*padabandha*).
Thus, the intrinsic nature of the factors (*aṅga*) has been explained.
As for their superimposed nature, since it is the opposite of that [intrinsic nature], it is not explained by the author himself, as its meaning is already implied.
Having thus explained the three types, he illustrates them in sequence with the words beginning "Therein" (*tatra*).
Regarding the phrase "Where [is] the improper act?": Bālapriyā says, "[The question is] whether union is immediately established again after death."
"Tīrtha" refers to a passage from the *Raghuvamśa*.
The reading is "dehatyāgāt" (from the abandonment of the body).
"Kāntayā" means with Indumatī.
"He is the Unborn.
"As a limb of delight" means as a limb of sexual pleasure.
Regarding the phrase "of death":
the meaning is "of that death which was indicated by the expression 'from the abandonment of the body'.
Since the hope for reunion was described in the preceding verse, the sense is that the role of death as a constituent of the *vipralambha* (separation) type of love is here made explicit.
The "composition of words" (padabandha) refers to the arrangement of words that provides a sense of repose through comprehension.
The phrase "by way of being restated" means by means of the expression "upon the abandonment of the body. This is the intended meaning.

"Atīti" means "even in that case," the sense being: even when there is the attainment, possibility, or realization of meeting with him again after a time that is extremely limited—that is, very short.
This is connected with the phrase "only the arising of grief."
The meaning of that is: for those who possess aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya), there should be only the relishing of the sorrow.
Some explain the intent of the passage beginning with "not for a long time" (*adīrghakāla*) in another way; repeating their view, he says: "Now," and so forth.
The word "atha" (now/then) indicates a question.
He replies with "hanta" and so forth.
The word "hanta" expresses either dejection or astonishment caused by the statement of something improper.
He concludes with his own view, beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Regarding the word *dīrgha*: the meaning of the term *dīrghakālatā* (long duration) here refers to the very composition of the words, since it rests upon the aesthetic intuition (*sahṛdayapratīti*) regarding death.
"But it has been brought about" means that "it is a factor" is the ellipsis. "The opposite of this" [is as follows].

The meaning is that because there is an absence of actual status as a constituent part (*aṅga*), its natural status as a constituent part is the opposite [of what it appears]. "Explained" means "demonstrated."

In the commentary, "of that" and so forth means "of that *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment). Or, for example, as in the description of the instruction given by the second young sage to Puṇḍarīka, whose intense passion for Mahāśvetā had already set in.

There is no fault when a subordinate status is attained by that which is inherent, as for example: "The poison born of the serpent-cloud forcibly produces in women separated from their lovers whirling, restlessness, languor of heart, dissolution, fainting, darkness, exhaustion of the body, and even death."
In such cases as these,
there is no contradiction even when [the quality] is superimposed— as in "pāṇḍukṣāmam" (pale and emaciated), and so forth;
or as in "kopātkomalalolabāhulatikāpāśena" (by the noose of her tender, trembling creeper-like arms out of anger), and so forth.

This eye [of the heroine] is afflicted by *vitarka* (reflection) through longing, by *mati* (intellection) through memory, by *śaṅkā* (doubt) through dejection, and by *dhṛti* (fortitude) through anxiety.
And this was stated by us at the very beginning of the second chapter (*udyota*).
"The second" refers to that.

The point is that even when one has ascertained the absence of passion through the cultivation of its opposite, such as dispassion (vairāgya), the intensity of attachment is said to remain because it cannot be severed. Regarding the phrase "in the case of superimposition" (samāropitāyām),
the ellipsis is "when it has attained the status of being a subordinate factor" (aṅgabhāvaprāptau).
O friend, your face pale and wasted, your heart full of longing, and your body languid, clearly announce within your breast a deep-seated disease of the blood.

Here, a disease appropriate to *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment) is established through the artifice of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), as indicated by the words "having bound" (*badhvā*) and "is being killed" (*hanyate*). Furthermore, the manifestations (*anubhāva*) of *raudra* (the furious sentiment)—which are superimposed by the power of metaphor—become subordinate elements precisely because they cannot be carried through to completion. And this has already been stated previously in the passage beginning with "not desiring an excessive conclusion" (*nātinirvahaṇaiṣitā*). [The word] "in between" (*antarā*) means "in the middle."

"Interruption of the flow" means the cessation of the stream of continuous reflection (*anusandhāna*). In the *Locana* [it says]: "having become adverse"—the meaning is that it has become an opponent to passion (*anurāga*).
"Of passion" means "of the passion directed toward Puṇḍarīka. In the commentary,
it says "bewilderment."
This passage beginning with "pāṇḍitya" is also cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
"Dizziness" (*bhrami*) is a certain internal transformation that manifests as if it were the whirling of the directions;
"dissolution" (*pralaya*) is the state of having lost all physical activity.
Fainting is the cessation of the activity of the external and internal senses;
darkness is blindness; "born from that" refers to what arises from the cloud itself, which is the serpent.
Poison is indeed water that has become venom;

here, because the manifestations (anubhāvas) such as wandering and so forth of the disease arising from compassion can also occur in the context of love-in-separation (vipralambha), their presence is natural and subordinate.
[The phrase] "pale and emaciated" [is used].
The heart is the chest;
it is "sarasam," meaning accompanied by the essence of food, or alternatively, accompanied by the essence of sandalwood and other such substances.
*Alasa* means incapable of external activity;
*kṣetriya* means that which must be treated in another body, implying it is incurable;
*roga* means disease (*gada*).

Some say that "kṣetriya" refers to the disease of consumption (*kṣayaroga*); [the text] reports this. The singular ending is used for each of the terms beginning with "vaktra" (mouth) with the intention of expressing their collective connection.

Regarding this, Locana states "atra" and so forth, explaining that the [poetic figure] is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) because of the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a disease appropriate to compassion upon the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).
The phrase "by means of the device of *śleṣa*" (paronomasia) means by way of demonstrating the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) common to both.
"Established" (sthāpita) means demonstrated as a constituent member by way of superimposition (āropa).
"Having bound," and so forth.
The meaning is "of the bonds and so forth.
"Because of its non-accomplishment" means "because of the non-accomplishment of the form."

"Aṅgatvam" means the state of being an auxiliary to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). In the commentary, "attaining the status of an auxiliary" refers to this distinct attainment of auxiliary status, which occurs when two mutually contradictory sentiments or emotional states (*bhāva*) both attain the status of auxiliaries within a single primary sentence-meaning that is the subject under discussion.
There is no fault even in that case, as stated in such verses as "Thrown aside, yet clinging to the hand," and so forth.
If it is asked, "How is there no contradiction in that instance? [the answer follows].
This is because both of those [statements] are established as being intent upon something else.
If it is asked: "Even if they are intent upon something else, how is the contradiction between two contradictory things resolved?", it is said:
"In the case of a positive injunction (*vidhi*), there is no coexistence of contradictories; this is the eye [of logic]. (*Locana*) "Something else" [refers to the following].
The meaning is that this is the fourth type.
For previously, it was stated that two conflicting [elements] serve as subordinate members (*aṅga*) to another rasa under discussion;
now, however, the remainder is that two conflicting elements serve as subordinate members to a different subject matter (*vastvantara*).
Regarding the term "cast aside" (*kṣipta*):

this has already been explained in the passage beginning with "when the primary meaning of the sentence is something else. Now, one might object: even if [the word] is subordinate to another purpose, its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) does not cease to exist.
And with the intention that the contradiction is indeed produced by their own intrinsic natures (svabhāva), he says: "even when directed toward another," and "of the two contradictories.
The qualification "of those two intrinsic natures" is intended to indicate the reason (hetu).

"It is said" means the following point: the contradiction or non-contradiction of entities depends upon their falling within a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and not solely upon their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for even cold and heat lack mutual contradiction [in certain contexts].
"In the case of affirmation" (*vidhau*)... [end of fragment]
The connection is as follows: "Do exactly that; do not do otherwise" is what is dear to the child, and this constitutes the attainment of the state of being a limb [of the beloved].
Regarding the phrase "even in that":
the meaning is "even when such a state of being a limb has been attained."
The explanation of the word "anyā" (the other) is given in the *Locana* as "the fourth.
It shows the distinction from what was previously stated with the words "previously," etc.
[It refers to] "the contradictory."

The meaning is "having as its constituent parts a rasa opposed [to the primary one]. Regarding the phrase "in another rasa," that is, "in a specific rasa," the word "in the subject matter at hand" (*prastute*) is to be supplied.
"Even when it has another purpose" means even when it serves as a subordinate element of something else.
"He says": [this refers to the following].
The meaning is "he asks.
Regarding the term "qualification" (viśeṣaṇam):
it means that it is a qualification of the two [words] being connected [to the preceding].
This is the meaning: this is the intended sense of the passage beginning with "vidhau" (in the case of affirmation).
To the question "What is it?", he says: "the totality of conditions" (*sāmagrī*), and so forth.
This is the point: among entities, the contradiction or non-contradiction of one with another is not caused by their mere intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
However, [contradiction] is also possible through the intervention of specific causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).

In this context, what is called "contradiction" consists of non-coexistence (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the obstruction of the production of one thing by another. For instance, the contradiction between pot-ness and cloth-ness, or between cold touch and hot touch, is a contradiction consisting of non-coexistence, which is produced by their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).

In this way, their lack of contradiction in the form of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with substances (*dravya*) and so forth, as well as with qualities such as color (*rūpa*), should be understood.

Furthermore, the contradiction between cold touch, pleasant fragrance, and so on, on the one hand, and the production of hot touch, unpleasant fragrance, and so on, in a substance composed of their own substrates, consists in the prevention of the latter; this is caused by the inclusion of a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī-viśeṣa*).

Likewise, the non-contradiction between cold and hot touches should be understood as being caused by the inclusion of a specific causal complex for the production of soft boiled rice (*komala-bhakta*).

In the case of affirmation (*pravṛtti*), one should grasp the contradiction or non-contradiction by taking up the causal complex for action (*pravṛtti-sāmagrī*) in the place of affirmation and the causal complex for cessation (*nivṛtti-sāmagrī*) in the place of negation, and then considering their mutual entry [into the same locus].
"Of the cold and the hot" means "of the sensations of cold and hot touch."
"Because there is no contradiction"—

the remainder of the phrase is "by way of entering into a specific causal complex" (*sāmagrīviśeṣānupraveśena*). He states the example for [the word] *vidhāti* and so forth with the words "that very same," etc.
By the word "that" (tat), one action is intended; "at one time" is the ellipsis;
thus [is] "as it is."
The meaning of "iti" is that the state of being defective is such and such;
the intention is that it is impossible for one person to perform both the doing and the non-doing at the same time.
He states the supporting reason with the words "ata eva" and so forth.
Or, its defectiveness lies in the restatement;
as [stated in] the *Locana*:
"In this context, predominance is expressed by the word 'injunction' (*vidhi*) on one occasion."
Therefore, those who know the nature of sentences maintain that the contradictory injunction "they take the ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra" results in an option (*vikalpa*).
[The term] "restatement" (*anuvāda*) means [the injunction applies] when it is a subsidiary to something else.
Precisely for this reason—because it is defective for two contradictory things to be predominant in one place at one time—as in the passage beginning with "atirātre":
in the Atirātra sacrifice, they take up the *ṣoḍaśin*, a particular vessel for Soma, as follows: "Come! Go! Fall down! Rise up! Speak! Observe silence!"
In this way, the wealthy play with supplicants who are seized by the demon of hope.
In such cases as these, there is no contradiction in the coexistence of injunction and prohibition because they are being restated; likewise, it will be so here as well.
For in this verse, neither the object of the erotic sentiment characterized by jealousy and separation nor that of the pathetic sentiment is being enjoined.

Because the extraordinary power of the enemy of Tripura (Śiva) constitutes the primary meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), and because those two [the moon and the lotus] are established as subordinate to it;

for, insofar as they are subordinate to the play, there is no mention here of contradictory meanings. Thus, according to the maxim of the two assassins stationed near a king, even though they are contradictory, there is no conflict between them since they are dependent on another and look toward his face.

The taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* vessel has been prescribed so that, due to its contradiction [with other rules], those who are ignorant might take it based on the principle established in the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*.

Furthermore, by the statement "one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* in the *atirātra* sacrifice," it is prohibited; thus, although there is a prescription for both the contradictory acts of taking and not taking, nevertheless, that prescription results in an option (*vikalpa*), meaning: "one may either take the *ṣoḍaśin* or not take it."
In the commentary:
"Come," O seeker, you come; "so be it."
The meaning is "in the manner described.
Regarding the word "āśā" (hopes): the meaning is "seized by those planets in the form of hopes."
The connection is that "the wealthy play with suppliants," meaning beggars.

Here, by showing that there is no fault because both going and coming—even though they consist of existence and non-existence—function as modes within the primary activity of playing (as in "they play by saying 'come! or "they play by saying 'go!'"), he states: [the verse].
"Locane"—meaning "as a part of the play," and so forth.
"Herein"—the meaning is: in the verse beginning with "Come," and so on.
"Of contradictory things" means of things that are mutually exclusive at one time and in one place, such as going and coming, falling and rising, or speaking and silence.
"Thus" (iti) indicates the reason.

"Regarding 'rāje'ti": the meaning is that by this same principle, there is a pair consisting of two men who, while stationed in the vicinity of a king and existing in dependence upon him, are intent on killing one another due to mutual enmity.
"Anye'ti" [refers to others].

"Looking to the face of another" means dependence on others; the meaning is that they have been made subordinate or secondary by that [dependence]. "Even though there is the recognition of one's own selves"—that is, the perception of the self occurring through the sequence of hearing such commands as "Come! or "Go! according to this aforementioned order—"let it not find rest."
The meaning is: "not attaining rest within their own nature. The intention is that they are connected as constituent parts of the play (*krīḍā*).
Regarding the phrase "in the form of one another": [this refers to their mutual interpenetration].

Regarding the phrase "the nature which is their mutual form": the meaning is that when one considers that [nature], no such thought arises at all. He states the distinction with the words beginning "only," etc., and "ruddy," etc.
The meaning is: "by the principle of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*.
