This connects with the word "is possible" (*sambhāvyate*).

In an injunctive sentence such as "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*), because there is a rule that case-factors must connect with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), the properties of being red, having reddish-brown eyes, and so forth—which are the referents of words ending in instrumental case-suffixes—are [connected] to the productive operation of purchasing Soma (*somakrayaṇa*) only while remaining mutually unconnected [to one another].

Subsequently, there is mutual correlation: nor can it be said that the linguistic usage of injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) does not exist among the *rasas*, since they are accepted as the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).

Regarding the sentence-meaning and the expressed meaning (*vācya*), whatever injunctions and restatements exist, let those which are possible as their subsequent, sentence-based relationship be analyzed by the *Locana*.
Anticipating the objection— "Is it not the case that there is an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding that which is to be expressed as primary,

whereas there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding that which is to be expressed as secondary? And you yourself have already accepted that rasa cannot be the object of expression"— the author refutes this with "Not so" (*na ca*).

The sense is that injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) are based solely on the distinction between primary and secondary importance, and these two functions occur even in the case of suggestiveness (*vyaṅgyatā*).
Furthermore, it has been stated that rasa alone is, in the primary sense, the meaning of a poetic sentence.
Therefore, since it is secondary, it is appropriate that rasa also possesses the status of being restated (*anūdyamānatva*) wherever that [primary] meaning resides.
Alternatively, if rasa is considered restated because it is implied by the restated excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, then he says: "of the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthasya*). For example:
"The cow which is Balapriyā’s is ruddy and yellow-eyed," and so on.
This is clear from the *Mīmāṃsā-paribhāṣā* and other works. The term "vākyīya" means that which is conveyed by a sentence (*vākya*).
"Of these," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is a subsequent logical connection (pārṣṭhikānvaya) such as "he who comes goes," and so on.
The connection is that, because of its contradictory nature, that [connection] shall simply fall apart.
In the commentary [it says] "of injunction and prohibition";
this means [the distinction between] going and coming, and so forth.
"[By way of being restated]"—this refers to the state of being that which is already established as a premise.
The phrase "in the ritual procedure" (*kriyāvidhāne*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. He explains what was stated with the words "tathā" and so forth by saying "'śloka' etc.
and "'the state of being prescribed' (*vidhīyamānatvam*)."
The meaning is "preeminence.
Locana introduces the passage beginning with "And not" and ending with "because of [our] admission" with the words "Now, etc.";
that is, "what is to be expressed," and so forth.
The meaning is "that which is the expressed sense.
In that regard, "prescription" (vidhi) refers to the intention that there is both a prescription and a restatement (anuvāda) of it.
He states the meaning of the refutation passage beginning with "teṣām" and ending with "yuktam," by means of the words "pradhāna" and so forth, namely:
"the injunction and the restatement."
The word "of the meaning" (*arthasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Even in the case of being suggested (*vyaṅgyatāyām*), that is, even though it possesses the state of being suggested,
he states where the rasa is what is being restated— beginning with "primarily," and so forth.
That meaning is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).
The phrase "or rather" (*yadivā*) indicates an alternative position.
By whom can those sentiments (*rasa*) implied by that [meaning] be prevented?
Alternatively, even by those who do not accept that rasa and the other elements constitute the direct meaning of poetry,
it must necessarily be admitted that they are at least the cause thereof;
nevertheless, there is no contradiction in this verse.

Since the cognition of a specific state (*bhāvaviśeṣa*) arises from the enjoined element, which has as its auxiliaries both the factors consisting of the occasioning causes (*nimitta*) and the objects (*vastu*) of the subordinate elements being restated, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

For it is observed that a specific effect is produced from a cause possessing two contradictory auxiliaries; indeed, it is contradictory for a single cause to produce two contradictory effects simultaneously, but it is not contradictory for it to have two contradictory auxiliaries. [Locana:
Or rather, let there be no coexistence of two contradictory *rasas* by virtue of their being restated.

He shows that there is no effort required here to establish a logical relationship of mutual dependence (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between two things that are entirely contradictory on the grounds that they will exist through cooperation— expressed by the words "yaiva" (that very [cause]) and "tannimittatā" (the state of having that as the cause).
"Tannimittatā" means the state of being those whose causes are the poetic objects such as the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, which belong to the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and the like.

Those factors such as the gestures (hastakṣepa) and so forth which are being restated, and which serve as the determinants (vibhāva) and other elements of the aesthetic flavor (rasa), have as their cause that twofold matter of rasa consisting of the pathetic (karuṇa) and the love-in-separation (vipralambha)— which is of the same genus as the primary rasa— and this acts as a cooperative factor for what is being enjoined, namely, the burning away of impurities produced by the fire of Śambhu’s arrow.

Therefore, there is a logical connection (saṅgati) in the sense that there arises a realization of the excellence of the Lord’s power within the specific emotional state (bhāva-viśeṣa) characterized by the ornament of the "dear one" (preyas), which pertains to the subject matter of rasa.

When two opposing qualities—cold and heat, which reside respectively in water and fire—are auxiliary to a cause such as rice, the production of a specific effect characterized by the preparation of soft boiled rice is observed;
for everywhere, the causal relationship in cases such as the seed and the sprout is exactly thus, and not otherwise.
Anticipating the objection that "in that case, opposition would be ineffective everywhere," he says: "having opposing effects" (*viruddhaphala*).
And so they have said: "There is no apprehension of that which is contradictory.
Now, [one might object]: if such a sentence were to occur in a poem intended for dramatic performance (*abhineyārtha*), then—[as explained by] Bālapriyā—the meaning is:
because it is already implied or encompassed by the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors being restated (*anūdyamāna*).
He says that; he states this with that intention.
He explains "having that as its cause" (*tannimittatā*) by saying "poetic" (*kāvya*), and so forth.
Connecting the phrase "the members being restated" (*anūdyamānāṅga*) and so on with the verse beginning with "is cast aside" (*kṣipta*), he explains it by saying "being restated," and so forth.
In the phrase "hand-gestures and so forth are the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth," a sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not intended;

for hand-gestures are among the consequents (*anubhāva*). Alternatively, there is a reading: "hand-gestures and so forth are the consequents (*anubhāva*) and so forth. The phrase "that cause" (*tannimitta*) [refers to this].
The meaning is: that [cognition] which has those as its signs (*nimitta*).
"Of the same genus as rasa" means having *rasa* as its essence, or having the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) as its essence.
This is the explanation of the very phrase "of that part which is being enjoined"— namely, "Śāmbhava," and so forth.
Since the term "from the part being enjoined" was explained as "of that part which is being enjoined" by virtue of its proximity to the substantive, he says "Therefore" in order to demonstrate this.
He explains this [statement], "the cognition of a specific state of being," with the words beginning "bhāva" (state of being).
The gloss of the phrase "in a specific state of being" is "in the domain of the *preya* ornament.
To the question "What is that?", he says the words beginning with "bhagavat" (the Blessed One).
"Everywhere," and so forth.
The meaning is that the production of an effect such as a sprout from a seed or the like occurs only through two opposing auxiliary conditions consisting of fire, water, and so on.
"Not the material cause" means: [it is not produced by the material cause alone].
It appears that the reading should be "notpādanam" (non-production). If it is asked how such a performance (*abhinaya*) should be applied regarding the meaning of words expressing such a negation,
the same principle that applies to the case of a statement being restated (*anūdyamāna*) will apply here as well.
Thus, by relying on the method of injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*), the contradiction in this verse is first resolved.

Furthermore, when describing the extraordinary power of some hero whose rise is to be celebrated, the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*) felt toward his adversaries does not produce dejection in discerning critics, provided that all the dramatic modes (*abhinaya*) are present. *Locana*.
Thinking, "In that case, how can a simultaneous representation (abhinaya) of contradictory objects be performed?", he raises an objection with the word "evam" (thus).
He refutes this with the words "anūdyamāna... (being restated).

This means: even in such a subject matter where the expressed object (*vācya*) possesses a contradictory form being restated—as in "Come! Go! Fall down! Stand up! and so forth—the same principle applies here as well.

This is what is meant: in passages such as "Cast off [by her], clinging to her hand," etc., the contextual meaning must first be demonstrated by way of establishing the glances of one terrified and overwhelmed, which are the primary elements here.

Although the *karuṇa* (pathos) rasa is also merely subordinate (*parāṅga*) in this context, its status as a contextual element is nonetheless more immediate than that of the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation), because it is useful toward the manifestation of Maheśvara’s power.
The *vipralambha*, however, is remote, as it arises only through the force of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) and simile (*upamā*) in the phrase "like a lover."

And thus, by means of the sequence of the enactment of the application of compassion— predominantly through lotus-eyes moist with tears, and only slightly through the indication of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) due to its similarity with *karuṇa* (pathos)—
and although in the phrase "like a lover" (*kāmīva*) an enactment appropriate to a lover's anger was performed, nevertheless,
that *vipralambha* which is implied there is [only] fully established by the grandiose enactment in the immediately following verse beginning with "May he burn away my sin" (*sa dahatu duritam*).
There is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that whatever power belongs to the Blessed One culminates in being a constituent part [of that cognition].
He concludes this resolution of the contradiction with the word "thus" (*evam*).
Then, he states the resolution of the contradiction in another manner regarding a different subject matter with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*).
"Desirous of examining" refers to the members of the assembly who possess discernment.
"No despondency" means that in such a context, no melting of the heart arises, because there is an absence of resting in the relish of compassion.

However, that very anger of the hero which undergoes a transformation (vyabhicāritā), this aesthetic flavor of compassion (karuṇarasa) which is its fruit, ultimately culminates in a superior relish of the heroic (vīrāsvādātiśaya) by means of manifesting its own cause. [The author] explains for the instruction of actors: "This is what was said," and so forth.
It is to be demonstrated and enacted;
"by the power of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) or simile (upamā)" means by the power of either poetic fancy or simile.
The connection is "having performed the dramatic representation.
He raises an objection with the words beginning "one who is full of desire" (kāmī), etc., and he provides the resolution with the words beginning "nevertheless" (tathāpi), etc.
"Made" (kṛta) means "the object of an action" (kṛtiviṣaya); the word "might be" (bhavet) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

He introduces the passage beginning with "kiñca" (furthermore) with the words "viṣayāntare 'pi" and so forth. "In another object" means in another location, such as in the verse beginning with "kuravaka.
"By another manner" means...
The meaning is "by the fifth mode.
Regarding the word "says" (āha): the meaning is that he says this as a consequence (prasaṅgāt).
"In such a subject matter" means in examples such as the verse beginning with "kuravaka.

Since what is called "distress" (vaiklavya) actually serves as a cause for an excess of joy, its power is blunted; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in that which produces a contradiction [with the expected emotion].

Therefore, it is logical to say that "contrary to rasa" means contrary to that rasa or bhāva which has become the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), and not to some [rasa] that has become a subordinate element (*aṅga*).
As it has been stated: "The action of the Furious (*raudra*) itself is to be known as the Pathetic (*karuṇa*) rasa."
Thus he says: "Excessive joy," etc.

An example of this is as follows: "O *kurabaka* tree, you shall be deprived of the pleasure of the sport of being struck by [their] breasts; O *bakula* shrub, you must remember the savoring of the wine from their mouths;
O *aśoka*, you will come to possess sorrow (*saśokatā*) when you are devoid of contact with their feet"—thus did the women of the enemies speak as they were abandoning their own city.
"Or of a state (bhāva)" means:

in that rasa, [it is the cause] of a dominant permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) or of a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*), as in the case of longing (*autsukya*) in the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation).
The *Bālapriyā* commentary states: "It is the melting of the mind (*cittadruti*)."

"Kuravaka," and there is also a reading "mukhāsavasevana. Thus: the Aśoka blossoms from a kick; the Tilaka and Kuravaka from being gazed upon and embraced; the Priyaṅgu from the touch of women; and the Bakula from the sprinkling of mouthfuls of *śīdhu* liquor.
This statement should be considered here.
In the commentary, "compassion is the rasa," the word "being composed" (*nibadhyamāna*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"In the excess of joy" means in the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*). "Of that" refers to...
The meaning is "of compassion.
Regarding the phrase "because its power is blunted":
the meaning is that its power is blunted because it serves as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) to something else.
The word "na doṣaḥ" (no fault) is connected with this [preceding statement].
"Tadvirodhavidhāyinaḥ" is a qualifier of "tasya" (of that); the meaning is: "those which bring about a contradiction with the excellence of the relish of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*)."
In the reading "akuṇṭhaśaktikatvāt" (because of having unimpeded power), the word "tasya" (of that) means "of the aesthetic relish of heroism" (*vīrāsvāda*).

In the phrase "tadvirodhavidhāyinaḥ" (of those effecting its opposition), the word ending in the ablative case is "karuṇāt" (from compassion), which is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He concludes with the words beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore).
The phrase "of that which has become the meaning of the sentence" means "of the primary subject under discussion. The phrase "in order to state that it is contrary to rasa" [is used].

In the passage beginning with "virodhira-se" (incompatible rasa), the word "virodhi" (incompatible) means "to be spoken of. Thus, the sense is that it is a defect to include a rasa related to a rasa incompatible with the rasa that constitutes the meaning of the sentence. This is what is meant by the phrase "not, however," and so forth.
The meaning is that it is not logical to call something "contrary to rasa" merely because it is contrary to some subordinate rasa or bhāva.
Thus, the point is that there is no fault in including that which is contrary to some subordinate element, provided it is connected to [the primary] rasa;
as in the example beginning with *akṣipta*, where there is the inclusion of what is connected to the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa, which is contrary to the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa.

Regarding the phrase "or of a state" (*bhāvasya*), the *Locana* states that by the word "state" (*bhāva*), both the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) and the transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) are intended; this is shown in the passage beginning with "In that" (*tasmin*).
"In that" refers to the rasa under discussion, the primary rasa.
The explanation of the phrase "of that which has become the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārthabhūtasya*) is "of that which is the principal element" (*pradhānabhūtasya*).

Alternatively, even when some object of the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*) has become the primary meaning of the sentence, its conjunction with an object of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-vastu*) by means of a particular stylistic device serves solely to nourish that [pathetic] rasa.

For objects that are naturally sweet, when they have fallen into a state of lamentation, produce an even greater intensity of grief when their former states are recalled through remembered amorous pastimes. As in the verse beginning "Now, in the very same [verse]... and so forth; here, he resolves the contradiction in another manner, starting with "Alternatively."

And this is the underlying point here: previously, it was stated that there is no contradiction because *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) and *karuṇa* (pathos) function as subordinate elements (*aṅga*) to something else.

Now, however, since that *vipralambha* has itself become a subordinate element of *karuṇa*, how can it be established as being contradictory? For it has been said that the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) called *karuṇa* arises from excitants (*vibhāva*) such as the calamity of a beloved person;
and "belovedness" is rooted in loveliness.
And thus, as if he were a lover who has committed a fresh offense, this [verse] is spoken with such a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

Upon observing the activity of the fire of Śambhu’s arrow, the past incident of their love-quarrel is recalled; now, because it has been destroyed, it becomes a determinant of sorrow (*śoka-vibhāva*). Thus he says: "by a particular mode of expression" (*bhaṅgiviśeṣa*).

In order to prevent the misconception that there is a different meaning for the passage beginning with "atha vā" (or else), [the commentator] introduces that very passage, starting with "adhunā" (now) and so forth.
Furthermore, instead of "atha vā," there is a reading beginning with "athavā" and ending with "doṣābhāvaḥ" (absence of fault).
In the *Vṛtti*, the text reads "athavā" and so on.
Regarding the phrase "of that which has become the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārthabhūtasya*): it means "of the expressed" (*vācyasya*).
The word "also" (*api*) indicates an apparent contradiction regarding the nourishment of rasa through the method just mentioned; this is shown by the phrase "of some" (*kasyacid*).
The meaning is "of something" whose form consists of the *vibhāva* (determinant) and so forth.
"Of the object of the *karuṇa-rasa* (the pathetic sentiment)" refers to one whose limbs are mutilated.
"By such [a means]" means by that which is equivalent to it in being the expressed (*vācya*).
Alternatively—by means of a contradictory erotic subject matter (*śṛṅgāra-vastu*), which is a constituent of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
He provides an example of what was stated, beginning with "This" (*ayam*) and so forth.
This verse is also cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
Applying what was stated in the passage beginning with "cast down in the present context" (*prakṛte kṣipta*), he says:
"‘He acted’ (*vyavaharati sma)*," the meaning of which is that he performed such acts as seizing the hand and so forth.
Because this intended meaning is not clear from the commentary (*vṛtti*), he states the underlying intention (*bhāva*) in the *Locana*: "And here... and so forth.
Elsewhere, [the phrase] refers to the extraordinary power of the Enemy of Tripura;
however, its connection with the word "now" (*adhunā*) is with the words "is established" (*vyavasthāpyate*).
"How is it contradictory?
means that it is not contradictory to compassion.
It has been stated [that this occurs] "due to the determinants" (vibhāva).
The word "muni" (sage) is to be supplied [as the subject].
"Ramaṇīyatāmūla" is a bahuvrīhi compound.
[The phrase] "ity utprekṣayā" means "by way of such a poetic conceit."
And this was stated with the intention of the position that there is the poetic figure of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) here;
"this has been said" means that the meaning which is about to be explained has been illuminated.
Regarding "śāmbhava":
it means by observing the activities of the Śāmbhava fire.
There is also a reading "avalokane" (in the observation).
This connects with the word "being remembered" (*smaryamāṇa*).
Regarding the term "prior" (*prāktana*): it means a prior experience, such as the account of a lovers' quarrel involving the inability to endure being grasped by the hand, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "being remembered":
the words "by the young women of Tripura" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding the phrase "by way of being destroyed": [the ellipsis is the same].
The meaning is "by way of being lost. After the phrase *śokavibhāvatām*, some manuscripts read *prakṛṣṭām* (excellent). Regarding the word *pratipadyate*:

thus, here, by the logic of the "qualification of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*), the Pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*)—enhanced by the sentiment of Separation-in-love (*vipralambha*)—reveals the extraordinary power of the Enemy of Tripura. [This is the hand] which used to pull up the girdle and press against full breasts...
The hand, touching the navel, thighs, and hips, loosened the knot of her lower garment.

In such passages as this, the lover Śambhu, whose offense was fresh, acted toward the young women of Tripura exactly as a passionate man would act; thus, even by this manner of interpretation, there is indeed an absence of contradiction.
Therefore, however one examines it, in every way there is an absence of defect here.
And thus— Treading upon the ground strewn with darbha grass with feet whose tender toes are reddened by the blood of their wounds, their faces washed by falling tears as if by liquid lac,
these wives of your enemies now wander in fear around the forest fire with hands grasped by their husbands, as if they were entering into marriage once again.
In this manner, the absence of contradiction among all these [elements] should be understood.
Thus far, the distinction between the spheres of coexistence and non-coexistence of sentiments (rasa) and the like with contradictory sentiments has been shown.
Now, in order to establish the proper sequence for their arrangement within a single literary composition, it is said:
"Free from vulgarity" (locanaṃ grāmyoktirahitayā) means [free from vulgar expression].
He provides an illustration for this very point: "Just as this...
Here, having seen Bhūriśravas’s arm fallen upon the battlefield, his beloved wives lamented in this manner.
"Rasanotkarṣī" means one who pulls up the girdle or waistband during moments of sexual enjoyment.
With the intention that by this method of resolving the contradiction (*virodhoddharaṇa*), a much greater number of instances (*lakṣya*) is established, he says: "And thus... [He further explains:
"Whether it be the water of tears produced by the smoke of the sacrificial fire, or that arising from the sorrow of leaving the house of kinsmen,"

"Fear" (*bhayam*) refers to the trepidation appropriate for young maidens. Thus, he concludes by summarizing what has been explained regarding the portion of the *kārikā* that pertains to the statement that such speech is "unrestrained" (*acchala*) when it reaches its full development through these stages: "In this way" (*evam*).
By the use of the word "so far" (*tāvat*), he indicates that there is further to be said. //20//
He introduces that very point with the words "Now," and so forth.
The construction is: "the sequence of those aesthetic flavors (rasas).
The sense is that he embellishes the state of being supported by them.
"He says that" means he says it with the aforementioned intention.
"By way of being non-vulgar" is the very explanation of that [term], namely "vibhāva," and so forth.
Regarding this, [the passage] beginning with "Bhūriśravas" and so forth—

in this verse, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) residing in the hero (*nāyaka*) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*) residing in the heroine (*nāyikā*), and such points should be examined in the *Kāvyapradīpodyota* and other works.
As for the word "by him" (*amunā*):
The meaning is "as has been stated.
To the question, "How can there be the rising of tears at the time of marriage? he says: "By the oblation," and so forth.
This verse as well has been cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
Everything should be understood here as well, just as in the case of the verse beginning with "kṣipta" (I.19). //20//
Now, regarding the phrase "of them" (*teṣām*) in the verse, he explains that word as "of the rasas" (*rasānām*).
As for the passage beginning with "the sequence," etc.:
even though it is well known that literary compositions are composed based on various *rasas*, [there remains a need for this clarification].
One who desires their excellence must accept that there is but a single rasa among them.
Even though compositions are established as being composed of various sentiments (rasas), one who desires their excellence must accept a single sentiment as the primary one. (21)

Although it is well known that in literary compositions such as mahākāvyas or dramas, many rasas are presented in a scattered manner through the relationship of primary and subordinate elements, for one who desires these works to possess an excellence of aesthetic luster, the more appropriate path is this: one should establish a particular intended rasa among those [rasas] as the dominant element (aṅgin).

Now, one might object: "If many other rasas have attained full development, how is it not contradictory for one [rasa] alone to be the primary element? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "The intrusion of other rasas does not impair the primacy of the rasa under discussion, provided that it appears as the stable emotion (sthāyin). (Dhvanyāloka 3.22)

The intrusion of another rasa which does not impair the status of the primary rasa as its subordinate is permissible, provided that the primary rasa manifests itself as the dominant stable emotion (sthāyibhāva). // 22 //

"In compositions," being introduced first and being repeatedly connected [with the mind], that rasa which is the *sthāyin* (the enduring emotional state) undergoes an "interpenetration" (*samāveśa*) by other rasas situated in the intervals, which pervade the entire composition—even though it is well-known, meaning even though it has been defined by the sage Bharata and others.
*Locana*. "Even though it is well-known":
the meaning is, even though it has been determined by the sage Bharata and others.
"Of these" refers to the compositions. In the phrase "in mahākāvya and so forth," the word "so forth" (ādi) indicates a class or type.
He states the varieties that are not intended for dramatic performance (anabhineya).
The second [type], however, consists of those [elements] to be enacted;
"by way of being dispersed" means by way of residing in the hero, the antagonist, the banner-hero, the secondary hero, and so forth.
"By way of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal" means by being centered upon a single hero (*nāyaka*). Regarding the term "more appropriate":

although in cases such as the *Rasavakāra* or compositions consisting of a series of synonyms (*paryāyabandha*), there is no single principal element, nevertheless, even in those instances, it is not inappropriate for such a [single hero] to exist.
The meaning of the word "tara" is that whatever composition there may be—such as a drama or a great epic (mahākāvya)—that is more excellent. // 21 //
The word "nanu" (surely) introduces the objection: if [the rasa] has attained its own full development (*paripoṣa*) by itself, how can it be a subordinate element (*aṅga*)?

Or, if its full development has not been attained, how can it be the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)? Thus, the status of being *rasa* and the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*) are mutually contradictory. Furthermore, since it is impossible for those [other rasas] to be subordinate elements, the point is: how can it be said that one [specific rasa] is the predominant element (*aṅgin*)?
Regarding the phrase "rasāntara" (in another rasa):

the meaning is that the word "krama" (sequence) is connected with the word "teṣām" (of those), referring to the primary rasa which pervades the entire plot of the work presented, and which, by virtue of its extensive pervasiveness, is fit to be the dominant element (*aṅgin*).
He explains the phrase "even though not established" (*prasiddhe 'pi*) with the words beginning "Bharata," etc.

He explains the commentary (*vṛtti*)—beginning with "great" (*maha*), etc.—and demonstrates the sense of the comparative suffix (*tarap*) in the word "more appropriate" (*yuktatara*) with the words "even though," etc.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "nevertheless, even for that [position], there is no lack of appropriateness."
"Of that too" means "of [the word] *samaba* and so forth as well. "Of such a kind" means:
The meaning is that it consists of various sentiments (rasas) while having a single predominant sentiment as its primary constituent. // 21 //
He states the meaning of the objection beginning with "nanu" (but surely) as follows: "svayam" (itself), etc.
Regarding the phrase "labdhaparipoṣatve" (when [the rasa] has attained full development), the word "of other rasas" (rasāntarāṇām) is to be supplied.
Now, [the opponent] says, "Let there not be the status of being an auxiliary (aṅgatva)"—to this he replies with "And of those," etc.
In the commentary, it is stated that this does not undermine its status as the primary element (aṅgitā);
and in order to demonstrate precisely this, it is said:
Just as a single effect is established as pervading a literary composition,
so too there is no contradiction whatsoever in the case of the manifestation of rasa.
Just as a single effect is established as pervading an entire composition, so too, in the case of the production of rasa, no contradiction whatsoever exists. (23)

The Locana states: "The integration and reinforcement of one rasa by other rasas—which, by virtue of being extended through the plot (*itivṛtta*), pervade only limited fragments of the narrative—does not undermine the status as the primary element (*aṅgitva*) of that [rasa] which appears as the dominant sentiment (*sthāyin*) pervading the entire plot;
rather, it only enhances its status as the primary element. This is the meaning.

This is what is meant: although the other subordinate sentiments (*rasas*), even when they have attained full development through their own respective collection of determinants (*vibhāvas*) and so forth in their own state, do indeed become objects of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), nevertheless that wonder does not find satisfaction or rest therein alone; rather, it pursues another wonder.
For this is the very same principle in every instance of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal.
As the venerable one has said: "A subordinate element that has undergone its own refinement serves the principal element;
for in this way, it functions more extensively toward the benefit of the principal."
Thus [ends the twenty-second].
"To establish" means by means of determining a suitable example;
and this very point is established through reasoning.

For one must necessarily accept that there is a single primary action (*adhikārikakārya*) which is pervasive and is assisted by other incidental actions (*prāsaṅgikakārya*). The relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) among the mental states of the hero (*nāyaka*), which follow upon that [primary action], arises solely by the force of that [action].
The point is: what is new in this [concept] that it should be called "occurring in the flow" (*pravāhāpatita*)?
The word "tathā" (thus) means by way of pervasiveness.
Alternatively, the particle *eva* (only/itself) is displaced in its order;

the meaning is that in that very same manner—namely, in the form of the relationship between cause and effect among the factors (*aṅga*) and the whole (*aṅgin*)—this [aesthetic flavor] also necessarily arises for the *rasas*.
And so the commentary will state: "in that very way. Regarding the term "effect" (*kārya*):
it refers to the seed as characterized by the statement, "that which, though released in a very small measure, spreads in many ways."
In some manuscripts, the reading "bahuṣu" does not appear;
furthermore, in place of the reading "kathamekasyāṅgitā na," the reading "ekasyāṅgitā" is seen.
He explains the verse with the words beginning "prastutasya."

The explanation of the word "asya" (of this) is "tasya" (of that). With this verse, he demonstrates the resolution of the doubt beginning with "nanu" (but surely), which was obtained [by the previous discussion], starting with the words "etad uktam" (this has been said).
The term "guṇa" (quality) [is used].

The quality (*guṇa*) is a subordinate member (*aṅga*). Having undergone refinement by another [element], that quality, thus refined, serves the primary element (*pradhāna*), the principal member (*aṅgin*), for a greater benefit; indeed, it exists for the sake of a more abundant assistance.
This verse is also shown in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
"By way of definition" means by way of demonstration.
"This very [thing]" refers to that.
The meaning is that it is precisely what will be stated by the words "the task" (*kārya*) and so forth. "Of those following upon that" means "of those connected with each respective task."
Regarding the phrase "of the mental states of the leaders":
by the word "leaders" (nāyaka), all [characters] such as the leader and the sub-leader are intended here.
"Precisely by their power" means:

The meaning is: "solely by virtue of the relationship of primary and subordinate between the constituent parts of the effects. He explains the word *tathā* found in the verse with the words "by way of pervasion" (*vyāpitayā*).
He provides another explanation as well, beginning with "or if... (*yadi vā*).
"Disordered sequence" (*bhinnakrama*) means that the restrictive particle *eva* (translated as "not at all") connects with the word *tathā* (translated as "in that way").

Just as a single, continuous, and pervasive causal effect is postulated for the body of a literary composition consisting of the junctures (*sandhi*) and so forth, and yet it is not confounded with other effects; [so too is the case here].
Nor does its predominance diminish even when it is intermingled with them;
likewise, there is no contradiction whatsoever when a single rasa is being composed.
On the contrary, for sensitive persons who possess discernment and the capacity for synthesis, such a state of affairs gives rise to an extraordinary degree of aesthetic delight.
Now, regarding those sentiments (*rasas*) which are not mutually contradictory—such as the heroic (*vīra*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), or the erotic and the comic (*hāsya*)—the *Locana* states:

"That which, from the very beginning, serves as the cause for the non-interruption of the purposes [of the plot] even when they are interrupted, and which persists until the conclusion of the composition, is the *bindu* (the drop).
Since this element in the form of the *bindu* extends throughout the work up to the final resolution (*nirvahaṇa*), it is described as "following along" (*anuyāyin*).
By this, "seed" (*bīja*) and "drop" (*bindu*)—the two types of *arthaprakṛti* (plot-elements)—are included.
Regarding the phrase "by other effects":

this refers to that which pertains to the definition of the "subplot" (*patākā*), which is based on the *arthaprakṛti*, as it is mentioned incidentally in the rule: "The subplot ceases either at the end of the embryo (*garbha*) or at the end of the deliberation (*vimarśa*)."

And as for those effects which, by having a scope even less than that, are characterized as *prakara* (sub-plot) effects— it is with these that the inclusion of the five thematic elements (*arthaprakṛti*) is stated through their syntactic unity within a single sentence.
"Of such a kind" [refers to this].

As in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*, by this verse both [points] are established: the illustration of the relationship between the constituent parts (*aṅga*) and the whole (*aṅgin*), and the fact that the relationship of primary and subordinate among the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) occurs by virtue of falling under the power of the plot (*itivṛtta*).
The commentary (*vṛtti*) text should also be understood with reference to both of these intentions.

There is no contradiction between the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the heroic (*vīra*), [the latter] consisting of battle, policy, valor, and so forth, as seen in cases such as the acquisition of a jewel-like maiden.
The status of the comic (*hāsya*) as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to it is, however, quite evident.

Although the comic itself does not possess the nature of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), it attains that status precisely by being a subordinate element of the erotic, through the production of even greater delight.
Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever even with the Furious (raudra) sentiment;
as it has been said: "And the Erotic (śṛṅgāra) is forcefully cultivated by them. [Regarding the word] "asau" (this): Bālapriyā.
The meaning is the relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

Demonstrating the intended meaning by means of the word *kārya* through its etymological derivation (*yogavyutpatti*), he explains it with the words "merely a small amount" (*svalpamātram*) and so forth.
The word "seed" (*bīja*) is connected with the word "pervades" (*vyāpnoti*).
"By this" means by the word "effect. He explains what is intended by the phrase "by other effects" with the words beginning "from the embryo," and so forth.
"Even less than that pervasion" means:
because of the manifestation of the meaning characterized by the banner from that [pervasion].
The phrase ending with "by them" is an elaboration of the term "by other effects."
He summarizes with the words "In this way," and so forth.
"Has been stated" means that it has been made known by these two [verses]: "The effect [is produced] by other effects," and so on.
He shows an example of the phrase "in such a case" with the words "as in the case of the ascetic.
He states the essential meaning with the words "thus," etc. [He explains] by the word "by this."
The meaning is [as expressed] by the words "the task," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: by this verse, two things have been defined: the determination of the examples for the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅga-aṅgitā*) within the relationship of the subordinates and the principal among the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), and the fact that this relationship occurs by the force of the plot (*itivṛtta*).
He establishes the non-contradiction of the flavors with the words beginning "by the erotic" (*śṛṅgāreṇa*).
"Non-contradiction" (avirodha) means that there is an absence of contradiction when they share a single substratum.
"Being its constituent" (tadaṅgatva) means being a constituent of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
Regarding the phrase "by means of producing the coloring of the *samādhi*":

let there be a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) among the Furious and the Erotic, the Heroic and the Marvelous, the Heroic and the Furious, the Furious and the Compassionate, or the Erotic and the Marvelous.
But how could such a relationship exist for those [rasas] that stand in a mutual relation of the sublated and the sublator?

For example—[considering] the cases of the erotic and the loathsome, the heroic and the terrifying, the peaceful and the furious, or the peaceful and the erotic—it is said in response to this [objection]:
"By them," meaning by those such as the Furious (Raudra), [specifically] by Rakshasas, Danavas, and arrogant men;
in that context, only the intensity directed toward the heroine must be avoided.
However, there is a coalescence of the *vīra* (heroic) and *adbhuta* (marvelous) sentiments due to the astonishment produced by such inconceivable acts as the sweeping of the earth;
as the Sage has said: "Whatever is the deed of a hero, that is the marvelous.

There is a coalescence of the *vīra* and *raudra* (furious) sentiments in characters such as Bhīmasena, who are *dhīroddhata* (haughty and bold), because there is no contradiction between wrath and energy (*utsāha*).
The Sage has also stated regarding both the Furious (raudra) and the Compassionate (karuṇa): "That action which belongs to the Furious alone is to be known as the Compassionate sentiment.
Regarding the Erotic (śṛṅgāra) and the Marvelous (adbhuta), it is as in the *Ratnāvalī* upon the sight of the magician.
Regarding the phrase "of the erotic and the loathsome":

for how could there be a relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin) between two states that arise precisely by way of uprooting one another? Furthermore, while love arises with its form immersed in the objective substratum (ālambana), loathing arises with its form fleeing from it; thus, by virtue of having a common locus, they possess the quality of mutually uprooting each other's latent impressions (saṃskāra).
Fear and enthusiasm should likewise be described as being mutually contradictory.

Even for one who is peaceful (*śānta*), whose very nature is devoid of all worldly exertion because he possesses the life-force of total world-weariness arising from the knowledge of reality, there is indeed a contradiction with attachment to sense objects and with love and anger, which are the life-breath of such attachment. // 23 //
There is also a reading: "by generating an excess of sweetness" (*bālapriyā smadhikarasotpādanena*). This means by generating an excess of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*).
Its being such [is its] being a human goal (*puruṣārthatva*).
"By that [expression] *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment). Regarding the word "it was said," the phrase "by the Sage" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He states the distinction with the words "only" (*kevalam*) and "unimaginable" (*asambhāvya*), etc.
For a hero experiences wonder through the attainment of an unimaginable object.
Regarding the word "stated":
the term "non-contradiction" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Here, non-contradiction is to be understood by virtue of having a single object of focus (*ekālambanaka*).
Since it is possible for *raudra* (the Furious) and *karuṇa* (the Compassionate) to have distinct substrata,
the phrase "even between *śṛṅgāra* (the Erotic) and *adbhuta* (the Marvelous)" implies that there is no contradiction [between them].
He explains the relationship of the sublated (*bādhya*) and the sublator (*bādhaka*) with the words beginning "for those two," etc.
"Of which two" means of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), and so forth;
"therein" refers to those two.
He shows the reason for the stated meaning with the words "ālambana" and so forth.
It "arises," that is, it manifests.
"From that" means:
The meaning is "from the object.
Regarding the word *jugupsate*,
the verb *uttiṣṭhati* (he rises) is to be supplied.
The word "iti" means "thus.
"By way of having a common basis" (samanāśrayatvena) means by way of having a single object of focus and a single substratum.
"Of those two" means "of delight and disgust.
"Mutually" [is the meaning].
The meaning is that it is the uprooting of whatever mutual conditioning exists— that is, its causing destruction.
"In this very way" [is the phrase].
The meaning is: by virtue of having a single basis. // 23 //
Whether it be non-conflicting or conflicting, a rasa should not be brought to full development when there is another primary rasa; only in such a case would there be non-conflict. (Dhvanyāloka 3.24)
Whether it be non-conflicting or conflicting, a rasa should not be brought to full development when another rasa is the primary element (the *aṅgin*); in that way, there will be non-conflict.

When there is a primary sentiment (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), which is manifested by the structure of the composition, any other sentiment—whether non-contradictory or contradictory—must not be allowed to reach full development. In that regard, the first way to avoid such development is this: the non-contradictory sentiment must not exceed the primary sentiment in intensity.
This is because even if their intensities were equal, no contradiction between them would arise.
For example: "the *locana* [is] non-contradictory or contradictory.

The intention behind the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) is this: when the excellence of another rasa is described in relation to the *aṅgirasa* (the principal rasa), then even if that other rasa is non-contradictory, its description would be objectionable.

However, if by means of reasoning it is possible to establish the subordinate status (*aṅgabhāva*) of the rasa within the principal (*aṅgin*), then even a contradictory rasa—when composed according to the application of distinctions of scope and so forth to be mentioned later—is not a source of defect.
Thus, contradiction and non-contradiction are irrelevant;
rather, the manner of placement alone is what must be considered.
In the word "aṅginī," the locative case is used in the sense of disregard.

Disregarding the specific aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) which is the primary constituent (*aṅgin*), he describes three ways in which its development may be neglected, starting with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*) and ending with "the third. Now, one might object: since it is stated that "deficiency must be avoided," what possibility is there for "excess," such that it is said that "excess must not be committed"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the case of superiority or equality.
"On one side the beloved weeps; on the other, the roar of the battle-drums."
The warrior's heart was tossed to and fro by affection and the passion for battle.
"This" (ayam) means that which is about to be described.
"In relation to" (apekṣayā) is connected with "superiority" (utkarṣe).
"Even that which is not opposed to him" means even that which is not opposed by Aṅgiras. "Aṅga" [is used here as an interjection].
The meaning is "by means of attaining the status of being a limb.
"Tat" means "in that case."
"Aṅginī" is a citation of the original term.
"Saptamī" means that the locative case is intended in the phrase "aṅgini rasāntare."
Regarding the term "anādara" (disregard):
the meaning is that the locative case is prescribed by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare* ("the genitive and [the locative] in the sense of disregard").
The phrase "rasāntarapada" is explained as "a specific type of rasa."
The phrase "having disregarded" (*anādṛtya*) is explained by "having set aside" (*nyakkṛtya*).
Regarding the statement "it should be said":
the meaning is that it must be stated that, in that case, the non-conflicting rasa should be made subordinate (*nyūnatva*) in relation to the rasa that is the primary constituent (*aṅgirasā*).
In the commentary, "of those two" means:
of the primary aesthetic flavor (rasa) and of another aesthetic flavor that is not in conflict with it.
As for "how": [it is explained as follows].
*Ekataḥ* means in one place;
*anyataḥ* means in another place. *Ḍolāyitam* means agitated by doubt.
‘From the neck’ means having cut [the serpent] from the neck;
‘having extracted Hāla from the neck’— here there is a metaphor (rūpaka) in the sense that he led away the lord of the venomous serpents by means of the very cord of his girdle.
Regarding the word "sandhyā":
it is understood that Sandhyā is the heroine (nāyikā).

By reason of the jealousy she felt toward her, the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati) was made to laugh; she is the one by whom the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), while serving Sandhyā, was thus caused to laugh.
The verse beginning with "hṛṣṭā santuṣṭā" has been interpolated;
it explains the equality of excellence (*utkarṣasāmya*) in the *Locana*: "he weeps," and so forth.
Thus, from this...
On one side his beloved weeps; on the other side is the roar of the battle-drums.
Through affection and the passion for combat, the warrior’s heart is tossed to and fro.

Or as it is said: "May that Goddess protect you all—she who was seen there while practicing her twilight rites, wearing a circle of rosary beads around her neck like a bracelet on her hand, having assumed the paryaṅka posture with the lord of serpents as the thread for her girdle, her indistinct laughter revealed by the quivering of her lips as she muttered false mantras, and who made even Paśupati laugh out of envy at her twilight devotion."
In this regard, there are two [possible interpretations]: first, that those [factors] contrary to Aṅgiras, being erratic, are not included in abundance;
or second, that even if they are included, the application of Aṅgiras’s rule regarding erratic factors follows immediately thereafter.
The word *locana* means "eye.
From the phrase "the beloved weeps," there is an intensification of the rasa of love (*rati*).
From the phrases "the drum of the nectar of rasa" and "of the warrior," there is an intensification of the rasa of energy (*utsāha*).
The phrase "it is swayed" expresses the equality of the two [the hero and the rival] through their lack of deficiency or excess;
however, some say that this applies only to the subject matter of independent verses (*muktaka*) and not to the subject matter of a continuous composition (*prabandha*), but that is incorrect,
because in the primary plots (*itivṛtta*) of major works, it is possible for the three aims of life (*trivarga*) to possess equal prominence as the fruit.

To explain: in the *Ratnāvalī*, with the intention that success depends upon the minister, the attainment of the sovereignty of the earth is the primary fruit (*adhikārika-phala*) and the acquisition of the jewel of a maiden is the incidental fruit (*prāsaṅgika-phala*); however, from the perspective of the hero (the king), the reverse is true. Thus, when these are unified according to the principle that "the fruit is the unity of the intentions of the master and the minister," it results precisely in equal primacy (*samaprādhānya*).

As it has been said: "By the effort of the poet, [the qualities] of the characters are appropriately [applied]. Enough with this digression; having thus defined the first type, he states the second: "The primary [element]," and so forth, ending with "non-inclusion."
The meaning is that it is expressed through the description of the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) consisting of weeping performed by the beloved, who has become a subordinate element (*aṅgabhūta*).
Regarding the phrase "the heightening of love" (*ratyutkarṣa*),
it is to be connected with the word "stated" (*ukta*) by means of transposition (*vipariṇāma*).
"Expressed" means manifested.
"Of those two" refers to the excellence of passion and the excellence of energy.
It is said that "equality has been stated.

Here, the rasa under discussion is the heroic (*vīra*), which is understood from the force of the phrase "of the warrior" (*bhaṭasya*); it is described with equal prominence alongside the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) which is not incompatible with it.

However, in the passage beginning with "from the throat," the rasa under discussion is the erotic-in-separation (*vipralambha*), and the comic (*hāsya*), which is not incompatible with it, is shown there with equal prominence.
"Etat" means that there is an equality of excellence between the two;
it refers exclusively to the subject matter of independent poetry (*muktaka*).
The meaning is "only in the case of independent verses" (*muktaka*).
Regarding the term *trivarga*: it means that which consists of the three aims of life (*trivarga*), namely the fruit; the sense is "of that which possesses equal primacy."
"It is indeed equal primacy"—the words "of the heroic (vīra) and the erotic (śṛṅgāra)" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
To complete the phrase "because of its placement as a subordinate element," he says: "being a subordinate member."
"Asau" (this) means that the rasa is a subordinate element (*aṅga*).
Furthermore, the third [type] consists of the repeated contemplation of the rasa as a subordinate element, even while that subordinate rasa is being brought to full development (*paripoṣa*).
In this manner, other varieties should also be inferred.
However, in the case of a conflicting rasa, its deficiency must be brought about in comparison with the rasa that serves as the subordinate element (*aṅga*),
such as that of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) when the tranquil (*śānta*) is the principal, or the tranquil when the erotic is the principal.

If it is asked, "How can that which is devoid of nourishment (paripoṣa) be a rasa?"—it has been stated here that this is with reference to the *aṅgin* (the principal). For the *rasa* that is the *aṅgin*—the word "rasa" being understood as the remainder—is what is meant. Anticipating the objection that "in this way, he [the opponent] would not be satisfied," he states another view: "or in its placement (*niveśane*)."
For this very reason, the use of the word "or" (*vā*) indicates the strengthening of the subsequent position (*uttarapakṣa*), not an option (*vikalpa*).
Thus, there is only one such method;
otherwise, there would be two.
The "pursuit" (*anusandhāna*) is the continuous following of that transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) which belongs to the dominant sentiment (*rasa*).

For example, in the verse beginning with *kopāt komala-lola*, anger is presented as a subordinate element within the dominant sentiment of love (*rati*); therein, there occurs the pursuit of the emotions appropriate to love—jealousy, longing, and joy—as evidenced by the expressions "having bound [her] firmly," "immediately weeping," and "laughing," which are introduced alongside the previously established resentment (*amarṣa*).
He states the third type with the words "as a subordinate element" (*aṅgatvena*).
In this regard, an example of the erotic sentiment of enjoyment (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) concerning Vatsarāja’s domain of Pajhavatī from the *Tāpasavatsarāja* should be cited.
[The phrase] "others also" refers to further examples.

Furthermore, one must not enhance the excitants (*vibhāva*) and ensuants (*anubhāva*) that are incompatible with the *Āṅgirasa* [sentiment], or else they should not be introduced at all; even if they have been introduced, they must be strengthened by the excitants and ensuants of the *Āṅgirasa*.
Even when the excitants and ensuants of a conflicting sentiment have been fully developed, their subordinate status must be restored, and so forth.
This can be inferred by oneself.

Having thus stated the manner that is common to both the contradictory and the non-contradictory, he further states another distinction—namely, the manner of avoiding the uncommon defects pertaining specifically to the contradictory subject—by saying:
"because the contradictory [element] is a subordinate part (aṅga) in the Rasa."
The connection with this [term] is through the word "upanibaddha" (bound/attached);
the meaning is that it is demonstrated by way of the *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations).
Regarding the word "tatra" (therein):
The meaning is "in anger";
that is to say, because of its deviation from that [state].
It should be cited as an example.
The sense is that it is a constituent part (*aṅga*) therein.
He explains the statement beginning with "others also" (*anye 'pi*) by saying "vibhāva," etc.;
this is a qualification of the term "of the excitants and ensuants" (*vibhāvānubhāvānām*), namely, "those that do not contradict the primary sentiment" (*aṅgirasavirodhinām*).
"Or even the settling [of the mind]"—
here, the two words ending in the genitive case are to be supplied.
"Even though it has been performed"— this means:
The word "niveśanam" (establishment) is to be supplied [from the preceding context].
"Aṅgi" means: having brought about the state of being of that single form—that which has the same nature as the *vibhāvas* and *anubhāvas* belonging to Aṅgiras. This is the meaning.

"Bṛhaṇīya" means nourishing. "Aṅgatvam" means they should be made to attend to their duties; they should be brought to a state of service. This refers to a mode that is common to both those who are opposed and those who are not.
The word "sambhavantam" (as it occurs) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the verb].

"Contradictory" (*virodhī*) means: by way of being contained within, that is, by way of being related to, that method of avoiding faults which has a contradictory object and is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). "Possible" (*sambhavī*) means:
Here he completes [the thought] with "pradhāna" and so forth;
in the commentary, it begins with "etacca" and so forth.
The connection is as follows: among compositions (*prabandhas*) containing many sentiments (*rasas*), this possession of relative excellence by a single sentiment cannot be denied.
Regarding the question of why [the relationship] cannot be rejected, it is stated here: "of the tastes," and so forth.
He explains this view with the words: "that which is to be benefited," and so forth.
"Otherwise" means:
To the extent that there is an absence of repose in one's own aesthetic wonder (*svacamatkāra*), to that same extent no further intensification (*paripoṣa*) of it should be attempted;
however, who can prevent an intensification that arises spontaneously?

Furthermore, this relative degree of excellence in a single rasa—even for one who does not accept the relationship of primary and subordinate among rasas within multi-rasa compositions—is impossible to deny. Thus [ends the passage].

In compositions where flavors (rasas) that are either non-contradictory or contradictory are combined through the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), there may be no contradiction.
And all of this is according to the view of the *Locana*, which holds that for those [theories], one flavor can serve as a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) for another flavor.
This is possible.
The phrase "because it does not contradict the principal [element]" is to be supplied as the remainder. And this means:
there is no relationship of beneficiary and benefactor among the *rasas*, because they rest solely in their own aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
Otherwise, it would be impossible for them to be *rasas*;

and even for those who hold the view that "in the absence of that [rasa], how could there be the relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgitā*)?", they too must admit that some *rasa* possesses excellence— that is, it pervades the majority of the composition— while others follow only a small portion of the composition, within the context of the structural arrangement of the plot.
This is because otherwise it would be logically untenable (*anyathānupapatti*).

Furthermore, if there were no connection whatsoever between the dominant sentiment (*rasa*), which pervades the entire composition, and other sentiments, then there would likewise be no connection for the plot (*itivṛtta*). If there is such a connection, it is precisely this relationship of the benefactor and the benefited (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*).
Nor is there any contradiction with the repose in the *sthāyibhāva* (the stable emotion), as was stated immediately prior; thus he says: "even by one who does not admit [this]."
The meaning is that he does not accept this on the basis of mere words; rather, he must be made to accept it even against his will.
However, another explains: the passage beginning with "And this is relative" refers to the second opinion, wherein there is no relationship of beneficiary and benefactor among the tastes.
For even there, predominance consists precisely in being more extensively pervaded by its function.

But this is incorrect; for in that case, the conclusion made by the word "all" in the phrase "and all this," which pertains to only one side, [would be undermined]—this is the meaning of the term *bālapriyā*. [The phrase] "the absence of that" refers to the absence of such predominance.

The meaning is the absence of the nature of rasa. As for the question "How can there be the relation of primary and subordinate?", it refers to the relation of primary and subordinate between two rasas.
The meaning is "how so?
The phrase "by them too" is connected with the word "must be admitted.
By the phrase "the excellence of some taste," the passage beginning with "this is relative" and so forth is explained.
He explains its preeminence with the words "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*) and so on.
The explanation of the phrase "incapable of being rejected" is "it must be accepted.
He states the reason for this with the words "the narrative" (*itivṛtta*) and so on.
Regarding the composition of the narrative based on past events (*itivṛttaghaṭanā*):

if one accepts this [position], then the relationship of mutual benefit between the benefactor and the beneficiary would also have to be accepted; thus he says "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*), etc., [and uses the word] "connection" (*saṅgati*).
The meaning is "connection.
"Tat" means "then."
"It would not exist"—
the term "connection" (*saṅgati*) is to be supplied here.
Nor is there any sense of wonder (*camatkāra*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that there is no contradiction whatsoever in resting within the marvelous (*camatkāra*). "He says that" means he speaks with that intention.
"By the word" means by mere speech;
"to be accepted" means [to be admitted].
"By means of reasoning" is the ellipsis. "The second view" means the view that will be stated later with the words "But in another view," and so forth.
"Of the flavors," and so forth; however, the intended meaning is "of those [flavors] accompanied by the transitory emotions" (sthāyibhāvas).
Regarding the phrase "even there":
The meaning is: "even in that opinion.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*) and so on:

the point is that, according to that view, being the primary element (*aṅgin*) consists in being pervaded by many narrative events, whereas being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) consists in being pervaded by few narrative events.
"By the word 'all'" means by employing the word "all.
"'Conclusion' (upasaṃhāra)" means...
The meaning is that this is a conclusion stated according to that [other] view.
"Regarding a single case" means that it concerns a single instance as stated: that one flavor [is the cause] of another flavor.

The introduction of the second position with the words "locanam matāntare 'pi" and so forth, which has this very position as its object, is extremely ill-fitting; therefore, enough of this protracted discussion with those of the former lineage.
Regarding the phrase "of whom":
at the conclusion of the *Bhāvādhyāya*, there is a verse: "Of many things combined together, that whose form is most frequent..."
That [rasa] should be considered the stable one (sthāyin); the remaining ones are regarded as transitory (sañcārin).
Thus,

some have explained that according to the sequence stated therein, the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) that pervades the primary narrative (*adhikāriketivṛtta*) necessarily appears as a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), whereas that which pertains to incidental episodes appears as a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*); consequently, at the time of aesthetic relish (*rasyamānatā*), there is no contradiction whatsoever between the permanent and transitory emotions.

And likewise, Bhāguri, having raised the objection as to whether there can be both a permanent (sthāyin) and a transitory (sañcārī) state for even the *rasas*, gave his answer by way of admission alone, saying, "Certainly, there is.

Others, however, maintain that even for a *rasa* that is recited as being permanent, there is the quality of being transitory within another *rasa*; just as anger (*krodha*), though recited as transitory in the Heroic (*vīra*) sentiment, possesses the very status of a permanent emotion within another *rasa*.
Just as *nirveda* (world-weariness), which manifests the knowledge of reality, is [classified as] *śānti* (tranquility);

or how even that which exists as a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) may, in relation to another transitory emotion, possess the very status of a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), as in the case of *unmāda* (madness) in the fourth act of the *Vikramorvaśīya*—it is to make this point understood that this verse was composed: "Among the many mental states that are *bhāvas*, that one which is most prevalent..."

They explain that form (rūpa) as it is perceived is the stable state (sthāyī bhāva), and that is the rasa, which is capable of being made into a liquid (sasīkaraṇayogya); the remaining ones, however, are the transitory states (sañcārin).
However, it is not stated that the *rasas* stand in a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgi*) by way of being the permanent (*sthāyin*) and transitory (*sañcārī*) emotions.

For this very reason, other readings such as *rasasthāyī* (with the genitive), *rasasthāyini* (with the locative), or *rasasthāyī* (with the accusative) in the sense of "resting upon" (*āśrita*) and so forth— along with the reading *bālapriyāḥ*—
are considered poorly constructed and are therefore rejected.
"Of many" means:
the ellipsis is "of many entities residing within [the self] that have come together";
the sense is "of specific modifications of the mind."
That state which, in the midst [of a composition], possesses a form that is abundant, extensive, and pervasive throughout the continuous flow,
is called the *sthāyī* (permanent) emotion (*rasa*).
The word division is *rasaḥ sthāyī* (the rasa is the stable emotion). The elision of the visarga is according to the rule *kharpare śari*.
The construction is: "That stable rasa is to be understood [as such]."
Regarding the word "the rest" (*śeṣā*): by transposition, it is to be connected with "the flavors" (*rasāḥ*). Demonstrating the meaning already stated, he says "therein," and so forth.
"In that [verse], by the sequence mentioned"—that is, by the sequence stated in that verse.
"At the time of being relished" (*rasyamānatā-samaye*); there is also a reading: "even during the state of being relished" (*rasyamānatāyām api*).
"Of the stable and transitory states" (sthāyivyabhicāribhāvasya);
the word "of the aesthetic flavors" (rasānām) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Thus it is said, and so forth.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that Bhāguri also spoke precisely by accepting [the existence of the suffix] with the word "certainly" (*bāḍham*).
He introduces the passage beginning with "another view" (*matāntara*) while demonstrating the justification for that opinion, starting with "others,
however" (*anye tu*) and ending with "Vīra" as a single sentence.
The second [section] should be understood as ending with "śānta," and the third as ending with "caturthe 'ṅke.
Regarding the word "unmādasya":
The phrase "in relation to initial mental application (vitarka) and so forth" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The explanation of the term "of those that are inherent" is "of states consisting of mental modifications.
The construction is: "that [state] is to be considered the stable emotion (sthāyin) and the aesthetic flavor (rasa)."
The explanation of "sthāyin" is "the permanent emotion" (sthāyibhāva). The explanation of "rasa" is "that which is fit for being aestheticized. The remaining [terms] are as follows.
The meaning is "other entities.
As for the phrase "but not," etc.,
the sense is that [they belong] only to those who abide.
The readings are *yuktā* and *uktā*.
[This refers to] "by the genitive," and so forth.
The intended meaning is that the analysis of the compound is "the stable emotion (sthāyin) which is the flavor (rasa) within the flavor (rasa).
This is stated according to that particular view;

however, according to another view, the stable emotions (bhāvas) are designated by the word "flavor" (rasa) through metaphorical usage, and their status as subordinate elements (aṅgatva) is entirely without contradiction.

Having thus established the general means of non-contradiction through the absorption of both non-conflicting and conflicting [emotions] into the dominant rasa existing as a continuum, the following is now stated to explain that same means specifically regarding the case of conflict: "But when a conflicting emotion that has a single locus should exist alongside a stable emotion (sthāyin), it must be made to have a different locus; even when such [an emotion] is nourished, there is no fault. (Dhvanyāloka 3.25)

However, that which is a contradiction residing in the same locus as the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) should be made to reside in a different locus; its cultivation also results in the absence of fault.
There are two types of contradiction: contradiction regarding a common substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya-virodhi*) and contradiction regarding immediate succession (*nairantarya-virodhi*).

In that context, regarding the dominant rasa (the *sthāyin*) which persists throughout the composition, any conflicting emotion (*virodhin*) that shares the same locus due to considerations of propriety (*aucitya*)—such as the Frightful (*bhayānaka*) rasa in relation to the Heroic (*vīra*)—must be placed in a different locus.
That is, the locus of the Hero, namely the protagonist of the story, must be assigned to the sphere of his adversary.

When this is done, even the intensification (*paripoṣa*) of that conflicting emotion is faultless; for in the description of an excess of fear directed toward an adversary, the Locana reads the compound *gami-gāmi-ādīnām*.
He says this with the words "even in another opinion" (matāntare 'pi) and "by the word *rasa*.

The meaning is: by that which is contained in the preceding kārikā, beginning with "the penetration of another rasa into the rasa currently under discussion" (*rasāntarasamāveśaḥ prastutasya rasasya yaḥ*). // 24 //
Now, concluding the common method and introducing the uncommon one, he says "thus" (evam).
"That" (tam) refers to the means for non-contradiction.
"Contradictory" (viruddha) [refers to the following].
The qualification contains the reason:

that which would be contradictory because its existence in a single substratum with another stable emotion (*sthāyin*) is impossible—such as fear [contradicted] by energy—that must be depicted as having different substrata, residing in the hero's adversary and so forth;
"of that" [is what is meant].

Even for that which is contrary [to the rule], when it is treated in such a manner and composed in such a way—as in the case of *gamyā* and so forth with respect to *āśrita* and so forth—the connection is with the phrase "or by the second [case-ending].
By this, the Vārttika "there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *gamyā* and so forth" from the sūtra *dvitīyā-āśrita-* etc., is recalled. // 24 //
"A common method" means a method that is common to both the contradictory and the non-contradictory, that is, a method for the means of non-contradiction.
"Concluding" means...
By this, the meaning of the function *pratipādya* (that which is to be established) ending with *ityanta* is shown.
[The term] *asādhāraṇa* (uncommon) refers exclusively to that which has a contradictory [object] as its domain.
By this, the meaning of the function *virodhiviṣaya eva* (only having a contradictory object as its domain) is shown.
"Contradictory" means "having a single locus that is contradictory. He explains the word "contradictory" with the words beginning with "permanent," and so forth.
That which has for its nature a single substratum that is not possible [otherwise]—
such is the stable emotion (*sthāyin*);
"of that" refers to it.
Explaining the meaning of that term, he says: "Even of its opposites," and so forth.
"Thus performed" means performed with distinct substrata.
This very point is further explained by the phrase: "of that which is not thus bound."
The excellence of the hero’s statesmanship, valor, and other qualities becomes most brilliantly illuminated.
This has been demonstrated with clarity in my *Arjunacarita* in the context of Arjuna’s descent into the netherworld (*pātāla*).

Thus, it has been shown how there is no contradiction when a stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), which otherwise opposes the primary sentiment (*rasa*) by sharing the same substratum, assumes the status of a subordinate element (*aṅga*) within the composition.
Regarding the second [type of rasa], however, it is stated in order to explain it:
"When based on a single substratum, there is no fault; when occurring in uninterrupted succession, there is a contradiction.
Therefore, a rasa should be manifested by one of keen intellect through the intervention of another rasa. (Dhvanyāloka 3.26)
When there is a single substratum, there is no fault; however, in the case of uninterrupted succession, there is a contradiction.
Therefore, a rasa should be suggested by a wise person through the intervention of another rasa. (26)

Furthermore, that which is non-contradictory when there is a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatva*), yet contradictory in the case of immediate succession (*nairantarya*), is [resolved] by the intervention of another rasa (*rasāntara*). This is because the eye [of the poem] is nourished; on the contrary, faultlessness arises from the enhancement of the hero's excellence, whereas the lack of such nourishment is indeed a defect.
The word "api" (even/furthermore) is to be understood as displaced in its position [i.e., it should be construed with "doṣa eva"].
The same applies to the *vṛtti* as well, because of the explanation.
"Co-location" (*aikādhikaraṇya*) is merely a connection with a single substratum; by that, there is a contradiction, for example, between fear and enthusiasm.

Even when they share a single substratum, it is possible for one to be incompatible with another due to their extreme proximity and lack of interval, as in the case of world-weariness (*nirveda*) being incompatible with erotic passion (*rati*).
This has been demonstrated.
"When the terrifying twang of Kirīṭin’s bow arose, a great panic seized the city of the enemies of Purandara," and so forth. // 25 //
"Of the second" means of that which is opposed to immediate succession.
"That" refers to [the aforementioned].

"Non-contradictoriness" (*nirvirodhitva*)— meaning "there is no fault in the lack of full development because they share a single substratum"— is explained by the passage beginning with "on the contrary," etc.
He states the meaning to be understood by the passage beginning with "as for the lack of full development," etc.

Regarding the word "api" (also/even): the meaning is that the word "api" is used [in the phrase] "there is no fault even in the case of nourishment. Regarding the phrase "from the commentary": [it refers to the following].
The meaning is that this is because of the commentary stating, "even for its opposite.

Thus, by explaining the verse (*kārikā*) through the commentary (*vṛtti*) passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*), he has shown that only the first part—beginning with "opposing the same substratum" (*aikādhikaraṇya-virodhī*)—is sufficient to dispel fear.
He now explains the phrase "opposing contiguity" (*nairantarya-virodhī*) with the words beginning with "one" (*eka*).
The connection is that even though they share a single substratum (*ekāśrayatva*), something [specific] is incompatible due to its being immediate (*nirantaratvena*).
The explanation of "due to its being immediate" is "by way of being without an interval" (*nirvyavadhānatvena*).
[The term] "arisen together" (*samutthita*) [is used].
The second half [of the verse] is: “At the sound of that, the life of all the wives of the Daityas, their bonds having been severed, grew slack.
The connection is with “the sound of the bow of Kirīṭin,” that is, Arjuna;
[it refers to] the Asuras, the enemies of Purandara.
This is a brief explanation of *upaplava* itself, beginning with the words "by hearing," and so forth. // 25 //

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "contradictory to having a common substratum" (*aikādhikaraṇyavirodhin*) is connected with the phrase "absence of contradiction when entering into the state of being a subordinate factor" (*aṅgabhāvagamane nirvirodhitvam*).

In the verse (*kārikā*), the locative case in both instances—"in having a single substratum" (*ekāśrayatve*) and "in continuity" (*nairantarye*)—is intended to signify the "cause" (*nimitta*); with this intention, he explains [the verse] as beginning with "by virtue of having a single substratum," etc. (*ekāśrayatvena*, etc.).
The explanation of the term *nirdeśa* is "not contradictory";
it should be inserted into the composition,
just as the sentiments of tranquility (*śānta*) and the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) are inserted in the *Nāgānanda*.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: a definition [of contradiction] based on proximity (*nimitta*) is not contradictory; rather, that which encounters contradiction through the proximity of two such mutually opposed sentiments (*rasa*) should be composed by inserting another sentiment in between them.
The term "composition" (*prabandha*) is used here with reference to its abundance.
This might also sometimes occur even in the case of independent verses (*muktaka*), as he will say: "even in the case of two [words] situated in a single sentence.
For example:

For in that [drama], beginning from the introduction with the verse, "I know it is the seat of passion, yet I have no conviction that it will perish," and continuing until the conclusion consisting of the gift of his body for the sake of another, the *śānta* (quiescent) rasa is present; the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa directed toward Malayavatī is its opposite. Therefore, the poet, intending to maintain a gradual progression by interposing the *adbhuta* (marvelous) rasa—which is not incompatible with either—[placed it] in between.
It was composed with the thought, "Oh, what a song! Oh, what music!
