For this very purpose, even that which is mostly devoid of flavor, such as the verse beginning "The manifestation [of the soul] by means of the manifesting element," is rendered exceedingly sweet here by virtue of its capacity to nourish the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*).
Thus it is said: "Maidens who perceive no faults [in this] regard this—[the composition]—which has human goals as its cause, as a result of the connection between the sign and the indicated."

And immediately following, there is the episode concerning the crest-jewel (*śekharaka*), which is assisted by the rasa of humor arising from the connection between the cause and its effect; this is opposed by the episode concerning the sight of the mass of bones in the carcasses of the female nāgas and so forth, which nourishes detachment (*vairāgya*) and tranquility (*śama*).
The explanation of the phrase "possessing opposition" (*virodhavān*) is: "it goes toward opposition" (*virodham eti*).
He explains the second half [of the verse] with the words beginning "sa" (he), etc.
Regarding the phrase "prabandha iti":
the meaning is that the mention of "prabandha" (continuity) is intended in the context of "it should be established within the continuity."
He explains how Śānta and Śṛṅgāra are established in the *Nāgānanda* with the words "Therein," and so forth.
The meaning is: "from that [point] which was introduced by the passage beginning with 'Thus,' etc.
The word "para" means...
The meaning is that the culmination consists in the surrender of one's body for the sake of others, which is the very essence [of the sentiment].
Regarding the phrase "the sentiment of tranquility (śānta)," the word "composed" (nibaddha) is to be supplied.
As for the words "of that," and so forth:
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "having made the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) the internal subject, it is composed. Regarding "in sequence" (*krama*):
the meaning is "by means of that intention (*abhiprāya*) which consists of the imagining of the gradual expansion—that is, the spreading of the erotic sentiment in the form of *rati*—upon the hero."
The connection is with the phrase "composed as follows" (*ityādinibaddham*).
Regarding the words "and thus" (*iti ca*):
the sense is that by stating "maidens who perceive no faults," the speaker reveals the manner in which passion does not arise within him.

Regarding the term *cittavṛtti*: it refers either to those outflows (*prasara*) of mental fluctuations such as passion and so forth, or to those objects (*viṣaya*) toward which there is an outflow of mental fluctuations; in these cases, *prasaṃkhyāna* is the discernment that perceives their defects.
Those for whom that alone is wealth;
he states their words beginning with "puruṣārtha" and so forth.
This is the first half of a verse from the Sāṃkhyakārikā.
"The subtle body (liṅga) exists like an actor due to its connection with the omnipresence of primordial nature (prakṛti)"—this is for the sake of the subsequent meaning.

"By way of the occasion" (nimitta) refers to dharma and so forth; "the occasioned" (naimittika) refers to the gross body and so forth, which are the effects of dharma and so forth. Through their "connection" (prasaṅga), that is, through their relationship, "this subtle body" (liṅga) [functions].
"It functions like an actor": just as an actor engages in activity by assuming various forms, so too does [the Self] engage in activity by assuming the bodies of gods and others.
For what purpose? To this he says: "for the sake of the person's goal" (*puruṣārthe*). This means: having the fruit that is the goal of the person.

The meaning is that, by the force of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) for various enjoyments, he conducts himself in such a manner solely for the sake of those respective enjoyments. To the question "From where does he derive such power? he says: "In the case of Prakṛti," and so forth.
This is its explanation.
And that nourishment which consists of the bliss of the exhaustion of craving (*tṛṣṇākṣaya*) is indeed perceived as having the characteristic of peace (*śānta*).

Thus it has been said: Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the exhaustion of craving.

The glance of Mitravasu—who had entered [the palace] and caused Malayavatī to depart—is described by the words beginning with "creeping forth on all sides. This [glance], though intervened by the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) aided by the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of anger as depicted in the poem, is nevertheless introduced [into the context]. Now, one might object: "There is no such thing as the *śānta* (quiescent) sentiment; for the Sage [Bharata] did not even teach its permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And the *śānta*..."

The destruction of cravings—that is, desires for sense objects—which consists in total cessation and is characterized by world-weariness (*nirveda*), is itself bliss; the nourishment of that very [bliss], which constitutes its state of being relished, is the defining characteristic of the *śānta* (peaceful) rasa. It is indeed perceived as such.
This is indeed conceivable through one's own experience at the time when the expansion of all desires for objects, such as food and so forth, has ceased.

Others, however, consider that the subsidence of all mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) alone is its stable state (*sthāyin*); for if the existence of craving were of the nature of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), it would lack the status of a mental fluctuation, and thus could not be a positive entity (*bhāva*).
But in the case of *paryudāsa* (presuppositional negation), this belongs precisely to our own position.
It should be understood that this statement supports the point that the attainment of those respective human goals, such as desire and so forth, occurs only in a gradual sequence.
Thus it is "established."
This point is clear to those of refined sensibility who observe the *Nāgānanda* drama:
that *nirveda* (dispassion) is of the nature of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Being of the nature of cessation, it is the cause of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*).
"Disgust" (nirveda) means the cognition of objects as things to be abandoned, produced by the knowledge of reality;
or alternatively, it means having the form of withdrawal from everything.
The meaning is that its nature consists in the withdrawal of the mind from all objects.
"Withdrawal" (nivṛtti) is a particular modification of the mind.
[This refers to] "of that which has become the stable state."
This is the explanation of the portion ending with "of pleasure.
The connection is: "that nourishment which is produced by being relished.
[The word] "ceased" (nivṛtta) [is used].

"From which person the expansion of desire for all objects such as food has ceased—that state of being is its 'tattva' (reality); or there is a reading: 'at the time of its expansion' (*prasarakāle*). It is 'conceived,' meaning it is known. Some say that tranquility (*śama*) is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*)."
He states that opinion: "Another [says]... and "Of all...
The meaning is that the "subsidence" (*praśama*) of all mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*), such as passion (*rati*) and so forth, is their complete cessation (*prakarṣeṇa śama*).
The meaning of the term "the destruction of craving" (tṛṣṇākṣaya) is also this very thing; such is the sense.
"Of this" means "of the one who is at peace."
Showing the fault if one intends by the phrase "the subsiding of all mental fluctuations" (*sarvacittavṛttipraśama*) the non-existence of all mental fluctuations, he says "thirst," and so forth.

This refers to the state of being the absolute non-existence—that is, the non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—of the existence and proliferation of all those mental fluctuations that are thirst;
the words "of the referent of the term 'subsiding of all mental fluctuations'" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
"By way of the absence of mental activity"—
the meaning is "because it is of the nature of non-existence.
[This is stated] because it is impossible for it to be an existent entity (bhāva).
The meaning is: because it is impossible for it to be included within [the category of] entities (*bhāva*).
Regarding the term "exclusion" (*paryudāsa*), the words "in what is intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣite*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The meaning is: when the sense is intended according to the principle of *paryudāsa* (exclusion). Just as the word "non-dharma" (*adharma*) has as its meaning a sin that is the opposite of dharma, so too the word "cessation of craving" (*tṛṣṇākṣaya*) or the word "pacification of all mental fluctuations" (*sarvacittavṛttipraśama*) has as its meaning that which is opposed to all mental fluctuations; [this is] the vision [of the truth]. Others, however, [say]: "Having encountered their respective causes, a state arises from [what was previously] tranquil."
But when the signs have further subsided, it dissolves into peace itself.

Having observed this *bharatavākya*, those who describe the *śānta* as having the nature of being common to all aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) consider the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the *śānta* to consist of a mental state in which no other specific [emotional] fluctuations have arisen. This view is not very far from our own position;
however, the distinction lies in whether it is characterized by antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).
And the destruction of cravings alone is logical, as it has been said: "Because birth is not observed in one who is free from passion.
This is indeed perceived.
Even the Sage himself accepts this when he says, "In some cases there is tranquility," and so forth.
Nor should his final state be described in such a way that, due to the cessation of all activity, it would become unperceivable for lack of manifesting emotions (anubhāvas).

Even for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, there is indeed a state of being undescribable at the stage of the fruit; however, at the preceding stage, it is said: "Its flow becomes tranquil due to latent impressions (*saṃskāra*);

during the interruptions of that [flow], other cognitions arise from latent impressions. This means that if a specific modification of the mental state (*cittavṛtti-viśeṣa*) is intended to be expressed, then this [point] belongs precisely to our own position.
The intended meaning is that [the term] culminates specifically in a particular mental state characterized by world-weariness (*nirveda*).
Regarding the phrase "each its own":
this verse is located in the final section of the sixth chapter.
The verse preceding this is as follows: "States such as passion (*rati*) and the rest are modifications (*vikāra*); the tranquil state, however, is considered the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
A modification born from the primordial nature dissolves back into that very same [nature]."
Thus:
"one's own" (*sva*) means belonging to oneself (*svīya*).

The "sign" (nimitta) is the form of a woman and so forth. "State" (bhāva) refers to passion and the like, arising from the internal organ (antahkaraṇa), which is the unchanging and quiescent primordial nature (prakṛti).
It conforms;

that is to say, it takes the form of that mental modification which has not produced any distinction [from its object], which does not depend on external objects such as women and the like, and which is internal, having the self as its object.
"Etad" means "the aforementioned view.
Regarding the phrase "not excessively," and so forth:
The meaning is that it is proximate to our own position.
Regarding the phrase "prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*):

the meaning is that while this [opponent's] position culminates in the prior non-existence of all mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*), our position, however, consists in the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of all mental modifications; such is the distinction.
"Yuktaśca" and so forth;
the meaning is that the position of the total destruction of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) alone is logical.
"As it has been said" refers to [the following].
The meaning is that it has been stated that there is the total destruction of all cravings; the author of the Nyāya Sūtras is the one who said this—this is the ellipsis. [The term] "vīta" [is used].
This is the sūtra located in the first section (āhnika) of the third chapter:
because birth is not observed in one who is free from passion— that is, devoid of passion and the like— therefore birth does not occur.
Therefore, this is the meaning;
however, the intention is that birth occurs only for one who possesses passion (*sarāga*).
This [argument] serves as a proof for the permanence of the self (*ātman*).
He explains "it is indeed understood" in another way, beginning with "by the Sage," and so forth. The grammatical connection is "by the Sage speaking.
The sense is that here the word *śama* (tranquility) refers, through its etymological derivation (*yoga*), to supreme world-weariness (*nirveda*).
For the cessation of activity and so forth are to be described as the *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) of one who is tranquil, yet they are not suitable for actual practice.
Therefore, some say that [the tranquil person] is not perceived by means of such *anubhāvas*;
in order to refute that view, he says "And not... and so forth.
"Tadīyā" means belonging to the peaceful;
it refers to the final state, which is the state of being free from activity.
"Being unperceived" refers to that which is "quiescent"— this is the ellipsis. "In the stage of the fruit" means:
The meaning is: "in the state of being in love.
Regarding the phrase "on the previous stage," etc., the connection is as follows: on the previous stage, even for one who is tranquil, the movements of Janaka and others are seen.

The observation of the mind’s states, such as agitation (*kṣipta*) and so forth, according to the principle of these two sūtras, consists of various activities like observances (*yama*) and restraints (*niyama*), or even the lack of such characteristics due to bearing the burden of royal power; this is indeed seen even in calm individuals such as Janaka and others.

Thus, because of the presence of the *anubhāvas* (consequent manifestations) and the existence of many transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) that are possible within the context of observances, restraints, and so forth, [the stable emotion] is certainly perceived.
If it is argued: "But it is not perceived, for its *vibhāvas* (determinant causes) do not exist"—we say: no.
This [permanent emotion] is indeed perceived;

and it must necessarily arise from such factors as the ripening of prior wholesome karma, the grace of the Supreme Lord, the study of secret treatises on the inner self, and the cultivation of those free from passion.
By this much alone, the existence of the determinants (vibhāva), consequents (anubhāva), and transitory states (vyabhicārin), as well as the permanent emotion (sthāyin), is demonstrated.
But surely, in that case, because there is an absence of resonance with the heart (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*), the very status of being relished (*rasyamānatā*) is untenable.
Who says that it does not exist?
For it has been stated that it is indeed perceived.

Is it not the case that for everyone, [the erotic sentiment] is not an object of praise? Then, for those free from passion (*vītarāga*), the erotic is not [pleasing]; these various states are called "stages" (*bhūmi*). These stages are dear to the ignorant (*bāla*).
Thus, the various conditions are termed "stages."
"Extremely tranquil," and so forth:

"From the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of its flowing in a state of extreme tranquility, other cognitions arise from those impressions during its interruptions"— these are [the words] from the *Yoga Sūtra*.

Regarding the first [of these], this is the *Bhojavṛtti*: "From the aforementioned cultivation of the cessation of that mind, there arises a state of tranquil flow; the meaning is that the mind becomes a transformation consisting of a similar stream due to the removal of distraction.
This sūtra is in the third chapter (*pāda*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "In the intervals of that," etc., this is the *Bhoja-vṛtti* on the fourth [sūtra]: "For one established in that samādhi, those other cognitions which arise in the intervals— that is, during the gaps— as forms of emergence (*vyutthāna*),
occur even though they are being diminished by the previously existing saṃskāras born from the experience of emergence, which take the form of 'I' and 'mine'."
"Citrākārā" means "wonder-inspiring.
"Rājya," etc., [follows].
The word "activity" (*ceṣṭā*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].

Here, the distinction is that during the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is activity such as restraint (*yama*), whereas at the time of emergence (*vyutthāna*), there is activity such as bearing the burden of sovereignty.
Regarding the phrase "of Janaka and others":
The great king Janaka is renowned as a mahāyogin;
the word "iti" indicates the reason;
"yamā" refers to [the restraint].

The meaning is: because of the possibility of those numerous transitory mental states—such as intelligence, fortitude, memory, and so forth—which may arise in the midst or interval between the limbs of yoga, beginning with the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama).
[This] is indeed perceived.
The word "rasa" (sentiment) is to be understood as "peaceful" (*śānta*); this is the remainder [of the sentence].
He raises an objection with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*), etc.; [the objection is] "But it is not perceived."
The word "peaceful" (*śānta*) is to be supplied [as the predicate].
To the question "Why?", he says: "Not of this," and so forth. He provides the resolution: "No."
Regarding the question "What are the excitants (vibhāvas)? he says: "Of that," and so forth.
The grammatical connection (anvaya) is that there must necessarily be excitants for that [rasa].
He states them as: "The former," and so forth.

The meaning is: by means of such factors as the ripening of past virtuous deeds and good actions, the grace of the Supreme Lord, and the thorough study of the secret spiritual scriptures such as Vedānta and the like, as well as among those free from passion;
thus he concludes with the words "iti" and so forth.
"By this much alone" means precisely by the manner already described.
He raises an objection with "But surely" (nanu);
therein, [the word] "in the peaceful" (śānte) refers to the heart (hṛdaya).
The word "of the practitioners" (*pratipattṝṇām*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He provides the response: "What?
[meaning] that "it has been stated" refers to the resonance within the heart (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*).

The word "by the author of the commentary" (*vṛttikṛtā*) is to be supplied as the remainder. He introduces the passage beginning with "If indeed... (*yadi nāma...*) with the words "Now, [it may be objected]... (*nanu...*).
The word "is perceived" (*pratīyate*) has "as tranquil" (*śāntaḥ*) supplied as the remainder.
He states a distinction with the words "of all.
He provides an answer by way of a counter-objection with the words "then," and so forth.
He says that even that *śṛṅgāra* [rasa] is such.
The meaning is that he spoke with that intention in mind.
As for the passage beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*):

even if this person, who is preeminent in virtue, does not possess a sphere of experience accessible to all people, it does not follow from this alone that his extraordinary state of mind—a great power common to the world—can be rejected.
Nor is it appropriate to include heroism within that [equanimity],
because the former is established as being composed of pride (*abhimāna*),
whereas this [heroism] exists as having the singular nature of the pacification of ego-grasping (*ahaṅkāra*).

And even though such a distinction exists between these two, if they were to be identical—such that the eye were praiseworthy, then it too would fall from the status of being a rasa—he says: "When indeed... [and so on].
Now, one might suspect that this is simply the Heroic rasa (vīra) where dharma is predominant; anticipating this, he says: "Not so," and "of that," etc.
"Of the hero," [meaning] "by virtue of consisting of self-conceit"; for the meaning is that *prāṇa* is indeed *utsāha* (enthusiasm), in the sense of "I am of such a kind."
"And of this" refers to the peaceful one. "And of those two" means:
even though these two are absolutely contradictory by virtue of being free from affliction (*āmaya*) and free from effort (*nirīha*), such is the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*).
Furthermore, there is no absolute contradiction between the heroic (vīra) and the fierce (raudra) sentiments;
they share the same form in their utility for the acquisition of virtue (dharma), wealth (artha), and pleasure (kāma).
But if this is so, would it not follow that the compassionate hero (dayāvīra), the virtuous hero (dharmavīra), or the generous hero (dānavīra) are nothing at all?
This is merely another name for tranquility (śānta) itself;

for thus the Sage [Brahmā] said: "Brahmā has declared that there are three types of heroes: the hero of generosity (dānavīra), the hero of righteousness (dharmavīra), and likewise the hero of battle (yuddhavīra), as well as the hero of aesthetic sentiment (rasavīra)."
The connection is that "the hero is dear to the simple-minded. This "he" refers to the peaceful hero, whose primary concern is dharma; thus he is the "dharma-hero.
The phrase "iti" and so forth [indicates the end of the definition].
The meaning is that, while entertaining such a doubt, he speaks in order to dispel it;
this is indicated in the commentary by the words "na ca" and so forth.
"Vīre" refers to the hero of dharma.
The connection is that it is not appropriate for "him," who is peaceful;
"him" means the hero.
"By being composed of conceit (*abhimāna*), by being composed of pride (*garva*).
He explains this point in the *Locana*: "For enthusiasm (*utsāha*)... and so forth.
Enthusiasm (*utsāha*) has heroism as its stable emotional state (*sthāyibhāva*).
The meaning of the phrase "one whose life-force is such" and so forth is that his very life is the cognition [that] "I am capable of accomplishing all this," and so on.
Regarding the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "of those two," he states the purpose [of using it] with the words "here" (*iha*), and so forth.
He explains what was stated—that the same [consequence] would apply to the *vīra* and *raudra* rasas as well—starting with the words "of the *vīra* and *raudra*" and so forth.
Regarding the word "dharma":
the meaning is that the utility and the common nature of the acquisition of dharma, artha, and kāma are likewise present.
The intended meaning is that, for this reason, there would be identity between those two.
He introduces the passage beginning with "dayāvīrādīnām" (of the heroic, the compassionate, and so forth) with the words "nanu" and so on;
that is, if one accepts the distinction between the heroic (*vīra*) and the peaceful (*śānta*) sentiments according to the manner previously stated.
"Dayāvīra," and so forth.
The meaning is that a "dayāvīra" (hero of compassion) is included within either the category of *dharmavīra* (hero of righteousness) or the category of *dānavīra* (hero of generosity).
Immediately after the term "dayāvīra," there is also the reading: "Who is designated [as such]? (*ko 'bhidhīyatām*).
He replies with the words "not that one," and so forth.
The term "hero of compassion" (*dayāvīra*) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. This means:
"not any such person."
The meaning is that he is neither a hero of righteousness (*dharmavīra*) nor a hero of generosity (*dānavīra*).
To the question "What, then, is his nature?", he says: "Of one who is peaceful," and so forth; this refers to the hero of compassion (*dayāvīra*).
The meaning is that the "hero of compassion" (dayāvīra) is merely another name for the "peaceful" (śānta), as he is included within the peaceful type itself.
Why? He cites the authoritative statement of the Sage [the Buddha] with the words "tathā" and so forth;
that is to say, "for thus... (tathāhi).
The meaning is: "because of the internal state of being peaceful in the hero of generosity" (dānavīra); this connects with the phrase "he declared it to be of three kinds.
Regarding "the hero of generosity" (dānavīra) and "conforming to the threefold [nature]": [this refers to the classification].
The meaning is that it is divided into three kinds.

If it were so conceived, the same consequence would apply to the heroic (*vīra*) and the furious (*raudra*) sentiments as well. Furthermore, because specific mental states such as the compassionate hero (*dayāvīra*) and others are entirely devoid of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), they are varieties of the peaceful sentiment (*śāntarasa*).
Otherwise, however, if it were established that [the peaceful sentiment] is merely a sub-variety of the heroic (*vīra*), there would be no contradiction.
Thus, the peaceful sentiment (*śānta-rasa*) exists;

and in a literary composition (*prabandha*), even when there is an intrusion of conflicting sentiments, it remains free from contradiction provided there is an intervention by a non-conflicting sentiment.
Regarding the subject matter as it has been demonstrated,
[the author] declared that there are exactly three types, preceded by scriptural authority (āgama), beginning with the term "the eye" (locana).
He states this by including the phrase "and of the heroic (vīra) sentiment of compassion (dayā) and so forth."
Because it consists of a loathing for sense objects, its inclusion within the *bībhatsa* (the disgusting) might be suspected;
however, that [disgust] is merely a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) for this [sentiment], and does not attain the status of a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*),
because at the final consummation, it is severed from its very root.
However, the author of the *Candrikā* maintains that the sentiment of tranquility (*śānta-rasa*) should not be composed as a dominant theme;
yet this point has not been examined by us here, due to the constraints of another context.
Furthermore, because it has liberation as its fruit and is grounded in the supreme human goal, this [poetry] is the most preeminent among all aesthetic flavors (*rasas*).

This very point was established by our teacher, Bhaṭṭatauta, in his *Kāvyakautuka*, and by us in our commentary on it, through extensive deliberations regarding prima facie arguments and final conclusions; so, enough of further elaboration. // 26 //
The phrase "preceded by the Āgamas" means that the intention is [to show] because it is stated, "Brahmā said.
By the restrictive particle *eva* in the expression "only the threefold nature," the exclusion of the *dayāvīra* (heroic compassion) is intended.
"He says that" means he says it with the aforementioned intention.

Immediately after the phrase "and of the compassionate-heroic [rasas] and so forth," the reading "by means of the word 'and so forth' (*ādi-grahaṇena*) before the word 'object' (*viṣaya*)," etc., is seen in all extant manuscripts.
Furthermore, since a connection with "of that object" (*tasya ca viṣaya*) and so forth is not tenable, it should be understood that the inclusion here is of the Dharma-vīra and Dāna-vīra;
or rather, it should be understood that the text should be read accordingly.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "of the specific modifications of the mind" (*cittavṛttiviśeṣāṇām*) is used.
The word "being chewed" (*carvyamāṇānām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Heroic compassion" (*dayāvīra*) is the energy (*utsāha*) consisting of the effort to desire the welfare of others.
"In every way" (*sarvākāram*) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
The meaning is "in every respect.
In the phrase "by virtue of being devoid of the notion of 'I'," the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the reason;
furthermore, the reading is *rahitatve* (in the state of being devoid).
The word "of the hero" (nāyakasya) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Otherwise," that is, if it were accompanied by egoism (ahaṅkāra).
Some maintain that because the tranquil (śānta) has the nature of loathing for sense-objects, it is included within the loathsome (bībhatsa).

In the *Locana*, he refutes that opinion incidentally with the words beginning "viṣaya" and so forth. The phrase "because it consists of a loathing for objects" implies the word "of the tranquil one" (*śāntasya*).
"Of this" means "or there is a subtraction";
"is suspected" implies that "by some" is the ellipsis.
He says "in reality it is not so" with the words "But that," and so forth.
That refers to the aversion;
"of this" refers to the peaceful one.
Regarding that disgust (*jugupsā*),
he says "liberation," etc., to show that peace (*śānta*) possesses superiority over all other aesthetic flavors (*rasa*).
And as for "that":
"Peaceful" is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "abundant," etc.: he is one for whom the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) have been determined and investigated to the greatest possible extent. // 26 //
To confirm this very point, it is said:
"For even when two sentiments reside within a single sentence, their mutual opposition ceases once they are separated by another sentiment. (Dhvanyāloka 3.27)
For even when two sentiments are situated within the same sentence, their mutual opposition ceases once they are separated by another sentiment. (27)
There is no doubt that the contradiction between two sentiments situated within a single composition is removed when they are separated by another sentiment;
for, according to the principle already stated, even two sentiments existing within a single sentence have their contradiction removed.
As, for example: "Those whose arms were perfumed by the pollen of fresh *parijāta* garlands, and who were smeared with the dust of the earth..."
They were being closely embraced by female jackals, while the spaces between their arms were clung to by celestial nymphs.
They were fanned by the quivering wings of flesh-eating birds, dripping with blood from their own bodies,
and were cooled by the sprinkling of fragrant sandalwood water and the silken garments of the wish-fulfilling vines.
Seated upon the couches within their celestial palaces, the heroes, overcome by curiosity,
beheld their own fallen bodies as they were being pointed out by the fingers of the women.
"In order to stabilize the eye" means "in the mind of the disciple.
By the word "also" (api), he shows that this meaning is established as the subject matter of the treatise—namely, [the verse beginning] "bhūreṇu... (with dust of the earth...).
By the qualifying attributes, it has been stated that being utterly remote is a ground for the impossibility [of identification].
By the word "svadeha" (one's own body), through the very conceit of being the body, there exists a common substratum (*ekāśrayatva*) because the possibility of identity is established;
this is indicated by the particle "api" (even).
The meaning is that by the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even when situated in a single sentence.
In the *Vṛtti*, it says: "O you whose dust is abundant," and so forth.
This has also been cited as an example in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
The connection is that the heroes saw their own fallen bodies.
There is one qualifying attribute for the bodies and another for the heroes, which contain the cause of their curiosity in due order:
"dīgdhān" means pervaded, and "vāsitaiḥ" [means scented].
The meaning is "made fragrant.
"The middle of the arm" refers to the chest.
"Of the flesh-eaters" means of those who consume meat.
[It was] such that it was sprinkled with waters of sandalwood;
[it was adorned] with "kalpalatā-dukūlas," meaning silken garments produced from the wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā),
or alternatively, the kalpalatās themselves serving as the fine silk fabrics (dukūla).
"Lalanāḥ" refers to celestial courtesans.
"By the qualifiers of the eyes"—
this means by the qualifiers of the body, such as "with the dust of the earth," and so forth.
The "ground of impossibility" (*asambhāvanāspada*) is the cause for the absence of the possibility of ownership;
"being far removed" (*dūrāpetatva*) means being extremely distant, that is to say, having an absolute difference in nature. This has been stated and suggested.

Is it not the case that there is a contradiction between the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) only when they have the same object and the same substratum, since joy (*rati*) and disgust (*jugupsā*) cannot arise in one person toward the same thing at the same time?

And in the present instance, because the earth is smeared [with blood], the loathsome sentiment has as its substratum the body of a hero in his unqualified state, whereas the erotic has as its substratum the body of a hero qualified by his divinity.

Anticipating the doubt as to how these two [emotions] can have a single object (*ālambana*), a single form (*ākāra*), and a single substratum (*āśraya*)— regarding the erotic sentiment— he says "his own," and so forth.
"Due to the conceit of being the body" means that for heroes, there is the perception of their own bodies even in the fallen bodies [of others].

In such passages as these, for instance, the coexistence of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) rasas, or their respective constituents (*aṅga*), is not contradictory when mediated by the heroic (*vīra*) rasa. One should determine contradiction and non-contradiction in all cases in this manner.
But specifically in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), this [poetic style] is indeed most delicate.
One should thus determine contradiction and non-contradiction everywhere;
however, this is especially necessary in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), for that is most delicate. (28)

Following the characteristics as they have been stated, a connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*) should determine the presence or absence of contradiction among all the *rasas*, both within a literary composition and elsewhere;
this is especially true in the case of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa.

For that [rasa] consists essentially in the nourishment of love (*rati*), and since love has the eye as its object, what contradiction could there be [between it and the eyes]? Otherwise, because their objects would be different, how could there be any contradiction?
Is it not the case that here the rasa is indeed the heroic (vīra), and not the erotic (śṛṅgāra) or the loathsome (bībhatsa)?
For it is love (rati) and disgust (jugupsā) that function as transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva) toward the hero.
Let it be so.
Nevertheless, the status of being the present example is indeed appropriate. Thus he says: "or rather, of its two limbs.
The meaning is: "the two stable emotions (sthāyibhāva) residing in those two limbs."
Regarding the phrase "by the heroic sentiment" (*vīrarasena*):

the point is that through the understanding of their enthusiasm and so forth—expressed by the words "the heroes [gave] their own bodies" (*vīrāḥ svadehān*) and so on—the agent and the object are perceived as following throughout the entire meaning of the sentence. Thus, even in the absence of the middle position [of the word], the heroic sentiment is all the more an interposer (*vyavadhāyaka*). This is the intended sense. // 27 //
The phrase "in other cases as well" refers to independent verses (*muktaka*) and so forth.
The connection is that this *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) is the most delicate (*sukumāratama*).

The sense is that the term "delicate" (*sukumāra*) refers to a specific class of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and the author uses his own word [to denote it] for the purpose of demonstrating this; such is the intended meaning.
The term "tādātmya" (identity) means the complete accomplishment of the cognizer's notion of oneness between the two bodies.

Thus, the intended meaning is that for one who identifies with the unity of the two bodies, the single heroic subject (*vīra*) is the common locus for both the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) sentiments arising from the celestial nymphs.
He introduces the passage beginning with "Or rather, in its limbs" (*tadaṅgayorvā*) with the words "Now, however" (*nanu*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "only the heroic" (*vīra eva*):

the meaning is that only the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is perceived, through the dominant emotion of valor—which is implied by the expressive state (*anubhāva*) of fearlessly falling into the midst of battle—and by the transitory emotions (*sañcārībhāva*) such as pride.
"Those are the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva)" means that for the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and the loathsome (bībhatsa), the stable emotions are love (rati) and disgust (jugupsā), respectively.
"And so forth," etc.
The meaning is that [the Heroic Rasa] is characterized by the experience of the body's falling and so forth, indicated by the term "vīrapadena" (by the word "hero").
By the phrase "utsāhādi" (energy and so forth), pride and other such qualities are included.
After the word "avagatya" (having understood), the words "vīro rasaḥ" (the Heroic Rasa) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

He explains the "separation by the Hero" (*vīravyavadhāna*) with the words beginning "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*). This refers to the agent, who is the Hero, and the object, which is the body of the fallen [hero].
The phrase beginning with "entirely" (*samasta*) and so forth follows.

In this context, "sentence" (vākya) means a collection of words; the meaning is that there is a cognition of the object (*karman*) through its connection with the sentence-meaning of "the earth," etc., and a cognition of the agent (*kartṛ*) through its connection with the sentence-meaning of "whether [he does it]," etc.
The word "iti" indicates the reason.
The word "bhāva" [refers to]...

The meaning is this: when the meaning of the qualifiers such as "dusty with the earth" (*bhūreṇu*) is understood, the *bībhatsa* (disgust) rasa is experienced; when the meaning of its qualificand is understood, the *vīra* (heroic) rasa is experienced—or rather, when the meaning of qualifiers such as "not [fearing]" is understood, the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa is experienced, and when the meaning of its qualificand is understood, the *vīra* rasa is experienced. Thus, by this process, there is an intermittent experience of the *vīra* rasa. However, if understanding occurs according to the sequence of hearing [the words], then first the *bībhatsa* [is experienced].
Regarding the application [of rasa] to awakening, it is said that at the outset there is the erotic (śṛṅgāra). // 27 //
Regarding the phrase "in another composition," he explains the word "another" as "in the *muktaka* (detached verse) and so forth.

For that which is most delicate (*sukumāratama*)—being liable to collapse even by a slight cause—is the most delicate of all rasas; it cannot tolerate even the slightest intrusion of a conflicting [rasa].
A true poet possesses an extraordinary degree of attentiveness toward that very rasa.
For negligence regarding that [object] is indeed perceived instantaneously.
Only a true poet possesses such excellence of attention toward that very rasa;
for any negligence regarding it is immediately perceived. (29)

And regarding that very rasa, which possesses an excellence of delicacy beyond all other rasas, the poet should be attentive and diligent; for if he is negligent therein, he will swiftly become an object of contempt among the connoisseurs. Indeed, because it is invariably within the range of experience for those in the cycle of existence, the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa is the preeminent one among all rasas by virtue of its loveliness.
And this being the case:

"In order to attract those to be instructed, or for the sake of enhancing the beauty of the poem, the touch of a rasa contrary to that [of the primary sentiment] does not constitute a fault in its subordinate elements. (Dhvanyāloka 3.30)

Whether for the purpose of turning the disciple toward [the teaching] or merely for the sake of enhancing the beauty of the poem, contact with a rasa incompatible with those [dominant] constituents (aṅga) is a defect. (30)
From that [the erotic], the pathetic; from that too, the erotic—thus there is no fixed rule. (28–29)
"And thus" means that he is in agreement with everything.
"That" refers to [the aforementioned].

Even in those [rasas] such as the Quietistic (śānta) that are opposed to the Erotic (śṛṅgāra), contact with their constituents—that is, the constituents of the Erotic—is not defective. By that method, even the excitants (vibhāva) and ensuants (anubhāva) belonging to other rasas should be described in such a way that they attain the status of being constituents of the Erotic.
As in my own hymn: "Touching you, O Moon-crested Lord, the Master of life, suddenly—though tormented by intense separation—"
Like a moonstone statue, my consciousness, though already dissolved, dissolves even further.
He explains [the verse] with the intention of the reading "sa" in the *kārikā*, beginning with "sa hi" and so forth.
"Of the nature of rasa" means possessing the genus (*jāti*) of *rasatva* (rasa-ness). // 28-29 //
He explains the phrase "if it were so" (*evaṃ cet*) with the words "since" (*yataḥ*).
The meaning is: because the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is an object of universal experience.

Intending to explain the meaning of the passage beginning with "those to be disciplined" (*vineyāni*), he first explains the latter half of the verse beginning with "contrary to that" (*tadviruddha*) using the words "that" (*tat*), and so forth.
He states the meaning of the passage: "By that," and so forth.
"In another rasa" means in [a rasa] such as the *śānta* (the peaceful), and so on.
"By which [description] they attain the state of being limbs of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
This means: by which manner of description (*bhaṅgī-varṇanā*) they come to possess the nature of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth of the erotic sentiment.
He provides an example for this, beginning with "tvām" and so on.
Intensely tormented by profound separation, or rather by the intense lack of your touch,
my consciousness— whether it be the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or its function (*vṛtti*)— which wanders among other objects, touches you and makes you a slight object of perception; then,
dissolving and attaining a connection with the state of having your form, it reaches that knowledge wherein there is contact with a sentiment opposed to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).

That which constitutes the limbs of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) does not merely fail to be faulty when there is a connection characterized by non-contradiction; rather, it is not faulty even when employed for the sake of attracting the disciples or for the mere beauty of the poem. It is not faulty even when employed for the sake of attracting the disciples or for the mere beauty of the poem.

For those who are to be instructed, having been made attentive by the elements of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), easily accept the teachings on discipline. Indeed, in this work titled *Locana*, even the determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*) of the tranquil sentiment (*śānta*) are described through the stylistic manner of the erotic;
the connection is that there is no fault whatsoever in doing so for the sake of that literary beauty which serves to make the students attentive.
By the inclusion of the word "or" (vā), another alternative is stated.
He explains that very point with the words "not only":
this is the explanation of the word "or."

The characteristic of non-contradiction, such as the avoidance of excessive elaboration and so forth, has been stated previously. Furthermore, there may be the coexistence of contradictory elements for the sake of enhancing the beauty of the poem in order to attract the attention of the audience; it is not only through the aforementioned modes that this occurs.
However, the beauty of poetry does not exist apart from attracting the attention of the audience.
Neither the presence nor the absence of an intervention is obtained as explained by others. "Pleasure" means preceded by attachment.

Now, one might object: "Poetry is by nature a form of play, whereas the discourses on instruction found in the Vedas and other scriptures are of a different character. Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "By the conduct of the virtuous" (*sadācāra*). This demonstrates that the meditator, the act of meditation, and the object of meditation all appear [within poetry].
The word "also" (*api*) indicates an apparent contradiction.
"Dissolving" (*vilīyate*) means the non-manifestation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or its mental modification (*vṛtti*).
By this, knowledge whose object is the mere thing to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*) is shown.
Alternatively, "even having dissolved, it dissolves" means that even having become liquefied, it becomes utterly fluid.

The melting of the hearts of devotees is well known; however, in the case of the statuette (putrikā), the meaning is that it becomes slightly moistened by the touch of the moonbeams and then becomes moistened again throughout all its limbs.

Here, through the perception of the heroine as being tormented by separation and so forth within consciousness and the like, she attains the status of an excitant (vibhāva) for the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra); thus he says: "the description by way of the mode of the erotic."
He explains the first half [of the verse] with the words "vineyān" and so forth.
He shows that the particle *eva* is connected with the negative particle *na* by saying "not at all" (*naiva*).
The phrase "another alternative" (*pakṣāntaram*) refers to this.
The meaning is that [the view] is other than the positions stated in the verses beginning with "Is it non-contradictory or contradictory? and so forth;
the intention is not that it merely illustrates these two positions here.
This is the explanation.
The meaning is that this is the explanation beginning with "not merely" (*sa na kevalam*).

Regarding the phrase "the application of the characteristic of non-contradiction" (*avirodhalakṣaṇayoga*), he explains the term "characteristic of non-contradiction" (*avirodhalakṣaṇa*) with the words beginning "paripoṣa" [and so forth]. The section from "vineyāni" up to "tadartham api vā" is a commentary on the *vṛtti* beginning with "vineyāni."
The explanation of the phrase "being produced" (*sa kriyamāṇa*) is "the coexistence of opposites" (*viruddhasamāveśa*).
He states the conclusion: "not only by the aforementioned modes.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "the coexistence of opposites is not defective."
However, the sense is that even when performed in this manner, there is no fault.
To turn the disciples toward [the subject], he provides a justification for what was stated as "whatever constitutes the beauty of poetry"—namely, the passage beginning with "but not," etc.
The syntactical connection is "it does not exist."
The meaning is "it does not exist.
Regarding the term "interposition" (*vyavadhāna*):
the meaning is that it does not exist even by way of an interposition or non-interposition with another taste (*rasa*).
"In some cases it is found" connects with both "poetic beauty" and "not [found]";
"as for example," and so forth.
The word "tathā" (thus) is to be connected with what precedes it.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the alternative explanation [of the verse] is intended either to attract the attention of those to be trained (*vineya*) or for the sake of the aesthetic beauty (*kāvyasobhā*) of the poem; this is the point of the disjunctive analysis.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase beginning with "śṛṅgāre" is an elaboration of exactly what was stated previously in the words "vineyān" and so forth.
It was indeed for the benefit of those to be trained that [the teachings] were brought down by the Sages.

Furthermore, because the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is so captivating and pleasing to the minds of all people, its inclusion as a constituent element in poetry nourishes an excellence of beauty; thus, in this manner as well, the inclusion of an element of the erotic sentiment does not constitute a contradiction even when it occurs within a conflicting sentiment.
Therefore, it is true that women are enchanting, and it is true that worldly splendors are delightful;
yet, life is as fickle as the flickering side-glances of an intoxicated woman.
In such passages as these, there is no fault of contradictory aesthetic flavor (*rasavirodha*).
Regarding the phrase "by the sages" (*munibhiḥ*), the meaning is "by Bharata and others.

Furthermore, we have already previously established that, compared to the treatises and histories which are like a master or a friend, drama and poetry possess the quality of being instructive by virtue of their resemblance to a wife, and this has been set forth with pleasure.
It has not been written here for fear of redundancy. [Objection:

Is it not the case that by the very description of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth through the technique of being subordinate to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), the arousal of passion is already achieved?
[Reply: No; there is another method.
Thus he says: "And what [more]? Regarding the phrase "an excellence of beauty":
the meaning is that it nourishes—that is, it makes beautiful—a specific ornament such as simile (upamā) and the like.
As it has been said: "The qualities (guṇas) are those attributes that produce the beauty of poetry, while the ornaments (alaṅkāras) are the causes of its excellence.

In the verse beginning with "mattāṅganā," while the transience of all things is being described as a determinant state (vibhāva) of the sentiment of peace (śāntarasa), no composition has been made using the stylistic devices of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
But what is the truth? To explain that "pleasure" is dear to the ignorant, he says:
"By means of attachment," and so forth.
This refers to the scriptures and histories which are regarded as equal to a master or a friend; that is, with reference to them.

Now, one might object: since it is the word itself—delimited by context and other factors—that simultaneously produces the cognition of both the expressed and the suggested meanings, what is the purpose of postulating a sequence between them?

for instance, there is the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) even from words such as songs,
yet there is no intervening reflection upon a denoted meaning in those cases.
To this we reply: it is indeed our own position that words possess suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) through the delimitation of context and other factors.
However, that suggestiveness of theirs is sometimes based on a specific nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*) and sometimes based on their denotative power (*vācaka-śakti*).

In that regard, if for those [words] whose suggestiveness is based on denotative power, that [suggestiveness] were accomplished merely by the cognition of their own form without the cognition of the denoted meaning, then it would not be based on denotative power.

Now, since the eye is seen to function merely as an instrument for perceiving sound in cases such as songs that lack words or are devoid of distinct phonemes (*svara*), it follows that the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and the intended suggested element (*vyaṅgya*), such as aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), appear together through a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Thus, there is no need for two separate functions of denotation (*vacana*) and suggestion (*vyañjana*); this is what he says with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). Even where the words of a song possess a literal meaning, the cognition of that meaning is useless, because the arising of aesthetic flavor is observed to follow the musical modes (*grāma-rāga*), which sets aside any adherence to the literal sense.
Nor is it observed that this [sound] exists everywhere;
thus he says "not" (na ca).
"Of them" refers to the sounds of songs and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), sounds such as those of musical instruments and lamentation are indicated. The meaning is that we have already stated [in the *Ślokavārttika*] that "wherever there is a meaning, whether it be through a word or [another means]. Thus is the sense.
"In that case, then," [it is argued].
Consequently, just as in the case of song, there would be a manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) from the words of poetry even without the comprehension of meaning;
yet this is not so, and therefore the denotative power (*vācaka-śakti*) must also be required therein.
And since that [denotative power] resides solely in the denoted object, it must be accepted that the cognition occurs first with respect to the denoted object.
Thus he says: "Now" (atha);
by this, he means the denotative power.
*Bālapriyā* says this:
the meaning is that he demonstrates the aforementioned doubt by means of the passage beginning with "nanu" and ending with "parāmarśa.
He introduces the text beginning with "na ca" with the words "yatrāpi," etc.
Regarding the phrase "useless" (*anupayoginī*), he states the reason: "village," etc., and "having cast aside" (*apa*).

"Having cast aside" means disregarded; that is, by that emergence of rasa (*rasodaya*) in which the following of the literal meaning—the pursuit of the comprehension of the expressed sense—is disregarded, the state of being so is its nature (*tattā*). By that [nature].
"It is so" means that there is a comprehension of the expressed meaning (*vācyapratīti*).
Regarding the phrase "of songs and so forth," he explains the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) with the words beginning with "and so forth."
*Vilapitam* means lamentation (*vilāpa*). According to Amara, "lamentation is meaningless speech.
In the commentary, it says "the capacity to suggest that" (*tadvyañjakatvam*);
this means the capacity to suggest when assisted by context and other factors.
"Of those words" means of those sounds. "In the specific nature" means in the specific nature of the sound.
Regarding the term "vācake" (in the denotative): that whose basis or cause is the power of denotation (*abhidhā*) is [the word].
The sense is that the manifestation (*vyakti*) is preceded by the cognition of the object to be denoted.

Regarding the phrase "of those" (*yeṣām*): the term "the state of being its manifestor" (*tadvyañjakatvam*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The word "that" (*tat*) means "the state of being a manifestor."
"Not then," he says;
and thus, since there is an absence of dependence on the power of denotation for the status of being a manifestor,
it is "like a song."
The meaning is "equal to song.
And it is not the case that it is not so;
"iti" is used in the sense of a reason.
"Residing solely in the expressed" means having the expressed as its very object.
As stated previously,
"based on that" means that it is necessarily established that the cognition of the suggested meaning occurs subsequent to the cognition of the relationship between the expressed and the expressive.
If that sequence is not perceived due to its rapidity, what then?
And if the apprehension of rasa were to occur solely through the word as delimited by context and other factors, even without the cognition of the expressed meaning (vācya),

then for those listeners who have not ascertained the context and who themselves lack proficiency regarding the relationship between the signifier and the signified, [the apprehension of rasa would likewise fail to occur].
Locana states: "By the relation of signifier and signified (vācyavācakabhāva)";
this very power of signification (vācakaśakti) is what is being referred to.
What is meant is this: let it not be that the signified (vācya) is the manifestor of rasa and so forth.

Granted that the cognition of that [meaning] arises from the word alone, nevertheless, it follows that the expressive power must necessarily depend upon that [word] as a cooperative cause when exercising its capacity to denote its own object; thus, the priority of the cognition of the denoted meaning is established.
Now, one might object: "In this case too, the expressive power is useless, just as in the case of the sound of a song.

Anticipating the objection that "when a poetic work is heard, the cognition of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) does not occur because the necessary cooperative causes, such as the comprehension of the context, are absent," he says: "And if... (*yadi ca*).
What indeed is meant by "understanding the context"? Does it mean being assisted by other sentences,
or is it the related meaning expressed by those other sentences?

Even when both types of thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) are present, the emergence of aesthetic flavor (*rasodaya*) does not occur if the meaning of the sentence under discussion is not communicated.
Therefore, it must be admitted that the comprehension of the expressed meaning (*vācyārthapratīti*) occurs first.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "atha" means "yadi" (if).
Regarding the phrase "tannibandhanam": the meaning is that it has "that" as its basis (nibandhana). The term "manifesting-ness" (vyañjakatva) is to be supplied [from the previous context].
‘Tad’ means ‘then’ (tarhi). ‘Sa tu krama’ means ‘but that sequence.’
The meaning is that the sequence consists in its being posterior in time to the cognition of the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
The word "of the cognition of the suggested" (*vyaṅgyapratīteḥ*) is to be supplied [to the compound].
Regarding the term *tannibandhana* ("based on that"), he explains the word *tat* in the *Locana* as "the expressive power" (*vācakaśakti*).
The readings are "saiva" (that very same) and "sa eva" (that very one).
The meaning is that it is precisely the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*).
He states the sense of this [in the words] beginning with "this," namely,
"that which manifests rasa and so forth."
The meaning is that it generates the manifestation of rasa and so forth.
"The cognition of that" means the cognition of rasa and so forth.
"By that" means by the word;
"when that [action] is to be performed."
The meaning is: "in the case of the cognition of taste and so forth that is to be produced.
The word "iti" indicates a reason.
As for the phrase beginning with "nanu" (but surely), etc.:
"Like the sound of song" means "as in the case of the sound of song. "Here too" refers to the word *kāvya* as well.

[Objection: "In that case, where the word is heard but the meaning is not understood, there would still be a perception of rasa. To this, he says: "As for that which... and so forth. Having raised this doubt with the words "As for that which" (*yattu*) and "where" (*yatra*), he replies.
The meaning is that he speaks with the intervening passage beginning with "iti śaṅkāpūrvakam" (thus, preceded by a doubt) and ending with "samādhānaṃ bhavet" (there would be a resolution).

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "only" (*mātra*) in the phrase "accomplished by the word alone" (*śabdamātrasādhyā*) is explained as "even without the cognition of the denoted object" (*vācyapratītim antareṇaiva*). [And] "when that has been determined" (*tadavadhārite*).
Therefore, that [is the case]:
for those by whom the context has been determined and understood,
[it applies] "when it is not being expressed," and so forth.
The meaning is: for those who themselves do not know the respective denoted objects of the respective expressive words.
"This" refers to the apprehension of rasa and so forth.
He explains this in the *Locana* with the passage beginning "context," etc.
"Comprehension through context" means that the meaning of the context is what is to be understood. Regarding the term "vākya":
it means that which has another sentence as its auxiliary (*sahāya*), that is to say, its nature is to have another sentence as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*).
This [cognition] would arise from the mere hearing of the poem;
furthermore, if they were simultaneous, the cognition of the expressed meaning would be useless,
or if it were useful, there could be no simultaneity.

Even for those [sounds], such as those of songs and the like, whose manifesting nature (*vyañjakatva*) is the cause for the cognition of their own specific forms, there exists a necessary concomitance (*niyamabhāvī*) between the cognition of their own form and the cognition of the manifested object (*vyaṅgya*). This is the sense: that the Locana [commentary] itself has merely been explained by some other person through the context alone.

Furthermore, the intention is that one should not, out of envy, foster anything beyond what is reasonable by denying the cognition of the expressed meaning (*vācya*), which is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), and instead taking refuge in the existence or non-existence of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
One might object: "Granted that there is utility for the cognition of the denotable [meaning] through reliance on sequence, what is the purpose of this?
For the utility consists merely in coexistence, characterized by dependence upon a single causal complex. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Together" (*saha*).
The sense is that if utility were thus [merely coexistent], it would be a mere application of a name to something that provides no assistance—a designation devoid of reality.
He says "of those [who are benefactors]" because you yourself have admitted that benefactors exist prior [to the benefit received].
The intention is that by that very example, we shall establish the prior existence of the cognition of the expressed meaning as well.
The words "of the present sentence" are to be supplied as the remainder of the phrase.
The word "atha" (now/then) is used in the sense of an inquiry.
Regarding the phrase "of other sentences," and so forth:
the meaning is "other sentences and their expressed objects."
"Both" means both the other sentence and that which is expressed by it. "In the cognition of the meaning of the sentence under discussion" [is the intended sense].
The meaning is: the non-comprehension of the respective word-meanings that constitute the sentence under discussion.
He explains the lack of proficiency regarding the relationship between the signified and the signifier with the words "merely the context," and so forth.
By the word "mere" (mātra), the signified object is excluded.
"Of whom" means "of certain practitioners.
It has been explained.
The meaning is that [the rasa] is awakened.

Now, one might raise the objection: "In the production of the apprehension of rasa and so forth by means of a sentence, a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) must also act as a cooperative cause; therefore, it is precisely due to its absence that rasa and so forth are not apprehended at times when there is no apprehension of the denoted meaning (*vācya*). He dispels this doubt with the words beginning "And not... (*na ca...*), and so on.
And the connection is "it does not nourish. Regarding the term *anvayā* (invariably concomitant):

the meaning is that it possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), such that when there is the cognition of the expressed meaning (*vācya*), there is the cognition of rasa and so forth, and in its absence, there is its absence.
"As the basis" means as the causal agent;
the words "of the perception of rasa and the state of being a word" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding "nanu" and so forth:
"upayoga" (utility) refers to the cognition of rasa and the like; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"By means of a sequence" (kramāśrayeṇa) means by means of a sequence consisting of the priority and posteriority between the cognition of the expressed meaning and the cognition of rasa and so forth.
To the question "In that case, what is the utility [of this sequence]?", he says: "Together" (saha).
Anticipating the question "Of what nature is that?", he says: "eka" (one).

The sense is that the coexistence with rasa and so forth consists in the fact that the cognition of the expressed meaning is dependent upon the causal complex that brings about the cognition of rasa and so forth.
"Upayogāḥ" refers to the referent of the word "upayoga" (utility/application).
"Having raised a doubt" means having suspected it at first sight.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "And in the case of coexistence," etc., with the words "For thus," and so forth.
The connection is that the application [of the term] to that which provides no assistance is merely the creation of a designation.
He explains the meaning of the word "merely" with the words beginning "the thing," etc.;
"thing" refers to the object in the form of being a provider of assistance.
"Previously cultivated" means existing at a prior time.
He explains the meaning of the final portion of the text, beginning with "by your own example," as follows: "sequence."
He introduces the passage beginning with "tattvit" and so forth by means of the example of yourself, such as the *Gītā* and other texts—namely, the words beginning with "nanu.
The word "śabdasya" (of sound) is connected with the word "kriyā" (action). [This refers to] sequence (*krama*).

That sequence of words, however, is not perceived in the case of *rasa* and the like—which are distinct from other denotable meanings and non-contradictory with the expressed sense—whether those [meanings] consist in the arrangement of actions and their results that cannot be accomplished by anything else, or in the cultivation of one's own mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Anticipating the objection, "If this sequence is real, why is it not perceived?", the author says: "That, however" (*tattu*). By the phrase "the sequence of actions," he states the essential nature of sequence; he explains it as "they are performed" (*kriyete*). *Locana*: Indeed, if the sequence is real, why is it not observed? Having raised this doubt, he says: "That, however.
By the expression "the sequence of actions," he states the very nature of sequence. He explains it thus: "they are performed."

If there are two functions—the function of denotation (*abhidhā*) and the function of suggestion (*dhvanana*), which is synonymous with manifestation (*vyañjanā*)—then no sequence between these two functions is perceived.
Where? In the domain of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth.

Of what kind? It must be entirely non-denotable, distinct from other denotable meanings and from the specific denotable meaning [of the words used]; it has already been stated that this must occur through a gradual process.
The meaning is that [the secondary function] occurs when it is not in contradiction with the expressed meaning, but when there is a contradiction, it is indeed indicated by indication (lakṣyate).

To the question "Why is it not indicated?", he states the reason—containing another underlying cause—by means of the locative case of reason (*nimitta-saptamī*), saying: "In cases where [the results] occur swiftly."

In the context of the composition of those effects which cannot be accomplished by anything else, the structural arrangements (*ghaṭanā*) characterized by sweetness (*mādhurya*) and so forth were previously explained during the discussion on the *guṇas*. These have "that as their effect," meaning that the perception of *rasa* and so forth is their result;

likewise, they have "that alone as their sole objective" (*ananya-sādhya*), for the perception of *karuṇa* and other *rasas* is not the objective to be achieved by a composition characterized by vigor (*ojas*).
This is what is meant: because a particular arrangement (*saṅghaṭanā*) is employed in a virtuous poem with non-overlapping domains, no sequence is perceived.
Now, let it be that such is the status of the arrangements;

but why is the sequence not perceived? To this he says: "In those [arrangements] which produce [the effect] rapidly, they bring forth the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and so on instantly, without even waiting for the time of the cognition of the expressed meaning. This means that the activity produced by the words occurs instantaneously.
He states the meaning of the term *kriyā* (action): "They are performed," and so forth.
To the question "Which ones? he replies: "The expressed [meaning]," and so on.
With the intention that "the action of the word" means "an action residing in the word," he says: "Or rather," and so forth.
He demonstrates the logical sequence with the words "of those two," and so forth.
"Of those two" refers to the two actions.
Here, it should be understood that the temporal sequence pertaining to the cognition of the expressed and the suggested meanings is superimposed upon their respective operations.
"In the object such as rasa" means:
thus, it refers to both the cognition of the expressed meaning (vācya) and the cognition of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) in the form of rasa and so forth.
"From the particularity of the denoted" [means...].
The meaning is "due to the particularity of each respective expressed object. He states the conclusion with the words "in every way," etc. "Inexpressible" means distinct from the expressed.
"By this" means by the statement that [it] is inexpressible.
"Thus it has been said" means...
The meaning is that this has been demonstrated.
"It is indeed perceived" refers,
for example, to [the verse] beginning with "O righteous one, wander about" (*bhrama dhārmika*).
The word "iti" [is used] when there is an expectancy for "thus"; that is, it signifies "in this manner. It is a locative case of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).
The phrase “by whose existence” (yasya ca bhāvena) means the locative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*), as instructed in the Sūtra.
“By another cause” (*hetvantara*) means by another cause characterized by the fact that the result cannot be accomplished by anything else.
He explains the passage beginning with "ananyā" (not other) with the words "ghaṭanā" (union) and so forth.
He provides the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) according to the sense of a *karmadhāraya* compound with the words "tāśca" (and those) and so forth.
The explanation of the term "ananya" (not other) is given as "tadeva" (that very same thing).
The meaning is that whatever is to be accomplished by a particular arrangement [of words] is precisely that.
He explains what has already been stated with the words "for not," and so forth.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that the apprehension of *karuṇa* (the pathetic) and other rasas is certainly not to be accomplished through an arrangement characterized by *ojas* (vigorous energy); rather, the point is that it is only the apprehension of *vīra* (the heroic) and other rasas [that is accomplished].
He states the meaning of what was said with the words "this," and so forth.
"By way of having an unmixed object" means by way of having as its object itself that which is not mixed with other entities.
He explains the phrase "in those [actions] that bring about misfortune" with the words beginning "to be spoken," and so on.
"Tāḥ" (those) means:
those which produce the relish of that [misfortune].

This is what is meant: because rasa and the like are manifested by the *saṅghaṭanā* (the structural arrangement of words), even when the cognition of the literal meaning (*artha*) has not yet occurred, the relish of rasa is already hinted at (*āsūtrita*) at the very moment of hearing the appropriate *saṅghaṭanā*. Therefore, although it is joined with a fully manifest relish that arises subsequent to the comprehension of the expressed meaning, it does not appear as something produced later [because its essence was already present].
Indeed, in the case of a familiar object, the sequence of perceiving the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is not perceived in this manner at all.

For this very thing is what constitutes "familiarity": that the [cognition] remains in a state of constant readiness to manifest, due to the strength of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), even without deliberate attention (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth. Thus, because the pervasion—that where there is smoke, there is fire—is established in the heart, only the knowledge of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is required.
The meaning is that [the cognition] takes hold of the locus of apprehension as "it exists";

for when the cognition of smoke has arisen instantaneously, aided by the recollection of its pervasion (vyāpti), and because there is no intrusion of other intervening cognitions— such as the pursuit of mental applications (praṇidhāna) toward things of a different class— the cognition of fire occurs with great swiftness, and thus the connection [of the inference] is established even for a child.
The explanation of the passage beginning with "rasādīn" (flavors, etc. is as follows: "tadāsvādam" (the tasting of that), and so forth.
He explains the answer to the objection—"Why is the sequence not perceived, which is obtained through the text beginning with 'tat'?"—with the words "etad" (this), and so forth:
"because it is suggested by the structural composition (*saṅghaṭanā*)."
It is "excessive" (atyartha) because it is suggested by the composition even without the application of knowledge of the meaning.
"Even previously" means even before the knowledge of the expressed meaning. It is "appropriate" (ucitā).
The meaning is "practiced. "Sūtritaḥ" means slightly manifested.
The word "tena" (by that) is connected with the word "na bhāti" (does not appear).
Regarding the word *vācya*:

although it is distinguished (*viśiṣṭa*) by being endowed with that clear relish (*parisphuṭāsvāda*) which arises—by way of its cause—as the occurrence (*bhava*) following the cognition of the denoted object (*vācyapratītyuttarakāla*);
[the reading *parisphuṭāsvādayukto 'pi* is also found].
"By being produced later" means by being produced at a time subsequent to the cognition of the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
"It does not appear"—
the words "to those with aesthetic sensitivity" (*sahṛdayānām*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Practice," and so forth.
Regarding "practice," the *Nyāyabhāṣya* states: "Practice, however, is the repeated occurrence of cognitions regarding the same object.
"Application," and so forth.
"The Nyāyabhāṣya states: ‘Concentration (*praṇidhāna*) is the fixing of the mind with the desire to remember (*susmūrṣayā*).*” Fixing (*dhāraṇa*) means making [the mind] one-pointed.
By the phrase "by means of concentration and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the signs (*liṅga*) and other factors mentioned in the Nyāyasūtra, such as "signs, binding, and practice."
The word "even without" (vināiva) is connected with the word "establishment" (sthāpanam) by way of the desire to awaken [the latent impression].
"Because of its strength" (balavattvāt) means because it possesses firmness in the form of the immediate presence of an awakener.
"By means of the desire to produce" means by way of being the condition that brings about the awakening of the form of memory;
it is a usage similar to expressions such as "the bank wishes to fall."

With the words beginning with "abhyasta" (practiced), he shows specifically what was stated in general; [this is expressed by] "evam" and so forth. The grammatical connection is: "because of such pervasion" (*vyāpteḥ*).
[And] "because of being situated in the heart" (*hṛdayasthitatvāt*).
The meaning is that [the cognition] exists within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the form of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

By the term "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "mere knowledge of the presence of the mark," such as smoke, on the subject (*pakṣa*), like a mountain, it is meant that there is simply the knowledge of the mark's subsistence in the subject.

By the word "merely" (*eva*), there is an exclusion of the "consideration" (*parāmarśa*), which consists of the knowledge that the subject possesses the reason qualified by its pervasion with the probandum (*sādhya*).
"Useful" means [useful] for the inference of fire and so forth; this is the ellipsis. "Thus" indicates the reason.

Regarding the term "parāmarśa": it is clearly held that this [inferential cognition] occupies the position of the *parāmarśa*. The word "jhaṭiti" (instantly) is connected with the phrase "recollection of the pervasion" (*vyāptismṛti*).
"Regarding 'tadvyāpti'": the meaning is that when there is an association with the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of fire and so forth by smoke and so forth.
"Tat" and so forth [refers to this].

From those two— the cognition of smoke and the recollection of the pervasion— there arises another cognition, distinct in kind, consisting of a mental reflection (*ālocana*) produced by means such as focused attention (*praṇidhāna*) or imitation, or by the act of focusing attention, and which is indeed clearly perceived in certain cases, as for instance in the cognitions of suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) in the form of after-sounds (*anuraṇana*).
If it is asked how this occurs even there, it is explained as follows:

In the case of *dhvani* where the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) consists of a resonance rooted in the power of the literal sense (*arthaśaktimūla*), there exists between the two cognitions— the cognition of the expressed meaning and that of the meaning implied by its capacity— a relationship of cause and effect that cannot be denied, since they are entirely distinct in that the latter differs from other expressed meanings; thus, the sequence of priority and posteriority therein is quite evident.

Just as in the first Uddyota, in the verses cited for the sake of establishing the suggested meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*), in such a context, because the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) are entirely distinct, it cannot be said that the very cognition of one is the same as that of the other. However, in the case of *dhvani* where the suggestion consists of a resonance rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla-anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya*)—as in the verse: "May the cows produce for you an immeasurable, supreme joy, [they who are] the purifiers of the eyes"—no sequence is perceived; and it is the same here as well.

If, however, the rasa were not in harmony with the expressed meaning (vācya) and the arrangement (ghaṭanā) were not appropriate, then that sequence would indeed be perceived. But the author of the *Candrikā*, following the maxim of "repeating what has already been read," explained [the passage] while closing his eyes like an elephant: "The fruit of that word, or rather its fruit consisting of the cognition of the expressed and the suggested, is its arrangement—that is, its production—since it cannot be accomplished by anything else."
Regarding the phrase "produced solely by the operation of words":

we do not perceive any reality of the meaning here in the explanation; therefore, enough with this extensive dispute with our predecessors. However, where there is no suggestiveness through structural composition (*saṅghaṭanā*), it is indeed indicated [by the word itself]; thus he says: "But in some cases... and so forth.
