He raises the objection—"In that case as well"—asking how there can be a distinction when suggestiveness (*vyaṅgyatva*) is equal.
[The response is] "It is quite clear":
that which has its expressed meaning unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*) is manifested by words and sentences.
And [this applies] to that other type of *dhvani*, namely that whose suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) consists of a resonance (*anuraṇana*).
The meaning is that, as previously stated, the arrangement of phonemes and so forth was not mentioned as its manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
Regarding the phrase "in the gāthās":
the meaning is "due to the absence" (*virahāt*), that is, the non-existence of "its penetration" (*tasya yo 'nupraveśaḥ*).
In the case of that which occurs instantaneously,
such as the cognition of fire upon a mountain and so forth when fire is inferred,
there is a sequence.
The ellipsis to be supplied is "of the cognition of smoke accompanied by the recollection of pervasion.
He concludes with the words "tadvat" (in the same way).
It should be understood that the similarity lies in being produced through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).
By the statement beginning with "vācyāvirodhitā," he expresses the meaning to be understood; [he does so] with the words beginning with "yadi.
He provides the *Candrikā* commentary on the passage beginning with "ananya" with the words beginning with "tasya.
[The phrase] "arthasatattvam" means...
The meaning is that the coherence of the sense is intended.
He establishes this very point—that the sequence [of words] is indeed manifest—by stating "avivakṣita" and so forth.
The connection is as follows: for it was stated previously that the arrangement of phonemes and so forth was not mentioned as its (the sentence's) suggester (*vyañjaka*).

In such cases, when two meanings are cognized through verbal cognition (*śābdī*), the cognition of the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)— which occurs in the absence of an explicit word for simile— is suggested by the force of the meaning (*artha-sāmarthyāt*).
Even there, the sequence between the cognition of the expressed meaning and the cognition of the suggested figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) is easily discernible.

Even in the case of *dhvani* where the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) consists of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) rooted in the power of words that illuminate the sense, when a qualifying word is capable of connecting with two meanings, its connection— even if not expressed by words— remains established through the force of the sense in the absence of a word that explicitly joins them; here too, as before, the sequence between the cognition of the primary meaning and the cognition of the mere ornament (*alaṅkāra*) implied by its capacity remains perfectly established.
"In the verbal" refers to [sentences] such as "O pious man, do not wander," and so forth;
these have been explained in that very same place.
The meaning is "even in the case of verbal [simile].
The words expressing comparison are *yathā*, *iva*, and so forth.
"By the force of the meaning" (*arthasāmarthyāt*) means:
This means "by the force of the sentence-meaning.

Having thus examined that which is rooted in the power of the word as manifested by the sentence (*vākya-prakāśa-śabda-śakti-mūla*), he examines that which is manifested by the word (*pada-prakāśa*) with the words "that which is manifested by the word" (*pada-prakāśa*).
[He specifies] "of the qualifying word" (*viśeṣaṇa-padasya*).
Regarding the term "insentient" (jaḍa):
"the unifier" (yojaka) refers to the synthesis [of the notions] "well" and "I" through their being in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇatayā).
The "subject matter" (abhidheya) and that which is implied by its power— of these two, which are merely ornaments—
their "sequence" (krama) is their perception in a temporal order of priority and posteriority; the meaning is that this is well-established and well-defined.
By the use of the word "mātra" (only), he shows that even there, the apprehension of rasa is one where the sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣyakrama*).
The intention is that by this [word], the lack of clarity regarding the priority and posteriority [of the stages] would occur.
[The phrase] "even in the verbal [apprehension]" means:
The meaning is: "even by means of denotation (abhidhā), which is produced by words.
By the word "api" (even/also), the position that the non-contextual meaning is suggested (vyaṅgya) is indicated.
Regarding the phrase "the absence of a word expressive of simile," he explains the term "word expressive of simile" with the words beginning "simile" (upamā).
In the commentary, "ākṣipte" means "produced.
"Abhidheye" means...
The meaning is: "of those two," namely, the cognition of the expressed meaning and the cognition of the suggested figure of speech.
This is stated with the intention of the view that the second meaning is also the expressed (abhidheya), while its mere simile is the suggested (vyaṅgya);
this should be understood in the same way in the instance that will be discussed immediately hereafter.
He introduces the *Locana* by way of a restatement of what has preceded, beginning with "Thus" (*evam*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "illumination of the words" (*padaprakāśam*),
the term "rooted in the power of the word" (*śabdaśaktimūlam*) is to be supplied as a connective adjunct (*anuṣaṅga*).
Having kept in mind the example stated as "to obtain by means of wealth," etc., he explains [the passage] with the words "of this [word] 'jaḍa'.
He states the meaning of the word *yojana* with the words "in a well," etc. And [he says] "both," etc.
The meaning is "both the well and the object.
*Saṃvalana* means mixing.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says: "even though not expressed by words."
The meaning is that it is not even conveyed by the word "yojaka" (the connector).
"Arthāt" means from suggestion (*vyañjanā*). "Avasthitam" means having become the object of comprehension.
He explains the passage beginning with "the subject matter" (*abhidheya*) and so forth: "The subject matter," etc.
Here, the ornament of illumination (*dīpaka*) is the subject matter, because the quality of insentience (*jaḍatva*) is connected to both [parts].
The simile is also implied by its power;
and both the expressed meaning and the figure of speech implied by its power are themselves "mere that"—this is how the meaning of the commentary (*vṛtti*) is to be understood.
Because the doubt that [the figure] might be undetectable must be dispelled, he explains it in accordance with that [doubt], saying: "well-defined" (*sulakṣitam*).
"By the inclusion of the word 'mere' (mātra)" means by the word "mere" (*mātra*) found in the phrase "mere ornament" (*alaṅkāramātra*).

Furthermore, even a suggested meaning (*ārtha-vyañjanā*), when it arises in a context where the understanding is according to the [speaker's] intention, is considered to be rooted in the power of words (*śabda-śakti-mūla*), as it is brought forth by the capacity of words capable of connecting with both meanings.

In the case of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is not intended to be primary, there is a rule that the manifestation of another meaning occurs only after a perception of turning away from its own well-known domain; thus, a temporal sequence (*krama*) necessarily exists. In that regard, because the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary, no consideration has been made regarding the sequential perception of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) along with the expressed meaning itself. Therefore, [the author] says "even though it is based on the meaning" (*ārthyapi*), anticipating the objection: "But if it is based on the meaning, then how can it be rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*)? This is contradictory. To this he replies: "Even though it is based on the meaning... (*ārthyapīti*). Regarding the phrase "like the cognitions of the denotative function and its object" (*abhidhānābhidheyapratītyoriva*): just as there is no sequential perception between the cognition of the denotative function and the cognition of its object, so too here. As for the statement "because it is based on the meaning," the sense is that although the power of suggestion is rooted in the power of the word, it is called "based on the meaning" because it depends upon the meaning as its cause. For example, in the verse: "O friend, having seen the moon risen, why do you not go to meet him? The night is now half-way through; the moon, the lord of the night, is rising; and the southern breeze, cool with the spray of the Malaya mountains, blows gently. Here, the suggested meaning—namely, the prohibition of going to meet him—is based on the meaning [of the words], yet it is rooted in the power of the word. This is because the power of suggestion is established by the very nature of the word's power, even when it relies on the meaning. Thus, the term "based on the meaning" is used to indicate that the power of suggestion is dependent upon the meaning, while the term "rooted in the power of the word" indicates that the power of suggestion is established by the power of the word itself. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the phrase "even though it is based on the meaning" is intended to show that the power of suggestion is distinct from the power of denotation (*abhidhā*) and the power of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For if it were merely a variety of the power of denotation, it would have been included within the discussion of the powers of the word. But since it is not so included, it is understood that it is a distinct power. Consequently, the term "based on the meaning" is employed to demonstrate that it is distinct from the powers of denotation and indication. Thus, the two terms are used to exclude the powers of denotation and indication, and to establish the existence of a third power, namely suggestion. Therefore, there is no contradiction. As for the phrase "the sequence is necessarily present": this refers to the sequence between the perception of the expressed meaning and the perception of the suggested meaning. However, in the case of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is not intended, because the expressed meaning is not intended, no investigation into a sequential perception of the expressed and the suggested meanings has been undertaken. Hence, the term "based on the meaning" is used to indicate that the power of suggestion is distinct from the powers of denotation and indication. Thus, there is no contradiction. As for the phrase "the sequence is necessarily present": this refers to the sequence between the perception of the expressed meaning and the perception of the suggested meaning. However, in the case of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is not intended, because the expressed meaning is not intended, no investigation into a sequential perception of the expressed and the suggested meanings has been undertaken. Hence, the term "based on the meaning" is used to indicate that the power of suggestion is distinct from the powers of denotation and indication. Thus, there is no contradiction. As for the phrase "the sequence is necessarily present": this refers to the sequence between the perception of the expressed meaning and the perception of the suggested meaning. However, in the case of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is not intended, because the expressed meaning is not intended, no investigation into a sequential perception of the expressed and the suggested meanings has been undertaken. Hence, the term "based on the meaning" is used to indicate that the power of suggestion is distinct from the powers of denotation and indication. Thus, there is no contradiction. As for the phrase "the sequence is necessarily present": this refers to the sequence between the perception of the expressed meaning and the perception of the suggested meaning
The sense is that there is no contradiction here whatsoever.
Since this has already been determined in detail previously, it is not stated again.
[Regarding the phrase] "its own object":
The respective objects of words such as "blind" are those whose eyes are impaired; in that regard, "aversion" means disregard.
Thus, no investigation has been made.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "by way of defining the names.
The sense is that it is improper to suspect coexistence here.

In this manner, the *rasas* and so forth constitute the life-force of the *vṛttis*—such as *kaiśikī* and others—which consist of portions of the plot (*itivṛtta*), as well as of the [styles] such as *upanāgarikā*.
And because all this dual operation of function (vṛtti) and linguistic usage has as its object that which is regulated by rasa and the like;

thus, in connection with what was introduced, the sequence of investigation was undertaken to establish that rasa and the like are distinct from the denoted meaning (vācya). He concludes this with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt), [meaning] that the cognition of rasa is [distinct from] denotation (abhidhāna).
The meaning is that there is a cognition of either rasa or a bhāva. "There too" means even in the case of what was described as being rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*).
In "prātu" and so forth, world-weariness (*nirveda*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Regarding "not here" and so forth,
the meaning is that there is no contradiction because the qualifying attributes such as "ubhayārthī" (serving both purposes) are present.

Having thus established the sequence between the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and the suggester (*vyañjaka*) in the case of the "intended but not primary" (*avivakṣitānyaparavācya*) type of meaning, [the author] says—in the commentary, starting with the words "in the unintended" (*avivakṣite*)—in order to demonstrate that such a sequence exists everywhere between the suggested and the suggester.

He explains the phrase "aversion toward its own object" (*svaviṣayavaimukhyam*) by means of the previously cited examples, such as "blinded by sighs" (*niḥśvāsāndha*), etc., beginning with the words "of the word 'blind,' etc. (*andhaśabdādeḥ*).
Here, "object" (*viṣayaḥ*) refers to the expressed meaning (*vācyārthaḥ*).
"Disregard" (anādara) means the abandonment of the literal meaning because it is sublated. In the commentary, the phrase "to another meaning" (arthāntare) [is used].
The meaning is "suggested" (vyaṅgya).
Regarding the word "sequence" (krama),
the ellipsis is "of the cognitions of the expressed and the suggested."

"In that case, because the expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed" means that in the context of suggestion where the expressed meaning is unintended (*avivakṣitavācya-dhvani*), the literal sense is not what is meant to be communicated.
"In sequence" [refers to the following].

The phrase "the investigation of the sequence" (krameṇa yā pratītiḥ tadvicāraḥ) means an investigation into the sequence between the cognition of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).
Regarding the statement "it has not been done," the *Locana* completes the sense with the words beginning "namely" (*nāma*), etc.
It expresses the underlying intention (*bhāva*) with the words beginning "together" (*saha*), etc.
Regarding the word *atra*:
it means "in the case of dhvani where the expressed meaning is not intended" (*avivakṣitavācya*).

Now, an objection is raised: the fact that rasa and so forth constitute the life of the function (*vṛtti-jīvitatva*) was introduced [at the beginning], and the sequence of the cognition of the expressed and the suggested meanings was concluded by the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so on.
Since this [poetry] is characterized by non-attachment (*asaṅga*), he introduces that very point with the words "In this way, the sentiments (*rasa*) and so forth," and so on.
The connection is with the phrase "of the styles (*vṛtti*) such as the *upanāgaraka*.
He states the reason why the sentiments and so forth constitute the life-force of both types of styles with the words "of everything," and so on.
The grammatical connection is: "that which was introduced and commenced has been examined in that context. Regarding the phrase "this very thing":
the meaning is the examination of the sequence that arose incidentally.

The cognitions of the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) are sequential because they stand in the relation of cause and effect, just like the cognition of a word and its denoted meaning. Thus, due to the causal relationship between the cognition of the expressed and the suggested, there is necessarily a sequence;
however, by the reasoning already stated, this sequence is perceived in some cases and not perceived in others.

Now, having thus defined the varieties of *dhvani* from the perspective of the suggester (*vyañjaka*), someone might ask: "What is this so-called suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*)? It is the manifestation of the suggested meaning."

For the status of being a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and the status of being manifested (*vyaṅgya*) regarding an object do not depend on the establishment of the manifestor for the object to be manifested, nor does the establishment of the status of being a manifestor depend on the manifested; thus, due to this mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), there is no stable determination.
[Objection: But surely, for a manifested meaning that is distinct from the expressed (*vācya*), there is first the cognition of the form of the word, and only then of the expressed meaning.
As the venerable [author] stated therein: "The meaning is not revealed by words that have not attained the status of being objects [of cognition]," and so forth;

therefore, because their form is not yet fully known, one asks, "What is being said? Furthermore, in this case as well, since the convention (*samaya*) is practiced in the same way as inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), even the sequence would not be perceived. Now, concluding what was stated at the beginning of the *Uddyota*—that the nature of *dhvani* is established by means of the manifestor (*vyañjana*)—[the author] explains the state of being a manifestor (*vyañjakabhāva*).

Although this was established in the first illumination (*udyota*), [the author] states the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in a single section so that it may be firmly impressed upon the hearts of the students: "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*);
"someone" (*kaścit*) refers to a Mīmāṃsaka or others.
"What is this?"—
this is the intention of the challenger (codaka) which is about to be stated.

[The author] explains [the passage] beginning with "of the expression" (*abhidhānasya*) and so forth, in order to dispel the suspicion that the example in the inference stated in the *Bālapriyā* commentary is deficient in its probans (*sādhanavaikalya*).
"Because he says" means "since he says.
[The phrase beginning with] "the state of being an object," etc., [follows].
"Objecthood" (viṣayatva) means being the object of cognitions such as those of hearing.
"By those not attained" means by those not known;
the meaning is that it is not manifested [by unknown things], but rather only by those that are known.
With the phrase "and so forth," he shows a portion of a verse among those indicated by that term: "ataḥ" (therefore), etc.
"Ataḥ" means:
because [the word] possesses the capacity to convey meaning only when its [referent] is already known; therefore, for that reason.
"Because its form is not cognized" means that when it is not properly heard by the ear, the specific nature of the sound remains undetermined.
"What is it that is said? is what is being asked.
The meaning is that he is being asked, "What do you say?
The intention is that this is out of a desire to know both the word and its referent.
He states "here too," and so forth, as an incidental remark.
Here too, just as there is an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) between the denotation and the denoted, so too there is an inseparable relation of convention (*samaya*),
that is, the linguistic agreement (*saṅketa*) of specific words for their respective meanings.

It is not perceived anywhere, yet it remains unperceivable; thus, the passage beginning with "that very [thing]" and ending with "among those things defined" is useless, and the definition of suggestiveness (vyañjakatva) starting with "some [person]" is redundant.
Therefore, he introduces the following by stating "at the commencement of the Uddyota," etc., in order to demonstrate its purpose.
By "praghaṭṭaka" is meant a section or context.
Regarding the word "kim" (what) in the phrase "What is this?", it signifies either a censure or a question; since the reason for this has not yet been stated, he says: "to be explained."

The meaning is that "there is no establishment [of the sequence] due to mutual dependence," as will be stated later. For the *codaka*, that is, the one who raises the objection; and in the *vṛtti*, it says "the manifestation of an object not previously manifested."
The meaning is "the capacity conducive to the cognition of the suggested sense.
After this, the word "if" (cet) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
He refutes [this] with the words "for not," and so forth.
The word "of sound" is to be supplied [to the sentence].
The establishment of sound has already been demonstrated; and since the establishment of the manifestor depends upon that [establishment of sound], what occasion is there for further questioning?
This is indeed true.

The establishment of an entity distinct from the expressed meaning has already been accomplished through the arguments stated previously; why, then, is that object designated specifically as "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*)?
And as for the point where there is no primary stability, [it was addressed] in the *Locana* earlier.
In the first chapter (*udyota*), during the refutation of the theory of non-existence (*abhāvavāda*),
the point is this: its establishment does not depend on the establishment of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*)— which would give rise to the suspicion of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—
but rather because it has been established by other means of proof (*hetvantara*).
Thus he says: "The accomplishment of that," and "But that [is]...
Let this be the second meaning.
If that [meaning] is given the name "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*), why is it not also called "denoted" (*vācya*)? Or, why is the name "suggested" not also applied to that which is considered "denoted"?

For being understood is what constitutes the status of being a word-meaning, and that itself is the state of being a signifier (*vācakatva*). Abhidhā (denotation), vyañjakatva (suggestiveness) of the meaning, and vyaṅgyatva (the state of being suggested)—these do not, indeed, fail to exist by themselves. [The particle] *hi* [is used here]. *Bālapriyā*: The status of being a word-meaning consists in being apprehended; that very same thing is the state of being a signifier. Denotation, suggestiveness of the meaning, and the state of being suggested—these do not "not exist by themselves. [This is the meaning. The particle *hi* [indicates this].
In the case of [the word] *prasiddhau* (in the established sense),
the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is to be supplied as the remainder; that is to say, it means "therefore, by way of elimination" (*pariśeṣāt*).
The state of being the manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*) depends upon the establishment of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), and the establishment of the state of being the manifestor depends upon the manifested;
"thus" (*iti*) means for this reason.
"There is no establishment, nor is there a fixed state. Alternatively, the word 'na hi' (for not) is connected with what precedes."

It is stated that the word alone possesses the quality of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*) while the meaning possesses the quality of being manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*), in order to indicate this very point.
Thus, the connection is as follows: since the meaning is what is manifested, the word alone is the manifestor; and that manifestation of the manifested meaning does not [occur otherwise].
He states the reason for this with the words "in the case of being a manifestor," and so forth.

If the reading "vyaṅgyatvam" (the state of being suggested) does not follow immediately after "vyañjakatvasiddhyadhīnam" (dependent upon the establishment of the suggestiveness), then the construction is as follows: "Suggestiveness is not the manifestation of a suggested meaning.
To the question "Why?", he says "vyaṅgyatvam" and so forth. The passage beginning with "nanu" is the respondent's (siddhāntin) refutation.
Anticipating the possibility of forgetfulness, he explains the word "previously" (*prāk*) found therein in the *Locana* with the words "firstly," etc.
He states the established conclusion (*phalita*) with the words "therefore," etc.
The particle "ca" (and) is used in the sense of restriction; he states the reason referred to by the word "therefore" with the words "by other reasons," etc.
"Tadāha" means "therefore he says"; this is the sense [of the expression].
In the *Vṛtti*, it says: "'dependent on its establishment' (*tatsiddhyadhīne*)."
The meaning is that [the cognition] is dependent upon the establishment of the suggested object (*vyaṅgya*).

Having restated what was said by the proponent with the words "It is true," etc., the opponent has set forth his refutation with the words "But that," etc.; he explains that passage with the words "Let this be so," etc.
The explanation of the phrase "that object" is: "this second object."
He explains by means of the passage beginning with "of that," joining the particle *eva* in two ways as "only by way of being suggested" (*vyaṅgyatayaiva*).
[The phrase] "it is not made" implies that,
for this reason, the ground for the application of the word "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*) must be stated for the sake of restriction.
The sense is that it would thus result in a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).

With the words "And where... and so forth, another refutation is stated, consisting in the non-establishment of the intended object as qualified by being *vyaṅgya* (suggestible); he introduces that passage with the words "by being apprehended," and so forth. "By being apprehended" means by being apprehended through the word.
"Being the meaning of a word" (*śabdārthatva*); thus, the meaning is that "being denotable" (*vācyatva*) consists in being cognizable through a word.
"That very [thing]" (*tadeva*).
The meaning is: "that alone which is the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) to the state of being understood when the object is reached.
That is to say, it is simply the state of making the object understood.
[The opponent asks: "Let this be so; what follows from that? To this he replies: "For expression," and so forth.
The term *abhidhā* (denotation) is included within the nature of being expressive (*vācakatva*), characterized by speech.
Regarding the phrase "that which is its limit":
that object which constitutes its limit is rightly designated there solely as the denotable (*vācya*).
Because the sentence is directed toward that [meaning],
the very function of the sentence which reveals it is its denotative power (*vācakatva*).
What is the use of postulating another function for it?
Therefore, that object which is the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*) is primarily what is to be expressed (*vācya*).

As for the intermediate cognition of another expressed meaning in such a context, it is merely a means (*upāya-mātra*) to the cognition of that [intended] meaning, just as the cognition of word-meanings is a means to the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
For it is appropriate that the denotative function (*abhidhāyakatva*) extends only as far as that [intended meaning].

And since that [suggested meaning] constitutes the culminating point when it has become the primary sense—just as the nature of *dhvani* was described as being "crowned" (preeminent)—it is logical that it should exist precisely there through the operation of denotation (*abhidhā*). Thus he says: "And where... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "that which illuminates it":
this refers to that sentence which necessarily illuminates what is intended to be manifested by it.
By the expression "merely a means," through the statement of its commonality, he indicates the prima facie positions (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Bhāṭṭas, the Prābhākaras, and the Grammarians.
For in the Bhaṭṭa school, the communication of word-meanings is an inseparable concomitant when words function toward the comprehension of the sentence-meaning,
just as the flame of wood is [inseparable] in the act of cooking.
The meaning is that it is dear to the ignorant;
in that very context, it refers precisely to that ultimate sense.
Now, let it be granted that it possesses denotative power with respect to that ultimate sense.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That being the limit," and so forth.
"That being the limit" means being the limit with respect to that denotation; it means being the boundary or the object of the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Regarding the phrase "in that": [it refers to the aforementioned].
The meaning is: "in that which is implied by what you desire.
Revealing the refutation of what was stated, he states the conclusion with the words beginning with "iti" and so forth.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (hetu).
The consecrated head is the primary [element] characterized by taste and so forth;
"form" means its own nature (*svarūpa*).
"In that very [place]" refers to that same location.

The word "only" (eva) is connected with the phrase "by means of the operation of denotation" (abhidhāvyāpāreṇa). Thus, it is logical that [the object] should come into being; therefore, the point is that what is called "manifestation" (vyañjakatva) is merely a name.
In the commentary, "yatra ca" and so forth means: in that [work] such as poetry, etc.;
"abiding primarily" means...
The meaning is that the object exists by virtue of being the intended scope (*tātparya-viṣaya*).
"Therein" means in poetry and so forth.
"This" refers to the object established as predominant.
"Locane—'tad' and so forth. 'Avaśyam' (necessarily):
the sense is that otherwise the beauty of the poetry would not be established."

"By this common statement" means by a statement shared by the three systems, in the sense that the cognition of word-meanings is merely a means for the cognition of sentence-meaning, just as [the cognition of] word-meanings is for the cognition of sentence-meaning. He introduces those three systems in order, beginning with "In the Bhāṭṭa system, indeed," and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "for the sake of cognizing the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthamitaye*):
the activity of those words is directed solely toward the cognition of the sentence-meaning by way of generating the sentence;

when that [sentence-generation] occurs, the communication of their own individual meanings follows as an inseparable consequence (*nāntarīyaka*) through the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

To explain this, as it were for the purpose of cooking food, it is said here: where a word, while denoting its own primary meaning, causes another meaning to be understood, there is either no distinction or there is a distinction between that which is its capacity to denote its own primary meaning and that which is its status as the cause for understanding that other meaning.
First of all, they are not without distinction.
For these two functions are indeed perceived as having distinct objects and distinct forms.

To explain: the function characterized by denotation (*vācakatva*) has the word’s own primary meaning as its object, whereas the function characterized by signification (*gamakatva*) has another meaning as its object.
That very meaning which is raised through the primary intention (*tātparya*) by means of the word-meanings understood from the term "locana" is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
And that very [sentence-meaning] is what is to be expressed (*vācya*).

Even in the Prābhākara view, there is a very long process regarding the sentence-meaning as the *nimittin* (the thing to be indicated), whereas the status of the word-meanings as the *nimitta* (the indicators) is indeed ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
However, for the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), that [distinction] is not ultimate; this is the difference.
Since we have already established this in detail in the very first *udyota*, we shall not labor over it again; rather, we shall merely proceed with the composition of the text.
These three points are to be applied to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Regarding this, "here" refers to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"It is said" introduces the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

There is a difference in essential nature between being a denoter (*vācakatva*) and being a signifier (*gamakatva*); and there is a difference in terms of object, as they apply respectively to one's own meaning and to another meaning.
Now, if that meaning is understood from that [sentence], how then can it be said to be a "different meaning" (arthāntara)?

If it were not so, then that [meaning] would not belong to it at all; what then would be the purpose of the activity of words, which—like the burning of wood intended for the pleasure of children—is directed toward an object?
Therefore, the function of denotation (*abhidhā*) of words extends only as far as the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, just as the function of wood ends with cooking; this is the meaning.
"Thus" (iti) means "by the method already stated.
[It is known] from the words understood [therein].
The phrase "exceedingly [beyond] what is understood from the words contained in the sentence" means that very [sentence-meaning].

By the use of the particle *eva* ("only/just"), there is an exclusion of the word-meanings, because they serve merely as the means for the cognition of the sentence-meaning and thus are not the intended object (*tātparya-viṣaya*) of the sentence.
Regarding the term "activity" (vyāpāra):
the phrase "of words consisting of sentences" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Regarding the term "causal" (nimittinī): [it refers to that which has a cause].

The meaning is: "in that which is occasioned," i.e., in the form of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Although the status of the word-meanings as the cause (*nimitta*) is established by the very statement that the sentence-meaning is the effect (*naimittika*), he says "but of the word-meanings" in order to show the distinction from the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).
The statement regarding the relationship of cause and effect between the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning is made with respect to their production (*utpatti*).
It should be understood that, according to the Prābhākara school, the cognition of the sentence-meaning occurs first because [words] denote what is connected to an action (*kāryānvitābhidhāna*).
That [sentence-meaning] is "not ultimately real" (*apāramārthika*);
the meaning is that it is not ultimately real because its nature is ignorance (*avidyā*).
He states the result of the presentation of the three views in summary: "This very [point]," etc.
The phrase "is to be applied" means that otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the teaching] being rootless; such is the intended meaning.
Regarding the word "it is said" (*ucyate*), he completes the sense with the words "the established doctrine" (*siddhānta*).

He clarifies the distinction between the essential nature and the object, which were stated in the commentary passage beginning with "where," by means of the passage beginning with "the state of being a signifier" (*vācakatva*).
[The phrase] "by way of the object" (*viṣayataḥ*)...

The word "distinction" (bheda) is to be supplied [to the previous statement]. The underlying sense is that because it depends upon convention (samaya), its denotative function (abhidhā) operates toward its own primary meaning; whereas because it does not depend [on convention], its cognitive operation (avagamanavyāpāra) functions toward other meanings.
He introduces the passage beginning with "And not in itself or in another," etc., with the words "Now then," and so forth.
"From that" means: because the cognition of the object to be expressed arises from that word;
"this" refers to that which is intended to be manifested (vyaṅgya).
[Objection: But surely it is not understood from that word itself, but rather by virtue of its connection [to something else]. To this, he says: "If not," and so forth.
"That" refers to the word together with [its object].
Furthermore, the linguistic usage regarding both oneself and others concerning the denoted (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya) cannot be denied.
One [meaning] is perceived as being directly related to the word, while the other is perceived as being related to that which is related to it.

For the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is indeed the direct relation of the word, whereas the other—the implied meaning—is drawn forth by the power of the expressed meaning and is thus related to that which is related to it.
If its relation to itself were direct, then the very designation of it as "another meaning" would not exist.
Therefore, the difference in the objects of those two operations is well-established;
the difference in their forms is likewise established. For the very power of denotation is not the same as the power of comprehension.

For even that which is non-expressive, such as the word "song" (*gīta*), is observed to bring about the comprehension of an object characterized by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth; and it is well known that even that which is non-verbal, such as gesture (*ceṣṭā*) and the like, reveals specific meanings.
Thus, having raised the objection with the words "by her face bent down from bashfulness, [her] glance... and so on, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
“It would not exist”:
the particle *eva* is displaced in its order;
the meaning is “it would certainly not exist.”

To the extent that there is no direct connection [between the senses and the object], a distinct operation toward a different object is indeed appropriate; thus, the difference in objects has been stated.

Now, one might object: "Even when the object is different, for a multi-sensed word such as *akṣa*, there is only a single function characterized by denotation (*abhidhā*. Anticipating this, he establishes the difference in form: "There is also a difference in form. He demonstrates this very point through common usage: "For not..."
He states the reason for one who holds a contrary view: "Even of that which is not expressive" (*avācakasyāpi*).

If being expressive (*vācakatva*) were the same as being indicative (*gamakatva*), then that which is non-expressive would not be indicative; and if it were indicative, it would likewise not be expressive.
And neither of these two applies to the word "song" (*gīta*), nor to anything other than sound, such as the downward-turning of the face, the trembling of the breasts, or the onset of tears;
this is the meaning of [the phrase] "none whatsoever.
The sense is that there is nothing at all that is either indicative (*gamaka*) or expressive (*abhidhāyaka*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Thus," and so forth.
"The object of the domain" (*viṣayārtha*) means an object in the form of poison;
or else, it means the meaning of the word "domain" (*viṣaya*).
"What is 'ka'?
means that there would be no object for the word as a distinct entity;
having raised this doubt, he says:
The meaning is that he says [this] with the words beginning with "na ca" and ending with "na syāt.
Regarding the word "eva": the meaning is the emphatic particle "eva" in the phrase "vyavahāra eva" (only in conventional usage).
He clarifies the meaning with the words "yāvatā" and so forth.

"Yāvatā" means "by which reason. Now, one might ask: since the desired conclusion is already established by the very demonstration that the objects are distinct, for what purpose is the demonstration of the difference in form? To introduce that passage, he says "nanu" and so forth.
In the phrase "of the word *akṣa* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the word *hari* and others.
Regarding the expression "of that which has many meanings": this means [the word] whose referents are manifold, such as the sense organs (*indriya*) and so on.
"It is one and the same" means that even though there is dependence on repetition, the function remains denotation (*abhidhā*) itself with respect to each respective meaning; this is the sense.
Having stated the well-known reason for the difference in essential nature, he shows the underlying motive for stating another reason by saying, "with regard to one who is in disagreement."

To one who asserts that "the state of being a signifier (*vācakatva*) is itself the state of being a communicator (*gamakatva*), and nothing else is experienced," he explains the nature [of this] with the words beginning "that which... He states the reason for the phrase "it would not be so" with the words beginning "in the state of being a communicator..."
The construction is as follows: "Even the status of being a denoter would not be absent when there is the capacity to convey meaning.
The sense is "it certainly would be so," with the word "since" (yataḥ) understood as a supplement.
In the verse beginning with "na ca," the specific function of movement as a cause for revealing meaning has indeed been demonstrated by the skilled poet.

Therefore, because they have different objects and different forms, the fact that a word expresses its own primary meaning and the fact that it is a cause for the comprehension of another meaning constitute a clear distinction between the two.

If it is argued that there is a distinction [between the two], then the designation of "denotability" (vācyatva) cannot now apply to the comprehension [of meaning], nor to another object implied by the capacity of the denoted meaning.
We certainly accept that such [comprehension] falls within the scope of the word's operation; however, that occurs solely as something suggested (vyaṅgya), not as something denoted (vācya).

The intended meaning is this: because it is observed that even that which is not expressive (*avācaka*) can produce comprehension by virtue of its fitness for a relationship with another well-known designation, and because even that which produces comprehension is well known as being non-expressive;
he concludes this with the words "Therefore, distinct...
and "In that case, then not...".
For "being denotable" (vācyatva) consists in being the object of the function of denotation (abhidhā), and not merely being the object of any function whatsoever;
for if it were the latter, one would be proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). This is what he states with the words "the function of the word.
[Objection: Granted that there may be no denotative power (vācakatva) in songs and the like, but here, even regarding another meaning, the denotative power of the word itself is asserted.
Raising the objection, "What indeed is that denotative capacity being restricted?", he says: "well-known," etc.
[The commentary] *Bālapriyā* explains: "This pair" refers to both denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) and indicative capacity (*gamakatva*).
The syntactical connection is that these two do not exist in the word "song" (*gīta*), in "outburst of tears" (*bāṣpāveśa*), and so forth.
However, the intended meaning is that there is indeed the capacity for comprehension.
By the verse beginning with "adho-vaktratva" (downward-facing nature), the meanings set forth in the verse—namely, the connection with shame—are demonstrated.
To the question "Why?", he says: "tasya" (of him), and so forth.

The meaning is that this is the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the commentary (*vṛtti*) passage beginning with "of that [sound], such as the sound of singing" and ending with "is indeed already demonstrated," namely, the phrase "of that which is non-expressive" and so forth.
"Etaditi" (this):
the meaning is that by establishing the distinction between denotative power (*vācakatva*) and suggestive power (*vyañjakatva*), the position of non-distinction is refuted.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says: "And there is a distinction."
The phrase "of those two" is to be supplied [from the previous context].
Regarding the term "of comprehension," the connection is that it refers to another object related to the operation of comprehension.
The reading is also "avagamanīyasya. He states the reason for its connection with comprehension in the passage beginning with "abhidheya" (the denotable).
He explains what was stated—that it is not to be designated as "denotability"—in the words: "for denotability consists in being the object of the function of denotation (abhidhā)."
The meaning is "directly having that as its object. "Merely an operation" means "a general operation."
"Tathātva" means "given that it has as its object merely an activity.
"Siddhasādhana" (proving what is already established) refers to that [already accepted] fact.

The meaning is that there is the fault known as *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established), because one is proving the state of being the object of the operation of a suffix (*vyañjana*), which is already established in our own view. He introduces the passage beginning with "But [if it is argued]... (*nanu*) as a response to an objection, stating:
"Let it not be the case that [the suffix] is expressive (*vācaka*)."
The sense is that this is because of the absence of anything to be expressed; however, the connection here is "of the word" (śabdasya);
"here" means in poetry (kāvye).
The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction;
[it refers to] the word as the signifier,
in relation to another meaning intended to be the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).
The word "api" (also/even) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
As for the phrase "what indeed," and so forth:
the intended meaning is that being a different object (*arthāntaratva*) does not serve as a restrictor of that [property].

Demonstrating the logical sequence, he explains the meaning of the particle *eva* (only) in the statement that "the expression [of the meaning] through illumination alone is appropriate," beginning with the words "by another word" (*śabdāntareṇa*), etc.
"By another word" refers to the word *gaṅgā* and so forth in expressions such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā.
"Of that other meaning" refers to qualities such as coolness and purity.

And in that case, since there is the cognition of that other meaning, regarding its being made an object by another word expressing its own primary meaning, it is only appropriate to speak of its "manifestation" (*prakāśana*), not of the word's "denotative function" (*vācakatva*). Furthermore, the relationship between the meaning of a word and the meaning of a sentence does not apply to the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*). For, as Locana states, the cognition of the word-meaning is indeed unreal; regarding that which is made an object [of cognition], it is only appropriate to speak of "manifestation" for the word, not of its "denotative function."
Nor is it logical to say that the object [of cognition] is denotable in that context;
for denotability consists in being a communicator without mediation by virtue of convention,
as is the case with that very word regarding its own meaning.
Thus he says: "by that which expresses its own meaning.

For being denotable (*vācyatva*) is, by the force of convention (*samaya*), the state of being conveyed without mediation, as in the case of that very same object with respect to another word. He says "well-known" (*prasiddha*): that which is the relationship with another well-known denoting term—that is denotability; or rather, it is the fitness (*yogyatva*) characterized by that [denotability] in that [object].
And such a denotative capacity of the word toward the object does not exist here, nor does that object possess the aforementioned status of being denoted (vācyatva) toward that word.
Anticipating the objection—"If it does not exist, then how was it said to be made an object [of cognition]?"—he says: "Because of cognition" (pratīteḥ).
And yet that meaning is understood; however, it does not do so through the operation of denotation (vācyavācakatva), which means that this operation is indeed distinct [from denotation].
Anticipating the objection—"In that case, let there be no power of denotation, but there will still be the power of intentionality (tātparyaśakti)"—he says: "And not... [in the verse].
[The commentary] *Bālapriyā* explains: "in that meaning."
The statement regarding "manifestation" (*prakāśana*) is a statement regarding "making understood.

Regarding the word—such as the word *gaṅgā*—the claim that it possesses "denotative power" (*vācakatva*) is not tenable; as the reason for this, he introduces the term "expressing its own meaning" (*svārthābhidhāyin*) after first defining denotative power, beginning with the words "For denotative power... and so forth.
Of that very word, such as the word "Gaṅgā" and so forth;
in its own primary meaning, such as the stream and so forth.
Thus he says, speaking with that intention.

He introduces the passage beginning with "it is well-known" (*prasiddha*) as a reason for the claim that "the statement of expressibility is not tenable," preceded by a definition of expressibility—namely, "for expressibility... and so forth.
[This refers to] the meaning, such as coolness or purifying power;
"another word" (*śabdāntara*) refers to words such as "coolness" or "purifying power."
He explains [the verse] in accordance with the context, beginning with "by the well-known," and so forth.
The word "as denotative" (*vācakatayā*) is supplied. "By another designation" means by another word, such as the words "coolness," "purifying," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "tatra vā": "tatra" means "in that state of being denotable," and "nirūpitam" means "defined by that. "Yogyatvam" means "fitness" or "worthiness."

The meaning is that "of that which is characterized by it" (*tenopalakṣitasya*) is an adjective for "of another object" (*arthāntarasya*). The intention is that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) in *yogyatvena* expresses the sense of characterization (*upalakṣaṇe*).
He concludes with the words "And not thus," etc.;
"the object" (*arthaṃ*) refers to such qualities as coolness and purity.
Regarding the word "of the word," this refers to words such as *gaṅgā*.

Because it is explained that the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the phrase "by way of fitness" (*yogyatvena*) functions as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the connection of that [fitness] with the word "perception" (*pratīteḥ*) is ruled out; thus, he introduces that term with the words "If [it] does not exist," and so forth.
By the phrase "if it does not exist," there is a restatement of what was previously said in the passage beginning with "nor is it of such a kind."
Regarding the phrase "the making into an object" (viṣayīkaraṇam) of that meaning such as coolness and purity:
the words "by means of the word 'Gaṅgā' and so forth" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The word "atha ca" (and then) is an explanation of the meaning of the "ca" (and) found in the verse.
That meaning refers to qualities such as coolness and purifying power.
Following the phrase "by means of its function," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "but by means of another function."
And thus he states the result: "Thus," and so forth.
He introduces [the next section] in accordance with the context at hand: "Now," and so forth. [The objection is:
"The power of intention (tātparya-śakti) will suffice."
This has been maintained by certain scholars.
Even those who do not accept its unreality must admit the analogy of the jar and its constituent causes regarding the relationship between the sentence-meaning and the word-meanings.

For just as when a jar is produced, its constituent causes are no longer perceived separately, so too, when the sentence or its meaning is cognized, the words and their respective meanings are no longer perceived as distinct entities at that time.
Only the cognition of the sentence-meaning would disappear;
however, this logic does not apply to the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya),
for when the suggested is being perceived, the cognition of the expressed does not disappear.
"By some," namely by the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). "By those as well," namely by Bhaṭṭa and others. He explains that very principle with the words "for just as... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of their material causes" (*tadupādānakāraṇānām*):
by this expression, the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), namely the potsherds, are defined.

Now, although according to the systems of the Sugatas (Buddhists) and the Kapilas (Sāṃkhyas), at the time of the jar, the material causes do not exist—either because they perish in a single moment in one view, or because they have become latent in another—nevertheless, they are not perceived as separate entities.
Thus, this much constitutes the illustration.
The phrase "it would become distant" means that there is an absence of identity with the chariot; this is the intended sense.
The word "arthāntara" (another meaning) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

The sense is that the power of a sentence which is conducive to the cognition of another meaning is indeed the power of *tātparya* (intentional import), and not that which you [the opponent] maintain it to be.
In the commentary, the phrase beginning with "na ca" (and not) [is used].

The meaning is that it is not logical to claim that, just as the sentence-meaning is understood through the power of intention (*tātparya-śakti*) once the word-meanings are cognized, so too another meaning [is understood] once the sentence-meaning is cognized.
For that "other meaning" would be cognizable by the power of intention because it is cognizable by the collection of words.
The inference "like the meaning of a sentence" is what the objector intends here. Regarding the phrase "and not," he states the reason with the words beginning "since.
By this, the reason "because of the disparity between the example and the subject" is shown.
"'It is indeed unreal'— the sense is that only the sentence-meaning in the form of *sphoṭa* is real.
[This refers to] "by the Bhaṭṭas and others" in the *Locana*.
By the word "etcetera" (prabhṛti), the Naiyāyikas and others are included.
Regarding the term "inherent cause" (samavāyin): that in which a thing being produced inheres is its inherent cause (samavāya-kāraṇa).
The "skulls" (kapālāni) are the fragments;
by this expression, namely the term "instrument of appropriation" (upādānakaraṇa),
they are defined and demonstrated.

One might object: "The general statement 'even by those who... is not tenable, because at the time of taking up [the doctrine], there is no material cause for the Buddhist (Saugata) and Sāṃkhya (Kāpila) systems. Thus he raises this doubt with the words "Buddhist," etc.
He states the reason for the phrase "not existence" with the words "in one case," etc.;
"in one case" refers to the Buddhist system.
It destroys; the phrase "of the appropriations" is to be supplied [to the verb]. For it is their doctrine that whatever exists is momentary.
Elsewhere, in the system of Kapila, [the author] provides a response—
beginning with "even so" (*tathāpi*) and so forth— to the objection that [the effect] would be unmanifest due to the concealment (*tirobhāva*) of the material causes (*upādāna*).
In the commentary, the words "sentence" (*vākya*) and so forth are used;
although it is indeed the meanings of words and sentences that are the subject under discussion,
the mention of "words" and "sentences" is nonetheless for the sake of providing an illustration.
Regarding the phrase "of the words and their meanings":
the ellipsis is "there is no separate apprehension.

The meaning is that once the sentence is perceived, and consequently once the sentence-meaning is perceived from those words, there is no apprehension of the words or their meanings as distinct [entities].
He demonstrates the fault in perceiving them separately with the words "of those," and so forth.
"Of those" refers to the words and their meanings.
"Then" means at the time of their cognition.
"By way of being divided" means by way of separation from the sentence and the sentence-meaning. "It would become distant" means it would remain far removed from the cognition of the word-meaning.

Here, he shows the underlying reason for this in the *Locana*: "Because of the absence of identity of purpose (*arthaikatva*)," since the cognition of the sentence-meaning and the cognition of the word-meanings manifest that [suggested meaning] through an inseparable connection with the manifestation of the expressed (*vācya*).
Therefore, the analogy of the jar and the lamp applies to these two;

for just as when the cognition of a jar has arisen by means of a lamp, the illumination of the lamp does not cease, so too the manifestation of the expressed persists during the cognition of the suggested.

As for what was stated in the first Uddyota, beginning with "just as [the meaning of a sentence is conveyed] by means of the word-meanings," that was intended to show their equality merely on the basis of being instrumental [means].

But if this were so, would it not follow that a sentence possesses two meanings simultaneously? And if that were the case, its very status as a sentence would be undermined, since that status is defined by having a single meaning.
This is not a fault, because those two are established through the relationship of subordinate and principal.

For in some cases, the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is primary while the expressed meaning (vācya) is subordinate; such is the logic of the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning. Locana. Thus [is the principle].

Having refuted the argument for the power of *tātparya* (intentional meaning) regarding the present subject, and in order to establish the intended power of manifestation (*prakāśa-śakti*), he applies the appropriate analogy of the lamp and the jar to the present case, saying "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since that analogy of the word-meaning and sentence-meaning is not applicable here, he applies the relevant analogy— preceded by its formal derivation— to the subject at hand, saying "Just as indeed" (*yathaiva hi*).

But was it not stated previously: "Just as the meaning of a sentence is understood by means of the meanings of its constituent words, so too is the cognition of that reality preceded by the understanding of the meaning of the sentence"?
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, why has that very same principle been so strenuously rejected here?", he says: "As for that...
The word "that" means not by way of universal equality.
"Thus" means in the manner of the simultaneous manifestation of both, like a lamp and a jar;
"of that" refers to the state of being a sentence.

The definition of "having a single meaning" (ekārthya) is that a sentence is said to be one because of the unity of its purpose; the meaning is that there is an absence of a single intended purpose [in the case of two separate sentences]. Furthermore, since remoteness (dūrībhāva) is not admitted [as a ground for syntactic separation], the implication is that the perception of those two as distinct entities should not be accepted.
He states the specific distinction regarding the subject at hand with the words "But this is not," and so forth.
To the question "Why?", he says "For not," and so forth;
the connection is that [it] does not indeed become distant.
He states the reason for this with the words "vācye" and so forth;
the meaning is that the suggested sense (vyaṅgya) is perceived separately from the expressed sense (vācya).
He introduces the passage beginning with "tasmāt" and so forth in the *Locana* with the words "evam" and so forth.
The "logic of the lamp and the jar" (ghaṭapradīpanyāya) refers to the logic of the original nature (prakṛti).
It is preceded by grammatical analysis and preceded by detailed exposition.
He shows what is excluded by the word "only" (*mātra*) in the phrase "similarity due to being merely the means for that" (*tadupāyatvamātrāt*) with the words beginning "but not" (*na tu*).

Regarding the phrase "the definition of having a single referent" (*aikārthyalakṣaṇam*): that which has a single referent (*ekaḥ arthaḥ*) is "that which possesses a single referent" (*ekārtha*); the state of being such is "having a single referent" (*aikārthyam*).
He states the authority for this being the defining characteristic: "because of the unity of the referent" (*arthaikatvāt*).

One might raise the objection that "having a single meaning" is not the defining characteristic [of *śleṣa*], since a sentence that is the subject matter of the figure *śleṣa* can also have multiple meanings. He dispels this doubt by demonstrating his underlying intention with the words beginning "sakṛt" (*at once*, etc.). Wherever, for a particular purpose, one of the two meanings is primary while the other is subordinate, it has already been stated that when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is primary, it is *dhvani*.
But when the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is predominant, another variety [of poetry] will be pointed out.

Therefore, this is established: even though poetry has the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) as its ultimate purpose, it does not follow that the suggested meaning is non-expressible; rather, it is indeed something that is suggested.

Furthermore, you must not admit that the suggested meaning possesses the status of being "expressed" (*vācyatva*) simply because it is not intended to be predominant, for the word is not directed toward that [predominance].
Thus, it is established that there is indeed a certain domain of words that is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

Even in cases where that [suggested meaning] is predominant, why should its very nature be denied? For when a word is heard, it brings about the recollection of a convention (*samaya*) only with respect to a specific object; if that object has already been conveyed by the word itself, then since there is no further operation [of the word] and because many recollections of conventions cannot occur simultaneously, what occasion is there for a difference in meaning? *Locana*: For when a word is heard, it produces the memory of a linguistic convention only with regard to that very [object] which has been understood through it. Since there is no further activity [of the word] once that is achieved, and because numerous recollections of conventions cannot occur at once, what opportunity is there for a distinction in meaning?
The meaning is that this [suggestion] is neither heard nor even remembered.
"Of those two" refers to the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya).
"Therein" [refers to the following].
"Between the two types" means when the first type [is intended];
"the other type" refers to that which is designated as *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).
"Being suggested" (vyaṅgyatva) means precisely "being manifested" (prakāśyatva).

Now, one might object: according to the principle that "whatever a word is primarily intent upon is its meaning," if the suggested sense is predominant, it is logical that it should be the expressed meaning (vācya); if, on the other hand, it is not predominant, why should it be considered "suggested"? To this we reply: our position is established.
He says this with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*).
Anticipating the objection that "let there be no suggestiveness (*vyaṅgyatva*) in the case of predominance," he says "even where" (*yatrāpi*).

*Arthāntaratva* (the state of being another meaning) consists precisely in being related to a correlate (*sambandhisambandhitva*), which is the state of having no established convention (*anupayuktasamayatva*); thus [says] Bālapriyā.
It produces— that is, generates— the recollection of the convention, which is the memory of the agreement, because it acts as a stimulus;
that is the meaning.

The connection with this [verse] is as follows: "If [the meaning] is understood by this very sound heard but once, that is, if it is brought to awareness through the cooperation of context and other factors, then what occasion is there for a difference in meaning? Thus is the link.

Now, if the recollection of convention (*samaya*) is the cause for the comprehension of meaning, then since there are many such conventions, one might raise this doubt. To address this, he refutes the first alternative—that they occur sequentially—by stating, "because there is no activity after having ceased. He refutes the second alternative—that they occur simultaneously—with the words beginning with "convention" (*samaya*).
Now, one might object that multiplicity of meaning is observed in the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia); to this, he says "again," and so forth.
In both instances—"whether heard or remembered"—the word "word" (*śabda*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Alternatively, "heard" (*śrutaḥ*) means "conceived" (*anusaṃhitaḥ*), and the word "word" (*śabda*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The word "remembered" implies that it is the object [that is remembered].
"Not this" means that neither the previous word nor the object is [the thing remembered].

Thus, the point is that in the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), because there is cognition through repetition (*āvṛtti*), the sentence and its meaning are distinct, and the identity of the two is merely figurative (*aupacārika*).
In the commentary, the phrase "this is not a fault" means that there is no fault consisting of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Regarding the word "guṇe" (in the quality): the sense is that in a sentence, neither a suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) subordinate to the expressed (vācya), nor an expressed meaning subordinate to the suggested, is presented as a single unified meaning. He introduces the passage beginning with "kiñca" (furthermore) in the *Locana* with the words "nanu" and so forth.
The phrase "it is logical" (*nyāyyam*) marks the end of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Then, having asked the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) what is appropriate if [the object] lacks primacy, [the author], restating the opponent's answer, says: "If it is argued that it is the state of being suggested" (*vyaṅgyatvam iti cet*), and so forth.
By this, the commentary passage beginning with "first of all, its existence... (*anenāstitāvad...*) has been explained.
He states the meaning: "the state of being a different object," and so forth.
"The state of being a different object" means having an object distinct from the primary object.
"The state of being related to that which is related" means... [end of fragment]

Thus, first of all, suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is indeed distinct from denotativeness (*vācakatva*); furthermore, suggestiveness is different from denotativeness because denotativeness has sound alone as its locus, whereas the other [suggestiveness] has both sound and meaning as its loci. Moreover, while denotativeness resides solely in the word, suggestiveness—whether through metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—can reside in both the word and the meaning.
However, even from that [distinction], the nature of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*) differs both in terms of its own form (*svarūpa*) and its object (*viṣaya*).

First, as for the difference in form: the fact that the eye is the basis for the state of being manifested only in a secondary sense, whereas it exists even in the primary sense, means that its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed not to be discarded; this is the intended meaning.
He concludes this with the word "thus" (evam);
the meaning is that [it occurs] through the distinction of objects and the distinction of essential natures.
By the word "for now" (tāvat), he introduces another point to be discussed.
He states this very point with the words "from this [it follows]" (*itaśca*).
By this, he demonstrates that because there is a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is also a difference in the cause.

And this has been explained in detail under the definition of *dhvani* in the passage beginning, "wherein the meaning or the word... (*yatrārthaḥ śabdo vā*), by means of the inclusion of the term "or" (*vā*).
Since we have already demonstrated in the first chapter (*prathamoddyota*) while explaining the doubling of the word "vyaṅktaḥ," it will not be elaborated upon here again.

Thus, having established the distinction between denotation (*vācakatva*) and manifestation (*prakāśakatva*) based on the difference in object, the difference in essential nature, and the difference in cause, one might raise the following objection: "If there is no distinction between the two bases [of the word and its meaning], then what is the difference between the capacity for manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) and secondary indication (*gauṇatva*)? Anticipating this, [the author] says, "even from that which is non-primary... (*amukhyād api*).
To explain this, he says: "the function of the qualities" (*guṇavṛtti*).
"Based on both" means based on both word and meaning.
*Bālapriyā* explains: the meaning related to the word—whether it be the expressed (*vācya*) or the indicated (*lakṣya*) meaning—the sense is that it consists in being related to that [word].
By this, its being cognizable through words is demonstrated.
He states the reason for its being a different object: "the state of not having a convention applied to it.
This means: the state of being the object of a cognition that does not depend upon the apprehension of a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).
The word "iti" means "this triad. Now, one might ask: "Let this be so; what does it have to do with the present subject? To this, he says: "And that," and so forth.
"Even though it is predominant": the word "of the suggested meaning" (vyaṅgyasya) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. This introduces another point to be stated.
The sense is that the word "first" (prathama) signifies priority.
"That very thing" means that it must be stated as something entirely different.

By the phrase "vṛttāvita" (in the commentary), the reason consisting of the difference in substrata—which will be stated later with the words "yat" and so forth—is referred to; having anticipated this, he explains [the passage] with the words "by this," etc.
"Due to the difference in the causal complex" (sāmagrībhedāt) means "due to the difference in the collection of auxiliary factors" (sahakārivargabhedāt).
He states that in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "substratum" (*āśraya*) refers to the cause, saying: "the difference in causes" (*kāraṇabheda*).

This means "due to the difference in the collection of auxiliary factors" (*sahakārivargabheda*). He further states that in the commentary, the word "substratum" refers to the cause, saying: "also the difference in causes."

Although the status of meaning as the substratum of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) is entirely dependent upon the word—such that the word alone is the primary substratum of manifestation just as it is of denotation (*vācakatva*), and thus there is identity of cause—nevertheless, due to the difference in auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), there is also a difference in the word itself as a cause. This is the meaning.
The explanation of the passage beginning with "of word and meaning" (*śabdārthayoḥ*) is provided by the words "and this," etc. (*etacca* etc.).
He introduces the passage beginning with "But the function [of words] as qualities" (*guṇavṛtti*) by first restating what has preceded, using the words "Thus" (*evam*) and so forth.

The connection is as follows: having thus established non-difference from the primary denotative function (*mukhyādvācakatva*), he says this in order to establish it even from the secondary function (*amukhyāt*).

To the question, "What now is that establishment?", the text beginning with "Because there is no difference in being based on both" (*ubhayāśrayatvāviśeṣāt*) and ending with "suspecting" (*āśaṅkayā*) is stated.
"Then" (tarhi) means:
if there is a distinction between being a denoter (*vācakatva*) and being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*), then [the following applies].
"Ka" means "no"; that is the sense.

One might have the confusion that the meaning is "both" in the sense of being characterized by metaphorical indication (upacāra); therefore, he explains the phrase "based on both" with the words beginning with "śabda," and so forth.
The function known as *guṇavṛtti* (secondary function) is well-established as consisting of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
However, the capacity for suggestion (*vyañjakatva*) is the primary function of the word itself.
Indeed, the cognition of the threefold suggested meaning—whether it be the object and so forth—is not perceived in the slightest as being anything other than primary.
And this is another distinction of essential nature: that which is established as denotative function (*vācakatva*) by virtue of its primary operation upon qualities is called [denotation] itself;
whereas suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*), however, is entirely distinct from denotativeness.
And this has been demonstrated.

This is another variety of metaphorical function (*rūpabheda*): when, in the process of figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*), an object indicates another object, then that [first] object becomes as if transformed into the very nature of the indicated object. As in the example, "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā," and so forth.

In the path of indication (*vyañjanā*), however, when a meaning illuminates another meaning, it is perceived as the illuminator of the other precisely while manifesting its own form, like a lamp—for example, in such cases as "Pārvatī counted the petals of her play-lotus.
And if the conventional usage of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is applied where a meaning, whose own manifestation is not suppressed, indicates another meaning; [then this is the case here].
This being the case, it follows that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone is the primary function of a word;

for, as a general rule, sentences manifest an object that is the focus of their intended meaning (*tātparya*), distinct from the directly expressed meaning (*vācya*). Since the essential nature of both metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) and indication has already been analyzed and determined in the first chapter (*udyota*), it is not written out again here.
"Primarily indeed" means by way of an unerring course. "The three suggested meanings" refers to [the following].
It consists of the substance (vastu), the ornament (alaṅkāra), and the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
"It is indeed the expressive power (vācakatva) itself" means that even there, the application of convention (samaya) exists in exactly the same way.
"It has been explained" means just now. "Transformed" means... [end of fragment].
The meaning is that [the word] does not manifest in its own form.
The intention is that the commentary (*vṛtti*) connects the phrase "that which is a quality-function (*guṇavṛtti*)" with "it rests upon both.
He recalls what was stated previously: "of metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."

Regarding the phrase "precisely as the primary [meaning]," he explains it in accordance with the context as "by way of unimpeded movement. He then clarifies that "the figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*) is indeed denotative power" with the words beginning "even there," and so forth.
"Even there" means even in the case of the figurative function;
"in the same way" means just as in the case of denotative power.
The application of convention (*samayopayoga*) means the application of grasping the linguistic sign (*saṅketa*).
The meaning is that it certainly exists;
the intention is that this is because [the term] functions as a quality (*guṇavṛtti*) by virtue of its cognition being inseparable from the denotatum (*abhidheya*).
In the commentary [it says]: "When one object [is related to] another object.
Here, "object" (*artha*) refers to the current and so forth;
"another object" (*arthāntara*) refers to the bank and so forth.
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is defined as the attainment of another form through the relinquishing of a previous form.
He explains the word "transformed" (*pariṇata*) in accordance with the context of the passage, beginning with "by its own [nature]" (*svena*), etc., in the commentary on the phrase "this [is it].
(*asāv iti*)
The meaning is "for the purpose of [counting] the flow" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the object (artha)": "object" refers to such things as counting the petals of a play-lotus.
"Another object" (*arthāntaram*) refers to shame and so forth.
He provides the example for the statement "while manifesting its own nature," etc., by saying "like a lamp.
He gives an illustration of the statement "an object illuminates another object" with the words "just as in play," etc.

Let it be that there is no identity in nature between the functions of *guṇavṛtti* (secondary indication) and *vyañjakatva* (suggestiveness) in cases where the expressed meaning is completely set aside;
however, in other cases, surely even in your own view, when a single meaning manifests three suggested meanings, what then is the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the word?
It is said in reply:

Since the capacity of a word to manifest an object in such a manner occurs precisely through the power of the word as delimited by context and other factors, how can the utility of the word in that regard be denied?
Furthermore, the difference in scope between the functions of *guṇavṛtti* (secondary indication) and *vyañjakatva* (manifestation) is quite clear;

for the scope of manifestation comprises three things: aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and the like, specific figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), and objects delimited by the form of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).

Regarding this, the *Locana* states: "The cognition of rasa and so forth is a figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*). [One might ask: "Of what kind is it? It is either primary (*mukhya*) or not; for there is no other alternative.
If it is primary, it is denotative (*vācakatva*); otherwise, it is a figurative function.
The sense is that a "figurative function" is the operation of a word mediated by a quality (*guṇa*), such as similarity, which serves as the cause.

"This very operation is primary; however, due to the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is distinguished from denotative function (*vācakatva*) and so forth"—with this intention, he says: "It is said. Thus, having explained the difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) of the illuminating function (*prakāśakatva*)—by way of three modes, namely: (1) because its movement is never faltering (*askhaladgati*); (2) because it does not depend on convention (*samaya*); and (3) because it appears as something distinct—and [having explained] the three contrary forms of the secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*), he now states the difference in their objects (*viṣaya-bheda*). The difference in objects...
[The author] says "pīti" [meaning "moreover"].
