With the intention that even a quality-activity (*guṇavṛtti*) has the mere object (*vastumātra*) as its domain, he qualifies it by saying "delimited by the form of the suggested" (*vyaṅgyarūpāvacchinnam*).
Anticipating the objection that this might be so, however, he refutes it with the words "yadi ca" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the conventional usage of indication" (*lakṣaṇāvyavahāra*): the ellipsis is "not the conventional usage of manifestation" (*na vyañjakatvavyavahāra*). The connection is that the primary function of a word is indeed indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
"'Thus it follows'— the word 'might be' (syāt) is the ellipsis. Here he states the reason, beginning with 'because' (yasmāt)."
The counter-argument by way of a parallel case against one who cannot tolerate what has been stated begins with "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth.
The *Locana* explains its intended meaning with the words "or primary" (*mukhyām*) and so forth.
It states the reason for not formulating an alternative possibility: "because there is no other mode" (*prakārāntarābhāvāt*).
To address the question, "If that were the case, what would follow?", he states the refutation in sequence, beginning with "In the case of being primary" (*mukhyatve*).

He establishes that if [the word] is not primary, it must function through secondary indication (*guṇavṛtti*), by explaining the meaning of the term "secondary indication" (*guṇavṛtti*) in the passage beginning with "The quality is the cause" (*guṇo nimittam*).
He explains the intent of the section of the text beginning with "It is said" (*ucyate*) in the passage beginning with "Primary" (*mukhya*).
This operation is the operation of the word.
Now, one might object that if [the word] were primary, there would be no distinction from being a denoter (*vācaka*); to this he says: "due to the difference in the causal complex" (*sāmagrībhedāt*).
In the commentary, the difference in the causal complex is demonstrated by the words "in the context," and so forth. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):

The meaning is: "by means of the object" refers to the context of manifesting the three types of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*). "'Utility' (*upayoga*)" means utility characterized by the state of being a suggester (*vyañjaka*).

Summarizing in a single passage the reasons for the difference in nature between the functions of *guṇa* (quality) and *vṛtti* (operation)—which have been stated in many texts—for the sake of easy comprehension, he introduces the subsequent section by stating its purport: "Thus," etc., ending with "because of having unimpeded movement.
This means: because of the absence of impeded movement.
"In any way whatsoever," and so forth;
the meaning is "because it conveys an object that has not been conventionally designated.
"Separately," [and so forth].
The meaning is that it is distinct from the literal sense (*vācyārtha*).
The phrase "in three ways" is connected with the phrase "the distinction in the nature of the figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*).
As for the word "this":

The meaning is: "of that [speech] which possesses the three types of form contrary to this, such as faltering movement (skhaladgati) and so forth. Regarding "guṇavṛtteḥ," it means "from the function of the qualities" (guṇavṛttitaḥ).
He states the result of the qualification beginning with "vyaṅgya" (suggested), etc., as "mere matter-of-fact (vastumātra)."

Even with such a qualification, one might ask how there is an exclusion of the scope of metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*); therefore, he states the intended meaning: "Of the state of being a manifester," and so forth.
It is not asserted by anyone, nor can it be said [that it is].
The cognition of the manifested ornament (*vyaṅgyālaṅkāra*) is likewise [not subject to such a restriction].
That which is intended to be communicated by not being expressed through its own word (*svaśabda*) for the sake of perceiving the beauty of the object is the *vyaṅgya* (the suggested).
And not all of that is the province of secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*), because we observe the use of figurative words even in accordance with established convention (*prasiddhi*).
This has been stated previously.
Furthermore, even that which is the object of *guṇavṛtti* (the function of poetic quality) is so only by way of entering into the process of manifestation (*vyañjanā*).

Therefore, there is an absolute difference between the manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) and the function of poetic quality (*guṇavṛtti*). Locana: That which is the object of manifestation is not the object of the function of poetic quality; moreover, another distinction regarding its objects should be applied. In this regard, he states the first type with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
"And it is not possible" means that,
as has already been stated previously, the collection of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇasāmagrī*) is absent therein;
"in that very way" [is said].
The meaning is that the operation of a quality (*guṇavṛtti*) is not appropriate there.
He explains what was previously stated as the qualification of the object: "for the sake of the cognition of beauty.
[He says] "not everything."
However, something does indeed occur, as in the example: "like a mirror blinded by its own breath.
As it has been said: "That [metaphor] may serve as an indication (upalakṣaṇa) of a certain particularity of sound (dhvanibheda)."
Words such as *lāvaṇya* (loveliness) and so forth are based on conventional usage (*prasiddhi*).

Expressions such as "he speaks while lying upon a bed of lotus leaves" arise from conformity to poetic meter (*vṛtta*) and conformity to worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), and so on. Thus [it is said] "pre-" and so forth.
In the first Uddyota, within the passage beginning "those which are not established in another object," he clarifies—
as we have explained— that "not everything" is so, by the words "even that which...
The term *guṇavṛtteḥ* is in the ablative case.

Now, because [the word] denotes [the meaning] by way of depending on one form from one thing and by way of depending on another form from that other thing—through this sequence—and because of its functioning as a quality (guṇavṛtti), let the mere object be the domain of the quality-functioning; however, that which is delimited by being suggested (vyaṅgyatva) is not its domain. *Bālapriyā*:
Let the mere object be the domain of the quality-functioning; but that which is delimited by being suggested is not its domain.
The meaning is that "suggestibility" (*vyaṅgyatva*) refers to being the object of the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vyāpāra*). "And another" means that which was stated in the first *udyota*.

"By way of its qualities and functions" (*guṇavṛttitaḥ*): it should be applied here as that which is to be understood. And since it cannot be stated [directly], he states the underlying reason for this in the passage beginning with "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
He explains the phrase "tathaiva" (in that very way) according to its intended meaning with the words beginning with "na":
"viśeṣaṇam" means the qualifier, namely, that which is delimited by the form of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*).
In the commentary, "the cognition of rasa and so forth" means "the cause of the cognition of rasa and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the object," and so on:
The connection is with the words "whatever object"; "in beauty" means "in the beauty of poetry."
Regarding the phrase "tadvyaṅgyam" (that which is manifested by it): the meaning is that what is intended by this is a manifestation of such a kind, delimited by the nature of being a manifestation.
By the word "sarvam" (all), the *Locana* states that he refers to what is being understood—namely, "something indeed."

Regarding the phrase "yaduktam" (as it has been said): the meaning is "because it has been stated. He explains this [phrase] "prasidhyanurodhābhyām" (by means of common consensus and logical necessity) with the words beginning "prasiddhitaḥ" (from common consensus), and so forth.
"By way of what is well-known" means by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). It has been explained as "something indeed exists," and this is how it has been explained.
Regarding the word "sphuṭayati" (it makes manifest), the word "itself" (svayam) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Since there might be a confusion regarding the genitive case in the phrase "guṇavṛtterapi," he states: "it is the ablative case."
Introducing the passage beginning with "vācakatva" (denotative power) as being intended to demonstrate the distinction [between the two types of metaphorical function], he says "now," and so forth.
Regarding the word "itara" (the other):
its form is the figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*); the meaning is that it depends upon that [denotation] and rests upon it as its support.
"From that other" means "because of its denotative capacity.
This refers to the phrase beginning with "from that other," and so forth.
The meaning is that its nature as a signifier (*vācakatva*) is otherwise, insofar as it depends upon that [signified].
Furthermore, although it is distinct from the functions of denotation (*vācakatva*) and secondary indication (*guṇavṛtti*), it is established as having both of those as its basis.
For suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is sometimes established by depending on denotation.
Just as in the case of suggestion where the literal meaning is intended but not primary (vivakṣitānyaparavācya),
and in some cases, as in suggestion where the literal meaning is unintended (avivakṣitavācya), by relying on the function of secondary indication (guṇavṛtti);
it is precisely for the purpose of demonstrating that both of these are its basis that the two primary divisions of suggestion were presented at the very outset.
Furthermore, because it depends upon both [the primary and secondary meanings], it cannot be said to have a single uniform form;
for its nature is not exclusively that of denoting [the primary meaning], since in some cases it functions by resorting to indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

And he establishes that the nature of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) is not of a single uniform character like the eye, even though it is distinct from duality—this by means of the words "denotative power" (*vācakatva*) and so forth.
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis and is displaced in its order;

the word *api* implies that it is not only the previously mentioned collection of reasons, but also that which is established as being based on both—that is, based on both the primary and the metaphorical—that belongs exclusively to that which is distinct from denotative power, quality, and function.
The formulation of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Therefore, this is the intended meaning: because it is established as the substratum of both, it is distinct from both.
This very point is analyzed as follows: "the state of being a manifestor" (*vyañjakatva*).
"First of all" refers to the passage beginning with "And that... in the first chapter (*uddyota*).
He also indicates another reason with the words "and not... (*na ca*).
"Because of the difference from the two modes of operation, namely denotation (*vācakatva*) and secondary indication (*gauṇatva*)," means "because it differs from that other [mode].
The meaning is: "from the manner of the mode of secondary indication.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "[it is] distinct in both cases."
"By way of sequence" means by order;
"and" (ca) refers to the word "ca" in the phrase "even though it is of a different character."
"Of inverted order" means that it should be construed with the word "of the dissimilar. The word "api" (also) implies "as well as."
The phrase "the sequence is broken" is to be supplied [from the previous context].
Furthermore, such a reading exists in some manuscripts;
the intended meaning is that the word "api" (also/even) is connected with the word "vyavasthānam" (establishment).
He states the meaning implied by the word "api" (also/even): "not only," and so forth.
The explanation of the phrase "by being the basis for both" is "primary," and so forth;
the meaning is "by being the basis for both denotation (*vācakatva*) and metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*)."

"Thus, the formulation of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)" means that the pervasion has been shown as follows: "whatever exists as a substratum is distinct from those [two]. Regarding the phrase "as the substratum of both": [it refers to the fact that the self exists as the substratum of both].
The word "of" (tasya) is to be understood as "of suggestiveness" (vyañjakatvasya);
the meaning is that suggestiveness is distinct from both denotative power (vācakatva) and secondary figurative function (guṇavṛtti), because it exists by depending upon both of them.
"This very [thing]" refers to this same point.
The meaning is that it has already been stated.
"He analyzes" means he demonstrates by way of analysis.
"First of all" [means:]...
He explains that the suffix *tarap* is used with reference to the second illumination (*udyota*), stating "the first," etc. In the commentary, the phrase beginning with "and not" (*na ca*) follows;
the word "that" (*tat*) is supplied by ellipsis (*anuṣajyate*).
The meaning is "the state of being a manifester.
"Precisely by virtue of being a property of both" means by the very reason of being the substratum for both denotation (*vācakatva*) and figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*).
"It does not possess each of those forms individually" means it is distinct from denotation and the others.
The connection is "thus" and "not so.
Regarding the phrase beginning with "as far as," it means "but rather."
Regarding the phrase "in the capacity of being expressive" (*vācakatve*):

the meaning is that even as properties belonging to those words which are devoid of the characteristics of being expressive and so forth, [the universal] does not possess each of those individual forms; this is to be supplied to complete the sense.
In the *Locana*, he introduces the passage beginning with "na cobhayā" (nor both) with the words "hetvantaram ityādi" (another reason, etc.).
This refers to what was stated regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), because it is established by relying on the capacity to denote (*vācakatva*).
Nor does that [probandum] fail to possess each of those two forms simply because it possesses the nature of both.
This is so even by virtue of being a property of sound that is devoid of forms such as denotative power (*vācakatva*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
For instance, even musical sounds possess the capacity for manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) with respect to aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and the like;
yet, in their case, neither denotative power nor indication is perceived in any way whatsoever.

Since the quality of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*) is observed even in objects other than sound, it is improper to assert that [manifestation] is a mode of the properties of words such as denotative power (*vācakatva*).

Furthermore, even if the modes of words such as denotative power and the like differ from well-known modes, since the quality of being a manifestor is observed [in them], it is improper to assert that it is a mode of the properties of words such as denotative power.

And if suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is postulated as a category [of verbal function] even though the types of word such as denotative power (*vācakatva*), indicative power (*lakṣaṇā*), and so forth, are distinct from well-known categories, then why is it not postulated as a category belonging to the word itself? The reason has been indicated [in the previous verse].
He elucidates that very point with the words beginning "for instance" (*tathāhi*),
etc.; [the word] "of them" (*teṣām*) refers to those [beings].
He also indicates another reason for [the existence of] words such as songs and the like— namely, "elsewhere than the word" (*śabdādanyatra*).

The reason indicated is that suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is something other than denotativeness (*vācakatva*) and secondary signification (*gauṇatva*), because it exists even elsewhere than in the word, just like knowability (*prameyatva*) and so forth.

One might object: "Granted that the power of suggestion (*vyañjakatva*) in non-expressive words may differ from denotative power (*vācakatva*) and the like; however, let the power of suggestion in expressive words be no different [from denotative power]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "If... The word "and the like" (*ādi*) includes metaphorical expression (*gauṇa*).
"Of the word alone" is the remainder [of the sentence]. He clarifies that very reason with the words "because of being expressive," and so forth.
The meaning is: because it is distinct from the occurrence of both denotative power (*vācakatva*) and figurative usage (*gauṇatva*), that is, because it functions while being devoid of both of them.
In the phrase "figurative usage" (*gauṇatva*), the term "indirect indication" (*lākṣaṇikatva*) is also implied.

With the intention that the passage beginning with "from sound" (śabdāt) and ending with "because of the observation" (darśanāt) does not connect with what precedes it, but rather connects with what follows, he introduces it with the words "another reason" (hetvantaram).
He then demonstrates that very same "other reason" along with another constituent part [of the argument], starting with "because of being expressive" (vācakatva), and so forth.

The passage ending with "it is divided" (*bhinnam*) is an explanation of the impossibility of stating that [the word] possesses the property of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) such as denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) and so forth;
this is introduced by the words beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).
Regarding the phrase "non-denotative" (*avācaka*): [it refers to the following].
The meaning is "in the case of the sound of a song and so forth. The phrase "non-distinct" (avilakṣaṇam) is to be construed with "denotative capacity and so forth" (vācakatvādeḥ).
"Gauṇam" means "secondary function" (gauṇīvṛtti). In the commentary,
the genitive case in the phrase "of the types of words" (śabdaprakārāṇām) is used in the sense of selection (nirdhāraṇe).
This connects with the phrase "by way of being a mode" (*prakāratvena*).
The meaning is: "by way of being that mode which exists among the various modes of words.
As for the phrase "even though it differs from well-known modes": [it means that although this mode is distinct from those commonly recognized].
The meaning is: "even though it is a reality that the nature of being a manifester (vyañjakatva) is distinct from well-known modes such as denotative power (vācakatva) and so forth.
Regarding the word "tat":
it means "then" (tarhi).
The phrase "by being a variety of word itself" means by being a sub-division of word.

[The question] "Why is it not postulated? [is answered as follows]: Thus, in verbal usage, there are three modes: denotative power (*vācakatva*), metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*), and suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*).

In that regard, concerning the state of being a suggester (*vyañjakatva*), when there is predominance of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*), it is *dhvani*. Its two divisions—*avivakṣitavācya* (where the literal meaning is not intended) and *vivakṣitānyaparavācya* (where the literal meaning is intended but has another purpose)—have been enumerated and previously determined in detail. Another might say: "But if 'the state of having the literal meaning intended but having another purpose' (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*) in *dhvani* and 'the function of qualities' (*guṇavṛttitā*) are considered synonyms for 'suggestiveness' (*vyañjakatva*) and 'denotativeness' (*vācakatva*) respectively, then suggestiveness would reside in the word... *Locana*: [This refers to the objection that if suggestiveness were merely a synonym for denotativeness, then suggestiveness would belong to the word itself.]
Why, then, is synonymy not postulated in this way?
Because there is no obstruction to one's desire.
However, since the distinct nature of manifestation has been demonstrated, how could it be reversed in another object?
The sense is that, in this way, smoke found on a mountain might even be produced by something other than fire.
Now he concludes the classification just established with the words "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*).
By the inclusion of the term "conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*), he excludes the roar of the ocean and similar sounds.

One might object: "The two reasons previously stated—that [the secondary function] depends on the form of denotation (*vācakatva*) and that it depends on the secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*)—are not established in the portion consisting of the unintended literal meaning (*avivakṣitavācya*), because that [portion] has as its sole body indication (*lakṣaṇā*). With this intention, he begins by saying, "Another might say...
Although this point was already determined by the statement, "Because it is established as being based on both of those," [he repeats it here].

Nevertheless, this introduction is intended to dispel the doubts of those who find it difficult to discern the distinction between *guṇavṛtti* (secondary function) and *avivakṣitavācya* (where the literal meaning is not intended).
This is the meaning of the phrase "syāt" (it may be so).
He explains this in the *Locana*: "The state of being a suggester," and so forth.
Regarding the term *iti*: the meaning is "the two words *iti*"; they are synonyms, having the same referent.
The phrase "it is also thus" means that this applies to both of these as well.
To the objection that they might simply be synonyms, he says: "of the state of being a manifester," and so forth.
"Distinct" means distinct from the denotative function (vācakatva) and so forth;
"it has been shown" refers to the fact that this is the case in the case of the sound of a song and the like— this is the intended meaning.
And for this reason, he states that it is incorrect to postulate [the nature of] denotativeness and so forth [in the word], beginning with "That... and so on.
"In another object" means:
in the capacity of being a manifestor residing in the denoter.
"How could they be inverted?"—
the ellipsis is "by way of having the nature of being expressive" (*vācakatva*) and so forth.
"For in this way," and so on.

The meaning is that if suggestiveness (vyañjakatva) were not based on denotative power (vācakatva) and the like, then smoke located on a mountain might as well not be produced by fire; therefore, such a reversal [of the logical relation] is not tenable.
He concludes the classification:
since suggestiveness has been demonstrated as distinct from both denotative power and the figurative functions (guṇavṛtti), the threefold division is indeed established.
The meaning is as follows:
"it excludes" means that [the word] lacks the capacity to denote the sound of the ocean and so forth; this is the sense.
The author introduces the intent [of the passage] with "nanu" and so forth.
"Upajīvaka" means that which lives depending upon or relying upon; "anujīvaka" means that which lives in close proximity [to another].

Regarding the phrase "vācakatva" and so forth, the fact that [the word] is based on both denotative power (*vācakatva*) and metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*) has been restated here in order to provide a refutation regarding a specific part [of the argument].

Anticipating the objection that "since this very objection has already been answered by the reason that [the two types of poetry] both rely on the meanings as previously described, raising it again and offering a rebuttal is redundant," he provides the following response: "Even though... and so forth.

The phrase "of that whose expressed meaning is not intended to be primary" is to be understood as referring to *dhvani* (suggestive poetry); the connection is that this is said for one who perceives the distinction [between the two types of poetry] to be difficult to define.
"Śāśaṅka" means the suspicion that [the nature of] dissimilarity is difficult to define.
That which is stated— "it does not exist"— is incorrect.

Since the comprehension of another meaning is preceded by the cognition of the signified (vācya) and the signifier (vācaka), how can there be the conventional usage of *guṇavṛtti* (metaphorical function) in such cases?
For in *guṇavṛtti*, either a word is superimposed upon another object by some cause while its own primary meaning is completely set aside— as in "The boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*) and so forth—
or else, without entirely abandoning its own primary meaning, it extends to another object through the medium of its connection with that [primary] meaning.
For this very reason, having first accepted the first type of division, this [section] is an introduction to the second type of division.
By the words "vivakṣitānyaparavācya" and so forth, he demonstrates his own acceptance of what has been admitted by others.
To show the reason for the absence of the conventional usage of "guṇavṛtti" (secondary function), he first presents the account of that very *guṇavṛtti* itself, beginning with "na hi."

The term *guṇavṛtti* means "functioning by way of a quality" (*guṇatayā vṛttiḥ vyāpāraḥ*). It refers to the functioning of a word through a quality (*guṇa*)—that is, by means of a cause such as similarity—and its application (*vṛtti*) even toward a different object, namely its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This demonstrates the view of the secondary (*gauṇa*) usage. Alternatively, [the phrase] "when it expresses its own meaning" (*yadā vā svārtham*) is the beginning of the *Vṛttikāra*; this is the commencement of the *Vṛttikāra*.
He states the supporting evidence for this with the words "for this very reason," and so forth.
Of the first variety, which is intended as having a meaning other than the expressed;
"the second variety" means that in which the expressed meaning is not intended.
Here he shows the reason with the words "vivakṣita" and so forth.
He introduces the passage beginning with "na hi" by showing its purpose with the words "guṇavṛtti" and so forth,
[stating] "in order to show the reason."
The remainder [of the definition] is "that which has a meaning other than what is intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).
He states the meaning of the word *guṇavṛtti* as being common to both the metaphorical (*gauṇa*) and the indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) types: "by way of quality," etc.
"By way of quality" means by way of being non-primary (*apradhānatayā*).
For the denotative function (abhidhā-vṛtti) is indeed primary;
[it is] the operation of the word.
The remainder [of the verse] follows.
By this, there is a summary of both the secondary (gauṇa) and the metaphorical (lākṣaṇika).
Regarding the secondary, he states another meaning for the word "guṇavṛtti" with the words beginning "by a quality" (guṇena), and so forth.
The explanation of "by means of a quality" (*guṇena*) is "by similarity, etc. (*sādṛśyādinā*).
"By a cause" (*nimittena*) is a statement of the meaning of the instrumental case.
The explanation of what was just stated is "even in the case of another object," and so forth.
In that case, the object is indeed a different meaning;
thus, it is figurative (gauṇa), as in "A hamlet on the Ganges" and so forth.
In such instances, the state of the expressed meaning being unintended (avivakṣitavācyatva) is established.

For this very reason, in the case of *dhvani* where the intended meaning is not the literal one (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*), the perception of the essential nature of both the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*), as well as the comprehension of the meaning, is observed; thus, the conventional usage of "suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatva*) is consistent with logic.

Since that which manifests its own nature while manifesting another is called a "suggester" (*vyañjaka*), in such a context, the usage of the term "secondary function" (*guṇavṛtti*)—which implies that suggestiveness is merely a form of denotative power (*vācakatva*)—cannot be applied as a rule.
The *Locana* demonstrates the definition (*lakṣaṇā*).
By means of these two divisions, it indicates that [the function] has not been accepted as consisting of the two divisions of "that whose expressed meaning is not intended" (*avivakṣitavācya*).

For this very reason, by the phrase "and by the word whose own meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtasvārtha*), it occupies another object," it shows those same two divisions with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva ca*).
The meaning is: for this very reason, it is not logical to employ the figurative usage (*guṇavṛtti*) [of "lamp"] there on the strength of the reasons already stated.
He demonstrates the uncontradicted reasoning in the form of common worldly consensus with the words "its own nature" (*svarūpam*).
By "is said," he refers to the lamp and so forth.
However, because the sense organs and so forth are instruments (*karaṇa*), they do not possess the nature of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) in the production of cognition.
The phrase "it shows" (*darśayati*) and so on means that,

with reference to the meanings of the words *guṇa*, *vṛtti*, and *śabda* as previously stated, he demonstrates the secondary function (*gauṇī*) by the passage beginning with "when by a cause" (*yadā nimittena*), and he demonstrates the indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) by the passage beginning with "or when its own meaning" (*yadā vā svārtham*).
Now, one might ask: "Even though the function of a word through its qualities (guṇavṛtti) possesses many forms, why has only this twofold division been shown with examples? To this he says:
"By this," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "it indicates" (sūcayati), he provides the reason for it: "For this very reason," and so forth.
"That very twofold division" means that it is precisely the twofold division of the unexpressed (avivakṣitavācya).
In the commentary, the phrase beginning with "for not," etc., [is used].
The connection is that, at that time, the state of having the intended meaning as its expressed sense (vivakṣitavācyatva) is indeed not tenable.
"In another object" means in the primary meaning of words such as "Gaṅgā. "Without abandoning a part" [is the meaning].

For the word "Gaṅgā" and so forth indicates the bank of the Gaṅgā specifically— either by way of its being the bank of the Gaṅgā or simply by way of its being a bank— and thus there is no abandonment of its own primary meaning in part.
The phrase "by means of its connection with that" means by means of the cause that is the connection with its own primary meaning, namely proximity.
"Another object" refers to the shore and so forth.
"It occupies" means it brings [that object] into its own domain;
the word "sound" is to be supplied [as the subject].

The meaning is "the word 'Gaṅgā' and so forth. Regarding "locane"—it means "the reasoning" (yukti); that is, the reasoning stated in the passage beginning with "conforming to reasoning" (yuktyanurodhī).
"It fulfills [the requirement]—such as a lamp and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Manifestation (vyañjakatva) is the state of being a communicator (jñāpakatva), and that belongs primarily to the sense organs and so on; therefore, why include the mention of lamps and such things which serve merely as auxiliary causes (sahakārin)? To this, he says: "But of the sense organs and so on..."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the inclusion of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is intended.
The connection [of the sentence] is that because they are instruments (*karaṇa*) in the arising of cognition, they do not possess the nature of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "in such an object" (*tathāvidhe viṣaye*) refers to this.
The meaning is: "in another object" refers to an object of cognition preceded by the cognition of the signified (vācya) and the signifier (vācaka).
"'Of the signifying capacity alone'" means "that which is based solely upon the signifying capacity.
"'How is it differentiated? [is the question].
The meaning is that it is not divided.
He states the reason for this with the words "of that" (tasya), and so forth.
But how is the suggestion (dhvani) whose literal meaning is unintended (avivakṣitavācya) distinct from the function of poetic quality (guṇavṛtti)?

Since it is evident that its two divisions consist of the two forms of the modes of qualities (*guṇavṛtti*), this too is not a fault. For *dhvani* whose literal meaning is unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*) may indeed rely on the path of the modes of qualities, yet it is not of the nature of the modes of qualities alone;
for the mode of qualities is seen even when it is not devoid of suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*).

And [the author] demonstrates the acceptance of the fact that suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is the cause of the aforementioned beauty, while showing the rejection [of the view that it is merely] indicative, by means of the words "when not intended to be expressed" (*avivakṣite*).
The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction from what preceded.
The word "its" (*tasya*) refers to...

Regarding the two subdivisions of that [type of suggestion] where the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary (*avivakṣitavācya*), two modes consisting of the metaphorical (*gauṇa*) and the indicative (*lākṣaṇika*) are observed—that is, they appear—therein. He refutes this with the words "this too" (*ayamapi*).
The meaning is: that which has as its basis—that is, as its cause—the two subdivisions of the path of metaphorical function (*gauṇavṛtti*), which reside in the preceding stage (*kakṣyā*).
And this has already been determined previously.
He states the reason for the absence of that nature [of identity]: "it is a function of qualities" (*guṇavṛtti*).
The meaning is that both forms—namely, the figurative (*gauṇa*) and the indicative (*lākṣaṇika*)—are included.
But how can the function of the qualities (*guṇa-vṛtti*) be empty of [direct] manifestation?
For it has already been stated: "Setting aside the primary function (*mukhyā vṛtti*), the perception of an object occurs through the function of the qualities;
with respect to that which is aimed at as the result, the word does not have a faltering course."

Thus [it is said]. Having raised the objection that "you yourselves have asserted that metaphorical usage (upacāra) is devoid of purpose, whereas the operation of suggestion (vyañjana-vyāpāra) resides in a portion of that purpose," he says "And as for suggestiveness" (vyañjakatvaṃ ca), meaning that the intended suggestiveness, which consists in the form of a point of rest (viśrānti-sthāna), does not exist therein.

Regarding "bālapriyā locane": the phrase "shows" implies that it is the opponent (pūrvapakṣī) who speaks. The explanation of the passage beginning with "guṇavṛtti" is provided by the words "gauṇa" and so forth.
He explains "it is perceived" (*lakṣyate*) in order to dispel the confusion regarding its meaning as something else: "it appears" (*nirbhāsyate*).
The phrase "in the manner stated by 'not indeed' and so forth" is the ellipsis to be supplied. "The preceding stage" (*prākkakṣyā*) means the stage prior to *vyañjanā*.

"Previously indeed" means: at the point in the text beginning with "For not... during the occasion of explaining the verse starting with "Do not wander, O righteous one. "The absence of that nature" refers to this.

The meaning is that there is an absence of being of the nature of a figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*). Now, one might object: "Since the absence of being of the nature of a figurative function for the unintended literal sense (*avivakṣitavācya*) is already established by the statement 'for a figurative function is indeed seen even when devoid of suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*),' what is the purpose of the passage beginning with 'and suggestiveness' (*vyañjakatvañca*)? To this, he introduces that passage with the words "Now, [one might object]... (*nanvityādi*).
[Objection: "But surely the previous statement must be intended for something else. To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth; and "thus," and so forth.
The meaning is that you yourselves have already stated that the other sentence should be set aside.
The phrase "the desired" is explained as "having the nature of the place of rest.
Regarding the word "therein":
the meaning is "merely within the function of the qualities (guṇas)."
Regarding the statement "it does not exist":
here, what is intended by "manifesting" is not merely the act of manifesting, but rather the act of manifesting that serves as a locus of rest.
The meaning is that this [metaphorical function] does not occur without the manifestation of a suggested sense that serves as the cause of beauty.
The commentary’s statement, beginning with "But the metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*)," is an elaboration of what was previously said: "It is also seen even when devoid of suggestiveness.
Indeed, the metaphorical function occurs both by relying solely on the properties of the expressed meaning and by relying solely on the suggested meaning.

It should be understood that the connection [of the words] "in the manner that" (*yathā*) and so forth with the sentence beginning "that which is" (*yāpi*) and so forth consists of the form of metaphorical transference (*abhedopacāra*), and there is an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) of the words "is denoted" (*vācyā*) and so forth, as well as "is suggested" (*vyaṅgyā*) and so forth.

In this context, the phrase "by resorting to the properties of the denoted" (*vācyadharmāśrayeṇa*) is explained in the *Locana* in accordance with the subject at hand: "the property which has the denoted as its object.
[Such a property] does not remain established without the suggested.

The function of quality (guṇavṛtti), however, is possible in the form of a metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra) based either on the attributes of the expressed meaning or solely on the suggested meaning,
as for example: "The boy is fire because of his sharpness," or "Her face is indeed the moon because of its delightfulness."

And just as in such cases as "there is no tautology regarding a beloved person," even that secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*) which takes the form of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs simply by relying on the connection with the indicated meaning, even without the perception of a beautiful suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*),
as in the case of "the platforms are crying out" and so forth.

"Locana says: 'The property of the expressed' means by way of relying on that function of denotation (abhidhā-vyāpāra) which is a property having the expressed as its object; the sense is that it serves to augment that [suggested meaning].

The point is that, just as in the case of *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard), the process culminates precisely in the establishment of another meaning—a suggested meaning—by means of the expressed meaning."
In that regard, he provides an example of [the view of] Gauḍa, beginning with "as for instance" (yathā).
He then begins to demonstrate the second type, which is devoid of suggestiveness, beginning with "and also that which" (yāpi).
"Beautiful form" (cārurūpa) refers to the locus of repose.
In its absence, that function of manifestation does not arise at all,
because [the cognition] reverts and comes to rest in the expressed meaning itself, like an ordinary man who has seen and lost a divine splendor in a single moment.

The phrase "of the reader who loves the simple" (*bālapriya-vācakasya*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. The explanation of the meaning of the term *bhāva* is given as "for the purpose of augmenting that," which means for the purpose of augmenting the subject matter (*abhidheya-artha*).
To explain how figurative usage (guṇavṛtti) serves to support that [primary meaning], he states "śruta" and so forth, along with an illustration:
Just as in cases such as "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," night-eating and the like are postulated as the means of establishing the fatness and other qualities already heard;
and that postulated further meaning culminates precisely in the establishment of the fatness and so forth—so too it is in the case of figurative usage.

The meaning is: because the function [of indication] terminates precisely in the establishment of the meaning denoted by another word, which is the indicated object (lakṣya) as a distinct entity (arthāntara).

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), by the word "only" (*mātra*) in the phrase "by resorting to the mere suggested" (*vyaṅgyamātrāśrayeṇa*), the primary suggested meaning that serves as the cause of beauty (*cārutvahetu*) is excluded. [The example begins: "O dear person... (*priye jana*).

It has already been stated that in the phrase "he is dear," because of its sharpness (tīkṣṇatva), there is a statement of a cause consisting of qualities such as excessive [heat] and so forth; furthermore, by means of the word "repetition" (punarukta), its lack of worthiness to be accepted is indicated.
In these examples, the excellence of qualities such as sharpness is suggested (vyaṅgya), but the sense is that this does not produce aesthetic charm (cārutva).

Regarding the term "upalakṣaṇīya" (to be indicated): it means by relying solely on that relationship—such as the relation of container and contained—which exists between the primary sense of the word "mañca" (bed/platform) and the object to be indicated (upalakṣya), namely the child and so forth who are situated upon the bed.
The phrase beginning with "cārurūpe" (of beautiful form) serves to state what is excluded by the word "mātra" (solely).
Regarding the example "mañcā" (the platforms):
here, because there is a plurality of boys situated on the platforms, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is singular; yet even that does not produce aesthetic charm (*cārutva*).
Locana explains this term "of beautiful form" (*cārurūpa*) as follows: "it rests" (*viśrānti*).

[Objection: "But surely, let the function of suggestion (vyañjanā) exist even without the perception of a beautiful suggested meaning (*cāru-vyaṅgya*. To this, he says: "In the absence of that," and so forth. "In the absence of that" means in the absence of a beautiful suggested meaning.
"That" refers to [suggestion] based on indication (*lakṣaṇāmūlaka*).
It "unfolds" means it shines forth.
To the question "From what? he says: "by turning back," and so on.
Regarding the word "moment":

Just as an ordinary, impoverished man whose divine splendor was seen for only a moment and then vanished returns to his former state of being merely ordinary, so it is with the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*): even in cases where that [function] is the cause for the cognition of a beautiful suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), it occurs precisely through its entry into the state of suggestiveness,
just like denotative power (*vācakatva*).

And where there is linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) with respect to an impossible object, such as in "the earth with golden flowers" and so forth, the cognition of the suggested beautiful form (*cārurūpa-vyaṅgya*) alone is the motivating factor; thus [Locana] says: "But where..."—anticipating the objection, "What should be done where the rest lies in the suggested meaning?"—he says: "But where... *Locana*: Now, one might ask: what should be done in a case where the repose lies in the suggested meaning? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But where... etc.

The meaning is that there is another function of suggestion (vyañjanavyāpāra) therein which is indeed quite evident. He states an example accepted by the opponent himself: "just like denotative power" (vācakatvavat).
The sense is that you yourself have already accepted the function of suggestion regarding denotative power, by not rejecting the first variety of *dhvani*.

Furthermore, when another primary object is possible, it is precisely that other possible primary object which is superimposed; the designation "superimposition" arises merely from the difference in the objects [of cognition]. This is the very lifeblood of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
However, since golden flowers are impossible from their very root, what kind of superimposition could there be regarding the gathering of them?
For the superimposition would have to be in the form, "the earth has golden flowers."

Therefore, in this context, it is the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanavyāpāra*) alone that is primary, not the conventional usage of superimposition (*āropavyavahāra*); the latter arises merely as something dependent upon the operation of suggestion. Thus he says: "because [it] is impossible."
Regarding the term "prayojikā" (the motivator):

for it is only the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) that constitutes the purpose (*prayojana*), as it is the locus where cognition comes to rest. If, however, [the purpose] were superimposed [upon the literal meaning], then since that is impossible, not even the suspicion of a resting place for cognition can arise.
The meaning is: because the resting place is found in the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) itself, therefore [it is the motivator].
In the commentary, "where," etc.;
"it" means the figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*).
"By entering into the state of being a manifestor (vyañjaka) itself"— the word "becomes" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He introduces this passage with the words "But surely," and so forth.
"Apart" means distinct, in the sense that it conveys a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) of beautiful form. "First" means...
The meaning is "that which has a suggested sense other than what was intended to be expressed. By not rejecting [the opponent's position]— that is, by accepting it—
he introduces the passage beginning with "asambhavini" (impossible) through its underlying purport, starting with "furthermore" (*kiñca*).
The particle *ca* (and) in the phrase "asambhavinā ca" (*and by that which is impossible*) is explained by the word "kiñcit" (*something*).

Regarding the phrase "vastvantare" (*in another entity*), and so forth: the meaning is that superimposition occurs only when both the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object of superimposition (*āropya*) are present.

As in the case of fire and so forth with respect to a young boy and the like. Now, one might ask: "If both [the object and the superimposed attribute] exist, how can there be the linguistic usage of 'superimposition'? To this he says: "merely by virtue of being another object.
The meaning is: "merely by the fact of being a different object."
The sense is that, in reality, there is no identity between those two.
Regarding the phrase "iti" and so forth:

the meaning is that the superimposition of one thing upon another—where both the object of superimposition (*āropya*) and the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) exist by their own nature—is the primary lifeblood of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
Let this be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "Of those with golden flowers," and so forth. "From the very root" means excessively.
"Its gathering" refers to the gathering of the golden flowers.
In that context, regarding the passage beginning with "suvarṇapuṣpām" and so forth,
the word "kaḥ" means "one who is devoid of a living soul."

[Objection: "In that case, how is the usage 'the earth with golden flowers' (suvarṇapuṣpāṃ pṛthivīm) justified? To this he says: "suvarṇa... and so forth. The connection is: "there would be a superimposition (āropa), for [it is] the intellect (dhī). The sense is that without such a superimposition, that usage by a great poet could not be sustained. He states the conclusion: "Therefore," and so forth.
"Metaphorical usage" (āropavyavahāra) means usage based on the figurative application (guṇavṛtti) rooted in superimposition (āropa).
He says this [to explain it].
The meaning is that he speaks with the aforementioned intention. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the term "motivating cause" (*prayojikā*) means "that which motivates worldly usage.
He states the essential meaning of the passage beginning with "of beautiful form" (*cārurūpa*) as follows: "the suggested meaning" (*vyaṅgya*), and so forth.
The phrase "in the form of a purpose" (*prayojanarūpam*) is a qualifying attribute containing a reason (*hetugarbha*).

[Objection: Even when the function of suggestion (guṇavṛtti) is present in a subject that is impossible [to be expressed literally], it is only the designation "suggestion" (dhvani) that accords with reason.

Therefore, in the case of suggestion where the literal meaning is unintended (avivakṣitavācya), the function of suggestion—which is not distinguished by a specific quality of suggestiveness—belongs to both varieties;

it is not, however, of a single form, for it is perceived as something that delights the hearts of the sensitive (sahr̥daya) because it serves as the cause of their perception in another object-domain (locana). [The phrase] "even when present" [is explained as follows].
The sense is: "when [the capacity] has been supported for even a moment for the sake of the perfection of the operation of manifestation (*vyañjana-vyāpāra*). Regarding the word *tasmāt*:

that which is characterized by the nature of being a manifester (*vyañjakatva*) is "not distinguished" (*aviśiṣṭā*) by that specific quality; the meaning is that she whose distinction—that is, differentiation (*bhedana*)—is non-existent, possesses no differentiation in her state of being a manifester.
Alternatively, she is "not distinguished" by the specific operation characterized as being a manifester, meaning she is not set aside from her own nature, but is rather completely pervaded by it.
Regarding the phrase "tadekā": that which does not possess a single form together with that characteristic of being a suggester (*vyañjakatva*) is so described [as *atadekā*].

In cases where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*), suggestiveness is distinct from the function of a quality (*guṇavṛtti*), because it is the cause of a beautiful cognition, just like the suggestiveness residing in cases where the expressed meaning is intended (*vivakṣitavācyanibandhana*).

For a figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*) cannot be the cause of the apprehension of the beautiful (*cāru*); therefore, one might argue that let the superimposed meaning alone, accompanied by the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), be the point of rest for the cognition—what is the use of resorting to a suggested meaning that is beautiful in form? To this, he says: "superimposed," and so forth.
The word "impossible" contains the reason [for the argument].

By the phrase "having been resorted to for even a moment," it is shown that the object which has become the domain of a figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*) is the scope of the intermediate intention (*avāntaratātparya*). In the commentary, the expression "in such a subject matter" means "in a sentence whose literal meaning is impossible."
He introduces [the following] with "Therefore," and so forth.

He explains the phrase "distinguished by the specific nature of being a manifestor" (*vyañjakatvaviśeṣāviśiṣṭa*) in accordance with the present context as "being a manifestor," and so forth. In the word "by that" (*tena*), the third case ending denotes the instrument (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*).
By means of the commentary, he states the established result—the meaning as it has been realized—beginning with "the state of being a manifester" (*vyañjakatva*) and so forth.
"Of that" refers to the figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*).

"Difference" (*bheda*) is a subordinate property (*avāntaradharma*). This is stated thus for the purpose of concluding the difference between the state of being a manifester and the figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*) which has already been demonstrated.

Having explained [the previous point], he now explains this passage— beginning with "Or rather" (yadi vā)— with the intent of concluding the discussion on the predominance of suggestiveness and the non-predominance of other [factors] as already established:
"Or rather" (yadi vā) means "and yet" (atha ca).
"Unqualified" (*aviśiṣṭa*) means that which is not qualified or distinguished.

Alternatively, taking the etymological derivation to mean "that which has no *viśiṣṭa*—where *viśiṣṭa* signifies a distinction (*viśeṣa*) or special regard (*ādara*)"—he says: "having its own nature suppressed.

Furthermore, intending the analysis as "unqualified by the distinction of being a manifestor" (*vyañjakatva-viśeṣeṇāviśiṣṭā*), and considering that verbal roots have multiple meanings, he states another interpretation: "pervading everywhere" (*āsamantādvyāptā*).
The word "yadi vā" (or rather) is to be supplied [to the previous sentence].

To the objection, "Even so, let it be that the function of a quality (*guṇavṛtti*) has a single form, namely that of being a manifester (*vyañjakatva*)," he says, "But it does not have that single form," and explains this with the words beginning "by that" (*tena*), etc.
The reason for the absence of identity with that [the literal meaning] is given by the words "sahṛdaya" and so forth. The word "not" (na) is to be supplied.

Since the function of suggestion (guṇavṛtti), which delights the hearts of connoisseurs (sahṛdaya) and is perceived, does not exist [in the case of the literal meaning], the connection is: therefore, it is not identical with that.

It should be understood that by superimposing upon the suggestiveness (vyañjakatva) the quality of delighting the hearts of the connoisseurs and the state of being suggested— which reside in the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya)— the identity of suggestiveness with figurative function (guṇavṛtti) is negated through the prior negation of those [qualities].
Thus, by demonstrating that figurative function lacks the singular nature of suggestiveness, it is established that suggestiveness is distinct from figurative function.
In this context, the phrase "because it is the cause of cognition" (*pratītihetutvāt*) serves to demonstrate the reason;
its meaning is "because it is the cause for the cognition of beauty," with the word "of suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatvasya*) understood as the ellipsis.
With the intention that this is the formal argument (*prayoga*), he says in the *Locana*: "where the expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed," and so forth.
"Separately" means "distinctly.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), [the phrase] is "devoid of that form."
The meaning is: "devoid of being a cause for the cognition of beauty.
The phrase "of the figurative function" (guṇavṛtteḥ) is to be supplied [from the previous context].
He introduces this passage—beginning with "for not," etc.—as being useful for the inference already stated.
Because it is seen as being empty of that form.
And although this has already been indicated previously, it is stated again for the sake of even clearer comprehension.
Furthermore, that property of word and meaning characterized by manifestation conforms to a well-established relationship; thus, it does not fall within the scope of anyone's disagreement.

For the operation characterized as suggestiveness (vyañjakatva) proceeds as something adventitious (aupādhika), arising from a connection with a different set of causal conditions, while strictly adhering to that well-known relationship between word and meaning called the signifier-signified relation (vācyavācakabhāva).

Therefore, it is distinct from denotative power (vācakatva); for denotative power is the fixed nature of a specific word, established through its inseparable concomitance [with the meaning] from the very time of linguistic convention (vyutpatti).
But that [cognition] is indefinite, because it is conditioned by external adjuncts (*aupādhika*).
The *Locana* illustrates this with the words "in another object."

In passages such as "Agni is a *vaṭu*," etc., [the author] shows— by the words "Moreover" (*api ca*)— how suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*), being non-fixed due to its being adventitious (*aupādhikatvena*), has a different cause than denotative-ness (*vācyavācakatva*), which possesses a fixed nature; this was stated previously in the first chapter (*prathama-uddyota*).

"Aupādhika" (conditioned) means that it is produced by the aforementioned variety of manifesting capacities (*vyañjakatva*). Consequently, it is, in other words, distinct from the denotative function (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) which is restricted by conventional agreement (*samaya*).
This very point is the explanation of the phrase "in another context" (*viṣayāntare*) used by the *Bālapriyā*—namely, in passages such as "fire is a vaṭa tree.

Furthermore, he introduces the passage beginning with "even though" (*athāpi ca*) with the words "niyata... and so on, with the intention that this text establishes the nature of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) against those who maintain the doctrine of non-existence (*abhāvavādin*), according to the maxim of "driving in a pillar" (*sthūṇānikhanananyāya*).
[The phrase] "due to its fixed nature" (*niyatasvābhāvāt*) means...
The point is that denotative capacity (vācakatva) has a fixed nature because it depends upon convention (samaya).
The reason for its lack of fixity is stated as "because it is adventitious" (aupādhikatvena).
As for the question "How so? and so forth:
The meaning is that the cause for the operation of denotative power (*vācakatva*) is indeed distinct from the cause for suggestive power (*vyañjakatva*).
In the commentary, the phrase "in another set of conditions" (*sāmagryantare*) and so forth means:
"due to connection with another set of conditions," that is, due to the presence of the primary set of conditions such as context (*prakaraṇa*) and the like.
"It functions conditionally" (aupādhikaḥ pravartate) means that it arises as something conditioned.
With the intention that the word "condition" (upādhi) here refers to another intermediate causal complex, he explains it with the words "in its capacity as a manifester," and so forth.
The "variety" (vaicitrya) in its capacity as a manifester consists in the subordination, predominance, and other such relations between the expressed meaning and the sentence.

[Objection: "Even if this operation is produced through connection with another causal complex (*sāmagrī*), since it is the operation of that which denotes, let it be *abhidhā* (denotation) itself. To this, he says: "For this very reason," and so forth.
"For this very reason" means: for the very reason that it is produced as adventitious (*aupādhika*) due to connection with another causal complex;
that is precisely what has been stated.
In the commentary, "of a specific word" means of a word that depends directly upon convention (*samaya*). "Self" (*ātman*) means its own nature (*svabhāva*).
"At the time of linguistic derivation" means "at the time of the convention";
such is the reading.
The word "tat" means "the word"; "tasya" means "of that denotative capacity";
and "sa tu" [means "but that"].
The meaning is that the function [of the word] is that of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*).
"By way of delimitation through context and so forth" means by way of the assistance of context and so forth;
for it is perceived through the delimitation of context and so forth, whereas otherwise it would not be perceived.
Now, if it is indeed indeterminate, what is the use of examining its essential nature?
This is not a fault; for its indeterminacy pertains to the nature of the word itself.
But it does not [apply] to its own object, which is characterized as the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Furthermore, the logic of being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*) is observed in this state of being a suggester (*vyañjakabhāva*),
just as the nature of being a logical mark has an indeterminate manifestation with respect to its substrata.
Because it is dependent on one's will;
and it is non-deviant with respect to its own object.
He clarifies this very point, as previously shown, by means of the example of the eye, saying "for this very reason."
He shows its conditioned nature (aupādhikatva) with the words "from context, etc.
[He asks] "What of it?
[The answer is: Because it is not fixed, one might imagine its ultimate form according to one's own preference; however, no such ultimate form exists.
The meaning is that an investigation of a non-entity is not tenable. "In the nature of the word" means in the mere form of the word, which is the locus of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).
Regarding the phrase "in their respective substrata":
for the capacity of smoke to indicate fire is not eternal, since we observe it indicating other things as well as its failure to indicate fire in certain instances.
"Due to dependence on desire.
Here, "desire" refers to the inquiry into the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), the wish to recall the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and so forth.
"Regarding its own object" means:
"Of that" means of suggestiveness;
"from the cognition" means from its manifestation.
The passage beginning with "context and so forth" does not indicate another reason.

However, [the author] says in the *Locana*— “it shows its being adventitious”— in order to provide an exposition of that which was already stated as “because it is adventitious. In the *Vṛtti*, the words “if it were not fixed” (*yadi aniyata*) are supplied with the word “that” (*sa*).

He states the existence of that suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) in the eyes [of the verse] with the words "because of its non-restriction," and so forth. "Because of its non-restriction" means because there is an absence of restriction to the denotative function (*abhidhā*).
"It could be conceptualized"— the remainder of the sentence is "its own nature.
He states the reason for this with the words "ultimately real," and so forth.
It follows the ultimate truth.
The word "iti" indicates the reason.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And not," and so forth.
The sense is that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even things such as a "sky-lotus" would have to be subject to investigation.
He explains what is intended by the phrase "consisting of sound" with the words "the locus of convention," and so forth.
By the word "only" (*mātra*), there is an exclusion of the object (*artha*).
In the commentary, the word "tasya" (of that) means "of the state of being a manifester.
As for the phrase beginning with "na tu" (but not), etc.:
The phrase "its indeterminacy" is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
"In its own," meaning in that which is related to itself;
"in the object characterized as the unmanifested," meaning in the sense that is to be manifested (*vyaṅgyārtha*).

The meaning is that for whatever possesses a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), it possesses the quality of being a suggester (*vyañjakatva*); thus, there is indeed a fixed rule regarding the suggester with respect to its object.
Here is the statement of an illustrative example: "In the case of being a logical mark" (*liṅgatve*), etc.
"The principle of being a logical mark" (*liṅgatvanyāya*) refers to the similarity of being a logical mark (*liṅgatvasāmya*).
"Being a mark" (*liṅgatva*) means being the indicator of fire and so forth.
"In the substrata" refers to smoke and so forth.
He explains the phrase "appearing in an indefinite manner" in the *Locana* with the words beginning "for not," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "not always present," he states the reason: "other," and so forth.
"Other" means distinct from fire.
"Of the non-indication of fire" means the absence of the indication of fire at some time;
"from seeing" means from experience.
Regarding the phrase "because it is dependent on desire" (*icchādhīnatvāt*), he explains the word "desire" (*icchā*) in accordance with the context as follows: "Desire," etc.
The "manifesting nature" (*vyañjakatva*) consists in the presence of the pervaded [property] within the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Furthermore, because it is not restricted to the nature of sound itself, it is impossible to conceive of it as having the mode of being a signifier (*vācakatva*).

For if that [conceptual content] were to have the mode of being the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*), it would also be restricted to the nature of that word, just like the denotative capacity itself.

And such a contingent property (*aupādhiko dharmaḥ*) of words cannot be accepted by one who knows the reality of sentences and maintains that the relationship between word and meaning is innate (*autpattika*), while asserting the distinction between human and non-human sentences.

For if he did not accept it, then even though the relationship between word and meaning were eternal, there would be no difference between non-human and human sentences in their communication of meaning; for the eye, once its own object has been apprehended...

He clarifies what was stated—that [the definition] does not deviate from the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) and so forth, and that no one harbors any doubt regarding it—with the words "And that" (*sa ca*).
The meaning is: "that which is characterized as being a manifestor."
Regarding the term *autpattika*:

"birth" (*janman*) is the second modification of being, consisting of existence (*sattā*). Through proximity or by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to non-origination (*anutpatti*); the desire to know that [non-origination] is *jijñāsā*.
The "desire to remember the pervasion" (*vyāptisusmūrṣā*) is the desire to recall the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhya*) by the reason (*hetu*).
By the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), the inquiry into the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and other such properties is included.

The ancients accepted that the desire to know the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) and so forth are the causal factors for inference; it should be understood that the status of being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*) is dependent upon them through these very factors.
The explanation of the intended meaning of the phrase "non-deviating from what is not its own object" is given by the words "in itself," and so on.
"In itself" means in the logical mark (*liṅga*) which is related to itself.
Regarding the object (*viṣaya*) and the probandum (*sādhya*);
or rather, there is also the reading "or regarding the object" (*viṣaye vā*).
This connects with the word "grasped" (*gṛhīta*).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the three characteristics" (*trairūpyādau*): the "three characteristics" (*trairūpya*) consist of the presence [of the reason] in the subject (*pakṣasattva*), its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), and its absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāsattva*), which constitute the members of inference; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), [properties such as] being unsublated (*abādhitatva*) and so forth are included.
Among these, the three characteristics pertain to the inferential mark (*liṅga*), while being unsublated and the other [criteria] pertain to the probandum (*sādhya*).

"Does not deviate" means that its status as an indicator (*jñāpakatva*) does not deviate with respect to its own object. However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "not deviating from its own object" means that the status of being an indicator does not deviate with respect to the indicated object, such as fire.
In the commentary, the term "in the form of denotative capacity" (*vācakatvaprakāratā*) is used.
The meaning is that it is a subordinate property of denotative capacity.
"Tad" means "in that case."

He introduces the passage beginning with "And that... by raising an objection: "Is it not the case that what was said—that the nature of being a manifester (vyañjakatva) is not subject to any disagreement—is incorrect? For since the relationship between word and meaning, characterized as the relation between the manifested (vyaṅgya) and the manifester (vyañjaka), is non-eternal, it would contradict the *Autpattika-sūtra*.
He then provides the resolution with the words "na kasyacid" and so forth.
It makes clear, that is to say, it renders manifest or establishes;
the construction in the commentary is "the property of words.
This was stated with the Jaiminīya sūtra beginning with "But the connection of a word with its meaning is innate" in mind.
This was stated with the Jaiminiya sūtra, "The relation of a word with its meaning is innate" (*autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena saṃbandhaḥ*), in mind; thus he says "innate" (*autpattika*) and so forth.
Therein, by the word *autpattika*, the meaning "eternal" (*nitya*) is intended; he demonstrates the manner in which that [meaning] is obtained with the words beginning with "by birth" (*janmanā*).
It is "characterized" (*lakṣyate*).
It is said that there are six modifications of entities: "it is born, it exists, it grows, it transforms, it declines, and it perishes.
In this context, the meaning is that the second modification, which consists of existence (*sattā*), is characterized by the term "birth" (*janman*) due to its proximity to it as a cause.
Because it might be conceived that mere existence is always non-existent simply because it is being characterized, [the author], being dissatisfied with that, says "contrary," and so forth.
By birth alone, there would be a state of non-distinction [between the Veda and other texts].

However, if that were admitted, then even for human-authored sentences— which, while not abandoning their connection with their own denotata, possess other functions superimposed through adjuncts (upādhi) in accordance with human will— there could also be falsehood.

The word *autpattika* is used here in its conventional sense as a synonym for "eternal" (*nitya*). Therefore, the meaning is: by that [proponent] who maintains that there is an eternal relationship between word and meaning characterized by *śakti* (potency), as Jaimini does.
Regarding the phrase "absence of distinction":
consequently, since the intrusion of human defects would be irrelevant, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) found in human utterances—which is based on those defects—would not be established.
For if the cognition of the cognizer itself is indeed of such a nature, then there is no fault whatsoever in the sentence; how, then, could there be invalidity?

Even in the case of a non-human (apauruṣeya) sentence, such [invalidity] might occur due to the deficiency of the cognizer. The word *bālapriyā* is to be supplied [as the subject]. The meaning is that "arising" (*janman*) is indicated by the cause which is the relation consisting of contradiction (*virodharūpa-sambandha*).

In this context, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is used in the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*) in both alternatives. Out of parsimony, he says "or by convention" (*rūḍhyā vā*), etc.; "by convention" means by the technical designation of the author of the Sūtras.
He states the conclusion: "By that," and so forth.
The connection is: "he who is a follower of Jaimini accepts.
[The term] "the definition of potency" refers to this.
The meaning is that it consists in the capacity for awakening [the understanding].

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase beginning with "innate" (*autpattika*) is stated as the seed of the aforementioned doubt, whereas the phrase beginning with "human-made" (*pauruṣeya*) is stated as the reason for its necessity to be accepted.
He states the fault in not accepting this with the words "that," and so forth.
"Of his" means of Jaimini, the knower of the true nature of sentences; the word "in the opinion" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Regarding the words 'in the word' (*śabde*) and so forth:
the meaning is that because the relationship between word and object—which consists in the word's capacity to convey the object—is eternal.
For validity (*prāmāṇya*) is indeed the power to produce a cognition whose domain is the object."
That capacity exists in sentences whether they are true or even untrue;
validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*),
whereas invalidity is produced by defects in the causes, subverting cognitions (*bādhakapratyaya*), and so forth— this Mīmāṃsaka doctrine should be noted here.

To avoid the objection that there would be a lack of distinction (nirviśeṣatva), he demonstrates the fault in such a lack of distinction with the words "And therefore," etc. Regarding "in the person":
it refers to the occasional intrusion of defects, such as error and the like, into the speaker who is a person.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "of that which is the entry of human error into the sentence.
"Because it is ineffective" means the sense is that there is an incapacity to subvert the eternal relationship between word and meaning.
In reality, that basis [of invalidity] depends on human defects.
In the case of human or worldly statements that do not correspond to reality, invalidity is caused by their lack of correspondence to reality;
therefore, the connection is that such [invalidity] would not be established [in the case of the Veda].

To the objection that a defect in the person (*puruṣadoṣa*) brings about the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of a sentence by way of the cognizer, he says: "of the cognizer," and so forth. "In that manner" means "by way of being non-conformable to reality (*ayathārthatayā*)."

He states another fault as well—beginning with "in the non-human" (apauruṣeya) and so forth. "In the non-human sentence" means in a Vedic sentence; "due to the depravity of the cognizer" means due to the defect of the person who understands it.
In that case, there would be invalidity due to the cognition of its being contrary to reality.

Regarding the acceptance of such adventitious properties (*aupādhika-dharma*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*), he states the merit [of this view] with the words "the acceptance of that" (*tadabhyupagama*), etc.,
and "the person" (*puruṣa*).

The meaning is: "of those [words] in which there is another operation that is superimposed—that is, imagined—and for that very reason adventitious (aupādhika), because they conform to human desire, namely the intention of the speaking person.

For it is observed that even entities that have not abandoned their own intrinsic natures (svabhāva) can possess contradictory functions when they are endowed with other adventitious operations produced by the convergence of other causal complexes (sāmagrī).

To illustrate: the rays of the moon and so forth, while carrying a coolness that soothes the entire world of living beings, are nevertheless perceived by people whose minds are being consumed by the fire of separation from their beloveds.
That [words] cause distress is indeed well-established.

Therefore, one who wishes to establish the falsity of human statements— even while acknowledging their natural connection with meaning— must clearly state some adventitious form distinct from their denotative capacity (*vācakatva*).
And that [function] is nothing other than being a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
For being a manifestor consists in the illumination of that which is to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*).
And human sentences primarily illuminate only the intention of the person [who uttered them].
And that [word] is indeed the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). Now, one might object: "Even if another property (*dharma*) is admitted, how can there be falsity?
For the word does not abandon its own property characterized by being a manifestor. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is seen," and "predominantly" (*prādhānyena*).
As he said: “In this way, there arises the cognition ‘this person knows,’ but not [the cognition] ‘this object is thus’.
Thus, it is the perception by another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) that is sublated here, and not the fact that the stated object is established by experience.

To the question—“What is the purpose of that statement [beginning with] ‘na tu... (‘but not...’)? which appears to state that the stated object is established by experience—he introduces the relevant passage with the words “nanu” and so forth.
"How so? means that it would not be established.
He states the reason for this with the words "for not," etc., [referring to] "that which has the characteristic of being an illuminator."
The meaning is that it consists in the capacity for conveying the sense;
for the connection is not "it abandons" [the sense].
By this, the maxim that "between what is already established and what is being postulated, the established is stronger" is demonstrated.
In the commentary, the phrase "of things" (abhāvānām) means "of categories" (padārthānām).
It refers to those things in which there exists another property that is adventitious (aupādhika), produced precisely by the convergence of a different causal complex (sāmagrī).
"Contrary activity" (*viruddhakriyatva*) means the production of an activity contrary to its own nature.
"The frost-rayed one" (*himamayūkha*) refers to the moon.
"Extinguished" (*nirvāpita*) means that by which the world of living beings has been brought to the cessation of its heat.

By the phrase "bearing such coolness," the fact that its inherent nature has not been abandoned is shown; and by the phrase "causing torment [despite] the presence of other causal factors such as separation from a beloved," the performance of a contrary action is demonstrated. As it is said in the *Śākuntala*: "The moon releases fire through its rays which contain frost."
He introduces [the argument] with "Therefore," and so forth.

He provides authoritative evidence for the claim that human sentences primarily manifest the intention of the person [who uttered them] by citing the words of the author of the *Bhāṣya* on Jaimini’s Sūtras—namely, what he says: "This person... and so on.
The meaning is "the person who speaks.
"Thus he knows" means that he understands exactly as it was spoken by him.
The construction is: "thus there arises a cognition"; the word "of the cognizer" is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
[this is] not, however, the actual meaning.
The meaning is this: the conviction that "the object is exactly thus" does not arise for the cognizer;
the underlying intention is that the object may be subject to sublation.
Therefore, the sense is that [words] primarily manifest only the intention of the person, which consists in the cognition of the respective meanings of those sentences.

But you [the word] are not the denotable object (*abhidheya*), because there is no relationship characterized by the status of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between it and that [meaning].
[Objection: But surely, by this same logic, the conventional usage of the term "suggestion" (*dhvani*) would result for all worldly sentences whatsoever.
Since all [words] are manifestors by this same principle,
this is true;
however, that quality of being a manifester which consists in revealing the speaker's intention is common to all worldly sentences without distinction.
That [meaning] does not differ from the denotative meaning because the suggested meaning is established therein as being inseparable [from it].
By the words "the word is the concomitant," the falsity [of meaning] in cases such as the sentence "the tip of a finger" is stated precisely due to the intrusion of the speaker's intention.
"Together with that"—[this refers to the aforementioned point].

The sense is that because it is not fixed, there is an absence of its being innate (*naisargikatva*). Regarding the phrase "by way of being inseparable" (*nāntarīyakatayā*): [the opponent objects]—"Let it be granted that the intention of the person (*puruṣābhiprāya*) is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), and let there also be a distinct function (*vyāpārāntara*) called suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) belonging to the sentence."
