Nevertheless, as to how there is falsity regarding the object, he says: "In that way," and so forth.
"In that way" means by the manner of manifesting the speaker's intention (*abhiprāya*); "here" refers to the subject matter of human speech.

"Observation by another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntaradarśana*) means observation by another means of valid cognition, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is the knowledge of the meaning of that sentence.
In some cases, it is sublated; that which is sublated is rendered [invalid]. Sublation (*bādhā*) means non-arising.

Because human speech conforms to human will, there is no necessity for it to correspond to an object as it is actually perceived; thus, at times, there arises perceptual or other forms of knowledge regarding an object different from what was seen.
The meaning is that because [the object] does not arise, it has a false nature. As for "but not," the word "is sublated" (bādhyate) is to be supplied.
The "verbal concomitance" (*śābado 'nvayaḥ*) is the natural relationship between a word and its meaning, characterized by the capacity to convey that meaning.
Showing this general statement in a specific instance, he says: "By this [phrase], etc.";
that is, in the case of sentences such as "On the tip of a finger" or "A hundred excellent elephants on the tip of a finger."

"It has been stated that [the meaning] is false" means that even for something whose referent is incoherent, it is possible for it to be intended by a person; this is the sense. Thus, although the relationship between word and meaning is eternal in the form described, because human sentences conform to the intention of the person, the falsity of the sentence-meaning intended by him [is established].
It should be understood that because those sentences have false meanings, they lack authority;

however, in the case of authorless (apauruṣeya) sentences, since there is no speaker, all of them possess authority. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "together with that" (*tena saha*) [is used].
The meaning is "together with the intention of the person. "'Of the designation'" means of the word.
"'Because of the absence of a relationship between the signified and the signifier,'" etc.
By this, it is shown that the relationship which exists between the word and its suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) does not possess the nature of the signifier-signified relation (vācyavācakabhāva).
Regarding this, he states the reason in the *Locana*: "Because of its non-regularity," and so forth.
The meaning is that because of the cause of non-regularity, there is an absence of inherent necessity (*svābhāvikatva*).
Now, relying on the statement that the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) is what is manifested (*vyaṅgya*), he raises an objection: "But by this... and so forth.
"Entailed" (*prasakta*) means arrived at, or alternatively, the subject of a logical consequence (*āpatti*).
He states the reason for this with the words "of all," and so forth.
He shows that this is an accepted conclusion with the words "true," and so forth:
"This is indeed true."
The meaning is that the quality of being suggestive (*vyañjakatva*), which arises through the manifestation of intention, belongs to all [words].
He states the distinction with the words "but rather" (*kiṃtu*) and so forth;
the connection is that this suggestiveness does not differ from denotative power (*vācakatva*).
In place of the reading "by revealing the speaker's intention," there is also the reading "by revealing the object qualified by the speaker's intention.

The term "unqualified" (aviśiṣṭa) means common (sādhāraṇa). He states the reason why [the suggested meaning] does not differ from the denotative [meaning] in the passage beginning with "for the suggested... and so forth.

But it is not by virtue of being intended [to be expressed]. However, for that suggested meaning which exists as something intended to be expressed, its capacity to suggest is the cause for the designation "dhvani. Locana: Even when the sentence "Bring the cow" is heard, although the intention is manifested, it is the object itself—qualified by that intention—that is fit for the action of bringing the desired thing, and not the mere intention alone which accomplishes anything.
"By virtue of being intended to be expressed" means by virtue of being primary.
"But for that which... [refers to the following].
The intended meaning is "in the examples of dhvani.
For from poetic sentences, one does not seek a cognition useful for such things as bringing or taking away;
rather, one seeks that which brings about the repose of cognition.
And that [suggestion] culminates in the intention itself, not in the object intended.

Now, one might ask: "If it is thus the intention alone that is suggested, how is it that it was stated that there are three kinds of the suggested? To this he says: "By way of being inseparable" (*nāntarīyakatayā*), which means "by way of being invariably concomitant" (*avinābhūtatvena*).
He explains the state [of affairs] in the *Locana*: "The word 'cow' (*gām*)," and so forth.
The connection is with the phrase "even when the intention is manifested.
This means: even when the intention to bring the cow for the purpose of taking milk and so on has been manifested.
The "meaning" (artha) refers to the meaning consisting of the cow as the object of the action and so forth.
However, as for the phrase "but not," etc.:

since the intended purpose cannot be accomplished without a meaning in the form of an action such as bringing the cow as the object, the implication is that suggestiveness (vyañjakatva) is not distinct from denotative power (vācakatva), just as the suggested sense (vyaṅgya) is not distinct from the expressed sense (vācya). This is the underlying thought.

Anticipating the objection that a negation is untenable because there is no attainment of the status of being intended (*vivakṣitatva*) for that which is manifested as a mental intention (*abhiprāya*), he explains [the verse] with the words "by way of predominance" (*prādhānyena*).

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), this is to be construed with the phrase "of that which is manifested. He fulfills the syntactic expectation regarding the expression "existence by way of being intended" by specifying "in the examples of *dhvani*."
In the commentary, the phrase "its being suggestive" (tad-vyañjakatvam) means "the state of being suggestive with respect to that [meaning].

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even in the examples of *dhvani*, as in ordinary worldly sentences, the expressed meaning possesses primacy, which is another term for being intended [as the primary sense]. Anticipating this doubt, the author states his intention with the words beginning "from the expressed meanings of poetry" (*kāvyavācyebhyaḥ*).
"Leading" (nayanā) means being instrumental for actions such as bringing [something] to its destination;
"comprehension" (pratītiḥ) refers to the comprehension of the expressed meaning (vācyārtha).
"It is not requested" means that it occurs by force; such is the sense. "But rather" (api tu) [indicates this].
The sense is: "What, then, is being requested? [The answer is:
"That which brings about the repose of cognition"—that is, that which brings about the repose of the cognition of the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "such a cognition is what is being requested."
The meaning is that the cognition of rasa and so forth is what is being sought;
the point is that this [cognition] consists in the cognition of the excitants (vibhāva) and the rest.
Now, one might object: let even that [rasa-cognition] terminate in the denoted meaning (vācya).
To the question, "Since it is rooted in that [the literal meaning], how can the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) possess primacy?", he says: "And that," etc.
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of "but" (tu).
It means that [the function] culminates precisely in the intended meaning (abhiprāyaniṣṭhā), which results in the suggested meanings such as aesthetic flavor (rasa) and so forth.
"Intended object" means the literal meaning (vācyārtha).
Therefore, the point is that in poetic sentences, the primary status of the expressed meaning is not characterized by its being the intended [or primary] sense.
He introduces the passage beginning with "But as for... (*yattu*) in order to dispel the doubt regarding its lack of purpose: "Now, [if]... (*nanu*), and so forth.

The connection is as follows: if that which is the specific intention (*abhiprāyaviśeṣa*)—the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*)—is manifested through the primary meaning (*tātparyeṇa*), being manifested by both the word and its literal sense (*śabdārtha*), then it becomes "intended" (*vivakṣita*).
"Intended" means "primary."

"That very [cognition]" means precisely that which consists of a specific intention; "of an unlimited object" is a statement containing a reason; however, the connection is with the phrase "but it is shown in such a manner."
‘In that way’ means in the manner described.
‘And having the form of not being intended’—
the word ‘intended’ is to be supplied [to complete the sense].

Regarding the phrase "no over-extension" (*nātivyāpti*) and so forth: as for that suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) in the form of a specific intention which is manifested by both word and sense, it becomes the intended [meaning] when it is manifested through the speaker's purposive intent (*tātparya*).
However, that alone is not the sole determinant for the application of the term *dhvani*, because it is not all-encompassing (*avyāpaka*).

Rather, everything—whether manifesting through its intended meaning (*tātparya*) in the form of the three aforementioned types of divisions, or being of the nature of intention (*abhiprāya*), or even non-intentional—is a determinant for the application of the term *dhvani*. Thus, the definition of *dhvani* consists in the specific quality of suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) as previously described.
There is neither over-extension nor under-extension [of the definition].

Therefore, according to the opinion of those who know the true nature of the sentence, the verbal operation characterized as "suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatva*) is not contradictory; on the contrary, it is observed to be entirely consistent.
This usage of the term *dhvani* proceeds precisely by relying upon the view of the wise ones for whom the *śabdabrahman*—the Word-Brahman—is perfectly determined and free from corruption.

Having thus demonstrated in the *Locana* that there is no room for disagreement here on the part of the Mīmāṃsakas, he shows that for the Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*) there is none at all, stating: "thoroughly ascertained" (*pariniścita*).

That which is thoroughly ascertained—established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), free from corruption, and devoid of the latent impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃskāra*) due to the dissolution of the manifold expansion of duality (*bhedaprapañca*).

"Brahman, which is called Śabda, whose nature is light and reflection, is pervasive; it is *bṛhat* (vast) because it is filled with specific powers, and it is *bṛṃhaṇam* (the nourisher/expander) because of its lordship over the power of creating the universe—by whom [it is known]... [The commentary] says: "By way of being inseparable. *Bālapriyā* [notes]: "By way of being inseparable."
The meaning is "by way of being inseparable.
He explains the state [of the word] in the *Locana* with the words "the cow," and so forth.
The connection is that [this occurs] when the intention has been manifested.
The meaning is: "even when the intention [of the speaker] to bring a cow for the purpose of obtaining milk and so forth has been manifested.
"The referent" (artha) means the referent such as being the object of the action of bringing a cow.
"But not," and so forth.

The sense is that, without an object in the form of an action such as bringing cow-products and so forth, the intended meaning cannot be established; therefore, suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is not distinct from denotative power (*vācakatva*), just as the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) is not distinct from the expressed (*vācya*).

Anticipating the objection that a prohibition is untenable because the suggested meaning in the form of an intention lacks the status of being "intended to be spoken" (*vivakṣita*), he explains [the verse] with the words "by way of predominance. In the commentary, this is to be connected with the phrase "of which suggested meaning."
He fulfills the expectation regarding the phrase "the state of being intended" by saying, "in the examples of dhvani.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the expression "its suggestiveness" (*tad-vyañjakatvam*) means "suggestiveness having that [intended meaning] as its object.

Anticipating the objection that even in the examples of dhvani, as in worldly sentences, the denoted meaning possesses primacy—which is synonymous with being intended—he states the underlying intention: "from poetic sentences..."
"Leading" (nayanā) means being employed in actions such as bringing [the meaning] about;
"cognition" (pratītiḥ) refers to the cognition of the expressed meaning.
"It is not requested" means that it occurs by force; such is the sense. "But rather" (api tu) [indicates this].

The sense is: "What, then, is being requested? It is that which brings about repose in cognition—that is, which brings about repose in the cognition of the expressed meaning (vācya). The word "cognition" (pratīti) is to be supplied [with the verb] "is requested" (abhyarthya).
The meaning is that the apprehension of rasa and so forth is what is sought after;
the point is that this [apprehension] consists in the apprehension of the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth.
But one might object: let even that [apprehension] terminate in the expressed meaning (vācya).
To the question, "Since it is rooted in that [the literal meaning], how can the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) possess primacy?", he says: "And that," and so forth.
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of "but" (tu).
It means that [the function] culminates precisely in the intended meaning (abhiprāya), which results in the suggested meanings such as aesthetic flavor (rasa) and the like.
"An intended object" means the literal meaning (vācyārtha).
Therefore, the point is that in poetic sentences, the primary status of the literal meaning is not characterized by its being the speaker's intended subject.
He introduces the passage beginning with "But as for... (*yattu*) in order to dispel the suspicion that the text is purposeless, starting with "Now, [one might object]... (*nanu*).

The connection is as follows: if the suggested element (*vyaṅgya*), which consists of a specific intention (*abhiprāyaviśeṣa*) within the function (*vṛtti*), is manifested through the primary sense (*tātparya*), then being manifested by both the word and its meaning, it becomes what is intended (*vivakṣita*).
"Intended" (*vivakṣita*) here means "primary" (*pradhāna*).
"That very [cognition]" means having the specific nature of an intention.
"Of that which has an unlimited object" is a statement containing a reason (*hetugarbha*). However, the connection is: "but it is shown in such a way."
‘In that way’ means in the manner described.
‘And having the form of not being intended’—
the word ‘intended’ is to be supplied [to complete the sense].

Regarding the phrase "no over-extension" (*nātivyāpti*) and so forth: in cases where the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), that specific intended suggestion which is manifested by both word and meaning becomes what is "intended," being manifested through the speaker's purpose (*tātparya*).
However, that alone is not the sole determinant for the application of the term *dhvani*, because it is non-pervasive.

Rather, everything—including that which takes the form of the three aforementioned types of distinctions, whether manifested through the primary sense (*tātparya*) as being of the nature of intention (*abhiprāya*) or of the nature of non-intention—is the determinant for the application of the term *dhvani*. Thus, in the definition of *dhvani* as a specific kind of suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*), [all these factors are included].
There is neither over-extension nor under-extension [of the definition].

Therefore, according to the view of those who know the nature of the sentence, the verbal operation characterized as "suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatva*) is not contradictory; on the contrary, it is observed to be entirely consistent.

It is precisely by relying on the opinion of the wise ones—who have attained certainty regarding the uncorrupted Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*)—that the conventional usage of "suggestion" (*dhvani*) is established.

Having thus demonstrated in the *Locana* that there is no room for disagreement here among the Mīmāṃsakas, he shows that for the Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*) there is none at all, by means of the words "pariniścita" and so forth.

"Pariniścita" means thoroughly ascertained, established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), free from corruption, and devoid of the impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃskāra*) due to the dissolution of the manifold expansion of duality (*bhedaprapañca*).

Brahman—known as *śabda* (the Word), whose nature is illumination (*prakāśa*) and self-reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), which is expanded (*bṛṃhita*) by being filled with specific powers (*viśeṣa-śakti*), and which is the cause of expansion (*bṛṃhaṇa*) due to its lordship (*īśvaratva*) over the power of creating the universe—is that [by which things are manifested]. By those [powers]... [is the meaning].

*Bālapriyā*: Since it exists in some cases, taking that [instance] into account, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) there; and since the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) [meaning] such as aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) lacks the nature of intention (*abhiprāya-rūpatva*), there is no lack of extension (*avyāpti*) in that situation either—this is the meaning.
He concludes with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
The connection is that [the means of knowledge] is not contradictory.

By explaining the meaning of the term "knower of the reality of sentences" (*vākya-tattva-vid*), he restates what has already been discussed; and by explaining the meaning of the word "wise man" (*vipaścit*) as qualified by the attributes such as "well-ascertained" (*pariniścita*), he elucidates the concluding passage.
He states the purport of the section about to be expounded with the words beginning "evam" (thus).
"Sā" (she) means "vimatiḥ" (doubt).

Following the passage beginning with "pariniścita" and such, as well as the words of Bhartṛhari beginning with "anādinidhanaṃ brahma," he explains [the Lord] as possessing a form (*savigraha*), starting with the word "paritaḥ.

With the intention that here the term *apabhraṃśa*—which denotes specific defects—is used to indicate the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of all defects, he explains [the verse] with "galita" and so forth;
that is, by virtue of having the manifold expansion of duality (*bhedaprapañca*) dissolved, meaning being devoid of association with the expansion of duality.
The third case ending is used in the sense of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are the causes for the state in which the proliferation of distinctions has dissolved.
The explanation of the words and phrases is called "the designation of word-meanings" (*śabdārtha*).
That which has the designation "sound" (śabda) means that its essence consists of name and form (nāmarūpa).

Alternatively, it means that in which there is the manifestation (sphuraṇa)—that is, the designation—of both sound and object; the sense is that it is the substratum for the delusion of sound and object.
He states its nature as being free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi) with the words "prakāśa" and so forth;
the meaning is that its essential nature is self-luminous knowledge.
With the intention of deriving the word "Brahman" from the verbal root *bṛh*, he explains it as "vast by virtue of its pervasiveness."

Having thus explained [the term] as being supreme in the sense of being without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), he explains it also as being supreme in the sense of having limiting adjuncts (*sopādhi*) with the words beginning "of the particulars" (*viśeṣa*).
The meaning is: by that fullness (*pūrṇatā*), which consists in being filled (*nirbhara*) with the powers (*śakti*) of all the particulars (*viśeṣa*) in their individualized forms;
[this] he connects with the word "vast" (*bṛhat*).
Intending to derive the word *brahma* from the root *bṛh*, he explains it as "vast (*bṛhat*) by virtue of its pervasiveness.

Thus, having explained it with reference to the supreme state free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), he now explains it with reference to the state possessing limiting adjuncts (*sopādhi*) as well—beginning with the words "of the particulars" (*viśeṣa*), etc.
The meaning is: by that fullness (*pūrṇatā*), which consists in being filled (*nirbhara*) with the powers of all the particulars in their individual forms (*vyaṣṭi*).
He connects this with the word "bṛhat. With the intention of deriving the word "brahman" from the verbal root *bṛh*, he says "expanded" (*bṛṃhitam*) and so forth.
In the word "expanded," the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
To explain how the form of nourishment (*paripoṣa-rūpa*) constitutes strengthening (*bṛṃhaṇa*), he says "of the universe" (*viśva*) and so forth.
Should one consider whether there is contradiction or non-contradiction with those powers whose objects are the various manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) of the universe?

For those who maintain that the relationship between word and meaning is artificial (*kṛtrima*) and who possess knowledge of reasoning, this manifesting nature (*vyañjakabhāva*) of words is established by experience; and like [the manifestation of] other objects, its lack of contradiction does not even enter the path of rejection.

The meaning of this "Locana" is as follows: first of all, the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas) maintain that there is some other entity denoted by the term "Brahman"; what then can be said regarding its being a signifier (*vācaka*) or a suggester (*vyañjaka*)?
Even in the case of the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*), they have indeed admitted another function.
And this has been explained in detail in the first chapter (*uddyota*).

Having thus demonstrated that this matter is beyond dispute for those who know the rules of sentences and words, he says "artificial" (kṛtrima) in order to show that even for logicians who know the true nature of reality, doubt in this regard is not tenable.
Those such as the Naiyāyikas and Sautrāntikas who assert that the relationship between word and meaning is artificial—meaning its very nature consists solely in convention (saṅketa)—have stated:
"The cognition of the meaning of a word does not arise from a [real] connection, because it is based on convention."
Likewise, words express that which is conventionally designated. "Of other objects" refers to lamps and so forth.
By those reasons, [He is] "dear to the ignorant" because He possesses lordship (*īśvaratva*), that is, the capacity to transform the universe;
or alternatively, *māyā* is the power of creating the universe,
and because He possesses lordship over it, the meaning is that He is the presiding substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for *māyā* as it transforms into the form of the universe.

The word "yair" (by whom) is connected with "pariniścitam" (ascertained); the word "teṣām" (of them) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. In the commentary, it says "virodhāvirodhau" (contradiction and non-contradiction).

The contradiction pertains to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), while the absence of contradiction pertains to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Now, even if the usage of the term *dhvani* proceeds by relying on the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), since the expressive word possesses the characteristic of being a signifier (*vācaka*), one must consider— just as the Mīmāṃsakas do— the contradiction or lack thereof in accepting a distinct power of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) separate from its power of signification (*vācakatva*).

Regarding the doubt that the statement beginning with "What [would happen] together with them? is improper, he states the intended meaning: "This has been said," and so forth. "In the state of Brahman" means in the stage of knowledge (*vidyā*).
The connection is "they do not desire. Regarding the word "other," the term "of Brahman" is to be supplied;
that is, in the context of the word *brahman*.
"What discourse? means that there is no discourse at all.
Therefore, the sense is: how can there be the occasion for considering contradiction or non-contradiction?
"Another operation" means the state of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*);
[this] is indeed already accepted.

The point is that, for this reason, there is no occasion here even to consider whether there is contradiction or non-contradiction. To the question, "How is it to be understood that another function has been accepted by them? he says: "And this," [referring to] "in the first Uddyota."
The intention is that this is an examination of the definition of *dhvani*.
Repeating what has already been stated, he introduces the following passage beginning with "evam" (thus) and so forth.

The explanation of the meaning of the term "yuktividām" (those who know the methods of reasoning) is "tārkikāṇāṃ pramāṇatattvavidām" (logicians who know the true nature of the means of valid cognition).
This is an elliptical expression for the Sugatas and others.
"Having convention as its sole nature" means that convention (*saṅketa*) is an agreement (*samaya*).
Some say that this [intention] is the desire, "From this word, this meaning is to be understood," and so forth; others say it is the instruction, "This is the meaning of this word.
The portion from "not" up to "of the cognition" is a Nyāya sūtra.
This is the resolution of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "the word conveys its meaning by way of an inferential mark (*liṅga*).
"No" means that the word does not convey its meaning by way of an inferential mark.
The reason for this is stated as "because it is conventional" (*sāmayikatvāt*), and so forth.
This means that the cognition or understanding of an object from a word is conventional, insofar as it is rooted in linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).
He states the Buddhist position with the words "words," and so forth.
The statement "like other objects" is given as an illustration to establish that this manifesting nature of words is indeed established by experience;
therein, he explains the phrase "of other objects" with the words "of lamps and so forth.
Let the disagreements among logicians proceed regarding the status of [words] as denoters.
[The opponent asks: "Is this [meaning] inherent to words, or is it conventional? and so forth.

But if [the word] is merely a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), then when that [manifested meaning] follows upon it, being common to other entities and already well-established in the world, what occasion is there for disagreements?
[Locana: Anticipating the objection—"But surely even the double moon and such are established through experience, and yet they are subjects of disagreement"—he says: "And there is no contradiction."
The meaning is that there is no contradiction—that is, no sublation consisting of an obstruction—by a second cognition; thus, it is established by experience and remains unsublated.
That which is established by experience is not to be rejected, just as [the capacity for] denotation is not. [Objection:
But surely, even in that case, they hold a dissenting opinion.

This is not so; for there is no disagreement regarding the capacity to denote (vācakatva) itself, but rather regarding whether that capacity is innate or artificial, and so forth. Thus he says: "For regarding the capacity to denote...

Having raised the objection that, in this way, the capacity to manifest (vyañjakatva) might also become a subject of dispute by way of its various attributes, he says: "But regarding the capacity to manifest..."
Regarding the phrase "bhāvāntareti":

having observed that while [gestures] such as the winking of an eye are conventional (*sāṅketika*), the capacity (*yogyatā*) of the eyes and so forth is beginningless (*anādi*), [the author argues that] just as a lamp and the like illuminate objects other than its own imagined object, so too does a word illuminate an object other than its conventional one;
thus, the sense is that this manifesting nature (*vyañjakabhāva*) of words is indeed established by experience even for them.
Regarding the passage beginning with "nanu" and so forth: it refers to experience produced by defects— that is, experience—
and to that [object], such as a double moon and the like.
In place of the reading *taccet*, there is the reading *na ca na*.
In accordance with the refutation, he explains the term *avarodha* [obstruction] as "non-existent," and so forth.
*Nirodha* means obstruction (*pratibandha*).
He states the conclusion with the words "by that" and so forth.
It is not to be rejected, nor is it a point of dispute.
By this, the following inference is shown: "The capacity to manifest [meaning] is not a point of dispute, because it is established by experience, just like the capacity to denote."

Here, with the intent of refuting the suspicion that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*), he introduces the passage beginning with "for [if] there is expressiveness" (*vācakatve hi*) by saying "But surely," and so forth.
Even in that case— meaning even if there is expressiveness—
for these logicians (*tārkika*).
"Not this" means that this is not tenable.
The reason for this is given by the words "for not," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is no disagreement regarding the subject (dharmin), namely "denotative capacity," but rather regarding its properties, such as being innate;
therefore, the intention is that the example lacks nothing in terms of the property to be proven (sādhyavaikalya).
"By way of another property" means by way of its being innate and so forth.
"Also being the object of misconception" [is the meaning].
The word "also" (api) signifies that [the capacity of words] is not established merely by experience.

He states his position—showing that while there is disagreement regarding the status of denotation (*vācakatva*), there is no such disagreement regarding manifestation (*vyañjakatva*)—with the verse beginning with "akṣi" and so forth.
"Akṣi" refers to the eyes; "contraction" (*nikoca*) and "expansion" (*vikāsa*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), contraction and so forth are included;
its "conventional nature" (*sāṅketikatva*) means its possession of convention (*saṅketavat*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that the relation with the object is established by convention (*saṅketa*).
"Capability" (*yogyatā*) means being the cause of visual and other types of cognition.
As it is said in the *Bhūṣaṇasāra*: "The capacity of the sense faculties toward their respective objects is beginningless.
Thus, it is said "having seen [this].
For indeed, all disagreements among logicians (*tārkika*) concern supramundane matters, but not mundane ones.
For indeed, regarding such realities as blue, sweet, and so forth—which are the objects of the senses for all people and are free from sublation—no mutual disagreements are observed.
For one who says that a blue object, which is free from sublation, is "blue" is not refuted by another saying, "This is not blue; it is yellow.
The same applies to the manifesting nature of both expressive words and non-expressive musical sounds, which do not consist of the form of speech.

Granted that there may indeed be doubt regarding [the nature of] movement and so forth, as they relate to the eye; however, the fact that sound possesses the quality of being a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) in revealing its denoted object is of exactly the same uniform nature as it is in other entities.
Thus, since its uniform nature is certain, what room is there for doubt? The meaning is this:
there is no disagreement regarding blue in the sense that "this is not blue."

Moreover, regarding the statement "this is composed of primordial matter (prādhānika)," "this is composed of atoms (pāramāṇava)," "this is mere cognition (jñānamātra)," or "this is void (tuccha)," these are indeed extraordinary disagreements concerning its creation;
this refers to "the speakers," meaning in the examples of *dhvani*.

*Bālapriyā*: The meaning is that although the eye and other sense organs are equal to the contraction of the eyes and so forth in their capacity to illuminate an object, one observes that the relationship of the former with its object is conventional (*sāṅketika*), whereas the relationship of the latter with its object is natural (*naisargika*).
Regarding the phrase "kāmam" and so forth:

The meaning is: "Let there be, if you wish, a doubt regarding the property of denotativeness—whether this denotativeness of a word is conventional (sāṅketika) or innate (naisargika)—just as there is a doubt regarding whether a word is eternal or non-eternal. [This refers to] its being a manifestor (vyañjakatva).
The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction.
"In other entities" means in things such as lamps and the like.
He provides the justification for the statement "but not the worldly" in the *Vṛtti* with the words beginning "for not," etc.
"In blue, sweet, and so forth" refers to substances such as blue or sweet things;
the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
"In reality" means regarding the nature of things; "those who are in disagreement" refers to people.
The word "people" (*janāḥ*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
He clarifies exactly what was stated [above] with the words beginning with "not" (*na hi*).
"Truth" (*satyam*) is that which is free from sublation (*bādhārahita*).
"Blue" refers to a blue substance such as a jar and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "saying 'it is blue,'" the word "this" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The author expresses his own position regarding this point with the words "This is not so," and so forth.
By saying "this is not blue" with respect to what is blue,
the word "this" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The phrase "by another," and so forth, is connected as follows: "it is not that this is denied, namely, 'this is blue' or 'this is yellow.
He states the existence [of the eye] with the words "not this," and so forth.
The connection is that there is no such misconception as "this blue is not blue," because it is worldly; this is the intended meaning.
A misconception (*vipratipatti*) is a contradictory apprehension.
"However," and so forth.
The connection is that "however, these misconceptions are indeed supramundane.
The statement of their types begins with "primarily [consisting of] the primary elements," and so on.
By the word "this" (idam), the entire world is intended in every case.
"Derived from the primary" (prādhānika) refers to a modification of the primary cause (pradhāna), which is the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti). "Atomic" (pāramāṇava) means produced from atoms (paramāṇu).
"Knowledge alone" means having the very nature of consciousness;
it is "insubstantial" or "void.
Herein, the doctrines of the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Vijñānavādin, and Mādhyamika are shown in succession.
"In its creation" means "in the cause of the world's creation.
However, if the reading is "in the vision of that," it means "in the vision of the cause of the world."
"Errors pertain exclusively to the non-worldly (alaukika).

This means that since errors are not observed regarding worldly things, whereas they are observed regarding non-worldly entities, it is established—by means of positive and negative concomitance—that these [errors] have exclusively non-worldly entities as their objects.
By this, the commentary passage beginning with "non-worldly" (*alaukika*) has been explained.
In the commentary, he concludes with the words "tathaiva" and so forth.
"Tathaiva" means exactly as it is, that is to say, precisely as it is in common worldly experience.
"By whom could it be denied?
means that it is indeed respected by everyone;
for how can that which is established by the experience of all people be denied?
For in the assemblies of the learned, various utterances and actions—whether formal or informal—that indicate a charming meaning which is not explicitly expressed in words, are observed.
What person of sound mind, wishing to avoid becoming an object of ridicule for himself, would intentionally deceive [others] by means of those?
"Not expressed in words" (*aśabda*) means untouched by the operation of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*). This is the sense.

"Delightful" (*ramaṇīya*) means that which becomes beautiful precisely by being concealed; by this, it is stated that the purpose [of the verse] is the attainment of an extraordinary perception through suggestion (*dhvani*).
"Established" (*nibaddhāḥ*) means well-known; "those" (*tān*) refers to such conventional usages (*vyavahārān*).

"Who would speak? means who would overreach [the truth] or fail to pay heed; the suffix *śatṛ* is used here in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). The meaning is that one who is characterized by the avoidance of the state of being an object of ridicule for oneself—which has become the object of the action—desires to completely abandon that state. The reason for this is stated here as "without sound" (*aśabda*), and so forth.
Intending the etymological derivation "that for which there is no expressive word," he explains the term *aśabda* [in the verse] with the words beginning "expression" (*abhidhā*) and so forth.
He clarifies it by showing that the state of being wordless (*aśabdatva*) is the cause of its loveliness, using the words beginning with "that which" (*yat*).
The underlying sense is that this is established by the analogy of the jar-like breasts of a beloved woman covered by the hem of her garment.
"Sundarī" means "one who is beautiful";
by this [phrase], the meaning is:
by means of the two qualifiers, "being without sound" and "being beautiful."
"In the state of being suggested" (dhvanyamānatāyām):
the word "of the meaning" (arthasya) is to be supplied.
"Uncommon" (asādhāraṇa).
The uniqueness of the realization consists in its being of the nature of aesthetic relish (*āsvādyamāna*).
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), there are two readings: "expressions" (*vyāhārāḥ*) and "conventional usages" (*vyavahārāḥ*).
"Thus, their operations": the meaning is that those whose operations— characterized by suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*)— are such that the object becomes both non-verbal and charming.
"Composed" (*nibaddha*) refers to those in the form of *muktaka* (single verses) and so forth;
"uncomposed" (*anibaddha*) refers to those in the form of prose (*gadya*) and so forth.
[As stated] in the *Locana*: "They are well-known."
The meaning is that they are well-known as being in the form of *muktaka* (isolated verses) and so forth.
He explains "one should not connect [them]" in a way consistent with the present context by saying "one should not care.
He explains "the conscious one" (*sacetāḥ*) by following the subject [of the verse] and saying "in the definition" (*lakṣaṇe*).
The meaning is that it has the sense of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
It is a defining characteristic because avoidance results from taking heed [of the danger].
[The form] *śatr* is a substitute (*ādeśa*).
The word "avoiding" (*pariharan*) is understood as a supplement to "here" (*atre*).
By means of that, he states the established meaning with the words beginning "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*), etc.
"Being subject to refutation" (*upasahanīyatā*) means being the object of ridicule by an assembly of learned people acting as the agents.
By "avoidance" is meant the preservation of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
He states the result [of this] with the words "that," and so forth.
In the commentary, it says "one should say."
The word "someone" (*kaścit*) is to be supplied as the subject.
He states their possible speech with the words beginning with "it exists" (*asti*).
To the question "how?", he replies with the words beginning with "the state of being a manifestor" (*vyañjakatvam*).
"And that" refers to the state of being a signifier (*gamakatva*).
"The state of being a mark" (*liṅgatva*) means the state of being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*).
"Therefore" (*ataḥ*) [means as follows].
The meaning is that being a signifier (*gamakatva*) consists in being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*).

The word "iti" indicates a reason. The construction is as follows: for those words, the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor (*vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāva*) is precisely the relationship between the possessor of the mark and the mark (*liṅgiliṅgabhāva*).
The explanation of the meaning of the particle *eva* is "there is no other whatsoever.
He establishes what was stated [in the previous verse] with the words "And therefore," and so forth.
"Therefore" means for the reason that is about to be stated.
The word "ca" (and) is a conjunctive particle that collects another argument.
"'This'" means that the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor is not distinct from the relationship between the possessor of a mark and the mark itself.
"It must necessarily be understood" means that there is no evidence for its existence as something additional; this is the intended sense.
He shows what follows from this by saying "because," and so forth.
To this he says: "And [it is] the intention of the speaker," and so forth.

One might argue that there is an opportunity for deception regarding the passage beginning with "the state of being a suggester" (*vyañjakatva*). For the suggestiveness of words is their capacity to convey meaning, and that is the state of being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*); therefore, the cognition of the suggested is nothing other than the cognition of the object possessing the mark (*liṅgin*). Thus, the relationship between the suggested and the suggester is simply the relationship between the possessor of the mark and the mark itself.
There is no other [means].

Therefore, this must necessarily be understood: since you have just now established that suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) depends upon the intention of the speaker (*vakrabhiprāya*), and the intention of the speaker is itself of the nature of an object of inference (*anumeya*).
To this it is replied: "Even if this were so, what is lost to us?"

We maintain that there exists a function of words characterized as suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*), which is distinct from the functions of denotation (*vācakatva*) and secondary indication (*guṇavṛtti*).
Even if this were so, there would be no loss [to our position].
For that suggestiveness may be the nature of being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*) or something else entirely.
In every respect, there exists a visual perception (*locana*) that is distinct from all well-known types of verbal cognition and is the object of the operation of words;
thus, its suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is not denied, yet it does not exist apart from reality, for this is simply the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*liṅgi-liṅgabhāva*).
"Right now" [is said] as follows:

In introducing the Jaiminīya position, [the author] says "yadi nāma syāt" (even if it were so). By means of this bold assertion (*prauḍhavāditā*), he demonstrates that even if one were to concede [the opponent's point], one's own position is nonetheless not established—hence the words "śabda... (sound...).
The "object of the word's operation" (*śabdavyāpāraviṣaya*) is that which, being the operation of the word, is its object;
others, however, [as stated] in the *Locana*— "suggestiveness," etc.—
state that it is not denied.

The phrase "by its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. That, however, namely the state of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*), is distinct— that is, different— from being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*).
The very relationship between the indicator (liṅga) and the indicated (liṅgin)— that is, the state of being an indicator as defined by the indicated—
is what constitutes "manifestation" (vyañjakatva).
This is what [the author] intends to say.
The meaning is "by this [statement].

Regarding the term *prauḍha*: even while accepting what has been stated by another, that debate which is conducted for the purpose of establishing one's own tenet is called *prauḍhavāda*; one who speaks such a debate is a *prauḍhavādī*.
The state of that is "tattayā" (by its being that); this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "one's own position" (*svapakṣa*):
it means the position of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), namely that the nature of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*) is not distinct from being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*).
"It is not established" means that this will be shown by the reasoning to be stated later.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase beginning with "in the capacity of a signifier" (*vācakatve*) is an elaboration of what was previously stated as "what, then, is lost for us? (*tat kiṃ naś chinnam*).
Regarding the word "prasiddha":
the meaning is that it is distinct from those well-known modes or properties of a word, namely *abhidhā* (denotation) and *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

Since it would have been more appropriate to say "the state of being a verbal operation" (*śabdavyāpāratva*), the expression "the state of being the object of a verbal operation" (*śabdavyāpāraviṣayatva*) might seem inconsistent; therefore, [the author] explains this in the *Locana* with the words beginning "śabda... and so forth.
"Object" (viṣaya) means an object of the intellect accompanied by the mind; that is to say,
something to be tasted.
He shows another interpretation with the words "another [says]": in the commentary, the word "of that" (tasya) means "of the state of being a manifestor" (vyañjakatvasya).

Addressing the opponent who thinks, "By saying that being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*) is being an inferential mark (*liṅgatva*), our desired conclusion is established," [the author] replies with the words "But not... and so forth.
We have no dispute at all regarding the fact that it (manifestation) exists;

however, this is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), namely, that being a manifestor is always nothing other than being an inferential mark, and that the cognition of the manifested is always nothing other than the cognition of the object of inference (*liṅgin*).

Furthermore, as for that which you have restated from our own words in order to establish your own position—on the grounds that you accept the "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*) as being the intention of the speaker, and thus maintain that words function merely as logical indicators (*liṅga*) when revealing it—we shall now explain this in detail according to our own presentation; please listen.
The objects of words are of two kinds: the inferable (*anumeya*) and the communicable (*pratipādya*).
In that context, the object of inference is characterized by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
And this intention is of two kinds: the desire to manifest the nature of the word itself, and the desire to manifest the meaning by means of the word.
Of these, the former is not a factor in verbal linguistic usage (*śābdavyavahāra*).
For the first [cognition] has as its fruit the mere apprehension of the fact of being a living being;
the second, however, although its result is mediated by the ascertainment of a specific word, is the basis for the linguistic usage that employs words.
Both of these, moreover, are the inferable objects of words.
The "communicable" (pratipādya), however, is the object intended as the focus of the speaker's desire to convey meaning.
And that is of two kinds: the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya).
For the speaker sometimes intends the object by means of his own words; regarding this, they say that the "particularity" (viśeṣa) is the specific object of the operation of the word.
"Furthermore," [it is said].

For even in cases such as a lamp and its light, there exists a relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), despite being devoid of the relationship between the signified (*liṅgin*) and the sign (*liṅga*). Thus, since the relationship between the signified and the sign is not a pervader (*avyāpaka*) of the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor, how could there be identity (*tādātmya*)?
Regarding the term "object" (*viṣaya*): [it refers to the following].

When the word is uttered, the connection is that "as far as [the term] *bālapriyā* [is concerned], this, moreover, is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Regarding this, he states the intended meaning in the *Locana*: "Like a lamp," and so forth.

"Devoid of the state of being the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) and the mark (*liṅga*)" means it is rendered empty by being defined as a mark in relation to a possessor of the mark; that is to say, it is not co-referential with that.

In the reading "in the void" (śūnye), that [term] is an adjective for "in the case of the light of a lamp and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the relation of the manifested and the manifestor," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "together with their respective objects, such as a jar."
The word *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*).

The connection is as follows: "the relationship between the possessor of a mark and the mark (*liṅgi-liṅga-bhāva*) is not a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor (*vyaṅgya-vyañjaka-bhāva*).
However, in the reading without the negative particle (*nañ*), the division is "it is not a non-pervader (*avyāpaka*)."
How is there identity (tādātmya)?

For if the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor were nothing other than the relationship between the signified and the sign, then wherever there is a relationship between the manifested and the manifestor, there would also necessarily be a relationship between the signified and the sign.
Furthermore, this [invariable concomitance] does not exist in the case of a lamp and so forth, because deviation is observed; therefore, the meaning is that there is no identity between those two.

Now, one might raise the objection: "But surely, for those Prābhākaras who maintain that the word is a *liṅga* (logical mark) because it makes known the speaker's intention—that is, they hold that the word is an inferential indicator of the speaker's cognition—this view is consistent with [the fact that] the speaker's intention is the manifester [of the meaning]. Anticipating this doubt, it is stated in the *Vṛtti*: "As for what was said... and so forth.
Immediately after the word *abhihita*, the word *tathā* (thus) is the ellipsis.
Since the word *viṣaya* is well-known in its [usual] sense, and since that [sense] is inappropriate here, he explains it as "the word" (*śabda*) and so forth in the *Locana*.
[The phrase] "as much as" (*yāvatī*)... [is used].
The meaning is "as much as is necessary. "To that extent" means that he sometimes desires to manifest [the object] by some specific purpose, even if it is not expressible by its own words.
Regarding the *locana*, it has been stated that the scope [of inference] is precisely practice (*pratipatti*).
In this context, both the desire to employ words and the desire to communicate a meaning are indeed inferable from the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*).
However, as for the object which serves as the direct object (*karman*) of the desire to communicate, the word is established here as the instrument (*karaṇa*); it is not itself inferable.
For in that case, only the desire to communicate that very object is inferred;

and since the word is not the instrument there, the procedure (itikartavyatā) belonging to the inferential mark (liṅga)—such as the apprehension of its presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatva) and so forth—is not present.
[The phrase] "the object of the comprehension produced by the uttered word" means that which is the content of the understanding generated by the word once it has been articulated.
In the commentary, the word "ādye" (in the first) means the desire to manifest the very form of the word itself. The word "śābde" (in verbal cognition) [is used].
The meaning is that it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to verbal usage—that is, to the cognition of an object which is produced by words.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of being a living being" (*prāṇitve*):

the meaning is that its result is the listener's apprehension of mere animacy (*prāṇitvamātra*), expressed as "this is a living being," by means of a word uttered with the intention of manifesting the word's own form; the word "mere" (*mātra*) serves to exclude the [specific] object.
"In the second [case]" means the desire to illuminate a meaning by means of a word. "In the word" [means...]

The ascertainment (*avadhāraṇa*) of a specific word—a sentence conducive to the cognition of the intended meaning—is the speaker’s mental coordination (*anusandhāna*). [The capacity of the word] is "terminated" (*avasita*) or "reached its conclusion" (*paryavasita*) therein; that is to say, it has fulfilled its purpose by producing that [coordination].
For this very reason, even though it is "remote" (*vyavahita*)—that is, even when there is an interval with respect to the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*)—[the word remains a cause].
Alternatively, the construction is as follows: "even though [the cognition] is separated [from the word], it terminates in the determination of the specific object of the word.

That is to say, when the specific object is determined by the word, the [cognition] terminates in the hearer's understanding; the meaning is that it produces that [understanding] through a causal chain.
Such being the case, this is the sense.

Regarding the word "śabde": verbal cognition (śābdabodha) is a linguistic usage (vyavahāra) for which sound (śabda) is the instrument; the meaning is that it is the basis (nibandhana), that is, the cause (nimitta), of such [cognition].
"But those two" means that, as stated previously, there is no intention to express two distinct types [of inference].

Regarding the phrase "the object of inference," one should understand here the following inference: "This person intends to speak of this [object], because he is a user of words of such a kind," and so forth.
In the *Locana*, he introduces the passage beginning with "therein, that which is to be inferred" (*tatrānumeya*) etc., while demonstrating its meaning: "Therein," and so forth.
"The desire to employ a word" (*śabdaprayuyukṣā*) means the wish to use a word.
"By that which is to be inferred" (*anumayā*).
"By means of the purpose, that is, by the employment of this or that word"—
this is the remainder [of the sentence].
"In the desire to communicate, it becomes the object."
The meaning is "that which is intended to be explained.
Regarding the word "therein" (tatra):
the meaning is that the object is the thing qualified by being intended to be explained.
"It is established as an instrument" means that it should be understood as an instrument with respect to such a purpose, because it serves as an instrument for the act of demonstration;
the sense is that it is not [established] as a logical mark (liṅga).
For this very reason, he says "but not," and so forth.
"This" refers to the intended meaning that one wishes to communicate.
"Having that as its object" means having that meaning as its object.

He confirms what was already stated—that this [word] is not an object of inference—with the words "And not," and so forth. The construction is as follows: in that case, regarding the object to be understood, the word exists there as the instrument (karaṇa), whereas the "procedure" (itikartavyatā) of the inferential mark (liṅga)—consisting of the apprehension of its presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatva) and so on—does not exist there.
Regarding the "mark" (*liṅga*), such as smoke and so forth, which is intended to function as a mark:
its "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*) refers to its auxiliary causes.
Having established the absence of a procedure for the mark, he states the existence of a procedure for the word, beginning with "But rather... (*api tu*).
"Another indeed": the phrase "there is a procedure to be performed" is to be supplied.
"Convention," etc.

The manifestation—that is, the recollection—of a particular word’s convention regarding a particular object is the twofold object to be communicated by words; however, it does not appear in its own form as something inferred (*liṅgitayā*), but rather through another relation, whether artificial or natural.
For it is the state of being the intended object of the speaker that is perceived by words as something inferred, and not the object's own form.

For if the operation of words in that context were by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), then the cognition of the word-meaning would be something entirely different—such as the manifestation of a convention (*saṃketa*) and so forth—and thus the word would not be a logical mark there.

Furthermore, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is twofold: by one [procedure] it effects the function of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*), and by the second, the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vyāpāra*).
He states this with the words beginning "there" (*tatra*).
"By some" means by [an intention] such as the desire to obtain beauty and so forth produced by concealment; this is the meaning of the word.
"The meaning of the word" [is as follows].
"Inference is dear to the ignorant" means that it is the beginning [of the path] for them. He concludes with "that," and so forth; "tat" means "therefore."

In this context, regarding the object to be established (the *pratipādyārtha*), the following inference is to be understood: "A word does not establish its meaning by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it establishes that meaning without depending on the consideration of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, just like the eye and other sense organs.

Since the reason for the twofold nature of the object to be established was not stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*), he now shows that the reason for it is the twofold nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of the word—beginning with the words "the procedure" (*itikartavyatā*) and so forth.
"By means of one" means by way of the manifestation of convention and so forth; "the function of denotation" is the meaning.
The meaning is "the cognition of the conventional object.
"By the second [cognition]" means by that which consists in the knowledge of the speaker’s excellence and so forth.
"Non-activity of manifestation" means the manifestation of some object; the word "performs" is to be supplied.
The word "sound" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. In the commentary, the phrase "by not being denotable by its own word" means "without being denotable by its own word."
The phrase "he desires to reveal the meaning" is to be supplied [to the previous sentence]. The reason for this is given by the words beginning with "prayojane" (with regard to the purpose).
He explains this [expression] "with regard to the purpose" in the *Locana* with the words beginning with "gopana" (concealment), and so forth.

The meaning is: by means of the concealment of beauty and the attainment or accomplishment of the charm of well-spoken words, beginning with that [beauty], through such things as the underlying intention (*abhisandhāna*).
In the commentary, the phrase "But he" (*sa tu*) and so forth refers to both types: the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
"Not to be indicated by a logical mark" (na liṅgitaya), and so forth.
The meaning is that [the object] is not made known by a cognition of a logical mark consisting of a word, which is assisted by the recollection of pervasion (vyāpti) and other factors.
To the question, "How then does it appear?", he says: "But rather," and so forth.
The phrase "both kinds" and so forth is to be supplied up to the word "of words.
The passage beginning with "by means of something artificial" is a statement of the different views.
[The phrase] "without another relation" refers to this.

The meaning is: "by means of a specific relation consisting of denotation (*abhidhā*) and so forth. He states the reason why [the object] does not manifest as something possessing an inferential mark (*liṅgin*): "if one intends to speak," and so on.
He establishes exactly what was stated: "for if," and so on.
"In that regard," concerning the object intended to be communicated;
"the operation of words as a mark" refers to the connection between words and their objects in the form of the relationship between a sign (liṅga) and the signified (liṅgin).
"'If it were so'" means if the object intended to be communicated were inferable from the mark consisting of the word itself, assisted by the recollection of pervasion (vyāpti) and other factors.
"In that case," then; "in the meaning of the word" means in the object presented by the word;
"correctly," and so forth.

The meaning is this: contradictory assertions such as "this matter is true" and "this matter is false," as well as doubts such as "is this matter true or false," would not actually arise; [the opponent's position implies] that their occurrence would not take place.

"Regarding 'as in the case of smoke, etc. (dhūmādo): the meaning is that it is just as in the case of another object of inference, such as fire, which is inferred by means of a mark such as smoke; the sense is that just as disputes do not arise in that regard, so too [is it here]."
Now, one might ask: "Once an object has been inferred, why would there be no engagement in dispute? To address this point, the *Locana* states: "Inference," and so forth.
Because [inference] is either correct or false, disputes simply would not arise, just as there are none regarding another object of inference already inferred from a mark such as smoke.

Furthermore, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), by being implied through the power of the expressed meaning (*vācyasāmarthya*), indeed becomes a relation of the word, just like the expressed meaning itself.
For whether a relationship is direct or indirect is irrelevant to its function;
moreover, it has already been demonstrated that suggestiveness (vyañjakatva) is based upon the relationship between the signified and the signifier (vācyavācakabhāva).
Therefore, the meaning is that the *locana* (the eye), which consists of the speaker’s intention, is indeed of the very nature of a definitive cognition (*niścaya*).
Regarding the phrase "as a limiting condition" (*upādhitvena*):

the meaning is that the speaker’s intention (*vaktricchā*) indeed results in an inference—specifically one in the form of a certainty—regarding some object, such as the meaning of what is expressed, by means of some inferential mark (*liṅga*).
By the use of the particle *eva* ("indeed"), doubt concerning that object which arises subsequent to it is excluded.

The intention is that inference is preceded by doubt, and that only a reason which is non-deviant from the object possesses the capacity to produce knowledge. Now, one might raise the objection: "If there were a relationship between the word and the meaning intended to be suggested (*vyaṅgya*), then its function [of suggestion] would be established; however, that very relationship does not exist. Anticipating this doubt, the author of the *Vṛtti* reminds us of what has already been stated: "And the suggested meaning... and so forth.
The instrumental case in "vācyasāmarthyākṣiptatayā" (by being implied through the power of the expressed meaning) denotes a causal relationship;
by this, an indirect connection (*paramparāsambandha*) is demonstrated. [This is clarified by the phrase] "like the expressed meaning."
The meaning is "equal to the expressed" (*vācya*). That is to say, "just like the expressed.

Now, one might object: "The connection with the expressed is direct, whereas that with the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) is mediated by it"; to this he replies with the words beginning with "directly" (*sākṣāt*).

The term "non-efficient" (aprayojaka) is used because it is for this very reason that the designation of conjunction, inherence in the conjoined, and so forth, as forms of "proximity" (sannikarṣa) becomes consistent; such is the intended meaning.

To strengthen the statement that the relationship with the suggested sense—since it is implied by the power of the expressed sense—is composed of the expressed sense itself, he recalls what was said previously, beginning with the words "in the expressed sense" (vācye).
He concludes the current discussion on the demonstration of the two-fold nature of meaning with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
[The phrase] "in the form of the speaker's intention" means in the form of the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*).
By the particle *eva* (only), there is an exclusion of the object that has been made the focus of that [intention].
‘By way of being an indicator’ (*liṅgatayā*), and so forth; the meaning is ‘the state of being made known by an indicator in the form of a word.
‘Having that as its object’ (*tadviṣayī*)... [etc.]
The phrase "the function of words" is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
The meaning is that the object which is the focus of the speaker's intention is what is conveyed by the words.
"[When that is being perceived]" refers to that [intended object].
The meaning is that [the suggested sense] is what is to be conveyed by the word.
Regarding the alternatives beginning with "by way of being the denoter" (*vācakatvena*), he refutes the first with "not, for now" (*mā tāvat*).
He says "by another relation" (*sambandhāntareṇa*).
The meaning is that whatever operation occurs through another relation is precisely the function of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*).
He recalls what was stated previously with the words "And not...
and so forth, ending with "because it is observed otherwise."
The meaning is that manifestor-ship is observed even in the absence of being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*).
He concludes with "therefore":
"the subject to be established."
The meaning is "that which is suggested.
"By way of being the sign" means by way of the relationship between the sign (liṅga) and the signified (liṅgin).
"Not related" [means as follows].

By this, the following inference is shown: "The meaning intended as the suggested (vyaṅgya) is not related to the word through the relation of indicator and indicated (liṅga-liṅgibhāva), because it is conveyed by the word, just like the expressed (vācya).
This has already been stated.
To demonstrate it, he says: "For that which," and so forth.
‘Of those’ words;
‘the object’ as it has been shown, characterized by the speaker’s intention (vivakṣā); ‘that which’ is ‘it’.
The meaning is that the object is characterized by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
Regarding the phrase "as a limiting condition" (*upādhitvena*),
the word "is perceived" (*pratīyate*) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis.

With the intention that the word *upādhi* here is a synonym for "that which distinguishes," he explains [the verse] in the *Locana* with the words "by the speaker’s intention" (*vaktricchā*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "appears as a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatvena bhāti*): by this, in the cognition "this meaning is intended by this speaker," the intention (*vivakṣā*) indeed appears as a qualifier of the meaning.

To reinforce what was stated with the words "therefore," he recalls the previously mentioned point: the operation of words toward the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is by way of being an indicator (*liṅga*);

however, toward that which is made their object by being presented for comprehension, whether it be of the nature of an intention or not of the nature of an intention, the operation is by way of denotation (*vācakatva*) alone, or through some other relation.
To that extent, it functions as a denotator, as previously stated;
however, by another relation, it is simply a suggestor (*vyañjaka*).
Nor is suggestiveness identical to the nature of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it is observed otherwise in cases such as light and so forth.
Therefore, the object to be established is not related to words as a signified (liṅgin) in the same way as the denoted (vācya).
For that object which is their related signified, as has been shown, is not perceived as a denoted meaning, but rather as a qualifying attribute (upādhi).
Furthermore, if the object of dispute were itself the subject of inference (*liṅgin*), it would follow that there could be no disagreements regarding that object made by ordinary people;
this has already been stated.
The word *locana* appears as a qualifier; [the phrase] "of the subject to be explained" means, by implication,
of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
"Being indicated" (liṅgitva) means "being inferable" (anumeyatva).
"By worldly people alone" (laukikair eva) [means...]
People do not disagree regarding the intention (*icchā*), but they certainly do disagree regarding the meaning (*artha*).

[Objection: When the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is understood, its determination as true is made by means of another instrument of knowledge, namely inference (*anumāna*); thus, it too would simply be a matter of inference.
[Response: Not so; for even the determination of the truth of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) occurs through inference alone.

In the *Bālapriyā* commentary, regarding the passage beginning with "of the object to be established" (*pratipādyasya*), the *Locana* explains this term in accordance with the present context as "of the suggested meaning" (*arthād vyaṅgyasya*). Now, one might ask: how can there be a certainty that [the suggested meaning] is not inferable simply from the fact that it is understood to be the subject of conflicting views?
Because a misconception might also arise regarding the object of inference (anumeya), he says: "In the case of desire," and so forth.
"In the case of desire" means in the case of the intention to speak (vivakṣā).
"In the object" means in the object that is the domain of the intention to speak.
"Only regarding disagreement" means "only regarding disagreements such as [theories concerning] truth and so forth.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The object under dispute is not inferable, because it is the subject of disagreement, just like the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), provided there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)."
He introduces the passage beginning with "And just as... with the words "Now, [one might object]... and so forth. Regarding the term "pratipanna" (cognized):
the meaning is that it is understood from the word preceded by the comprehension of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).
Regarding this suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) which has been presented,
there is a reading in some manuscripts immediately after the phrase "from inference alone" (*anumānādeva*), namely "from another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntarāt*).
[The word] "is produced" (*kriyate*) [is used].
The word "by the practitioners" (pratipattṛbhiḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The intended meaning is that a verbal cognition possesses validity regarding its own object only when it is assisted by another corroborating means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The particle "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (hetu).
"Again," and so forth.

The sense is that although the indicated (vyaṅgya) object lacks the status of being a logical mark (liṅgitva) in relation to the word, it certainly possesses the status of being a logical mark in relation to another corroborative means of valid cognition (saṃvādaka-pramāṇa).
First there is the comprehension of the meaning from the word, and subsequently the operation of the inference that corroborates it.

He provides the following resolution— beginning with "Not so" (maivam)— to the objection that since the object itself (*arthasvarūpa*) is the domain of verbal testimony, whereas the truth residing in that object is the domain of inference, inference does not infer an object already apprehended by verbal testimony.

And just as when the correctness of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is apprehended through the accompaniment of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), even though that [correctness] falls within the domain of another means of valid cognition, there is no loss of its status as being within the domain of the operation of the word—so it is with the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) as well.

As they say: "If there is the nature of inference here because of the commonality of non-deviation from the statement of a reliable person (*āptavāda*)," yet by this much the apprehension of the expressed meaning does not become inferential; rather, the truthfulness (*satyatva*) which exceeds that [expressed meaning] will also apply to what is suggested by it. Locana.
This is what he says with the words beginning "And just as," and so forth.
This has been stated even while granting [the opponent's position]; by the word "also" (api) in the phrase "of the expressed also" (vācyasyāpi), the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is included.
As for the words "as they say":
In the section on the Sentence (*Vākyādhikaraṇa*), the phrase “the author of the Ślokavārttika” is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Regarding the word *āpta*:

in the printed edition of that same work, however, the reading is as follows: “If it is argued here that [the Veda] is an inference because its words are reliable (*āptavāda*) and non-contradictory (*avisamvāda*).”
As for what remains of this: "The determination [of truth] would be established by that much; however, the arising of cognition is not caused by that.
For truthfulness is indeed something else, having the status of being the word of a reliable person as its cause."
Furthermore, since the meaning of a sentence is known to be something entirely distinct [from its constituent words],
if its truth is then inferred therein on the basis of the statement being from a reliable person (āpta), [then that inference would be superfluous].
"How could there be inference here for one who has the cognition of the meaning of a sentence?
To this, the statement of the reason is: "Because the word of a reliable person is non-contradictory.
"Here" refers to [the case of] the sentence-meaning.
The meaning is: "in the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
"Anumānatā" means the state of being an inference (*anumititva*).
After the word "ced" (if), the word "na" (not) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "The determination, for its part," and so forth.

The sense is that through these statements, it is understood that the truth of the meaning of the sentence must be ascertained by means of inference based on the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*).
The reading "The non-contradiction of the reliable person's word [is established] through inference by way of generality" is seen in many texts.

This is its meaning: the non-contradiction regarding the object of its own content— which is the truthfulness, that is to say, the state of having a true object— of an authoritative statement (āptavāda), i.e., the word of an authoritative person,
is cognizable through inference based on generality (sāmānyāt), namely by means of an inference such as "because it is the word of an authoritative person."
[Objection: "In that case, let it be accepted that even the cognition of the denotable object (*vācya*) is purely inferential. To this, he says: "And not," etc.
[Objection: "Is it then that there is no inferential cognition at all here? He says, "But rather," etc., to show that there is indeed such a cognition.
Regarding the phrase "of truthfulness":
the word "inference" (ānumānikī) is to be supplied [to the word "cognition"].
[The opponent argues: "It will also exist in that which is indicated by it."
The meaning is that truthfulness will also exist in the suggested sense (*vyaṅgyārtha*).
The point is that while the suggested sense is conveyed by the word, its truthfulness is to be understood through inference.
As for the phrase "and this":
The meaning is that the truth of the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) is inferential, as stated in the passage beginning with "yathā ca" (and just as).
Regarding the phrase "abhyupagamya" (having admitted):
it means having treated as existing what is in fact non-existent, namely, its possessing a purpose (*prayojanavattva*).
He establishes the lack of necessity for [external] motivation with the words "For not," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the subject matter of poetry, the investigation of whether the cognitions of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) are true or false is entirely irrelevant; thus, an examination of the operation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that context results only in ridicule.
Therefore, it cannot be asserted that the cognition of the suggested meaning is everywhere identical to the cognition of a probandum (*liṅgin*).
However, that capacity of words to manifest an object that is suggested by the inferred form [of the meaning] is not a factor for the conventional usage of the term *dhvani*.
Thus they say: "We have no need for this," and "And in the domain of poetry... (*Locana*).
Regarding the point that they lack a motivating purpose (*aprayojakatva*):

for it is not the case that the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of those sentences is sought by way of conveying a true meaning— like the sentences concerning the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth— in order to incite action, because they terminate in mere pleasure (*prītimātra*).
And because aesthetic delight (*prīti*) itself—which consists of a transcendental wonder—is a necessary factor for the cultivation of poetic sensibility (*vyutpatti*);
this has already been explained at length previously.
[The phrase] "only for the sake of ridicule" [is used].

"This person is not a man of aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*); his heart is merely hardened by the onset of dry logic (*śuṣkatarka*), and thus he is incapable of grasping [the nature of] apprehension (*pratīti*)"—this is the mockery [of the opponent].

Now, one might object: "In that case, let it be that wherever there is suggestiveness (*vyañjakatā*), there is not necessarily inference (*anumānatva*); but how can it be denied that wherever there is inference, there is suggestiveness? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As for that which is to be inferred... and so forth.

The sense is that the capacity to suggest (vyañjakatva) is not the defining characteristic of *dhvani*, because it does not apply to objects other than the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*). Now, if that suggestiveness which has the intended meaning as its object—which shares the same status as inference (*anumāna*)—is not the ground for the conventional usage of the term *dhvani*, then for what purpose [is the example] given? "Like the sentences concerning the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and so forth," with reference to those [sentences] which have the form of poetry.
This is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa dṛṣṭāntaḥ*).
