It is sought after— that is, investigated— in order to bring about its functioning, meaning to accomplish its capacity to induce activity.
"Merely pleasure" (*prītimātra*):
by the word "merely" (*mātra*), the capacity to incite action (*pravartakatva*) is excluded. To the question, "Why does it terminate in mere pleasure? he says: "Because of pleasure," and so forth.
"It has been said" means that this was stated at the occasion of defining the nature of rasa; such is the intention.
He states the nature of ridicule with the words "This is not," and so forth.
"Śuṣka" means that by the employment of dry logic—that is, inference—one has a harsh heart; the meaning is that one is devoid of aesthetic sensitivity (*arasa*).
"Pratītim" means... [the cognition].
The meaning is: "the nature of the cognition produced by poetry.
[The phrase] "let it not be" implies that there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of light and so forth.

The word *iti* means "this very thing. In the *Vṛtti*, it was stated that the capacity to manifest that [sound] is not the cause for the conventional usage of the term *dhvani*; however, the reason for its being non-causal was not stated. Therefore, showing the intended reason, he says: "That," and so forth.
"Thus, it is the state of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*).

This means that the manifesting power of a word has as its object the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) which consists of the speaker's intention (*vaktrabhiprāya*), which is itself an object of inference (*anumeya*).
It is not, however, the definition of *dhvani*, nor is it the definition of that which is the subject of the conventional usage of the term *dhvani*.
Regarding this, he states the reason for the lack of pervasion (avyāpti) with the words beginning "abhiprāya" and so forth.
"Abhiprāya" means the intention to speak (vivakṣā).

The "object distinct from that" refers to the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) in the form of rasa, figures of speech (alaṅkāra), and so on. The meaning is that there is no operation—that is, an absence of functioning—toward that [suggested meaning].

In that case where the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) exceeds the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*)—which is the domain of the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*)—there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*), because the capacity to suggest (*vyañjakatva*) does not exist with respect to a suggested meaning that is merely inferable (*anumeya*) in the form of an intention.
[The author] introduces the following by raising the doubt of a contradiction with his own previous statement, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*), etc.
[He says: "exclusively inferential" (*anumānaika*).
The meaning is that it shares the same status and security as inference (*anumāna*).

However, this has been introduced for the purpose of demonstrating that the operation of words characterized as "manifestation" (*vyañjakatva*) must be accepted even by one who maintains that the relationship between word and meaning is innate (*autpattika*).

For this manifestation—whether in the form of a logical mark (*liṅga*) at times, or in some other form at other times—is something that cannot be rejected by any proponent of any theory, whether regarding expressive words or non-expressive ones; this is the effort we have undertaken.

Thus, because of its being distinct from categories of words such as those expressing qualities (*guṇa*), functions (*vṛtti*), and so forth, suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*) is necessarily different [from them]. Anticipating the objection that this was already introduced previously, he says: "But rather... He explains this very point in brief: "For that... etc.

For precisely because suggestiveness is observed to be assisted—sometimes by inference in cases such as intention (*abhiprāya*), sometimes by perception in cases such as the light of a lamp, sometimes by causality in cases such as the sound of singing, sometimes by denotation (*abhidhā*) when another meaning is intended, and sometimes by secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*) when the literal sense is not intended—it follows that its nature is established for us as distinct from all of those [other means of cognition]. Thus he says: "Therefore, in this way... (*tadevam*).

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is the contraction of the form of that which is already well-known—such as the function of denotation (*abhidhā*), the operation [of suggestion], or metaphorical function (*guṇavṛtti*)—being performed? [The answer is:
because of the intervention of another set of causal conditions (*sāmagryantara*), it becomes something distinct from what was previously introduced;
this is the meaning of what has been presented by the passage beginning with "of such a kind" (*tathāvidha*).
"Etadeva" means "exactly what was stated.
Explaining the meaning of the passage beginning with "tadevam" in connection with the passage beginning with "taddhi," he says: "yataḥ," and so forth.
In some places, "in [the case of] intention and so forth" is the commentary on *atyasya*; it should be understood similarly for what follows.
In other places, "by means of another form" is the commentary on the text of the *Vṛtti*, namely "by means of perception" and so forth.
The explanation of "tadevam" and so forth is as follows: "tata eva tebhyaḥ" and so on.

For indeed, the manifesting capacity (*vyañjakatva*) of a word with respect to its intended meaning and the like is established by inference (*anumāna*), while the manifesting capacity of light and so forth with respect to objects such as a jar is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), namely, by visual cognition of the jar and the like.
The suggestiveness residing in things such as songs and sounds, which possesses an object, functions as a cause by way of producing rasa;
the suggestiveness residing in that which is intended but not primary (vivakṣitānyapara) is supported by denotation (abhidhā);
and the suggestiveness residing in that whose expressed meaning is not intended (avivakṣitavācya) is seen to be supported by metaphorical function (guṇavṛtti).
The meaning is "from that very [source].
The point is that these [factors] possess only the nature of being manifestors (vyañjaka) and sustainers (anugrāhaka), but they do not possess the same form as the object itself (tattādrūpya).
"From all of those" means from those consisting of inference and so forth. "Distinct," etc. [follows].

By this, the following formal argument (*prayoga*) is demonstrated: "The nature of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*), which is the subject of dispute, is distinct from the modes of inference and so forth, because it appears as persisting even when those [modes] are excluded;
for whatever appears as persisting even when these are excluded is different from them, just as a thread is different from the flowers [strung upon it].
Thus he says.
The meaning is that he states its distinction from that.
As for the passage beginning with "nanu" (but surely), the connection is as follows:
for what purpose is the contraction of the form of well-known [functions] such as the operation of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) and secondary function (*guṇavṛtti*) being performed?
The remainder of the sentence is: "by postulating a distinct quality of being a manifestor. In the phrase "guṇavṛttyādi," the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
To the question "How then should it be stated?", he says: "Of that very [cause]," and so forth.
"Of that very" means of the very same [cause], such as the operation of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*).
"In another causal complex" (*sāmagryantare*)—means:

The meaning is that it consists of the knowledge of the excellence of the speaker, the listener, and so forth. Even if that [excellence] is forcibly included within the aforementioned categories, the elucidation of its specific nature—whether for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions or for the instruction of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*)—is certainly not to be disregarded;
for the definition of a mere generality does not preclude the definitions of useful particulars.
It is possible to do so;
for if it were thus, once existence (sattā) alone had been established as the definition, there would follow the consequence of redundancy regarding all the definitions of existing things.
Thus it is: that which was always a subject of dispute among the wise, whose true nature remained unknown—
Anticipating the objection that "the eye is form, and that very thing may be called the manifestor," he says: "even though it falls within that.
The intended meaning is: "We do not deny the application of designations and so forth.
"Disagreement" (*vipratipatti*) refers to the absence of such a specific distinction; "ascertainment" (*vyutpatti*) is the removal of doubt and ignorance.
"Not so," [it is said].
Regarding those characteristics which belong to specific useful things,
by the word "useful" there is the exclusion of useless things such as the teeth of a crow and the like.
"Thus indeed" means:

since "existence" (*sattā*) has already been defined as that which causes the confusion of the three categories (substance, quality, and action), it is the specific form (*viśiṣṭaṃ rūpam*) of the Vedas, Smṛtis, Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and so forth;
that is to say, its own nature (*svarūpa*) is distinct and different from other states (*avasthāntara-paryāyam*). This is the meaning.
"Let that very state of being a manifester (vyañjakatva) be asserted," [says the opponent].
The sense is that this is due to parsimony (lāghava) compared to the postulation of a distinct entity called "manifester-ness.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the construction is: "even if its inclusion within that [category] is asserted by force."
"In its inclusion therein" means in its inclusion within the categories of "functioning as a quality," "denotative," and so forth.
"Of that"—that is, of suggestiveness.
Regarding its specific variety, [the author says] in the *Locana*: "We do not," and so on.
The meaning is: we do not deny the application of designations such as "establishment" (*niveśana*) and so forth;
if a designation such as "manifestation" (*abhivyañjana*), which is distinct in its essential nature from [our own] intended "manifestorship" (*vyañjakatva*), is employed, then we do not deny that.
The meaning is that doubt regarding a real entity is appropriate, for it is not merely a matter of names.
Intending the etymological derivation of *vipratipatti* as "contrary apprehension" (*viruddhā pratipattiḥ*), he explains that term with the words beginning "of such a kind" (*tādṛk*).
Such a specific quality consists in the nature of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*).
He states what is intended by the word "vyutpatti" (derivation/understanding): "saṃśaya... etc.
He explains the passage beginning with "upayogī" (useful) as follows: "upayogiṣu" means among those things useful for the conduct of worldly life.
"In the particulars" means in specific entities; that is to say, "those pertaining to them.

He states the purpose of the qualification "in those that are useful," beginning with the words "by the word 'useful,'" etc., immediately after the enumeration of the categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth in the Vaiśeṣika system.

In the sūtra beginning with "existence, non-existence, eternal," the definition of the three categories—substance, quality, and action—as possessing existence (*sattā*) and so forth was stated; keeping that in mind, it was said in the commentary (vṛtti) "in mere existence" and so on.
He explains that [commentary] as follows: "the three categories," etc.
"Tripadārthasaṅkarī" means "that which is mixed with three categories.
The reading "tripadārthasaṅkīrṇā" is correct;
it means "pervading the three categories, such as substance (dravya) and the rest."
He explains what is intended by the passage from "sakaletyādi" up to "prasaṅga" with the words "śrutītyādi.
He shows the subverting argument (bādhaka) against the non-commencement [of the inquiry] with the words "sakaletyādi.
He concludes the commentary with the words "tadevam," etc.
The verse beginning with "vimati" is included within the commentary.
This very mode of poetry, designated as "sound" (*dhvani*), which is characterized by the non-cognition of reality, has been manifested here.

Another variety of poetry is seen in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya), wherein the beauty of the expressed meaning attains excellence through its connection with the suggested meaning. (Dhvanyāloka 3.34)

Another variety of poetry is seen in which the suggested meaning is subordinated (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya), wherein the beauty of the expressed meaning attains excellence through its connection with the suggested meaning. (34)
The meaning is that there would be no undertaking of the *Locana*, which is useful for the maintenance of the entire world.
The reason for its being a subject of doubt is given as "whose true nature (*satattva*) is unknown.
For this very reason, in order to demonstrate that from this moment onward no one shall have any doubt regarding this [work], the word "was" (*āsīt*) has been used. (3.3)

Thus, having explained everything up to the specific nature of sound— including its divisions and subdivisions— as well as that nature which appears through the medium of the diversity of manifesters,

[the author] has composed this section on the theory of manifestation (*vyañjakavāda*) in order to instill, all at once, the vital relationship between the manifested and the manifester into the minds of his students; thus, whatever was to be said regarding *dhvani* has already been stated.

Now, however, [the author] says—by way of establishing that this very [suggested meaning], even when it has become a subordinate quality (*guṇībhūta*), sanctifies the poet’s speech—to support its status as the very soul [of poetry]:
"The reason for the state of being an object of dispute... [Locana explains the utility of this statement:
It is well known that doubt is rooted in the non-determination of specific distinctions.
He states the purpose of the past-tense designation "it was" (āsīt) with the words "for this very reason," and so forth.
"For this very reason" means: since misconception is based on a failure to understand the true nature of reality, it cannot arise once that [true nature] has been ascertained.
The meaning is "from that very [source]. He explains the word "now" by analyzing it as follows: "from this moment," and so forth. "In order to demonstrate."
The meaning is "in order to indicate. // 3.3 //

Now, in order to introduce the subsequent body of the text—which is devoted to the exposition of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion)—without first stating its specific purport, [the author] briefly states the meaning of the textual composition from the beginning up to this point, starting with the words "In this way" (*evam*), etc. The connection is as follows:
"In this way, everything that was to be said regarding *dhvani* has indeed been stated."
In the first chapter (udyota), the general definition of *dhvani* was indeed stated along with its preliminary introduction;
in the second, however, its divisions—such as that in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*)—and their sub-divisions were demonstrated.
Thus he says: "its own form, together with its divisions and sub-divisions."
By the phrase "and whatever," the meaning of the third chapter is stated;
by the phrase "having explained all that," he demonstrates that the exposition of the nature of *dhvani* is fully accomplished by that much alone.

By the phrase "the very life-breath," the absolute necessity of defining the relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is demonstrated. By the phrase "in a single section" (*ekapraghaṭṭakena*), the suspicion of redundancy is dispelled. By the phrase "with reference to *dhvani*," he indicates the existence of other subjects to be expounded.

Now, one might object: "Since it has been accepted that *dhvani* is the soul of poetry (*kāvyātman*), and since [this work] functions solely to establish the nature of *dhvani* which constitutes the soul of poetry, for what purpose has the exposition of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) been undertaken?

For that [subordinate suggestion] lacks the status of being the soul of poetry. Anticipating this, the author introduces the following passage—beginning with "Now" (*adhuna*)—while revealing his underlying intention:
"This suggested" (*ayaṃ vyaṅgyaḥ*) refers to the type of suggested meaning already described.
The sense is that even though it has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), it is not merely [subordinate] but remains primary (*pradhānabhūta*).
"It purifies" means that it produces an excellence of luster (*chāyātiśaya*).
"By this door" means by way of introducing the principle of *kaimutya* (the argument from the obvious). "Of that very [door]" means...
The meaning is "of the resonance (dhvani) alone.

For it was stated previously [in the verse beginning] "And this [suggestion] is manifested in such a way," up to "like royalty" (*nāratvamiva*). Since the connection with the suggested meaning was shown in the *kārikā* as the cause for the excellence of beauty, it is not merely the connection with the suggested; rather, it refers to that suggested meaning—resembling the loveliness of a beautiful woman—which has been explained.

It has been stated that when [the suggested meaning] is predominant, it is called *dhvani*. However, when that same [suggested meaning] becomes subordinate due to the excellence of the beauty of the expressed (*vācya*), a distinct variety of poetry named *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) is postulated.

In that regard, when a mere fact (*vastumātra*) as the suggested meaning—which might otherwise be preferred over those cases where the expressed is subordinated—becomes subordinate in relation to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) consisting of the expressed form, there occurs the state of being *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*.
For example: "What indeed is this other ocean of loveliness here, wherein lotuses float together with the moon;
wherein the temples of elephants emerge, and wherein there are other stalks of plantain trees and lotus fibers?"
Regarding the term *locana*:
the meaning is that the connection with the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) constitutes an embellishment (*upaskāra*) of the expressed sense (*vācya*).
Regarding the term *pratipādita* (established): [it refers to what has been demonstrated].

Regarding the statement, "But that which is suggested is indeed something else," the word "stated" refers to the passage beginning with "Where the meaning or the word... In that context, among the three types of suggested content—namely, the thing (*vastu*) and so forth—he demonstrates, in sequence, the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of those varieties of the suggested thing that have been previously mentioned. Thus: "Therein..."
Regarding the word *lāvaṇya*: this is the speech of a certain youth, containing longing and wonder. Here, by the word *sindhu* (ocean), fullness is expressed.
By the word "lotus" [he meant] the flashes of her sidelong glances;
by the word "moon," her face; and by the word "temples of an elephant," her pair of breasts.
By the word "plantain trunk" (kadalikāṇḍa), the pair of thighs is indicated;
by the word "lotus stalk" (mṛṇāladaṇḍa), the pair of arms is indicated.

Since their own literal meanings are in every way untenable in that context, they possess the quality of having their expressed meanings set aside (tiraskṛtavācyatva), according to the principle stated by the word "blind" (andha).

The *Bālapriyā* states: "What is intended here as the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is not merely that, but rather its status as the locus of a specific excellence produced by its connection with the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya)*. Thus he says: "It is the embellishment of the expressed.

Furthermore, since it should have been stated that the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhāva*), he says—“the suggested consists of the three types beginning with the fact (*vastu*)”—in order to dispel the suspicion of inconsistency regarding the demonstration of the subordination of the fact and so forth in the commentary.
The word "stated" (uktam) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In the commentary, it says "in beauty" (lāvaṇye);
"here" (atra) means in this place.
"Another indeed" means unprecedented;
"this river of loveliness" (lāvaṇyasindhu) is a stream of beauty;
"in which" means in her.
‘By the moon’ means by the full moon;
‘they converge’ means they become joined together;
‘it emerges’ means it rises up.
‘Dviradaḥ’ means an elephant. Regarding ‘yatra’ and so forth,
the word ‘santi’ (exist) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
‘Kadalikāṇḍaḥ’ means a plantain stalk.

Intending to demonstrate in due order everything stated in the *Vṛtti*—beginning with “of the mere matter that is suggested” (*vastumātrasya vyaṅgyasya*)—the author first prepares the introductory framework in the *Locana*, starting with “desire” (*abhilāṣa*), etc.
The sequence is such that wonder (*vismaya*) comes first, and then desire (*abhilāṣa*).
Therefore, it was stated that [the intention] contains desire and wonder because it is not intended to be expressed.
As for the phrase "of someone," no specific person is mentioned because such specification would be useless.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "by the word *sindhu*," [it means] "perfection (*paripūrṇatā*) is suggested by the word *sindhu*," and so forth.
Regarding "perfection": [it refers to the state of being complete].
The meaning is "distinguished by fullness. In accordance with the use of the plural ending in the word *utpalān*, he says "glances" (*kaṭākṣacchaṭā*).
The connection here is made by modifying the verb to "is suggested" (*dhvanyate*).
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
it means "given that there is suggestion (*dhvani*) of the aforementioned objects.
This refers to these words, such as *sindhūtala* ("ocean-lotus") and so forth.
This is connected with the phrase "the state of having the expressed meaning set aside.
He states the reason for this in the passage beginning with "of its own meaning" (svārthasya) and so forth;
that is, of its own meaning, such as the river, the blue lotus, and so on.

Even from words whose expressed meanings are not set aside, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) that is perceived sometimes imparts a shadow of beauty to the expressed portion when that expressed meaning is internalized within a statement such as, "What indeed is this other [beauty]?"— that specific suggested sense being perceived even while the expressed remains primary.
This is because the very expressed meaning (vācya), by means of its own immersion, causes the submerged class of suggested meanings (vyaṅgya) to appear as beautiful;

and this beauty consists in the fact that the collection of objects such as the *kuvalaya*— which are the essence of the entire world and whose union was previously considered impossible— attains a form of conjunction within a most charming substratum, thereby being preceded by the realization of a marvelous discovery (*vismaya-vibhāvanā-prāpti*) and being further embellished by the suggested sense.
Likewise, because only that which is manifold [the determinants] becomes the cause of longing and so forth through the emergence of the form of the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
"As in the case of *andha*" means: by that same principle which was stated in the explanation of the word *andha* in the verse, "like a mirror blinded by breath."

By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even though it is being perceived," he shows that it is contradictory for that which has naturally attained the status of the primary element to undergo a reversal and become subordinate (*guṇībhāva*).
That "particular meaning" (*arthaviśeṣaḥ*) refers to the entire range of suggested meanings (*vyaṅgyārtha*) to be explained.
The phrase "something else indeed" (*aparaiva*) and so forth follows.
The meaning is that [the object] is embraced as a universal essence by the two expressions "for it is indeed something else" and "what is this?
In the denoted portion— that is, in the sentence-meaning composed of the river and the blue lotus which are the denotations of the words *sindhu* (river) and *utpala* (lotus)—
there is a "beauty of charm," a splendor that serves as the cause for the perception of poetic beauty (*kāvyacārutva*).
"Vidhatte" means "he effects.
By this, the subordinate status (*guṇībhāva*) of the suggested meaning is demonstrated.
Here, he provides the authority for this by relying solely on the experience of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*), beginning with the words "of the expressed alone," and so forth.
The connection is that [the suggested meaning] appears as beautiful precisely because it is the expressed meaning itself.
Here, he shows the qualifying attributes which contain the reason for this, beginning with "its own self" (*svātma*).
This refers to that which is characterized by the emergence (*unmajjana*)—that is, the standing forth with its neck held high—of the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the expressed meaning itself.

Likewise, for that [suggestion] by which the aforementioned collection of suggested meanings (*vyaṅgyajāta*) is submerged—that is, the submergence of the collection of suggested meanings consists in their remaining in a subordinate state by looking toward the face of the expressed meaning (*vācya*). But how can such an expressed meaning be beautiful? To this he says: "And its beauty," and so forth.
Regarding this subject matter:

at the beginning of this verse, he states that the subject matter primarily consists of the excitants of wonder—beginning with "asambhāvya" and so forth. Those for whom the meeting is "asambhāvya" (unimaginable) means those who have reached a state where it is impossible even to conceive of such a reunion.

Likewise, by reason of that state of being a collection— a collective form obtained through the resting, which is the state of remaining in close union, of those classes of objects such as the *kuvalaya* (blue water-lily) and others that constitute the essence of the entire world, upon that which is exceedingly beautiful, namely the heroine who serves as their single substratum.
The reading "puraskāreṇa" (by way of placing before) or "purassarīkāreṇa" (by way of making precede) refers to the attainment of the state of being a manifesting cause (*vibhāva*) for wonder.
He states the reason for the attainment of the state of being a manifesting cause for longing and so forth with the words beginning "vyaṅgya" (the suggested).
"Of that which is embellished by the suggested meaning" means of that which is embellished by the collection of suggested meanings such as side-long glances, facial expressions, and the like.
Thus, it refers to that which has attained a specific state of variety through the embellishment of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).

Now, if it is argued that only when embellished by the suggested meaning do longing and the other [emotions] function as *vibhāvas*, and not in their own right, then it would follow that the suggested meaning is primary, since it alone is the cause for attaining the status of a *vibhāva*; to this he says: "by means of the emergence of the form of the expressed" (*vācyarūponmajjanena*).
The meaning is: by means of the emergence of the nature of the expressed meanings, such as Kuvalayacandra and so forth.

When these [meanings] become subordinate in relation to the beauty of the poetry (*kāvyacārutva*), there is the state of "subordinate suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatā*), as exemplified by the verse beginning with "The twilight is full of passion" (*anurāgavatī sandhyā*).

Because it is made manifest by the very statement of the speaker himself, it occupies a subordinate position (*guṇībhāva*), as has been cited: "The lover’s mind was fixed on the time of the tryst" (*Locana*). Therefore, although the expressed meaning (*vācya*) possesses predominance to this extent, nevertheless, in the case of *rasadhvani*, even that [expressed meaning] is subordinate; this should be understood for all instances of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* according to the present context.
For this very reason, it has been stated many times that this is the very nature of *dhvani*.
Others, however, maintain that this statement refers to a river made beautiful by the liquid splendor of young women who have descended for water-sports;
even in that case, the interpretation follows the same method as previously described.

Or, for instance, [the verse] concerning young women who have descended to bathe near a river; in every case, the suggested quality (*guṇa*) reaches its fullness through the operation of a face of wonder. Thus it has been illustrated.

The meaning is that for the *bālapriyā*, the perception of the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*)—such as the side-glance or the face—in the form of the expressed objects like the "Kuvalayacandra" (the moon-lotus) is indeed the cause for generating longing and other such emotions.
"For this very reason" means: precisely because the suggested sense has become subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) according to the manner described above.

The meaning is that the object extends from the attainment of the state of being the manifesting cause (*vibhāva*) of wonder up to the attainment of the state of being the manifesting cause of longing and so forth.
However, immediately thereafter, that [object] becomes merely subordinate; thus he says "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), and so on.
In the case of *rasa-dhvani*, that is, in the *dhvani* of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others.
He says "of that which is to be expressed" (*tasyāpi vācyasyāpi*) to show that this applies not only to this specific case, but to everything— hence he says "of all," and so forth.
To provide support for this point, he says "for this very reason," and so forth.

The sense is that if, among the varieties of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) alone were to possess primacy, then the repeatedly proclaimed doctrine that "suggestion (*dhvani*) is the soul of poetry" would be inconsistent. Since this verse is not found in any specific literary composition (*prabandha*), it must be understood as a *muktaka* (isolated verse) whose description of the particular object to be praised follows the requirements of propriety; demonstrating this, he states another view with the words "But others," and so on.

By the phrase "the river made beautiful by the liquid of loveliness," the expression "ocean of loveliness" (*lāvaṇyasindhu*) is explained; the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "an ocean (*sindhu*) consisting of loveliness (*lāvaṇyamayī*), or made beautiful by loveliness (*lāvaṇyasundarīkṛtā*)."
The intended meaning is that the word *sindhu* is not a suggester (*vyañjaka*) while its primary denoted meaning (*vācya*) is set aside.
However, regarding words such as *utpala*, the process of suggestion has already been explained; thus he says, "And there too," and so forth.

In this view, the attainment of beauty resulting from the union of the *kuvalaya* (blue lotus) and other elements within a single, exceedingly charming substratum does not occur with full consistency; indicating this lack of satisfaction by the phrase "in this [view]," he states another position: "If..."
"Vetyādi" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the vicinity of a river":

because it is pervaded by a flood of unsurpassed beauty residing in young women, it is a river (*sindhu*) consisting of beauty; thus, even in this interpretation, the word *sandhu* retains its primary meaning.
The sense is that the previously mentioned fault does not apply, because it is the young woman herself who is to be described.
He states "sarvārtha... and so forth to show that in all three positions, the status of being a variety of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) as intended is beyond dispute.
[He concludes] with "nirūpitam" (it has been explained).
The meaning is that it has been demonstrated how, in this instance, the suggested matter—the narrative of the hero—attains the status of a subordinate element (*guṇībhāva*).

Now, one might object: even if words such as *saṃdhyā* (twilight) convey meanings such as a heroine through their non-suppressed literal senses (*atiraskṛtavācya*), the word *anurāga*—which is well-known as denoting "love"—must necessarily employ *jahatsvārthalakṣaṇā* (indication where the primary sense is abandoned) with respect to its actual subject matter, namely "redness," since it is [otherwise] established as signifying only affection.

Desiring to dispel the doubt as to how there can be "non-suppression of the expressed meaning" (atiraskṛtavācyatva) given that [the word] must be explained [otherwise], [the author] states, on the contrary, that by virtue of its etymological and conventional power (yogarūḍhi), that very word denotes "redness" (raktimatva) alone, and not in the sense of "love" (prema), and so forth.
The subordination (*guṇībhāva*) of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) consisting of rasa and so forth has been shown in the context of the *rasavat* ornament;
and in that case, their subordination is relative to the principal sentence (*ādhikārikavākya*), like a king followed by servants engaged in marriage.
Regarding the subordination of a suggested ornament (*vyaṅgyālaṅkāra*), the scope concerns [the ornaments] beginning with *dīpaka*.

And this has been explained in the very first Uddyota of the Locana: with the intention that the word *anurāga* (passion/attachment) functions through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being colored by that [desire], just like the word *lāvaṇya* (beauty), its status as having an unobscured literal meaning (*atiraskṛtavācyatva*) was stated;
[the phrase] "of that very" refers to the mere object (*vastumātra*).
Regarding the phrase "rasa and so forth":
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), elements such as the emotional states (bhāvas) are indicated; by the word "rasa," figures of speech (alaṅkāras) such as the "erotic" (preyas) and others are implied.
Now, one might ask: how can rasa and the rest, which are the absolute primary elements, be subordinate?

Anticipating the objection, "Even if it were subordinate (*guṇībhāva*), how could there not be a lack of beauty?", he shows by means of a well-known example that, on the contrary, there is actually beauty—introducing the phrase "In that case" (*tatra ca*).
This refers to the domain of figures such as *rasavad* and so forth.

Having thus demonstrated the subordination of both the factual matter (*vastu*) and the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) etc., he now demonstrates it for the third type of suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which consists of a figure of speech itself—introducing the phrase "of the suggested figure" (*vyaṅgyālaṅkārasya*).
[The suffix *ka* is applied] after [a word ending in] *upama* and so forth. // 3.4 //

Having thus demonstrated that all three types [of indication] possess the status of being subordinate (*guṇabhāva*), he says "likewise" (*tathā*) in order to show that this [indication] has a wider scope of application (*bahutaralakṣyavyāpakatā*).

However, *Bālapriyā* shows that it is indeed appropriate for the indication to be "established" (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) when the expressed meaning is not set aside, by saying "of the word *anurāga*" and so forth;
[the word *anurāga*] refers to longing (*abhilāṣa*) and love (*preman*).
The word "that" (*tat*):

the meaning of the term "that" is that very object; it is "colored" (*uparakta*) by that [quality], and the means [of designation] is that quality which acts as the colorer of the object. By this cause, [the designation occurs] through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is like the word "loveliness" (*lāvaṇya*).
The meaning is that it is like the word *lāvaṇya* (beauty) when applied to a particular excellence (*suṣamāviśeṣe*).
It should be understood that the meaning in the form of love (*prema*) is exclusively suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
[This is stated] by the term "rasavat" (possessing rasa).
The meaning is: "by the word *rasavat* used in the passage where the *rasavat* ornament was shown.
Furthermore, the reading in the commentary (*vṛtti*) is: "the subject matter of the *rasavat* ornament was shown previously.

With the intention that the fruit of demonstrating the subordinate status (*guṇībhāva*) of rasa and the other elements—preceded by the presentation of examples—is the removal of the doubt regarding their impossibility, he raises the doubt with the words: "But [is it not] excessively," and so forth.
Since even the expressed meaning possesses a relative primacy, the word "excessively" (*atyartham*) was used.
Why?
The sense is that the coexistence of primacy and subordination in a single [object] is indeed contradictory.

One might object: "Why should the subordinate status of even a primary element such as *rasa* not occur by virtue of the poet’s intention? To this, he says: "Or in the case of subordination. [The phrase] "by means of a well-known example" means "by means of an example well-known for its beauty."
For it does not appear unseemly for a king to follow his servants when they are engaged in a marriage;
on the contrary, even the particular excellence of the servants will serve to enhance the king's own preeminence, and thus, the sense is that it nourishes beauty alone. // 3.4 //
The word "asya" (of this) means "of that in which the suggested meaning is subordinate" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).
The connection is: "clear" due to their association with the quality of lucidity (*prasāda*), and "profound" because they suggest a further implied meaning.
By the phrase "bringing happiness," this very same method should be applied to them as follows:
"Poetic compositions with clear and profound words bring happiness;
and in those [compositions], this very same method should be applied by one of keen intelligence. (Dhvanyāloka 3.35)

Those compositions which possess clear and profound words, are repositories of poetic art, and bring happiness—for them, this very same method should be employed by one of excellent intelligence. (35)

Furthermore, all those poetic compositions— which, though possessing infinite varieties, are delightful through their manifestation of such meanings and bring joy to the discerning— must be understood as employing this very mode known as *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is subordinated).
For example:
Lakṣmī is the daughter, Hari is the son-in-law, and the Gaṅgā is his wife.
Their eyes are clear due to the quality of serenity and profound because they suggest a deeper meaning;
thus, the words [of this verse] are "bringing happiness," which is the cause of its beauty.
The meaning is that this very method applies there as well.
Regarding the term "sumedhasā" (by the wise one):

the implication is that whoever is unable to apply this method to that [case] would become an object of ridicule, being described as one whose eyes are closed by the cultivation of a most false sense of aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdayatā*).
Lakṣmī, the daughter who is the object of desire for all people,

is his daughter-in-law— Hari, who is constantly striving to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon everyone. Likewise, Gaṅgā is his wife, for whom every desirable object has lost its status as a means of attainment.
And his two sons were Amṛta and Mṛgāṅka;
here, "amṛta" refers to *vāruṇī* (wine).

Thus, [the verse describes] the enjoyment characterized by drinking parties during moonrise, which results from the fortune obtained through hundreds of means such as bathing in the Gaṅgā and propitiating the feet of Hari.

With the intention of showing that "the primary fruit" refers to being the essence of the three worlds, and that "dear to children" indicates that such a quality is the cause of beauty, he says: "the cause of beauty," and so forth.
In that context, "in such a poetic composition."

He states that the phrase "by one of keen intellect" (*sumedhasā*) is used to show that the attainment of the status of a connoisseur (*sahṛdayatva*) is based solely on skill in applying these various methods; therefore, those who desire this should exert great effort in this regard. He says: "But he who...
and so forth, ending with "...unreal.

This person is not a true connoisseur, but rather, through the cultivation of a false state of being a connoisseur—that is, by cultivating an unreal sense of being a connoisseur—he sits with eyes half-closed to manifest a mental state of being overwhelmed by the tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*).
The meaning is that one who perceives his deceptive nature would become an object of ridicule in the assemblies of the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
Lakṣmī is his daughter, Hari is his son-in-law, the Gaṅgā is his wife,
and nectar and the moon are his two sons— such indeed is the family of the great ocean.
Thus ends the shadow-commentary (*chāyā*).
Showing the range of meanings suggested (*vyaṅgya*) by the words contained herein, he provides the syntactical construction (*yojanā*), beginning with "Lakṣmī" and so forth,
and "Sakala" and so forth.
The passage beginning with "samasta" and that beginning with "yasyā" explain the meanings suggested by those respective words.
Regarding the term "amṛta": [it means] nectar.
The meaning is "the substance of nectar.
Regarding the term *vāruṇī*:
the intention is that it is not the *pīyūṣa* (the nectar of immortality), because, like the rising of the moon, that is not common to all people.
"By that" means by the aforementioned collection of meanings.
This is the meaning of the passage from "gaṅgāsnāna" up to "anubhavati," which [describes how the primary sense] undergoes subordination.
She from whom [merit] is obtained through bathing and the like, and through her worship and so forth—that Gaṅgā is indeed his wife; that Hari is indeed his son-in-law;
and that Lakṣmī is indeed his daughter.
Having obtained her, O moon-faced one, both my daughter and the family of the great ocean have truly flourished.
This section on verbal ornaments (vācyālaṅkāra), when accompanied by suggested elements (vyaṅgyāṃśa),
is generally observed in actual usage to possess a supreme luster.
This section on verbal ornaments, while existing as a subordinate element following upon the suggested meaning,
is generally observed in actual usage as bearing a supreme luster.

This section on verbal figures of speech has been presented by the authors of the *Lakṣaṇa* [treatises] only partially, as they follow the respective application of the suggested element—whether it be a figure of speech or a mere fact—to demonstrate its superior aesthetic charm (*chāyātiśaya*).
Yet, when examined, almost all such figures are observed in actual literary usage (*lakṣya*).
For instance, like the figures *Dīpaka* and *Samāsokti*, other figures are generally seen to be in contact with other suggested figures or other factual elements.
Being perceived as the *locana* (the eye), it experiences a state of subordination due to the word "aho" in the phrase "aho kuṭumbaṃ mahodadheḥ" ("Oh, what a family of the great ocean!"). // 3.5 //

Having thus stated that poetry—which, when devoid of ornament, appears merely as something flat and trivial—is sanctified by this internal essence, he shows that even ornament becomes more beautiful by means of this very [essence]: "In the expressed," etc.
"Partiality" (aṃśatva) means being merely a quality (guṇamātratva). "By a single part," etc.
By this, the *ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka* (partial metamorphosis metaphor) is demonstrated.
Since Lakṣmī—in the form of prosperity—is not enjoyed [by him] and thus remains as if unattained, the primary fruit at the time of moonrise is indeed the enjoyment of wine (*vāruṇī*).

That the moon and that wine assume the very state of being his sons—this much meaning is understood here through the operation of suggestion (*dhvani*), namely, that the Great Ocean alone is the essence of the three worlds.
And that [meaning], once understood, assumes a subordinate status by being touched by the word "family" (kuṭumba);

for it is only when the expressed meaning is embellished by the collection of suggested meanings that it attains the state of being an excitant (vibhāva) for wonder and produces an excellence of aesthetic charm (camatkāra). // 3.4 //
He introduces the subsequent verse by first stating the intended meaning of the preceding verse, beginning with "evam" (thus) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "niralaṅkāreṣu" (in those devoid of ornaments): the sense is that in the previously cited example beginning with "lakṣmīḥ" (fortune), no ornament whatsoever is clearly perceived.
"In its manifest state" means in its immediate appearance; it is to be connected with the phrase "the poem as it appears."
The reading is also "bhāsamānam api" (even though it appears). By this subordinate suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*),
[it is meant] "with its inner essence."
"Being internal" means possessing an innate excellence even when subordinate, according to the analogy of silver [perceived] during childhood play.
"Of the ornament" (*alaṅkārasya*) is used in the singular to denote the genus.
"By this very [fact]"...
The meaning is "by means of the subordinated suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) alone.
Regarding the term "more beautiful" (*ramyataratva*): the suffix *-tara* is used because it is inherently more beautiful due to its status as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
For this very reason, it is said that "it is the supreme shadow" and "the excellence of shadow.

Regarding the phrase "the following of the suggested portion," he explains that the status of the suggested as a "portion" relative to the expressed means nothing other than its being subordinate; thus he says, "the status of a portion is the state of being a mere quality.
By this, it has been demonstrated.

The intention is that, according to the maxim "the mention of a name includes the mention of a part of the name," the word "ekadeśa" (part) refers here to a *rūpaka* (metaphor) that manifests as a part. For, first of all, the inclusion of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) can be achieved in all poetic ornaments;
indeed, when this is employed by great poets, it nourishes a certain unique splendor in their poetry.

For how can there be the possession of excellence when [a figure] is employed according to the propriety of its own subject? In poetry, this is the meaning: regarding the *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) metaphor—such as in the verse "The lake-kings were fanned by the autumn-like royal assembly"—the fact that the swans are perceived as chowries (*cāmara*) attains the status of a subordinate quality (*guṇatā*) within the expressed meaning, namely the kings; this is exactly what has been shown by the authors of the treatises on poetics.
The meaning is that this particular type has been indicated by means of this door [of classification].
Others, however, have explained it as "unmanifest" (*anudbhinnam*), on the grounds that it consists merely of a variety within the denotative portion (*vācyabhāga*) of a single part.
Those [figures] which touch upon another suggested figure (*vyaṅgya*) or another factual matter (*vastvantara*) and embrace them for the sake of their own refinement are described as such.
Regarding the phrase "by great poets," this refers to Kālidāsa and others.
To provide the reason for what was stated—that [the figure] nourishes the beauty of poetry—he says: "For how... and so forth.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the reason.
How could the possession of excellence (*atiśayayogitā*) not bring about preeminence (*utkarṣa*) in poetry? The meaning is that there is no other such mode [of expression].
If the poet, by means of that propriety (*aucitya*) residing within his own heart regarding his particular subject matter, brings about that hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), [then it is successful].

As Bhaṭṭendurāja says: "That [state] in which the eyes, having rested, look about repeatedly yet remain motionless; that in which the limbs daily wither like the stalks of plucked lotuses. [The author asks: How is that demonstrated by means of a *rūpaka* (metaphor) that undergoes partial transformation (*ekadeśavivartin*)? To this he replies: "This is the meaning," and so forth.
[He explains: "[It is] what is implied" (*pratīyamāna*).

The meaning is that the description of the lakes as "kings" (*nṛpati*) is expressed through words (*śābda*), while by its power (*tatsāmarthyāt*), the swans—which serve as the means for fanning—are suggested (*vyaṅgya*) to be chowries (*cāmara*).
It should also be understood that here the autumn season’s role as a female chowrie-bearer (*cāmaragrāhiṇī*) is likewise suggested.
[This occurs] when it has arrived.

"It has been shown" means that here, because it is the expressed meaning (vācya) alone— when embellished by the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya)— that produces aesthetic charm (camatkāra), the subordinate status (guṇībhūtatva) of the suggestion is made clear.
"Only so far," etc.
The specification of the temporal limit is for the purpose of indicating its extreme clarity.
By the word "tāvat" (just),
the intended meaning is that at the very moment of seeing it, this [object] is to be clearly apprehended without depending on anything else.
"By this door" means by way of an illustrative principle (*upalakṣaṇanyāyena*).
"This method" refers to the method stated in the verse (*kārikā*).
He states the explanation of others regarding the phrase "shown by way of a single part" with the words beginning "others," etc.
The explanation of the phrase "by way of a single part" is given with the words beginning "the expressible," etc.
[The term] "unmanifested" (*anudbhinnam*).
The meaning is that [the sense] is unclear.
He says "the suggested" (*vyaṅgyam*) and so forth, applying this as an adjective qualifying both [the word and the meaning].
The explanation of the term "touching" (*saṃspṛśanti*) is given by "of its own self" (*svātmanaḥ*) and so forth.
"For the sake of refinement" means for the sake of attaining excellence;
"in poetry" connects with what precedes it.
"It does not exist at all," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is no variety of poetry whatsoever that has not attained excellence through its connection with hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
To the question "Is this so in every respect? he replies: "In its own domain," and so forth.
That is, in its own domain—namely, that which is the object of its own hyperbole.
Propriety is characterized by the quality of being plausible.
Therefore, "by that which resides in the heart" means characterized by that propriety residing in the poet's heart.
The connection is that if one were to do so, such a mode [of expression] would simply not exist;

it would not bring about excellence (*utkarṣa*). This is also what Bhāmaha stated in his definition of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the *Locana*: "That dense paleness on the cheeks which mocks the blade of *dūrvā* grass—this very state of attire is found among young women when a youth is present."

For here, since this extraordinary excellence regarding the fortune of the Blessed One, who possesses the form of the God of Love, is indeed conceivable, a supermundane splendor shines forth in that poem. But by impropriety, splendor would surely be lost;
as for example: "Without considering even a small cause, the Creator [created] the sky..."
Such will be the swelling of your breasts when they come to pass.
Thus [it is said].
Now, as for what was stated—that hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) remains entirely latent as a suggested element within all poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*)—how is that so?
For Bhāmaha declared that hyperbole is the common form underlying all poetic figures.

Anticipating the objection—“The universal (sāmānya) does not manifest as something distinct from the word because it is perceived as a particular (viśeṣa), nor does it appear subsequently; so how can it be suggested (vyaṅgya)?”—he says, “by Bhāmaha. Regarding that, he provides an example consistent with propriety, beginning with “yat,” etc. This verse has already been explained.
The phrase "of the Blessed One" refers to [the Blessed One] who possesses the form of the God of Love;
and the phrase "and that is indeed possible" provides the reason for this.
"Is indeed possible" means: [it is possible].
"Thus it would be" means that it is precisely what is being conceived by those who practice;
and this is the reason.
"It is indeed possible" means that it is precisely what is conceived by practitioners as "it might be so.
By the word "indeed" (eva), the exclusion of its being impossible is indicated.
"This is an excellence regarding the domain of good fortune" means an excellence of qualities such as beauty that is implied by the description of a particular state of a woman;
"in such a poem" refers to a poem of that kind.
Clarifying this very point by way of a counter-example, he says: "By not being in a state of union," and so forth.
"It surely dissolves" means: what talk can there be of the radiance of beauty? This is the sense.
"Small" means "a small creation"; the sense is that there was no sufficient space for both breasts.
"This" means that which is being perceived;
"of such a kind" means [as follows].
The meaning is that it is impossible to describe.

Here, by describing the creation of even the vast space—which is of the nature of infinite room—as being small, the breasts are perceived as possessing a greatness that surpasses even that; thus, the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
However, because such a magnitude in the breasts is inconceivable and therefore improper (*anaucityavatī*), it is not capable of producing excellence in the poem; this is the intended sense.
To the question, "For what purpose is the passage beginning with 'By Bhāmaha also' relevant to the present context?", he introduces it with "Now then" (*nanu*) and so forth.
The meaning is that the point being made is by the passage stating: "The inclusion of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) within all poetic ornaments can be accomplished."
"How so? means "it is illogical.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because," and so forth.

Bhāmaha refers to the teacher named Bhāmaha, who stands as a preeminent authority among those who define poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*). "He said" means that he stated [this] by means of the passage beginning with the words, "This indeed is all *vakrokti*."
"Every *vakrokti* (indirect expression)" means every single poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).

"This very one" refers to this aforementioned *atiśayokti* (hyperbole); thus, the meaning is that while *atiśayokti* constitutes the general form, it is also the specific nature of those various individual ornaments.
To the question, "Let that be so; what does that have to do with the present subject? he says: "And not," and so forth.

How is this [suggestion] something to be suggested (*vyaṅgya*)? For that which is suggested is perceived from the word as distinct from the expressed meaning, following the cognition of the latter; whereas universals (*sāmānya*) are perceived otherwise. This entire "oblique expression" (*vakrokti*), such as the word "cow" (*gaur*), has its meaning manifested by this [suggestion]; therefore, the poet must exert effort toward it. What poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) could exist without it?
Thus [it is said].

In this regard, hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) presides over that poetic figure, for it possesses an excellence of beauty through the power of the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*). This is the meaning that must be understood in what was stated by Bhāmaha as well;
such is the connection, albeit at some distance.
What was said there?
"That very [hyperbole]"—that hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) which has been defined is itself every variety of *vakrokti*, that is, every type of poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
This is because of the statement: "The expression of words with a crooked (indirect) meaning is desired as the ornament of speech."

For the "crookedness" (vakratā) of the word and the "crookedness" of the denoted meaning consist in their existing in a form that transcends the ordinary world; this alone is the nature of ornamentation (*alaṅkāra*) in an ornament.
And this very transcendence of the worldly is what constitutes excellence (*atiśaya*);
therefore, hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is the common characteristic of all ornaments.
For instance: by means of this hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), the object—though rendered ancient by being enjoyed by all people—is conceived as being fresh through its wonderfulness;
likewise, the pleasure garden and so forth are brought to the state of being an excitant (*vibhāva*).

The meaning is as follows: since the general and the particular appear simultaneously and not as separate entities, the appearance of them as distinct—which is the pervader (vyāpaka) occurring after the cognition of the specific figure of speech—is excluded; and by its exclusion, its own pervaded (vyāpya), namely "suggestibility" (vyaṅgyatva), is also excluded. Therefore, the assertion of its suggestibility is improper because it contradicts the statement of Bhāmaha.
He demonstrates the connection [of the verse] despite its separation by stating "by Bhāmaha as well," and so forth.
That which was stated by Bhāmaha is what has been said.
He explains the verse beginning with "ya" and so forth.
"Lakṣitā" (defined) means defined by such passages as "That speech which [proceeds] from a cause" (*nimittato vaco yattu*).
"Vakrā" (crooked) means distinguished by the crookedness (*vakratā*) of the nature that is about to be described.
He explains with the intention that "utterance" refers to the meaning being expressed, starting with the words "yat... and so forth.
"Lakṣitā" (indicated) means indicated by the passage beginning with "But that speech which [is based] on a cause," and so on.
"Vakrā" means distinguished by the crookedness (*vakratā*) of the nature that is about to be described.
He explains [the term] with the intention of referring to the meaning— that which is being spoken— as "a variety of ornament" (*alaṅkāraprakāra*),
meaning a specific type of poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).

Regarding the fact that the word *vakrokti* signifies an "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*), he corroborates this with the very statement of Bhāmaha: "It is *vakrokti*"; the readings are *alaṅkṛtiḥ* and *alaṅkriyā*.

With the intention that the word *vakra* (crooked/deviant) here—its own literal meaning being impossible—indicates [the *vyaṅgya*] through similarity by virtue of possessing a different form that transcends the well-known path, he says "lokottīrṇena" and so forth.
"By a form transcending the world" means by a form excluded from those scriptures, histories, and so forth, which are well-known in the world.
And that form is characterized by the attainment of fitness for the manifestation of the intended aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
"This alone" means this very form that transcends the world, consisting in its fitness for manifesting rasa.
"The status of being an ornament for an ornament" means the quality of being an ornament (such as simile) belonging to [another] ornament.

And thus, the sense is that the term *vakrokti* (oblique expression) signifies an *alaṅkāra* (poetic figure). Nevertheless, one might ask: how can it have the nature of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole)? To this he says: "The very state of being transcendent (*lokottaratā*) is *atiśaya* (exaltation). He states the conclusion: "Therefore... (i.e., *tena*).
He explains the portion beginning with "by this" (anayā) with the words "for it is thus" (tathāhi), and so forth.
"For it is thus" means that what is about to be stated serves as the proof for what has already been said.
"Sakala" means made old, brought to a state where it is no longer palatable.
The explanation of the meaning of the prefix "vi" is "by way of variety."
The meaning is: "by virtue of possessing ever-new distinctions.
It is cultivated (bhāvyate) and brought to completion.
As they have said: "And this is the nature of things, that they are not directly [perceived] as such."
He shows that by the phrase "and another two meanings are to be contemplated," what is intended is as follows—beginning with "in that way" (tathā) and so forth.

As for the mention of "the pleasure garden and so forth," this refers merely to the poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*); however, because it is capable of assuming the body of all ornaments through the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*), one should understand that this very thing is the form of all ornaments.
And regarding her [the Goddess of Speech], Locana states that she is "mingled with other ornaments" and is "especially brought to consist of rasa";
to the question of what that meaning is, he replies: "By means of metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra), she herself takes the form of all the ornaments."
He states the cause for the metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) with the words "possessing all ornaments" (*sarvālaṅkāra*).
He states the purpose of the metaphorical usage with the passage beginning "hyperbole" (*atiśayokti*) and ending with "merely a figure of speech" (*alaṅkāramātratā*).
Furthermore, the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*) is shown right here with the words "by the power of the poet's creative intuition" (*kavipratibhāvaśāt*), and so forth.

The intended meaning is as follows: if hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) were indeed the universal form underlying all poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), then it would culminate in identity (*tādātmya*); consequently, no poetic figure distinct from it would ever be observed, and thus the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhāna*) would not need to be taken into account therein.
[The word] "meaning" (*artha*) is supplied [from the previous context].
"Is cultivated specifically" is the detailed explanation of this very point—namely, "the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)," and so forth.
"Thus," and so on, is the statement of the summarized meaning.
"To that extent" refers to non-contradiction.
"In that regard" (tatra) means "in that statement.
"This one" (asau) refers to...
The meaning is that this is what is intended by the word "this" (*idam*) in the phrase "this very [thing]" (*ayameva*).
For in a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), a triad must necessarily be stated:
the cause (*nimitta*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*).

In this context, he states "the metaphor" (*upacāra*) and so forth to present the grounds that establish the relationship between the subject matter and its definition, beginning with the words "all ornaments" (*sarvālaṅkāra*). By saying "he states the ground," the intended meaning is that the ground is the similarity to the primary sense (*mukhyārtha*), which consists in the capacity to assume the nature of the body of an ornament (*alaṅkāraśarīra*).

He states that "hyperbole" (atiśayokti) and so forth serve to provide the purpose, saying: "metaphorical transference" (upacāra), etc. In the commentary, the phrase "this [figure] presides over the ornament" means that by which ornament it becomes connected.
‘Of that’ means ‘of that which is connected with hyperbole.
‘Of another’— meaning:
The meaning is "of that which is unrelated to hyperbole" (*atiśayokti*).
Thus, the intention is that the purpose [of simile and the like] is to manifest an excellence of beauty through their connection with hyperbole.
In the *Locana*: "In this very [context]."
The meaning is: "in the very passage that presents the purpose.
In response to the inquiry, "How is the sublation of the primary meaning understood by this? he reveals the underlying intention, saying, "This is the sense," and so forth.

Just as the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*) is a universal because it persists through particular instances such as the "dappled" or the "hornless," so too, because the "hyperbole" (*atiśayokti*) persists through particular instances such as "simile" (*upamā*) and the like, it constitutes their universal essence; thus, all "figurative speech" (*vakrokti*) is that [hyperbole] alone, and there is a designation of non-difference.

Alternatively, having considered the following dilemma in one's mind— whether, by this mode of expression, the primary intention is to reject the position that *dhvani* alone is the soul of poetry due to a lack of desire to distinguish between the general and the particular, or whether it is intended to assert that poetic excellence (*atiśayokti*) is the life-breath of poetry— the author refutes the former with the words "If, first of all," and so forth.
"Ending in identity" (*tādātmyaparyavasāyinī*):

the sense is that just as [individual cows] such as the dappled or the hornless are of the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*), so too all figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) would become identical in nature with hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
To the objection, "Let there be this identity," he says: "Thus, distinct from that," and so forth.
"Distinct from that" means distinct from hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). In that regard, it would not be so because there is no dependence upon the application of hyperbole.
Just as sugar-candy and other such things possess the form of "cowness" and so forth by their very nature without depending on anything else, so too does the excellence of a simile and the like;

thus, the degree of excellence produced by the varying degrees of a poet's creative intuition is observed sometimes as the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and sometimes as the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Furthermore, suggestiveness (*vyaṅgyatva*) would not be seen as anything more than a mere ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
If, on the other hand, it is intended here as the very life-breath of poetry (*kāvyajīvita*),
even so, it would remain such [the life-breath] even when composed with impropriety (*anaucitya*).

If it is argued that "propriety (*aucitya*) is the lifeblood [of poetry]," we reply: since there is nothing else that serves as the basis for propriety except rasa, bhāva, and so forth, one must admit that these alone constitute the primary inner life, and not propriety itself.

By this, those who have said—"In a poem composed of beautiful words and meanings fashioned by propriety, what need is there for another 'suggestion' (*dhvani*) as its very soul?"—have themselves provided the testimony for the existence of *dhvani*.
Those who hold such views have been answered.
Consequently, it is established that the excellence of the expression (*atiśayokti*) possesses the nature of being suggested (*vyaṅgyatva*).
As for what was stated regarding its inclusion within other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), that very point is divided into three parts, beginning with the words "of that" (*tasyāśca*).
Regarding the phrase "as being denotable": that too becomes denotable, as in— "For what indeed is this other [beauty] here?"
The meaning is that even in this case of *rūpaka* (metaphor), it would contradict [the definition] because of the presence of *atiśaya* (exaggeration).
He states another objection: "merely an ornament," and so forth.
It is observed that there exists some mere ornament (*alaṅkāramātra*) which is not embraced by *atiśayokti*.
The meaning is that even that would be untenable.
Having raised the second [alternative], he refutes it with "atha" (now/if).
That is the *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).

Although it was stated here that "all this is *vakrokti* (figurative expression)" in order to demonstrate that it constitutes the very life of poetry— this being intended as a statement indicating a debate while provisionally accepting that position—
is it intended that mere *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) alone constitutes the life of poetry, or rather some specific variety thereof?
He states that the first position is not tenable with the words "even by impropriety.
The word "it" (sā) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis,
as in the passage beginning "only a small portion was created."
Likewise, the lifeblood of poetry is the second [quality], which is restated as "possessing propriety" (*aucityavatī*),
as in the verse beginning with "yad viśramye" and so forth.
He says, "The basis of propriety," and so forth, [meaning] that what we maintain is thus established.
It has already been stated that rasa and the like are precisely what bring about propriety.
The reason for its primacy is given: "the inner controller."
"But not that" refers to that hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) characterized by propriety (*aucityavatī*).
He states "by this," and so forth, as an incidental digression.
The connection is that they are "refuted by this.
"By one's own words alone" means by the very statement that it is constituted by propriety (*aucitya*).
Regarding the phrase "the existence of *dhvani*":

the meaning is that since propriety (*aucitya*) is based on *rasa* and so forth, it would serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for accepting the existence of *dhvani* consisting of *rasa* and so forth.
He concludes with the words "Therefore," etc.
"This is merely a metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra).
The meaning is that this entire figurative expression (vakrokti) is a designation based solely on metaphorical identification, just like [the expressions] "The face is the moon" and so forth.
He states the result of establishing its metaphorical nature with the words beginning "And therefore," and so on.
Showing the connection of this passage beginning with "tasyāśca" (and of that) with the present subject, he says: "yaduktam" (as has been stated), etc.
"Uktam" (stated) means what was previously stated by way of being the basis for metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
"Acceptance as another figure of speech" means the state of not being mixed with other figures of speech.
He explains that the word "of her" (tasyāḥ) is also connected with the phrase "by way of being the expressed meaning" (vācyatvena)— namely, "she too," and so forth.
That is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).
Here, he shows that the example already stated beginning with "lāvaṇya" (loveliness) is indeed [an instance of it]—starting with "yathā" (for example), and so on.
In this context, while demonstrating the expressed ornament (*vācyālaṅkāra*), he states that there is an absence of *atiśayokti* as a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyatva*)—starting with "atra," and so on.
Since the eyes and so forth are metaphorically represented as blue lotuses and the like, the status of the *rūpaka* (metaphor) as a directly expressed (*vācya*) figure is indeed clear;
however, the case of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) is such that it may sometimes be predominant and sometimes subordinate.
In the former case, it belongs to the path of directly expressed figures of speech (*vācyālaṅkāra*).
In the second case, however, there is inclusion within *dhvani*;
in the third, however, it takes the form of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*.
And this type exists for other poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) as well.
However, their scope is not universal;

whereas hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), on the other hand, can indeed have all poetic figures as its scope—this is the distinction. Furthermore, in those figures where the attainment of identity occurs by way of similarity, such as metaphor (*rūpaka*), simile (*upamā*), "equal union" (*tulyayogitā*), "illustration" (*nidarśanā*), and so forth...

Among these, only that similarity which exists by way of the very nature of the object being traversed possesses an excellence of beauty; thus, all of them, being endowed with an excellence of charm, belong to *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* alone. [The commentary] says "In that regard" (*tatra*) to state the division of the scope of this threefold [classification], which touches upon the word (*śabda*).
Among those types, regarding that which is the first type:
one might object, "If this is indeed nothing but *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), then why was the sequence indicated by saying 'first of all'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And this..."—referring to that which has been defined as *atiśayokti*, which consists in its capacity for inclusion within other poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) as well.
Anticipating the objection, "Even if this is so, with what intention was it said that [the suggestion] is 'first'? he says: "Of these" (teṣām).

Having thus stated that there is indeed a touch of the suggested (vyaṅgya) in the figures of speech (alaṅkāras), he explains the classification by asking, "In which [figures] does what appear as the suggested?"—this is expressed by the words: "And in those... (yeṣu ca).
The essential nature (*svarūpa*) of *rūpaka* and the other figures has already been explained.

Regarding *nidarśanā*, however, although it begins to exist as something suggested (*vyaṅgya*) by the very action (*kriyā*) of its own meaning—as stated in the *Bālapriyā*—it nonetheless falls into the status of being directly expressed (*vācyatva*), because it is touched upon by another word, namely "another" (*aparaiva*). Thus, the meaning is that both [the action and the word] are directly expressed.
According to the view of the Neo-Logicians (*navya*), however, in the phrase "another" (*aparaiva*), there is an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) based on a distinction.

In the verse beginning with "yatrotpalāni" (where there are lotuses), there is the figure of speech *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbolic metaphor); however, according to the opinion of Bhojarāja, this is *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression). Thus, one should understand these various differences of opinion.
Regarding the word "asya" (of this):
The sense is that, since there is no distinction between the objects [of these figures], demonstrating their threefold nature would yield little fruit.
The first type consists of both the expressed and the implied essence.
By the words "this and so forth," an extension (*atideśa*) of this aforementioned type to other figures of speech has been made.
To explain why this is so, he introduces the passage beginning with "nanu" (but surely) and so forth.
The word "ced" (if), used here where there is no doubt, is an expression of doubt [used rhetorically].
This would be appropriate only as a hyperbolic statement (*atiśayokti*).
The sense is that it has been stated that she is worthy of assuming a body adorned with all ornaments.
Regarding the phrase "as has been described," etc.: for sequence can only apply when there are many existing things that occur successively.
The meaning is "not otherwise.
Regarding the word "nirūpita" (demonstrated),
the word "prakāra" (manner) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
With what intention was it said "first"?
The meaning is: one must state that "first" refers to primacy; and what is the basis for this primacy? He says: "Of those... and so forth.
The meaning is that he says [this] with the passage beginning with "of these" and ending with "the distinction.
"Having stated that there is a touch of the suggested" means having stated it by means of the textual passage beginning with "this class of expressed ornaments."
"What is it? means: is it another figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) or another subject matter (*vastu*)?
In the commentary, it says "the attainment of reality" (*tattvapratilambha*).
The meaning is that it attains the status of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). Regarding the phrase "in *rūpaka*," etc.,
one should understand that in *rūpaka* and other such figures, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*), whereas in *upamā*, similarity is the very nature of the figure itself.
"By the action of the eyes"—
this definition is the presentation of that which is distinguished by the manifestation;
these are the objects.

In cases such as *samāsokti*, *ākṣepa*, and *paryāyokta*, however, because their status as figures of speech is established solely through the inseparable connection with the suggested element (*gamyamānāṃśa*), their nature as *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggestion is subordinated) is beyond dispute.
Furthermore, regarding that state of being *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*, there is a rule that some figures of speech contain within them specific other figures;
for example, that *vyājastuti* contains within it the figure *preyaḥ*.
For some figures of speech, there is a rule that they contain only a single figure within them,
as is the case when metaphors and the like contain similes within them.
For other figures of speech, it is also possible for them to contain one another within them.
As in the case of the two types known as *dīpaka* (illumination) and *upamā* (simile):
among them, *dīpaka* is well-known for having *upamā* at its core,
while *upamā* sometimes follows the shadow of *dīpaka*.

Just as in the case of the "garland simile" (mālopamā), so too in such instances as "like a lamp with its flame possessing great radiance," the shadow of the "lamp" (dīpaka) is clearly perceived. [As stated:
"The Locana considers this desired in the case of the 'illustration' (nidarśana)."
The example: "This sun, its luster dimmed, desires to go toward the setting;
it announces to men that rising is for the sake of falling."
It is called *prayoktṛlaṅkāra* (the ornament of the speaker), because it culminates in flattery; and that has already been illustrated by us in the second chapter (*uddyota*).

Regarding the phrase "having the nature of being pregnant with a simile" (*upamāgarbhatva*): by the word "simile" (*upamā*), all its specific varieties such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and so forth are included;
or else, since similarity (*aupamya*) is the common denominator of all, everything is already implied by it. [The phrase] "it is indeed clear" means:

By the phrase "he was both purified and adorned by her," the *dīpaka* (illuminator) figure—functioning like a lamp—is introduced here through its implied meaning (*pratīyamānatayā*). Furthermore, the statement of a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) and the "abduction" (*haraṇa*) are according to Bhāmaha. [The word] *yiyāsati* means he begins to go.
How the simile is suggested (vyaṅgya) in this instance is clear from the *Kuvalayānanda* and other such works.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says: "The scope belongs only to that where the suggested meaning is subordinate" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyasyaiva viṣayaḥ*).
The intended sense is that the implied property (*gamyamānadharma*) serves as a factor for the establishment of the expressed meaning (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*).

"‘Establishment of the categories [of poetry]’ (tattvavyavasthāna) means the establishment of [the types of poetry] such as *samāsokti* (speech with ellipsis). ‘That in which the suggested meaning is subordinate’ (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*)..."
The intended meaning is that [it serves] as an embellishment for the expressed sense (*vācyārtha*).
Locana states "cāṭu" (flattery) as the reason for its being pregnant with the *preyas* ornament;
and "sā ca" (and she).
The meaning is that this is "vyājastuti" (feigned praise).

Regarding the phrase "in some cases, being composed of mere figures of speech," since the term "mere figures of speech" (alaṅkāramātra) denotes figures of speech in general, the subsequent mention of "being composed of simile" (upamāgarbhatva)—which refers to a specific type—is contradictory; therefore, "those specific types" refers to specific types of simile.

The intended meaning is based on such statements as: “Metaphor (rūpaka) is considered to be nothing other than a simile (upamā) in which the difference [between the object and the subject] has become concealed. Regarding the phrase “metaphor and so forth,” the word “intended” is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
