He states "or rather," and so forth, to show that the word *upamā* here does not denote the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), but rather the state of similarity (*aupamya*).
He explains "common to all" as meaning common to all [figures], such as simile, metaphor (*rūpaka*), and the rest.
He establishes how the shadow of a lamp is understood through the simile of a heap (*mālopamā*) with the words beginning "by that," etc.

[The phrase] "because of illuminating by means of that which stands in the place of a lamp" demonstrates the etymology of the word *dīpaka* as either "like a lamp" (*dīpa iva*) or "that which illuminates" (*dīpayati*).
This is clear in the *Kuvalayānanda*:
the connection is that the *dīpaka* (lamp simile) has entered here by way of being implied—
that is, by way of being suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
In this context, regarding the instance of the "garland simile" (*mālopamā*) such as "possessing great splendor" (*aprabhāmahatya*), and so forth:

thus, when there is contact with a suggested element (*vyaṅgyāṃśa*), all poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) such as metaphor (*rūpaka*) and the rest—which possess an excellence of beauty—constitute the path of "subordinated suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*). And the state of being subordinated suggestion is the common characteristic of all those of that kind, whether they have been explicitly mentioned or not.

In the definition of *tallakṣaṇa* (that characteristic), all these [examples] are indeed [instances of] *locana*, by way of a clear mode of expression (*abhidhāprakāra*) regarding the simile (*upamā*). "Of such a kind" means those possessing an excellence of beauty.
Regarding the term "well-characterized" (*sulakṣitā*): that which is indeed their form when freed from those [attributes] is not to be sought in poetry.
For a simile (*upamā*) is like "as a cow, so a gavaya";
a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is like "the threshing-post is a sacrificial post."
*Śleṣa* (paronomasia) is exemplified by *dvirvacane 'cīti*, which is based on the principle of *tantra*.
*Yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence) is exemplified by *tudīśālātureti*. *Dīpaka* (illumination) is exemplified by *gāmaśvam iti*.
The doubtful (sasandeha) is "it might be a post";
the concealment (apahnuti) is "this is not silver";
the periphrasis (paryāyokta) is "the fat man eats by day."
*Tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) is illustrated by [the rule] *asthādhvoricca*.

*Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description) is illustrated by all the *jñāpaka*s (indicative evidence), such as the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) in the definition of a technical term (*pada-saṃjñā*), as in: "In other cases of the prescription of a technical term, when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, the rule of extension to that which ends with it (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply. *Ākṣepa* (Paralipsis) occurs in both types of optional rules (*vibhāṣā*) because, with the intention of expressing a specific alternative, there is first a negation of even a desired injunction, thereby employing a prohibition. Here, showing the reason for this, he says: "Because it is common," and so forth.
"In this simile" means "in the *mālā-upamā* (garland simile). "By the mode of expression" means by the operation of expression (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*).
By the word "eva" (only/itself), the exclusion of the literal object (*vyañjana*) is intended.
This is the meaning: here, in this simile, the quality required—such as purity (*pūtatva*) and so forth—is explicitly stated by the words "by her" (*tayā*) and so on;
it is not, however, an object standing in the place of a lamp according to the intention of a *dīpaka* (illuminator).
For first of all, there arises an understanding of the three meanings of the sentences beginning with "he is purified" through that [splendor], like a lamp with its great radiance; thereafter,

however, it is perceived that both "purification" and "adornment" follow upon the multiple instances consisting of the three similes such as the lamp and the subject of comparison, Mount Himavat— thus, *dīpaka* (the illuminator) enters here as a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).

In the case of the *mālopamā* (garland simile) where more than one attribute is employed, the connection of the attribute with both [the subject and the object] is clearly expressed; thus, there is no entry of the *dīpaka* (lamp-figure) as a suggested element (*vyaṅgya*). Therefore, it is called *mālopamā*.

Regarding the phrase "of such kinds" (*tathājātīnām*), he states "beauty," etc., explaining that the word *jāti* (kind) here refers to an adventitious property (*upādhi*) consisting in the possession of an excellence of beauty.
Now, one might object: this is indeed a different variety of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).

Furthermore, since there are other ornaments such as simile (upamā) and the like, how can it be established that they are included when the definition of "subordinated suggestion" (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya) has been formulated? To clarify this intention, he says: "yatkila... and so forth. The word "eṣām" means "of these," namely, of simile and the rest.
"Exempt from that" means devoid of the state of being a subordinate suggested meaning (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatā*).
"It should not be requested" means that it is of no use for the status of being an ornament (*alaṅkāra*); this is the intended sense.
To provide a justification for what was stated, he says: "For the comparison... and so forth. In this sūtra, *dvirvacana* (reduplication) refers to two meanings.
Regarding the word *tudī*:
for in the sūtra beginning with *tudī-śālā*, there is a connection according to the respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyena*).
In the case of *gām aśvam*, that [connection] is to be understood as being through a single action.
Regarding the rule *sthādhvoḥ*:
by this sūtra, one [form] is prescribed for two [roots].
All [these rules] are indicators (*jñāpaka*).

The intended meaning is that various technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) and so forth are understood from their respective words occurring within the sūtras. The phrase "not thus" implies "it makes known [this]."
In both cases, they are well-defined.

However, it is not possible to ascertain them in their true nature through a recitation of individual instances that lacks a general definition and merely describes the specific form of each one, because of their infinity.
For the varieties of verbal expression are infinite, and the poetic ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) are of precisely those same kinds.
According to the maxim "the eye is made level [with the forehead]," this is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), as in "The ocean is a water-pot" or "Vindhya grew tall and swallowed the path of the sun.
The same applies to other such cases.
Nor is this merely a poetic song;

rather, it is precisely the state of being a subordinate suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatā*) that constitutes the essential core of "ornamentality" (*alaṅkāratā*) here, as it has been characterized. He characterizes them well, such that by means of this [definition], they become fully defined and thus subsumed.
Otherwise, however, there would necessarily be a lack of pervasion (avyāpti). Thus he says: "of each one.

Furthermore, it is not possible for hyperbole (atiśayokti), indirect speech (vakrokti), simile (upamā), and so forth, to possess the nature of a general category if they were devoid of beauty (cārutā).
The general definition of "subordinate suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatva*) is precisely this: that beauty (*cārutā*) depends upon this [suggested meaning].

Furthermore, the beauty of the suggested meaning consists in its fitness for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), while the essence of *rasa* itself is the nature of bliss, being the very locus of repose. Thus, there is no infinite regress; this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Regarding the phrase "they are indeed infinite":
this has already been explained in the very first Uddyota within the passage beginning with "because of the infinity of verbal conceptualizations.
Now, one might object: in all poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), no other figure appears as the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
How then, O Bālapriya, can there be a discussion regarding "guṇībhūtavyaṅgya" (subordinate suggestion) and so forth?
This is clear to grammarians:
[the rule] "samudaḥ kuṇḍika."

The sense is that by taking the water-pot as the subject for the purpose of demonstrating an abundance of water and designating it as "the ocean," there is the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) in the form of identity despite difference.
In examples such as "the Vindhya [mountain]," it is *atiśayokti* in the form of a relation where no relation exists.
Concluding, he says: "In this way, other [cases] also," and so forth.
"Evamādi" means "the aforementioned examples and so forth.
"Iti" is used in the sense of a reason.

The explanation of the statement "all these are well-defined within the definition of the tallakṣaṇa" begins with the words "guṇībhūta," etc. "Yathā" (as) means "by way of being subordinated as a suggested meaning" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatayā*).
"Otherwise" means:

without the previously stated general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), there would be the mere statement of each respective specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*). However, in some manuscripts, the passage beginning with "For [comparison]... and ending with "...are included" is not seen.

Now, it might be objected that the general definition of all figures of speech (alaṅkāra) is simply the state of being a subordinated suggestion (guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatva), and thus the claim that they are well-defined by their own specific definitions is incorrect; for since hyperbole (atiśayokti) and the like constitute the very nature of the general category of figures of speech, they would have their purpose fulfilled by that [general] definition alone. To this, he says: "And not," and so forth.
The connection [of the sentence] is that it is not possible for figures such as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) to possess the nature of a "general" (*sāmānya*) if they are devoid of beauty (*cārutā*).
To this, he asks, "What follows from that? and replies with the words beginning "beauty," etc., [stating]: "dependent upon this."
The meaning is that [the beauty of the poem] depends on the state of being *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is subordinate).

Now, one might object: "The beauty of the *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* must itself be explained as being caused by the beauty of the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*); but that [beauty of the figure] too would be caused by something else, and that too by something else—thus there would be the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To this, he says: "Of the suggested meaning," and so forth. Having raised an objection to the statement "all these are well-defined" made in the definition [of *dhvani*], he introduces the subsequent passage with the intent of providing its resolution, beginning with "Now, one might object," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in all [cases]":

while it shines forth in some instances such as the *dīpaka* and so on, it is indeed the domain of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) as well, even by way of another mode characterized by the pursuit of a suggested meaning through *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis) and other figures.
Therefore, this second type of subject matter of great poets, which is an outflow of *dhvani*, is exceedingly beautiful and should be defined by connoisseurs.
"In no way at all is there a comprehensive inclusion of all poetry that captivates the hearts of the sensitive (sahr̥daya) by means of what has been characterized [in the *Locana*].

Do not say so; for either a mere matter (*vastumātra*) or a rasa will be the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) while being subordinate (*guṇībhūta*). He says this very thing: "And of the subordinate-suggested" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyasya ca*). That is, of that which is characterized by another mode, namely, by the nature of a matter or a rasa.

Or, if this is the introduction: "Now, if figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) have been characterized by means of 'subordinate suggestion' (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), then their definition must be stated; why has it not been mentioned? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By subordinate [suggestion]," etc.

"The state of being an object" (*viṣayatvam*) means the state of being that which is to be characterized (*lakṣaṇīyatvam*). By what is there the state of being characterized? The meaning is: by that very definition which is the mode other than *dhvani* called the "pursuit of meaning as suggestiveness" (*vyaṅgyatvena arthānugama*).
The intended meaning is: since the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) has been characterized and its subordination (*guṇībhāva*) has been examined, what else remains for it to be defined?
Having thus established that "Suggestion (*dhvani*) is the soul of poetry," he concludes with the passage beginning with "Therefore, this... and ending with "...good fortune. This is the sense.
*Bālapriyā*: [This indicates] that it is not so.
"How is that so? and so forth.
The sense is that it is not a defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*) because it is not all-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).

In the expression "the state of having a subordinate suggested meaning" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatva*), by the word "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*), one does not intend to refer merely to a poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).
However, he says "not so," etc., to show that this [definition] is not non-pervasive because of the presence of things such as *vastu* (matter-of-fact description) and *rasa* (sentiment).
The meaning is: "or merely a thing" (*vastumātra*) refers to those instances where, in the case of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) does not shine forth.
The phrase "by means of that which has as its characteristic the following of the suggested meaning" is explained by the sense of the words "the suggested [meaning] will become subordinate.
The "following of the meaning" by way of being suggested is its state of subordination (*guṇabhāva*) with respect to the expressed (*vācya*).
That is the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), meaning either the unique property or the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that other mode [of poetry]; such is the meaning of the compound.
He states "by another way" (*prakārāntareṇa*) as an indication (*upalakṣaṇe*), using the instrumental case; thus he says "of that which is indicated" (*upalakṣitasya*).

This is a qualifier for "of that in which the suggested meaning is subordinate" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyasya*); and its meaning is: "of a subordinate suggested meaning that is any one among [the categories of] fact (*vastu*), aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), or poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*)."
The connection is with the words "the state of being an object (viṣayatva) certainly exists.

The phrase "in the case of ornaments" (alaṅkāreṣu) is to be supplied by modification. Thinking that the aforementioned composition of the work is something to be accomplished through great effort, he says "or else" (yadi vā), etc., by way of another alternative.
"Are perceived" (*lakṣitāḥ*): the word "might be" (*bhaveyuḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Of that [type of poetry], namely, that in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).

Because it is stated "by means of a definition" (lakṣaṇena), the meaning that "the state of being an object" (viṣayatva) implies "the state of being definable" (lakṣaṇīyatva) is established; thus he says: "the state of being definable. The phrase "in what manner is it definable? serves as the introduction to the alternative formulation [expressed by] "by another way" (prakārāntareṇa).
[The term] "distinct from sound" (dhvanivyatirikta) [is used].
The distinction is that previously [the classification] was in relation to *alaṅkāras* (figures of speech), whereas now it is in relation to *dhvani* (suggestion).
"Following the meaning" (*arthānugama*) means existing in a subordinate state (*guṇībhāva*) with respect to the expressed sense (*vācya*).
A "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*).
Now, one might object: "This definition was not stated previously; therefore, how can it be mentioned here as if it were already established? To this, he says: "The suggested" (*vyaṅgya*), etc.

The meaning is that the definition of the suggested has indeed already been stated in the first chapter (*udyota*) by the passage beginning with "where there is the connection of the suggested," and the state of being subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) has also been determined therein.
He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the conclusion beginning with "Therefore, this... by showing the specific nature of the matter to be concluded:
"having brought it to completion" means having fully accomplished it;
"the manner" refers to that which possesses beauty through its contact with the implied meaning.
Therefore, this supreme secret of poetry should be contemplated by the wise:
"Even for the words of great poets that bear ornaments, this suggested shadow is the primary ornament, just as modesty is for women. (Dhvanyāloka 3.37)
This suggested meaning (pratīyamāna) is the primary ornament even for the words of great poets that already possess formal ornaments; it is like modesty is for women. (37)
By this [work], even a well-known subject matter is endowed with a certain degree of loveliness.

To show that what was stated previously—that it constitutes the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of all the poetry of true poets—is not to be regarded as mere deception or as a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), [the author says]: "This very [work]... (3.6).
"Ornament is primary" means that even for those who bear ornaments, provided they are devoid of verbal figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*),
there is a radiance or beauty produced by what is implied (*pratīyamāna*).

The meaning is that Bhīma’s intention was directed toward the fact that the path of peace favored by Yudhiṣṭhira was intolerable—that is, its unacceptability.
This is expressed by the phrase beginning with "iti" and so forth.

The intended meaning is this: it is not the case that there is first the cognition of the negation of churning and so forth—such as "I do not churn"—and only later the cognition of the negation of that negation—such as "I indeed churn"; rather, at the very moment of utterance, by the force of the *kāku* (intonation), there arises a cognition in the form "It is not that I do not [churn]" (*na na mathnāmi*), wherein the negation of churning and so forth functions precisely as the counter-positive of that negation. Therefore, the negation of the expressed negation of churning and so forth is indeed suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
In this context, he addresses the Mīmāṃsaka with the words beginning "darśa" and so forth.

The word *darśa* is applied to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) based on the etymological derivation that "the moon is not seen here. Thus, the point is that in this instance, there is an indirect indication (*viparītalakṣaṇā*) of the absence of seeing from the verbal root *dṛś*.
This is clear in the commentary on the Śrautasūtra, [3.8].
Regarding the term "confused subject matter":

where it is impossible from the very outset to establish a restriction to either one [of two alternatives], and where there is an investigation of reasoning (*yukti*), one should apply a designation based on that which possesses the assistance of reasoning.
One should not be a lover of "suggestion" (*dhvani*) in every instance.
For example: "Touch the crescent moon on your husband's head with this," said a friend jokingly;
having dyed her feet and received the blessing, she struck her with silence.
"Her husband's eye"—by this [it is meant]:

for the moon, when stained by lac, attains its superior luster [only] through incessant falling at his feet and acts of propitiation; and thus it is taught that a woman who wishes to follow her husband's will immediately must be one who acts accordingly.
By saying "she even treats with contempt that digit of the moon borne upon her head," the defeat of the world of rival wives is expressed.
Regarding the term *nirvacana*:

although by this [statement] such things as shame, dissimulation, joy, envy, trepidation, pride in one's good fortune, and so forth are suggested (*dhvanyate*), [the primary function remains denotation].

Nevertheless, it merely serves as an embellishment for the meaning of the etymological word, which is characterized by being unfamiliar to young maidens; yet, when thus embellished, that meaning attains the status of an auxiliary to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). [The phrase] "without him" means "without that object."
Since the category of "reason" (*yukti*) as accepted by the logicians is impossible here, he explains that term with the words beginning "beauty" (*cārutva*), etc.
Here, in the context of investigating the true nature of the meaning of poetry,
if that attainment of mental wonder arises from the expressed meaning (*vācya*) alone, as embellished by the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), [then...]

The meaning is this: when the suggested sense is subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), it is so; but when the expressed sense is eclipsed by the suggested sense alone, then it is *dhvani*. Thus, the determination of either one of these two states is established solely through the force of the effect, which is the perception of beauty. With the word "touch" (*spṛśa*) as the end, he shows the two meanings being manifested—beginning with "alaktaka" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "attaining a superior state":
the sense is that this is due to the moon's extreme whiteness and the lac's redness.

Having stated the suggestion arising from the specific qualifying attribute of being stained by lac, he describes the suggestion conveyed by the act of touching the head with the foot—beginning with "uninterrupted," and so forth.
"Bhaktaṭi" means by the force of compulsion arising from the power of innate and unsurpassed passion (*rāga*).

By means of the feminine gender indication, which is assisted by the qualification "having the head as its locus," he expresses the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) with the words "held by the head" (*śīrodhṛtā*), and so forth.

"Is stated" means "is manifested. By the commentary passage beginning with "the definition," he demonstrates the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) and its subordinate status (*guṇībhāva*), [introducing this] with the words "by this," and so forth.
By this [statement], "he struck with a definition," the word "that" means the collection of things manifested by shame and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "fit for a maiden":
by this, the suitability of the expressed meaning (vācyārtha) to produce aesthetic charm (camatkāra) is demonstrated.
As for the phrase "the meaning is refined" (upaskṛta): [this refers to its being embellished].
The meaning is that the expressed sense (vācyārtha)—namely, "he struck [him] inexpressibly"—is embellished by the suggested sense (vyangya) already mentioned.
Regarding the term *śṛṅgāra*: it means *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment of separation).

Intending that the word *uccais* means "situated in a high place" and functions as an adjective qualifying the flowers, he explains it with the words "those which are high" (*uccairyāni*), and so forth.

And as follows: "When the proud woman was presented by her lover with flowers from the lineage of his rival, she said nothing at all; with eyes clouded by tears, she merely scratched the ground with her foot."

In this context, because the suggested meaning is expressed through negation—by saying "he struck [her] with a retort" or "he said nothing"—it is appropriate that its status as a subordinate element (guṇībhāva) alone prevails, since it has been made into an object to some extent.
When the suggested meaning is understood primarily without the use of indirect expression (vakrokti), then it possesses predominance (prādhānya).
As, for example, in the verse beginning "While the divine sage was speaking thus... and so forth.
Furthermore, since there is repetition here by way of a stylistic turn (*bhaṅgī*), the expressed meaning (*vācya*) also possesses primacy.
Therefore, the designation of *dhvani*—in which the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*)—should not be applied here.
Thus says the *Locana*: "He bestowed [it]."

"Highly" (*uccaiḥ*) means those flowers which were plucked by the beloved herself because they were impossible for her to reach; our teacher (*upādhyāya*), however, [explains] that "highly" refers to the most heart-pleasing flowers. *Amuke* [is used here].
"Take it, take it!"—thus he spoke in a loud, resonant voice to show his extreme eagerness while offering it;
for this very reason, she was "caused to receive" it.
"Nothing at all"—this refers to [the fact that]...

In such occasions of love-making, it is not appropriate here to merely display indignation by thinking, "He remembers only her"; rather, the intended suggestion (vyaṅgya) is an extraordinary accumulation of resentment, which serves as the refinement (saṃskāra) of the expressed prohibition itself.
As he will say later: "There is a statement through a particular turn of phrase."
"Of that" refers to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
"In this [context]" refers to instances such as *patyuḥ* (of the husband).
"Even of the expressed meaning" (*vācyasyāpi*) refers to the literal sense.
The word "api" (also/even) is displaced [in the sentence];
it qualifies the word "dhvani" (sound/resonance). //39//
The *Bālapriyā* explains what is suggested by this qualification, beginning with "by the beloved" (*kāntayā*).

It states that its own intended meaning is that the word *uccais* signifies a high-pitched tone (*tārasvara*) and functions as an adverbial qualifier for the act of giving; thus it says "our," and so forth.
[It refers to] "so-and-so."
"Into a vessel such as the palm of the hand" is the meaning;
this is connected with the word "flowers. The explanation of "loudly" is "with a high-pitched voice."
He says "ādara... to indicate that the loud voice is intended to manifest an excess of respect toward the offering of flowers.
He provides the subsequent phrase beginning with "ata eva" to reinforce the consistency of the stated meaning;
"ata eva" means precisely because of the offering of flowers with a loud voice.
Showing the purpose of the phrase "he said nothing," he states the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) with the words beginning "in such cases" and so forth.
"The indication of pride" means that it occurs through the medium of the consequent emotional state (anubhāva), such as the rolling of the eyes.
The word "that" (tat) means that the suggested sense, by virtue of being an embellishment of the expressed sense, functions as if it were itself the expressed; this is the meaning.
The phrase "the order is reversed" (bhinnakrama) refers to this.
The sense is that otherwise there would be a contradiction. "Qualifier" means the qualifier such as "resonance" (*anuraṇana*) and so forth.

The sense is that the qualifying term [‘suggestion’] indicates that the nature of *dhvani* characterized by imperceptible sequential suggestion (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgyadhvani*) exists here as well. // 3.9 //

This type, although it is of the nature of *guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), nevertheless assumes the form of *dhvani* (suggestion) through a thorough consideration of its ultimate intent (*tātparya*) toward rasa and the like. (Dhvanyāloka 3.40)

Furthermore, this type, although it is of the nature of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), assumes the form of *dhvani* (suggestion) through a thorough consideration of its ultimate intent (*tātparya*) regarding rasa and the like. (40)

Even a type of poetry where the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) becomes *dhvani* itself when one considers its ultimate intent to be the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotion (*bhāva*), and so forth—as in the two verses just cited above, and as in the following:
"O fortunate one, Rādhā is difficult to propitiate; for even this tear of yours has fallen upon her, who is the mistress of your life and whose garment is being scorched by this very [fire]."
"This very [work] is the *Locana*":

the meaning is that it is precisely that which was indicated when it was stated in the aphorism (*sūtra*) that the "suggested meaning as subordinate" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) takes the form of *dhvani* consisting of rasa and so forth.
"Of equal luster" means:

In the case of *patyuḥ* and so forth, as well as *prayacchata* and so forth, since it is understood that the suffix denoting the abstract action (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*) serves to embellish the expressed meaning in the form of a prohibition, those two possess an equal luster (*tulyacchāyatva*).
Regarding the verse beginning with *durārādha*:

"O fortunate one! Since this fallen tear is being wiped away by you even with this [your own] life-force, wealth, and garment, Rādhā is difficult to propitiate; the heart of a woman is hard, so enough with these formal courtesies."
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O you who have desisted from [worldly] entreaties, may Hari, thus addressed, bring about your welfare.
Intending to explain the verse (*śloka*), he prepares the introductory framework (*pīṭhikā*) with the words beginning "without cause" (*akāraṇa*).
He indicates the collection of meanings suggested by the words contained in the verse, beginning with "O fortunate one" (*subhage*) and so forth.
Regarding the word "he" (*yaḥ*),
the word "you" (*tvam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"It is not possible," thus [he spoke];
the meaning is that Rādhā’s intention was revealed in this way.
The word "was manifested" (vyajyata) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The same should be understood for what follows as well.
He states another suggested meaning: "And that very [same thing]"—the word "this" is to be supplied here.
He clarifies this [statement] "thus honored" with the words beginning "that which...

By using the present-tense suffix in the word *mṛjataḥ* ("he cleanses"), he expresses the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) through the statement of the non-cessation of cleansing—namely, with the words beginning "for by this, on the contrary...
He states the suggested meaning of the verbal root portion (*prakṛti*) with the words beginning "and this much..."
"Māmita" means "even me standing before you";
the word "manyase" (you think) is also connected here.
"The heart of a woman is hard; enough with these formalities, desist!"—thus addressed, Hari spoke these auspicious words of conciliation to you.
"O Locanā, since you have forgotten me, you consider her alone to be angry;
otherwise, how could you act in such a way?
[She is] fallen."
The meaning is that even the opportunity for weeping has now passed.
If it is asked, "Even with such devotion as this, why do you not relinquish your anger?", what can be done? The heart of a woman is hard by nature.
For the term "woman" refers merely to a specific object, since it lacks [qualities such as] love and the like;
and this is its very nature:

that women possess tender hearts. Thus, there is nothing in their hearts more adamantine than this, such that even upon the direct perception of such an event, they do not shatter into a thousand pieces.
"By means of attentions" means those employed out of courtesy.

By the use of the plural "in entreaties," it is stated that for this man who has many favorites, this very state of affairs persists again and again, thereby expressing the excellence of his good fortune.
In this way, this garden of suggested meanings (vyaṅgyārtha) adorns the expressed meaning (vācya);
for that expressed meaning, once adorned, attains the status of being a constituent part of the erotic-in-separation through jealousy (īrṣyā-vipralambha).
As for the one who explained in all three verses that it is only the suggested meaning that serves as a constituent of rasa—
He sold the deity and performed that festival procession;
for in this way, the very state of being subordinate (guṇībhūtatā) which was intended for the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) would be utterly destroyed at its root.

For the suggested meaning, when distinct from rasa and the like, possesses only the quality of being a constituent part of rasa. Thus, by using the past tense in the word "patita" (fallen), he indicates the suggested meaning through the words "gata" (gone) and so forth.
Intending to explain the passage beginning with "harsh" (*kaṭhora*), he says "if," and so forth.
After the word "you release" (*muñcasi*), the word "thus" (*iti*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The connection is that [the statement] "if" refers to what is being said.
In that case, he states that this very [object] is indicated by the word "woman"—namely, "love and so forth.
The connection is: "for this [word] 'woman' is [this]."
"‘This’ means ‘hard-heartedness.
Having thus stated the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) directed toward the person to be enlightened, he states the suggested meaning residing in Rādhā, beginning with ‘ātmani’ and so forth."
"And this in the self" means that what is about to be stated is the suggested meaning residing in Rādhā. "Thus" (iti) [indicates the end of the citation].
The meaning is "it is thus";
"nothing at all" means that which is not ultimate reality.

He states that the aforementioned class of suggested meanings (vyaṅgya) serves as a subordinate element (aṅga) both with respect to the expressed meaning (vācya) and with respect to the aesthetic flavor (rasa), beginning with the words "In this way" (evam).
He restates another interpretation, beginning with the words "But he who," and so on,
[concluding with] "only of that which is being perceived" (pratīyamānasyaiva).
By the particle *eva*, there is the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of the expressed meaning as it is perceived or as it is embellished.
He explains [the passage] with the words "he explained" (*vyācaṣṭe sma*).
The intention of this commentator is as follows: for that which is primary or principal, such subordination (*guṇībhāva*) is indeed improper.
He shows by way of a sarcastic remark that this explanation—that the rasa alone is the primary element—is not the best, with the words "sa devam" and so forth.

Just as someone, out of poverty, might sell a deity to acquire wealth and then begin to perform a festival procession for it, so too has this author, having set out to establish the *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), resorted to a certain method that contradicts it; thus, his "great skill" is a subject of derision.
To the question, "How could this be severed?", he says: "rasādi" and so forth.
This refers to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), consisting of either a matter (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), which is distinct from rasa and the like.
[He then says] "rasāṅga" and so forth.

The meaning is this: since rasa and the like, whose sole nature is suggestible (vyaṅgya), possess primacy by their very own nature, whereas anything distinct from them possesses it only as a subordinate element (aṅga) to them; therefore, when that [other element] becomes a subordinate element to them, its primacy itself follows, and not its status as a subordinate quality (guṇatva).

This being the case, although the words specified in the verse beginning with "Indeed, this very [insult]" (*anyakkāro hyayameva*) convey a denoted meaning qualified by a suggested sense, their status as suggestors (*vyañjakatva*) is stated in relation to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that constitutes the meaning of this entire sentence; one should not entertain the misconception that these words constitute *arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya* dhvani, for their denoted meanings are intended (*vivakṣita*).

For in those cases, it is the expressed meaning that is perceived as being qualified by the suggested meaning, rather than the expressed meaning having been transformed into the form of the suggested.
Therefore, in such instances, the sentence constitutes *dhvani*,
while the individual words are instances of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).

Furthermore, it is not only words that possess subordinate suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) which are manifestors of *dhvani* with imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgya*), but even those forms of *dhvani* where the literal meaning is transferred to another sense (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*).
For example, in this very verse, the word "Rāvaṇa" functions as a manifestor in the form of another variety of *dhvani*.

However, in a sentence where there is no primary intent toward rasa and so forth, even if such meanings are brought to light by words possessing subordinate suggestion, the status of being "subordinate-suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatā*) remains the property of the whole.
For example: "Skilled men indeed serve even a king, consume even poison, and take pleasure with women."
"Locana" means preeminence; there is nothing else [of such importance], so enough with this dispute regarding the predecessors.
"Thus established" means that when the distinction between *dhvani* and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* has been established in the manner just described.
In order to explain the word "api" (also/even) found in the *kārikā*, he says: "And not...
This verse has already been explained previously, so it is not written again here. As for the phrase "But where... [the following applies].

Although there is here a perception of the sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*) consisting of world-weariness toward objects, nevertheless, this aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) resides solely in the expressed meaning (*vācyaniṣṭha*).

As for the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), such as its improbability or its contrary effects, it is subordinate to the expressed; therefore, the sense is that its status as a subordinate element must be stated only with respect to the expressed meaning.
In the commentary, the words "of the words" (*padānām*) and so forth appear.
The suggested meanings (*vyaṅgyārtha*) have been explained previously.
[The phrase] "in the rasa that has become the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthībhūtarase*) [is used].
The meaning is "the sentiment of wrath" (*raudrarasa*).
He states "not for them," etc., as an incidental remark.
To dispel the suspicion that the passage beginning with "nor merely" is not based on the sūtra, he says in the *Locana*: "the kārikā," etc.

Regarding the word "api" (also) in the phrase "guṇībhūtavyaṅgyo 'pi": the sense is that the word "api" serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. Thus, it means "to explain [the term] 'api'."
One might object: "How can there be an absence of intent toward rasa and so forth in passages such as 'the king' (*rājānam*)?

Since all worldly activity—characterized by service to a king and the like—is equivalent to consuming poison and produces a distaste for its objects, it must suggest the *śāntarasa* (the sentiment of tranquility). Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*), etc.
"This" means that which is experienced by those possessed of aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*).
"Residing in the expressed meaning" (*vācyārthaniṣṭha*) means...

The meaning is that because even kings and others perform service and so forth [for them], therefore humans are called "skilled" (kuśala); this is the sense of the word's application to its literal meaning (*vācyārtha*).
This occurs in such passages as the above.
A supreme effort must be exerted in distinguishing between the predominance and subordination of the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya),

so that the respective domains of *dhvani*, *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*, and poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) may be clearly understood without confusion. Otherwise, however, delusion persists even regarding the well-known domains of the poetic figures themselves.

For example: "The eye follows that very [object]," where the word *api* is joined on both sides, the word *ca* is joined to the three positions, and the word *mānava* is touched by the word *khalu* joined on both sides; thus, it becomes subordinate (*guṇībhūta*).
He shows that this perception of distinction is not useless by saying: "of the expressed and the suggested."
And regarding the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*):
where there is no suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) at all, those [ornaments] in their pure form possess predominance.
"Otherwise" means...
The meaning is: "if it is not brought about by one who exerts effort.

The intention of the particle *eva* (only) is that the type of suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyaprakāra*) which was previously conjectured by me is undoubtedly a ground for delusion. By the particle *eva*, the exclusion of its being restricted solely to the sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*) is indicated.

But even so, does not the impossibility of serving a king and the like being suggested here, and is it not from that very fact that the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) arises? To this, he says: "The suggested meaning," and so forth.
[He explains] "contrary" (*viparīta*).
The meaning is "having a result contrary to the stated result.
"Of that very [thing]" means "of the expressed object itself. "An attendant" (anuyāyin) means...
The meaning is "it is a constituent part" (aṅga).
He establishes that very point by demonstrating the reason—starting with "And that," and so forth.
The connection is: "And that [is] indeed touched."
"By both being joined" means:

they serve even a king and they consume even poison; thus, it means by both being joined through action (*karman*) and activity (*kriyā*). A king, for his part, is one who is consecrated (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*) over things that are difficult to approach, and he is the locus of action.
Because the service activity involves dangers that arise at every moment, it is difficult to carry out even for those whose minds are concentrated;
this should be understood in other cases as well by means of the word "ca" (and) joined to the three locations.
The meaning is that, according to the maxim "one illuminator [applies] to many as the last," the particle *ca*, which has the sense of conjunction, is to be joined with all three verbs.
By the phrase "by the word *khalu* joined on both sides," it is meant that the word *khalu* is to be connected with both the word *kuśala* and the word *mānava*.
The construction is with the word "mānava" (human).
"Touched" means slightly illuminated.
The word "iti" indicates the reason.
To the question, "What is the non-overlapping domain of the figures of speech? he says: "Where," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of them":
The meaning is "of the ornaments.

By means of the particle *eva* ("only"), he shows the sense that [these ornaments] apply only to the domain of well-known ornaments, let alone to the domain of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*), as he says: "But the variety of the suggested," and so forth.
"Imagined" (*utprekṣita*) means shown after having been imagined.
The state of being an occasion for delusion is the state of being an object of delusion.
He demonstrates the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) of the words contained in the cited verse, beginning with "wealth" (*draviṇa*): "by the word 'wealth'... and so forth.
The meaning is: by superimposing the nature of wealth (*draviṇatva*) upon beauty (*lāvaṇya*). "It has been stated" means: it has been manifested by beauty.
By using the word "gaṇita" (calculated) instead of "vidita" (known), he expresses a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), namely: "after a long time," and so forth.
The word "tatra" means "in such an expenditure."
"Ananta" means:
even for those who perform emanations—that is, the creation of extremely subtle forms—over an infinite and boundless time;
the expenditure of the wealth of beauty was not reckoned, great suffering was accepted, and the fire of anxiety was kindled for people living according to their own will.
This poor girl too has been destroyed by the very lack of a husband equal to herself; what purpose did the Creator have in mind when he fashioned her slender form?

Regarding this, the claim made by someone that the poetic figure (alaṅkāra) is *vyājastuti* (feigned praise) is not clever; for if this subject matter were to terminate merely in the nature of that poetic figure, there would be no elegance [of expression].
This is because this is certainly not the thought of some passionate person.
For such a statement as "this poor woman too is ruined because she lacks a lover as charming as he" would be logically inconsistent for him.
Nor could it apply to one who is free from passion (*nīrāga*);
by the word "wealth" (*draviṇa*), it is expressed that [the eye] is like his entire possession and is cherished through many of his own activities.
Regarding the term "calculation":

for that expenditure which is accomplished over a long duration and not instantaneously like a flash of lightning, there must necessarily be calculation. However, since not even a trace of discernment arose in the Creator, who fashions the infinite expanse of time, his lack of foresight is supreme.
For this very reason, he says: "The affliction is great. Regarding the term *svacchandasya*, it means "of one who is unrestrained."
"Even this" means that what is created by oneself is the very same thing that is destroyed; thus, the word "even" (*api*) and the syllable *va* express a great calamity.
What is the meaning?
The meaning is: not for oneself, nor for the world, nor for a created being.
Regarding the word "his":
for one possessed by passion, there follows speech embraced by wretchedness—such as "Alas, she is ruined"—which is struck by inauspiciousness and followed by lamentation.
"Because there was no woman of equal beauty"—this means that she did not appear; the sense is that it was because of her lack of consideration for this rule.
Of this injunction.
"Lack of circumspection" means acting without deliberation;
the word "stated" is to be supplied [to complete the sentence].
He provides the reason for this—namely, the phrase beginning with "for this very reason"—when he intends to express the absence of both emanation (*nirmāṇa*) and suddenness (*jhāṭiti*).

When one examines the meaning of any single one among the three [meanings] stated in the three quarters [of the verse], no suitable purpose is observed; thus he says, "Not for its own self," and so forth.
The word "meaning" (*artha*) is to be supplied [from the previous context].
In the commentary, it is stated that the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is "Praise by Disguise" (*vyājastuti*).
The sense is that the heroine's praise is perceived through the medium of censure.
Regarding the phrase "not well-knit" (*na suśliṣṭatā*): it means there is no perfect coherence.
He states the reason for this with the words "since," and so forth.
The word "this" means that which was stated in the verse.
‘Vikalpa’ refers to the object of various conceptual constructions.
He states the reason for the negation [of such a construction] with the words ‘tasya’ and so forth.
To explain how it is that for one possessed of passion (rāgin) such a statement is untenable, he establishes this in the *Locana* with the words ‘rāgiṇo hi’ and so forth.

The connection is as follows: the words "wretched" (varākī), which signify being embraced by misery, and "stricken" (hatā), which signify being afflicted by inauspiciousness, are indeed inappropriate for one possessed of passion (*rāgin*). For how could one whose mental state is immersed in that [object], who holds her alone in high esteem, and who relishes the nectar of the exquisite beauty of her form, ever contemplate her wretchedness or inauspiciousness? This is the intended meaning.
"Because there is no equal object of pleasure," etc.; this is the statement of one who possesses passion (*rāgin*), as the phrase "of one who possesses passion" is to be supplied.
"In oneself," etc.
The eye [directed] toward one's own self is utterly improper for the self;
if even regarding oneself there were an impossibility of such a form or a state of passion, one would be no different from a beast.
But surely, even for one who is passionate, or for one like Rāvaṇa who has undertaken a vow for a certain period of time for some particular reason—
