means "What is the report? The syntactical connection is that [the author] speaks by means of two verses.

Since the distinction is established merely by showing this division, the classification of poetry is presented on an equal footing as *śabdacitra* (verbal artistry) and *vācyacitra* (artistry of the expressed). When the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is predominant, it is the type of poetry known as *dhvani*; when it is subordinate, however, it is *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (poetry where the suggestion is subordinated).

Other than these, there is poetry that lacks intent toward rasa, bhāva, and so forth, and is devoid of the power to manifest any particular suggested meaning; composed solely by relying on the variety of the expressed and the expressive, it is comparable to a painting.
That which merely appears [like poetry] is a painting;
it is not primary poetry,
for it is merely an imitation of poetry.
In this regard, "verbal ornament" (*śabdacitra*) refers to such things as difficult feats (*duṣkara*) and *yamaka* (rhyme).

"Verbal-ornamented" (*vācyacitra*) is that which is other than verbal ornament; it is devoid of contact with a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), exists primarily as the sentence-meaning itself, and is devoid of intent toward rasa and so forth—such as poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) and the like.
Now, what is this that is called "ornament" (*citram*)?
Where there is no contact with a suggested meaning—
since the threefold nature of the suggested meaning has already been demonstrated previously—
that indeed is the domain for those who would conceive of *citra* (the pictorial) poetry, wherein no other suggested matter (*vastu*) or ornament (*alaṅkāra*) exists.
However, that variety of poetry in which rasa and the like are not the objects of apprehension is simply impossible;
for it is not tenable that poetry should lack contact with reality (vastu).
And every single thing existing in the world necessarily becomes a constituent of some rasa or bhāva, at least by way of being a determinative factor (vibhāva).

For rasa and the like are indeed specific modifications of mental activity (cittavṛtti), and there is no object whatsoever that does not produce a specific modification of mental activity; or, if it does not produce one, it should be understood as being equal to a mere visual object, such as a painting— this is the sense of the phrase "resembling a painting" (ālekhyaprakhya).
The meaning is that it is devoid of the vital principle (*jīva*) of taste and so forth, and consists of the primary form and its representation.
Now, regarding the objection "What is this?", the intended meaning will be stated below. The answer to this is: "Where [it is] not."
The objector shows his own intention by saying "is perceived" and "not touching upon a real entity.
The meaning is that it is either meaningless, like the sounds *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa* and so forth, or its meaning is incoherent, like the phrase "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*) and so forth.
He states the intention behind the use of the term "bālapriyā" (dear to children) with the words beginning with "yamaka," etc.
The word "bandhādi" (composition, etc. is a separate word.
[The phrase] "is indeed well-known" means:

The meaning is that since forms such as *yamaka* (paronomasia) consist of specific arrangements of syllables, their status as "pictures" (*citra*) has indeed been determined by those who know the science of poetics (*alaṃkāra*).
To the question of what the basis for their being like a painting is, he says: "Because of rasa and so forth," and "primarily," etc.
The meaning is that it is an imitation of *dhvani* by virtue of possessing beauty created through qualities (*guṇas*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāras*).
To show the reason for the objection "What is this?", he says "to be explained" (*vakṣyamāṇa*).
He explains the term "non-contact with reality" (*avastusaṃsparśitā*) in two ways, beginning with "ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa, etc. (*kacaṭatapādītyādi*).
"Let it not be so.

The meaning is that it is appropriate for only *dhvani* (suggestion) and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) to be the domain of the poet. He clarifies this intention with the words beginning "In poetry," and so forth.
"It is not designated [as poetry]" means that its essence is not primary poetry, because of the statement: "for this is a mere imitation of poetry.
The word "this" (asau) refers to that.
The meaning is that it is an object of poetry (*kāvya*).
It would not even be an object of poetry if it were not described as something possessing poetic quality (*citratayā*); yet, some such thing is indeed delineated as an object of poetry.
To this, it is replied: True, there is no such variety of poetry in which the *rāsa* and other [rasas] are not perceived.

However, when a poet composes a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) or a semantic ornament (*arthālaṅkāra*) devoid of the intention to convey rasa, bhāva, and so forth, then, with respect to that intention, the meaning is considered to be devoid of rasa and the like;

for in poetry, the meaning of words is precisely that which has ascended to the poet’s intention. And by the power of the expressive capacity [of the words], even in the absence of the poet’s intention, the perception of rasa and the like occurs in such a case, though it is extremely weak. [Objection: "But surely, let it not be the domain of the poet! Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And it is the domain of the poet... (*locana*).

Although it has not been explicitly designated as having the form of poetry (*kāvya*), it must nevertheless be understood as being within the scope of the poet; for it is improper to mention anything else here that would be equivalent to the account of Vāsuki. And if it is indeed within the scope of the poet, then surely delight must be produced by it;
and that [delight] necessarily culminates in the *vibhāvas*, *anubhāvas*, and *vyabhicāribhāvas*—this is the intended meaning. As for the word "but" (*kiṃ tu*): [it introduces the following point].

The meaning is that when one does not follow the method of examination stated at the beginning— namely, that [the *alaṅkāra*] exists through the speaker’s intention being directed toward it, and never as a primary element (*aṅgin*)—
then there is an absence of rasa and so forth.
In that case, there is no apprehension of rasa at all, as in the case of a particular preparation of meat cooked by a cook who is ignorant of culinary arts.

Anticipating the objection—"But surely, due to the inherent beauty of the subject matter, such a savor must sometimes arise even in a *śikhariṇī* verse composed by one unskilled [in poetry]," he says "vācye" and so forth.
By this [statement], he means: "even by this [poet]."
Previously, its emptiness in every respect was stated; now, it is stated "of another" (*anyasya*). This means "of that which is other than what has been made the object of the poet's vision.
[It refers to] "that which is equal to the account of Vāsuki."

The meaning is "of that which is not the primary subject. Now, let it be granted that [the object] falls within the scope of the poet; what follows from that? To this he says: "And of the poet," and so forth.
As it has been said: "This is the very nature of objects, that they are not [perceived] by him directly in such a manner."
They are savored as they come within the range of the words of a true poet.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Granted that there is the quality of producing delight, even so, how is the absence of being devoid of aesthetic flavor (rasa) and so forth established? To this, he says: "And that," and so forth.
The sense is that the specific pleasure produced by poetry is invariably based solely on the relish of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "But rather" (*kiṃtu*) as follows: "the intention to speak," etc.
[He says] "when it does not follow," etc.
The sense is that, in accordance with that [principle], the very application of figures of speech constitutes their status as being subservient to rasa.
He states this point with an illustration, beginning with "not at all," etc.;
the word "therein" refers to that context.
The meaning is: in a case where an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is composed without following the method of examination that has been stated. Regarding the phrase "the perception of *rasa*":
by the word *rasa*, both the erotic and other sentiments (*śṛṅgārādi*) as well as aesthetic flavors such as the sweet (*madhurādi*) are intended.
"Tathāsvāda" means the tasting of flavor (rasāsvāda).
"As if in a *śikhariṇī* [verse]" means as if in a poem composed in the *śikhariṇī* meter.
*Śikhariṇī* is a specific kind of food mixed with curd and other ingredients.
By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even by this," he explains the meaning of that term, beginning with "previously," etc.
Its emptiness is the emptiness of flavor (*rasa*).
Regarding the term "weakness":
the phrase "of the relish for flavor" is to be supplied as the remainder.
By the word "becomes," the object of the painting is established by imagining it to be devoid of flavor in this manner.

This has been stated as follows: "When there is an absence of the intention to express [the aesthetic] flavor (rasa), emotion (bhāva), and so forth, that composition of ornaments (alaṅkāra) is considered to have the 'picture' (citra) as its domain."
But when there is an intention to express rasa and so forth, which possesses *tātparya*,
then that poetry does not exist at all where it is not within the scope of *dhvani*.

And this [distinction] has been postulated by us because we observe that for poets whose speech is unrestrained, there is an engagement in poetry even without regard for the primary intent of rasa and so forth.
However, when the proper system of poetics is being established for contemporary times, there is indeed no variety of poetry apart from *dhvani*.
For the literary activity of mature poets does not shine at all in the absence of an intent directed toward rasa and the like.
And when there is an intent toward rasa and so forth, there is simply no such thing as an element that, being brought into the service of a desired rasa, does not become effective.

For even insentient entities—whether by virtue of being appropriate excitants (*vibhāva*) of a rasa or through their association with the activities of sentient beings—are certainly not non-existent insofar as they do not become constituent parts of a rasa.
Thus it is said: "But [the word] 'also' (*api*) has the sense of 'even weakness' (*daurbalyam*)," according to the *Locana*.

And regarding a *śikhariṇī* verse composed by one who is ignorant, alas, there is no aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) arising from the knowledge that it is a *śikhariṇī*; rather, people say, "This is curd, jaggery, and black pepper that have been combined in an improper manner.
The word "stated" (*uktam*) means "by me alone."
The meaning is: "the composition of figures of speech pertaining to both word and sense.
Now, one might ask: what is the point of teaching this [separately] with the statement, "that is called *citra* (pictorial poetry)"?
For it has already been stated that such a work does not possess the nature of true poetry (*kāvya*).

If it is argued that it is taught as something to be abandoned because once a jar is made, one is no longer a poet—anticipating the objection that this too ought to be stated, [the author] establishes that it is indeed so taught as something to be abandoned by poets, using the passage beginning with "And this... and ending with "of those who possess maturity.
For those women possess a maturity characterized by the appropriateness of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) regarding the subject matter of word and meaning.
By the statement "they become those who say 'it is dear to the ignorant,'" the weakness of the aesthetic relish (*rasāsvāda*) is shown.
By the word "stated" (*uktam*), he dispels the misconception that it was stated by someone else, saying "by me alone";
the meaning is "by me alone," that is, by the author of this commentary (*vṛttikāra*).
"Having the nature of non-poetry," and so forth;
the grammatical connection is that "it is indeed said to have the nature of non-poetry. The meaning of the word *tat* (it) is "the picture" (*citram*).
In the middle, he raises an objection: "by way of being something to be abandoned," and so forth.
"By way of being abandoned" means by way of being relinquished.
That is surprising.
He replies with "the jar," and so forth.
"Composed by him" means that a poem of variegated beauty has been composed.
Now, it is said:
"In the boundless universe of poetry, the poet alone is the Lord of Creation;
those words which abandon their capacity for substitution revolve according to how he pleases, and thus this entire world is transformed."
If the poet is possessed of the erotic sentiment, the world becomes full of aesthetic flavor within his poetry;
if he is free from passion, all of that becomes devoid of flavor.
Just as a skilled poet, through his independence, treats entities in his poetry— rendering even insentient things as if sentient, and sentient things as if insentient— according to his own will.

Therefore, there is simply no such thing that, for a poet whose intent is focused on rasa in its entirety, does not assume the status of a constituent of the desired rasa by virtue of his will. Or, even if it is so composed that it does not produce an excellence of beauty perceived by the eye, or if words themselves abandon their susceptibility to substitution (*parivṛtti*), one must still state that this is solely due to the propriety of the rasa; otherwise, it would be without cause.
"Apāra" means without beginning or end. He states a transformation according to his preference: "the erotic one," and so forth.

It should be understood that [the poet] consists of the cognition in the form of the relish (*carvaṇā*) of the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) as expressed in the *Śṛṅgāra* [chapter], and not that he is a mere addict to women.

For this very reason, the sage Bharata employs the word "poet" (*kavi*) itself in such expressions as "the internal state of the poet" (*kaver antargataṃ bhāvam*) and "he brings the meanings of poetry to life" (*kāvyārthān bhāvayati*). He uses it as the most preeminent term.
And this has been explained on the occasion of determining the nature of rasa:
"the world," meaning because of immersion in that rasa.
Those proficient in the arrangement of words call that "maturity of expression" (śabdapāka).
Since this statement expresses a different definition of *pāka* (poetic maturity), he says: "The words... and so forth.
[This applies to] one addicted to women;
the ellipsis is "one who is an object of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*)."
"Vyasana" means attachment.
Regarding the meaning already stated, such as "one who is erotic" (śṛṅgārī) and so forth, he provides support by saying "for this very reason," etc.
[The word] "of the poet" (kaveḥ).
One who brings to life the internal state of the poet through speech, physical gestures, facial expression, spirit, and dramatic representation is called a *bhāva*.
This verse and the passage beginning with "the meanings of poetry" (*kāvyārtha*) exist in the seventh chapter of the *Nāṭyaśāstra*.

By means of representation (*abhinaya*) consisting of speech, bodily gestures, and facial expressions, as well as by the representation characterized by inner being (*sattva*), [the rasa is manifested].

Of the poet who is skilled in description, that which is internal—consisting of innate predispositions (*saṃskāra*) and creative intuition (*pratibhāna*), which, due to the absence of distinctions such as place and time, becomes common to all and is fit for aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), and is characterized by a state of consciousness (*cittavṛtti*)... [is the rasa].
"Bhāva" means that; "bhāvayan" means making it relishable by bringing it to taste; "kāvyārthān" means the meanings of poetry.

What is *kāvyam*? It is that which is to be praised (*kavanīyam*) by the poet (*kavateḥ*). In this regard, both the meaning of words and the meaning of sentences culminate in the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*). Because of this unique quality and its preeminence, the "meanings" (*artha*) of poetry are the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*); for they are "sought after" (*arthyante*).
This has been explained in the *Abhinavabhāratī*.
To address the question of how the world consists of aesthetic flavor, he says: "That aesthetic flavor," and so forth.
Regarding the characterization of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*):
[the word] *puṇṇāti* [is used].
All of this is seen in the poems of the Māhakas.
We too have demonstrated this accordingly in our own poetic compositions.

And this being the case, every variety of poetry does not transcend the nature of *dhvani* when one takes into account the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth; even the variety characterized as "subordinate suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) assumes the status of a subordinate element to that [flavor], as was stated previously.

However, when rasa and the other elements are established as subordinate members within flatteries (*cāṭu*) or hymns to the deities, or in certain heart-touching verses containing wisdom (*saprajñakagāthā*) where the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is distinguished by its being subordinate to the expressed (*vācya*), that too is merely a manifestation (*niṣpanda*) of *dhvani* in which the suggested is subordinated (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), as was stated previously.

Thus, while this instruction on the method of poetry for contemporary poets is being given, if those beginners who seek practice engage primarily with the *citram* (the "figured" or "ornamental" poetry), [it is acceptable].
But for those who have attained maturity, the eye [of aesthetic perception] is the locus of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), which is the indicator of rasa;

"that very [eye]" means that as long as one is not a connoisseur (*rasika*), then even though this range of emotions (*bhāva*) being perceived provides only worldly pleasure, pain, delusion, or neutrality, [it does not yield aesthetic flavor].

Nevertheless, the meaning is that [beauty], without ascending to the description of a great poet, does not attain the state of being an experience of aesthetic flavor (rasa) that transcends the world.
The connection is as follows: that which does not nourish an excellence of loveliness simply does not exist.
Regarding the word "sveṣu" (among one's own):
"Behold the play of the god of uneven arrows (Kāma) among those who possess hearts"—
that is, among those well-known in the circles of Prakrit poets as "hiaalalia" (those whose hearts sport).
Thinking that the *phalahīlā* creepers would surely become as tall as those leaping into the sky,
the village women fulfilled the farmer’s wish by making them grow.
The meaning is that it indicates the commonality of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
He explains the passage beginning with "If he is free from passion" (*vītarāgaśced*) as follows: "As long as he does not become a connoisseur of rasa," and so forth. [Regarding the word] "sukha":

That which stands in the middle is "the middle" (*madhyastha*); its state is "equanimity" (*mādhyasthya*). The meaning is that the equanimity toward pleasure, pain, and delusion is a singular experience consisting of that alone.
By the word "alone" (*mātra*), the tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*) is excluded.
It "bestows" (*vitarati*).
The meaning is that the category of existents (bhāvavarga) consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
This is the explanation of the term "hṛdayavatīṣu" (those possessing hearts), namely: "hialaliā" and so forth.

Regarding the term *trivarge*: the meaning is that one should be skilled in those means (*upāya*) which constitute the very goal (*upeya*) to be known— the triad of the three aims of life beginning with dharma.
"Laṅghia" means:
"The cotton creepers have leaped across the sky," as she says this,
the neighbor's wife extinguished the blessing of the plowman.
Thus she said:
"O plowman! The cotton creepers—the cotton stalks that serve as your means of livelihood—have surpassed the sky;
they are exceedingly tall."
"May they be so"— thus, by a certain woman who repeatedly uttered this benediction of a plowman, increasing his prosperity;
"prāti" means a neighbor, specifically a bride living next door.
"Nirvāpitā" means she has been brought to a state of rest.

By the phrase "rest was secured"—meaning, "I shall now sport without hesitation with the farmer on that spot where the cotton creepers have fully matured"—the bride's longing for that illicit sexual enjoyment is suggested;
however, this suggestion remains subordinate.
This very point he explains with the words "here," and so forth.
It is established that poetry is indeed *dhvani* (suggestion).
Thus, here is the summary: that in which either rasa or a bhāva is manifested as the primary purport.
Where two things are expressed through conventional usage, there is either a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) or indeed the subject matter itself.
In the path of poetry (*kāvyādhvan*), *dhvani* is based solely on the predominance of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyaprādhānya*).

Regarding this, [the example] from the *Locana*: "While the rose-apple fruits are ripening in abundance within the thicket of creepers along the banks of the Godāvarī, the farmer’s wife wears a garment reddened by the juice of the rose-apples"—this is an instance of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion), wherein the excellence of the garment's redness—suspected to have been caused by a hurried sexual encounter—is concealed. Enough of this.
In short, sound alone is poetry (*kāvya*).

In reality, there is no difference between the self and that which possesses the self; however, this distinction is made for the sake of instruction. Furthermore, the reading in the *Locana* is: "and the neighbor was brought to peace."
That too is excellent;
following that, the verse and its shadow-translation (*chāyā*) should be recited.
In this context, a certain woman, desiring sexual union with a neighbor who is devoted to her and seeking a place for a rendezvous, [speaks] spontaneously.
It should be understood that by thus addressing the farmer with a blessing, she signaled the place of their rendezvous; the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is her longing for union with him.
Regarding "golākaccha":
it refers to the *jambū* fruits ripening in abundance within the bower at Godākaccha.
The beautiful young wife of the Suhāli bird fastens her garment, which is dyed with the juice of the jambu fruit.
Thus is the shadow [of the meaning].
The word "bhareṇa" (with abundance) means "atiśayena" (with excess).
In the passage beginning with "locane agode," it should be understood that there is a lacuna such as "godāvarī."

He demonstrates the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) as being subordinate (guṇībhūta) with the verse beginning "tvarita" and so forth: [the lover] is one who, on account of having quickly fallen upon a *jambū* fruit in a bower where a garment (*sicaya*) was spread as a bed, is characterized by— that is, rendered probable, brought into being, or inferred due to its cause— the state of being stained by the juice of the *jambū* fruit resulting from that secret amorous encounter (*cauryasambhoga*).
The "other part" (parabhāga) refers to the attainment of a different color in various parts of that [garment]; its "concealment" (nihnavana) means the desire to hide it.
Regarding the term "subordinate suggestion" (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya):
by the wearing of a garment dyed with the juice of jambu fruits across all its parts, the concealment of that [natural color] is understood.
The meaning is that this [suggestion] has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) to the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).

Now, one might object: since *dhvani* and poetry stand in the relationship of soul and body, their designation in the commentary as being in grammatical apposition—stating "poetry is indeed *dhvani*"—is untenable. To this he replies with the words "of the soul and its own," and so forth;
"its own" refers to the body.
"For the sake of proficiency" means for the purpose of instructing students.
Regarding "the division":
sound (*dhvani*) is the soul of poetry; in all cases, it should be understood as the object of focus by sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*).

Together with its own subdivisions—those in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (saguṇībhūta-vyaṅgya) and those accompanied by figures of speech (sālaṅkāra)—it shines forth again in many ways through both commingling (saṅkara) and combination (saṃsṛṣṭi). (Dhvanyāloka 3.43)
Together with its own subdivisions— including those where the suggested meaning is subordinate (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya) and those accompanied by figures of speech (sālaṅkāra)—
it shines forth again in many ways through the two modes of combination (saṅkara) and collocation (saṃsṛṣṭi).

And when the classification of that sound (dhvani) is established through its own sub-varieties, through suggestion where the suggested meaning is subordinate (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya), and through verbal ornaments (vācyālaṅkāra), a great multiplicity of types is observed in actual literary examples (lakṣya).

For instance: mixed with its own sub-varieties, combined with its own sub-varieties, mixed with subordinate suggestion, combined with subordinate suggestion, mixed with other verbal ornaments, combined with other verbal ornaments, mixed with combined ornaments, and combined with combined ornaments.
The sound manifests in many ways;
this means that the *locana* has been composed.
By the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), there is the inclusion of what was previously mentioned, such as its semblance (*tadābhāsa*) and so forth.
"By way of concealment" (saṃvṛtyā) means by virtue of being hidden, which results in the attainment of beauty.
"From poetry, [arises] resonance" (kāvyād dhvani).
"On the path of poetry" (*kāvyamārge*).
"The object" (*viṣayī*): that is to say, the threefold *dhvani* is the object within the path of poetry. // 41, 42 //
Having thus stated the summary of the meaning in two verses, he recites the following to demonstrate its manifold nature: "Together with the subordinate" (*saguṇīta*).

The intended sense is that *dhvani* is of infinite varieties through its being mixed or combined with its own subdivisions—those which exist together with the subordinate-suggested (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) and with the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
He demonstrates this manifold nature by saying: "For instance" (*tathāhi*).

It is manifested through its own subdivisions, through suggestion where the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), and through figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*); thus there are three divisions.
Furthermore, each of these is divided into six by means of both commixture (*saṃkara*) and combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*).

Within commixture, there are three types: by way of the relationship of the assisted and the assistant (*anugrāhyānugrāhakabhāva*), by being a locus of doubt (*saṃdehāspadatva*), and by entering into a single word (*ekapadānupraveśa*). Thus, there are twelve divisions in total.

Furthermore, the thirty-five varieties previously mentioned belong to *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (poetry where the suggested meaning is subordinated) as well; this is the meaning of the division that "poetry consists of word and meaning" (*śabdārthamayaṃ kāvyam*).
Regarding the phrase "by the use of the particle *vā*":
the meaning is "by the particle *vā* [in the expression] 'or the state' (*bhāvo vā*)."
The explanation of the phrase "stated by way of convention" (*saṃvṛttyābhihita*) is: "having attained beauty through being concealed.

With the intention that by stating that [suggestion] is the object of *dhvani*, it follows that it is the object of the path of poetry (*kāvyamārga*), he says: "that [which is] of three kinds," and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "in which," etc.:

The grammatical connection is as follows: wherever this path of poetry shines forth everywhere, there *dhvani*—which is based solely on the predominance of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)—is to be known by sensitive people (*sahṛdaya*) as its proper domain. (41, 42)
He explains the *kārikā* with the words "together" (*saha*), and so forth.
The intention is that in the phrase "arising," the word "sound" (*dhvani*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

With the intention of showing the divisions by stating that these [two types] are obtained each together with their own sub-varieties, along with figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), and through the extensive discussion of the combinations of *saṅkara* (blending) and *saṃsṛṣṭi* (juxtaposition), he presents the classifications with the words "with their own sub-varieties," and so on.
The readings are *prakāśyate* and *sammiśryate*. Regarding "twelve":
there are nine [types] formed by the combination [of the three] with their own subdivisions and so forth.
The phrase "the three produced by combination" means twelve.
And as for the thirty-five varieties mentioned previously—

at the point of explaining the commentary passage at the end of the second chapter, which states, "Having thus set forth the divisions of *dhvani*," those thirty-five varieties therein may sometimes be mixed with their own subdivisions through the relationship of the assisted (*anugrāhya*) and the assister (*anugrāhaka*).
For example, in passages such as "When the divine sage had spoken thus," etc.,

a variety of *dhvani* with an imperceptible sequence of suggestion (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya-dhvani*) is perceived as being supported by a variety of *dhvani* consisting of suggestion arising from the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktyudbhava-anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya-dhvani*).
Thus, there may sometimes be a doubt due to the convergence of these two varieties.
For example:
"O brother-in-law, this neighbor who visits at night was said something by your wife;
she is weeping in the upper chamber of the house—please go comfort that poor woman."
The *Locana* states that these should be considered:
first, there are seventy-one figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) including their own subdivisions;
when multiplied by the three types of *saṃkara* (commixture) and by *saṃsṛṣṭi* (coexistence), they amount to two hundred and eighty-four.
By multiplying those by the thirty-five principal divisions, there are seven thousand four hundred and twenty varieties.
However, because ornaments are infinite, they are beyond numbering.

Desiring to provide examples for a few of these divisions to facilitate understanding, and since his own subdivisions were stated as the primary meaning of the compound (in the *kārikā*), he states four examples based on them—beginning with the word "tatra" (therein).
Regarding the term "being favored":
for when shame is recognized,
the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) based on longing is here favored by way of being a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*).

"O brother-in-law, a festival is being held there and she was brought here by invitation. This poor woman, having been said something by your wife, is weeping; let her be consoled in the empty upper chamber of the house."

The statement, "She was indeed infatuated with her husband’s brother, and something was said to her by his wife who had learned of the situation," means that the account of that situation was explained by Bālapriyā herself.
As for "te" (they),
it means the thirty-five varieties.
"Own subdivisions" means the intermediate distinctions of sound. "As many as those" [means...]
The meaning is "thirty-five.
Regarding the term "ornament" (alaṅkāra):
the meaning is "that which is delimited by the property of being an ornament."
"Then," and so forth;
the meaning is that seventy-one is multiplied by four.

Following the statement "two hundred and eighty-four," there is the reading: "When those [two hundred and eighty-four] are multiplied by the thirty-five principal divisions, they become seven thousand and twenty-four."
This is seen in many texts; its meaning does not appear consistent and must be determined by the learned.
Regarding the term "incalculability" (*asaṃkhyatva*):
the intended meaning is that, because it is delimited by the nature of being an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), only one [instance] should be understood as such.
This is because it functions as the referent of another word (*anyapadārthatvena*).
The meaning is: by way of being the referent of the other members (*anyapadārtha*) of the two *bahuvrīhi* compounds beginning with "saguṇībhūta" (become endowed with qualities).
Here, he explains what was stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with "by the power of the meaning" (*arthaśaktyā*), starting with "by shame" (*lajjayā*).
[He does so] by means of its being a pervasive cause (*vyabhicāribhūtatvena*).
The meaning is: "by reason of [shame] being a transitory state (vyabhicāribhāva) of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
Regarding "the festival":
it should be understood that this festival pertains to the brother-in-law (devara).
The literal meaning of the word *prādhuṇikā* is "a guest" or "one who has arrived.
Its intended sense is explained as "brought by invitation.
By this, the necessity of persuasion is indicated.
The phrase beginning with "devare" (brother-in-law) is an illustration by means of a shadow [of meaning].
"Something" (kimapi) means that which is improper.
The connection is as follows: "Because she weeps, therefore that poor, wretched woman should be consoled by you.
He explains this verse, beginning with "She," etc., after first introducing it.
"She lies" means that she who was the guest for a moment is now the heroine (*nāyikā*).
[The verse continues: "O brother-in-law, this guest for a moment has been told something by your wife."
She weeps in an empty upper chamber; let this poor woman be consoled.
[Thus is the shadow.

For here, this word "let [him] be conciliated" is conceivable both as having its literal meaning transferred (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) and as having its expressed meaning intended but subordinate to another (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).
And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determining one side over the other.

However, regarding the state of being suggested (*vyaṅgyatva*) through the entry of a single suggester (*ekavyañjakānupraveśena*), [the Locana] observes that for the suggestion of imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgya*), this occurs in relation to its own internal subdivisions. In this context, a certain woman—having seen her husband’s brother-in-law, a thief and lover, with another woman, and wishing to provoke a quarrel on both sides by saying, "Your housewife has discovered this affair"—speaks as follows. In this case, there is a transference (*saṃkramaṇa*) of the expressed meaning (*vācya*) into another sense, namely: "Let him be gratified by an enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) appropriate for a secluded place."
Alternatively, if [the speaker] intends to say that she is devoted only to him, then the conciliation is intended for another purpose— namely, out of a focus on jealousy and anger;

or, if the conciliation is intended to mean "she is now the proper and irreproachable object of love," while implying "we have now become objects of reproach"— in either case, since his own intention is being revealed, it has been stated that there is no evidence for determining one alternative over the other.
For that which is intended to be expressed is [the woman] who, while remaining in her own true nature, is intent upon another;
"devare" means she is enamored with the husband's brother (devara).
"Viditā" means: by her who has learned the account of her [the woman] and the god-king, such as their mutual passion and so forth;
"tadvṛttāntam" refers to that account.
The meaning is: "the account of what was said by his wife and so forth. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "this is the speech of the amorous woman.
He says "there," and so forth, to show that the statement "something was said by the wife" is merely an indication of the cause for weeping, and that there is no other result to that speaking.
In the phrase "tadvacane," the connection is with "tatra ityevamāha" (there he spoke thus); "sā" (she) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"To quarrel on both sides" means to cause a mutual dispute between the husband and his wife;
he explains the "confusion of doubt" mentioned in the commentary with the words beginning "Therein," and so forth.
In that context, regarding the statement "tathā" (thus):
the connection is with the phrase "in such a form, [there is] another meaning.
Of the expressed [meaning], that is, of the expressed sense which causes one to incline toward [it].
Regarding the term "transition" (*saṅkramaṇam*):
it is a displacement of the word "intended.
The expressed meaning of the root *anu-nī* is an activity such as speaking kindly that produces satisfaction, considered as such.

The meaning is that here, he is intended to be characterized by his form as the *sambhoga* [rasa]. Furthermore, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) to be understood here is such things as, "I have learned of your passion for her," and so forth.
"In this very one" means:
The reading "devaras tasyām eva" means "the brother-in-law [should approach] that very woman who weeps. The word "iti" indicates the reason.
"Jealousy" (īrṣyā) means: the sense is that it refers to the jealousy and anger residing in the speaker and the beloved respectively.
"Conciliation" (anunayana) means:
The meaning is that the literal sense (vācyārtha) inclines [the listener]; "intended for another" means intended for [expressing] jealousy, anger, or the like.
He provides the justification for what was stated—beginning with "this" and so forth.
The connection is that this is intended to be expressed as having that [prior] purpose.
"In both ways" means:

"Inclines" means that [the word] is intended to convey another meaning, either by shifting to a different sense or by being intended for something else. "His own intention" means the desire residing in the speaker's beloved.
"It has been said" means that the author of the commentary (vṛttikṛt) is the one who spoke; this is the ellipsis. He states "of the intended [object]" and so forth as an incidental remark.
It occurs predominantly,
as for example in "snigdhaśyāmala" (glossy-dark) and so forth;
and its state of being mixed with its own subdivisions is as in the previous example.

For here there is a combination of the type where the expressed meaning is transferred to another sense (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*) and the type where the expressed meaning is entirely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*). An example of its being mixed with *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) is as follows: "This very fact that my enemies exist is indeed an insult to me," and so forth; or as in: "The one who was the author of the deceits of gambling, who set fire to the lac-house, who was full of arrogance, who was clever at seizing the hair and upper garments of Draupadī—he whose servants were the Pāṇḍavas... [and so on].

"Where is that Duryodhana—the king who is the elder of a hundred younger brothers beginning with Duḥśāsana, the friend of the King of Aṅga? Tell me; we have come here not out of anger, but to see him."
"Transference" (*saṃkrānti*) is the assumption of that [other's] form;

or rather, this is a statement made by a woman who is in love with her husband’s brother (*devara*), concerning the account of his being seen and enjoying himself with another woman, as indicated by the address "husband’s brother."
In the previous explanation, however, the address "devara" was explained with reference to that [context].
Regarding the phrase "in abundance":

in every poetic work there is, at the very least, an intent toward rasa and so forth; therein, the manifestation of both *rasadhvani* and *bhāvadhvani* occurs through a single manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

In the verse beginning with "snigdhaśyāmala," there is the relish (*carvaṇā*) of the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation) and its transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*), which consists of agitation due to grief (*śokāvega*). Having thus explained the three types of *saṃkara* (commixture), he illustrates *saṃsṛṣṭi* (collocation) with the words "svaprabheda" etc. Regarding the phrase "for here": [The verse: "O slender-waisted one, having seen you, whose face is like the full moon, who are lovely as a fresh lotus, and who possess a form that is the very essence of nectar, my heart has become such that it cannot endure even the touch of a flower. Here, the *rasas* of *śṛṅgāra*, *karuṇa*, and *adbhuta* are present; these are not merely commingled, but rather exist in a state of collocation (*saṃsṛṣṭi*). This is because they are perceived separately, each maintaining its own distinct character, without one being subordinated to another. Thus, the meaning is that when multiple *rasas* or *bhāvas* coexist in a single sentence or verse, each retaining its individuality, that is *saṃsṛṣṭi*. Therefore, it is said: "For here...
