The meaning is that in words such as *lipta* (smeared), the expressed meaning is subordinated (*tiraskṛta*), whereas in words such as *rāma*, it is transferred (*saṃkrānta*).

Having thus illustrated the four varieties with respect to its own subdivisions, he provides examples with respect to the subordinated suggestible (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) by stating "guṇībhūta... and so forth.
Of the denoted object abiding in its own nature;
of that denoted object;
"attainment of this form" means the acquisition of another intended form.
"Of one who is attached to her husband's younger brother" means:
of one who is attached to him who is her own husband's younger brother.
The word "with" (saha) is connected with the word "in sexual union" (sambhoge).
He states the indicator for the meaning already explained: "by the brother-in-law," and so forth.
"In relation to her" means in relation to her who had been the guest.
The meaning is that the state of being the best among gods (devaratva) as determined by that [quality] is to be understood.
This verse is also cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
He establishes that this occurs extensively with the words "everywhere," and so forth.
The connection is that it is called "manifestation" (*abhivyañjana*) because it is to be chewed (*carvaṇīyatvāt*).
Regarding the phrase "in the case of words such as *lipta*," and so forth:

in the verse "the sky was smeared with the glossy, dark luster [of her body]," there is that which belongs to a liquid substance by way of pervading all its constituent parts (*sarvāvayavāvacchedena*).
Because the literal meaning (vācyārtha)—namely, "smearing" which consists of a physical contact—is sublated, the verbal root *lip* indicates "contact" and thereby suggests its excellence.

Similarly, in the phrase "those for whom the clouds are friends," because the literal meaning is sublated, the word "friend" (suhṛt) indicates the state of being a benefactor and manifests that excellence; this is the meaning.
[The phrase] "in the case of Rāma and so forth" refers to this.
The meaning is "in words such as 'Rāma'"; the word "denoted" (vācya) is to be supplied;
[and] "transferred" (saṅkrānta).
How this transition occurs has been explained in the second Uddyota.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the case of Rāma and so forth," words such as Rāvaṇa found in the verse beginning with "insult" (*anyakkāra*) are included.
The verse beginning with "the doer" (*kartṛ*) is from the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*.

For here, in both examples [indicated by] "atra hi," there is a commingling of the suggestion whose sequence is imperceptible—which has become the meaning of the sentence—with words that express the denoted meaning as qualified by that suggestion.

And for this very reason, even though there is a mixture of the *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion), which rests on the meaning of individual words, with the *dhvani* (suggestion), which rests on the meaning of the sentence, there is no contradiction, just as in the case of its own other internal varieties.
This is what is meant by "here" (*atra*) in both examples.
Regarding the phrase "of that whose suggested meaning has no perceptible sequence":

by the expression "distinguished by the suggested meaning" (*vyaṅgyaviśiṣṭa*) in relation to the Furious sentiment (*raudra*), it is stated that the suggested meaning possesses the status of a poetic quality (*guṇa*).
The instrumental case in "by words" (*padaiḥ*) is used in a figurative sense (*upalakṣaṇe*).
The state of being mixed (*saṃkīrṇatā*) consists in the blending with that meaning indicated by the [word], which exists as a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) in a subordinate capacity (*guṇībhāva*).

This [blending] occurs through the relationship of the assisted and the assister (*anugrāhyānugrāhakabhāva*), through the connection of doubt (*saṃdehayoga*), and through the entry into a single manifestor (*ekavyañjakānupraveśa*); it should be applied, as the case may be, to the two examples.

For instance, in the verse beginning with *me yadarayaḥ*, the Furious sentiment (*raudra*) alone is assisted by all the word-meanings, such as "I," "enemy," and so forth, by way of their constituting the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors.

In passages such as "kartā" (the agent) and so forth, it is certainly possible to imagine suggested meanings for every individual word, for each subordinate sentence, and for every compound; however, these have not been written down.
The phrase "pāṇḍavā yasya dāsāḥ" (the Pāṇḍavas are whose servants) is an imitation of his own speech.
In that case, it is also possible to apply the category of subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatā*).
Because the expressed meaning alone serves as the excitant of the anger,
there is also the nature of a resonance based on the power of the contextual meaning (artha-śakti), namely that the master must certainly be seen by the servants who have completed their tasks.
Since beauty exists in both ways, there is no evidence to favor one side over the other.

"Entry through a single manifestor," however, occurs because those very same words manifest both the subordinate suggested meaning (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) and the predominant rasa by way of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
[The author] explains—saying "in both examples"—to prevent the misconception that the word "here" (*atra*) in the commentary refers merely to the example of the agent;
[he does so] with the words "of the Furious [rasa]" (*raudrasya*).

The meaning is that in passages such as "nyakkāra" (insult), there is the perception of anger residing in Rāvaṇa, and in passages such as "kartā" (the doer), there is the perception of anger residing in Bhīmasena.
Regarding the phrase "vyaṅgyaviśiṣṭa" (qualified by the suggested meaning), the sense is: "by means of stating the qualification by the suggested meaning."
Regarding the term "guṇatā" (the state of being a quality):
the remainder [of the sentence] is "in relation to the expressed meaning.
It has been stated, that is, demonstrated.

Because the literal meaning of the phrase "mixed with the words" (*padaissammiśratā*) is contradicted, he explains it thus: "the word 'words' (*padaḥ*) is used figuratively (*upalakṣaṇe*), and the third case ending [indicates] that.
The meaning of the third case in "by those" (*tadaiḥ*) is "being made known" (*jñāpyatva*).
He demonstrates that very same meaning by saying: "characterized by those" (*tadupalakṣitā*).
To the question "With what is it mixed?", he says: "The object," and so forth.
"The object" means the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*).
"By that" [is meant by that literal meaning].
The meaning is "by means of the expressed [meaning] which has become subordinate" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyena vācyena*). And the phrase "that [is]" means "it is a state of commingling" (*saṅkīrṇatā*).
The three words ending in the third case (instrumental) are connected with this [word "by"],
as well as with "agent" and so forth;
the word "by means of categories" (*padārthaiḥ*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
[Objection: But have not the suggested meanings (vyaṅgyārtha) in the verse beginning with "nyakkāra" and so forth already been explained?
Why then are they not present in the verse beginning with "kartā" and so forth? To this he replies: "In the verse beginning with 'kartā'... [and] "His words... (tadīyokti).

The meaning is that Duryodhana says, "The Pāṇḍavas are my slaves. By the phrase "only the Furious [sentiment] is favored," he demonstrates the commixture (*saṅkara*) through the relationship of the favored and the favorer; then, by means of the application of doubt (*sandeha*), he shows that same commixture with the words beginning "therein" (*tatra*).
It should be understood that this includes the inferiority and other qualities residing in the Pāṇḍavas.

The phrase "ityarthetyādi" means that what was stated regarding the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) being rooted in the power of the sense (artha-śakti-mūla) applies to its form as well; the word "capable of being joined" (yojayituṃ śaktā) is to be supplied [to the end of the sentence].
"Or otherwise," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is a confusion through doubt between the *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) and *dhvani* (suggestion).
"By them" refers to those [who hold this view].
The meaning is: "by means of [verses] such as *me yadaraya*.
The connection is that this occurs because rasa is manifested through the medium of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.

Having thus explained the phrase "for this very reason," [the author says] "those very [elements]" and so on; for just as other varieties of *dhvani* do not mutually intermingle, nor are they contradictory by virtue of being based respectively upon the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) or the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*).

Furthermore, while the relationship of primary and subordinate is contradictory when based on a single suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), it is not so with respect to a plurality of suggested meanings; therefore, there is no contradiction here either.

Moreover, this conventional distinction between "commingling" (*saṅkara*) and "conjunction" (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) should be understood as being entirely without contradiction even in the case of the relationship between the suggester and the suggested, just as it is in the case of the relationship between the signifier and the signified among many elements in a single instance.

However, where certain words have their literal meanings unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*), or where the suggested meaning follows from the literal meaning (*anuraṇanarūpavyaṅgya*), there exists a conjunction (*saṃsṛṣṭatva*) between *dhvani* and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*.
For example: "Of those who were friends to the amorous play of the cowherd women," and so forth.

For here, the words *vilāsasuhṛdām* ("friends to the amorous play") and *rādhārahaḥsākṣiṇām* ("witnesses to Rādhā’s secret trysts") are of the nature of a specific type of *dhvani* (suggestive poetry), while the words *te* ("those") and *jāne* ("I know") are of the nature of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).
Locanam: "And for this very reason... [etc.]

The meaning is: "because it is seen here in this object of characterization (lakṣya), therefore [it exists]. Now, one might object: "Is it not a contradiction for the suggested (vyaṅgya) to be both subordinate (guṇībhūta) and primary (pradhāna)? Even though it is observed, it should not be accepted because it has already been stated [to be impossible]. Anticipating this doubt, he shows that there is no contradiction due to the difference in the suggestors (vyañjaka), stating:
"For this very reason."
Regarding the word "sva" (its own):
since its internal subdivisions were previously illustrated through their intermixture, he now provides an illustration of those very same ones.
He explains that very point with the words "yathā hi" (just as).
In this case as well, the word "so too" (tathāpi) must be supplied here;
or else, the reading is "for thus" (tathā hi).

Now, one might object: "Granted that the first two types of difference may be resolved by the difference in manifesters (vyañjaka), but what is to be said when they enter into a single manifester? Anticipating this doubt, he states the ultimate resolution with the words "furthermore" (kiñca): from that... [text continues].

"Or [it may be] suggestion (vyaṅgya). Since one suggested element is subordinate while another is primary, what contradiction is there? One might object: 'This technical usage of "commixture" (saṃkara) and so forth is heard in the context of expressed figures of speech (vācyālaṅkāra), but not in the context of the suggested. Anticipating this doubt, he says: 'And this...'"

"It should be reflected upon" (*mantavya*) means that it should be determined as such through the cognition (*pratīti*) resulting from reflection; the sense is that in both cases, cognition alone is the refuge.

Having thus illustrated the three varieties of the commingling (*saṃkara*) of subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), he illustrates their coexistence (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) with the words: "But where the words... and so forth.
By the words "some [say]," he introduces the section of the text ending with "contradiction for the simple-minded" (bālapriyāvirodha), beginning with "But surely," etc.
The word "dṛśyamānam" ("being seen") has the word "lakṣye" ("in the object to be defined") as its ellipsis.
The word "sva" (itself) connects with the verb "dṛṣṭāntayati" (illustrates by way of an example).
The meaning is that by the phrase "like its own internal divisions," he demonstrates the illustrative example.
"Of the first two types of division" means:
of those two types of commixture (*saṅkara*) which occur through the relationship of the assisted and the assister, and through the connection with doubt (*sandeha*).
"What need is there to say more? [means: what further explanation is required?
"What is to be done?"—
this is also the reading;
the sense is that there is no difference in the manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*).
He states the underlying intention: "since [it is] internal," and so forth.

He explains the term "to be contemplated" (*mantavya*) in accordance with the context: "by means of reflection" (*mananena*), and so forth. "By cognition" (*pratītyā*) means by the cognition of those who possess aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*).

"By this [statement]" means by the statement that some [poems] have a literal meaning that is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitavācya*), while others have a literal meaning consisting of a resonant suggested sense (*anuraṇanarūpavyaṅgyavācya*).
"A friend," and so forth.

The intermixture (*saṅkīrṇatva*) of the two primary types—the expressed (*vācya*) and the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*)—is well-established everywhere in poetry that possesses rasa and figures, when compared to that where the suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgya*).
Even for other sub-varieties, such intermixture certainly occurs at times; as in my own work: [the *Locana*] refutes the possibility of such intermixture.

In the words "friend" (*suhṛt*) and "witness" (*sākṣin*), there is suggestion (*dhvani*) where the literal meaning is not intended; although the mass of extraordinary qualities is manifested by the word "those" (*te*), it remains subordinate (*guṇatva*), because the literal meaning itself—the act of remembering—is the primary cause of beauty.
By the word "I know" (*jāne*), which suggests infinite attributes being imagined, the literal meaning itself—the form of the imagination—is made predominant.

Thus, four varieties have been illustrated for the subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) as well. Now, he shows those [varieties] pertaining to figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) with the words "the expressed figure" (*vācyālaṅkāra*).
The intention of the word "expressed" (*vācya*) is that when figures of speech are suggested (*vyaṅgya*), they are included within the eight varieties already mentioned.
Regarding the term "poetry" (*kāvya*): for poetry is precisely of such a nature;
it is well-structured.

From the examples in the second *udyota* of the *Mūla* under the rule "by the speaker’s intention being directed toward that," the three types of *saṃkara* (blending) and *saṃsṛṣṭi* (coexistence) are indeed obtained.

For instance, in the verse beginning "calāpāṅgāṃ dṛṣṭim," the previously explained *rūpaka-vyatireka* (metaphor-cum-distinction) serves as an auxiliary to the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment), and there is a mutual interpenetration (*ekānupraveśa*) between the *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state) and the *śṛṅgāra*.

In the *gāthā* "uppaha jāyā" (born on the path), in the absence of contextual factors (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, there is no evidence to determine whether it is a *svabhāvokti* of a commoner or a *dhvani* (suggestive poetry).

Although an ornament (alaṅkāra) necessarily favors rasa, nevertheless, regarding what was stated with the intention that "there is no excessive desire for the conclusion" (*nāti nirvahaṇaiṣitā*), because of the impossibility of a single ornament (*saṅkāra*) there, it is indeed a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of ornaments with the suggestion of rasa (*rasadhvani*).
As, for example, in the verse: "Having bound [him] firmly with the noose of her vine-like arms... (*bāhulatikāpāśena baddhvā dṛḍham*).
The phrase "of other varieties as well" refers to those distinct from the dhvanis of rasa and so forth.

In the case of the non-sentient vine-cottages, the terms "friend" (*suhṛd*) and "witness" (*sākṣin*) would be contradicted; therefore, the word "friend" indicates [the cottages] by way of being helpful, and the word "witness" indicates them by way of being proximate.
The meaning of the word *dhvani* is the excellence residing in the *upakāra* (benefit) and so forth, which is the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*).
The connection is that it is "manifested by the word.
Regarding the term *guṇatva*: [it refers to its status as a quality].
The term "the rest" refers to what is to be expressed (*vācya*).

Regarding the phrase "the state of being mixed with a figure of speech that is to be expressed," he demonstrates the purpose of the qualification "being expressed" (*vācyatva*) applied to the figure of speech by saying "in the case of being suggested" (*vyaṅgyatve*), and so forth.
The phrase "the eightfold division mentioned" refers to the aforementioned classification.
The meaning is that there are eight varieties produced through combination (*saṅkara*) and intermixture (*saṃsṛṣṭi*).
"Of such a kind" means possessing rasa and being adorned with figures of speech (*sālaṅkāra*).
He demonstrates its well-established nature with the words "the desire to speak," and so forth.

Regarding "being a supporter of the erotic sentiment" (*śṛṅgārānugrāhakatvam*): the meaning is that there exists a relationship of the supported and the supporter (*anugrāhyānugrāhakabhāva*) between it and the erotic sentiment.

The meaning is that the sight of the various gestures of another hero (nāyaka) directed toward her serves as an excitant (*uddīpaka*) for passion (*rati*). Regarding the phrase "in the verse," the remainder is that it refers to the verse previously cited.
The locative case in "prakaraṇādyabhāve" (in the absence of context, etc. denotes the occasion [for the application of the rule].

Having thus demonstrated examples of the threefold commingling (*saṅkara*) of verbal figures of speech, he says "yadyapi" and so forth, intending to show the scope and the examples of their coexistence (*saṃsṛṣṭi*).
The meaning is that this was said with the intention [of showing] the absence of being beneficial; "in this regard" means in this context.
For here, the meaning is that there is indeed a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) of the *rasa* with the *rūpaka* (metaphor).
He states "niṣpādana" and so forth in order to provide the justification that will be explained later.
He explains the words beginning with "vyāpāravatī" by means of the passage beginning with "tatra."

That which is the active, ever-new vision of certain poets for savoring aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), and that which is the scholarly vision whose manifestation has as its object established meanings—this is the eye.
[The commentary] says "the active eye.
For it has been stated that *rasa* has its life-force in its production (*niṣpādana*).

In this context, *varṇanā* consists of the composition of the *vibhāva*s and so forth; from that point until the final *ghaṭanā*, it is the action or activity (*vyāpāra*). [The *kāvya*] is constantly joined with that.
"Rasān" means:
to savor the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva), whose essence consists in being savored; that is, to render them capable of attaining the state of being savored.
"A certain [woman]" refers to one who is emerging by abandoning the state of consciousness fallen into worldly discourse.
For this very reason, they are poets because of their capacity for description; thus,
"new" means that at every moment they weave the worlds with ever-new varieties.
Regarding the term "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*):
it consists of intuition (*pratibhā*).

In this context, "vision" refers to visual cognition; thus, the statement that it "tastes" flavors such as *ṣāḍava* involves the poetic figure of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*), and for this very reason, it is novel.
And sound is assisted by that [intention],
for visual cognition is not intended [to convey meaning], because it is absolutely impossible [for it to do so];
nor is it directed toward anything else.
Rather, however, it has been transferred to another object—an object characterized by intuitive flash (*pratibhāna*) that arises from the repeated practice of sensory cognition.
And in the process of this transfer, the contradiction is merely a contributing factor;
as he will state later with the words, "by means of the figure of speech *virodha*," and so forth.
*Bālapriyā* explains:
"From the manifestation" (*vibhāvāt*) means "from the meaning of the manifesting factors, the ensuants, and so forth.
"Composition" (*ghaṭanā*) [is the sense].
The meaning is the conjunction of those respective words. "It would be performed" means a mental activity consisting of the synthesis of those respective [words].
He states that the suffix *batu* is used in the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*) with the words "by that" (*tena*), and so forth.
The state of being joined (*yuktatva*) is to be understood through the relationship of the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*).
The explanation of the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) of the word *rasān* is: "those whose essence is the state of being relished" (*rasyamānatāsārān*).
By the word "rasa," he states what is intended in the present context— namely, the "stable emotions" (sthāyibhāvas).
The phrase "cognition fallen into the course of worldly life" means knowledge concerning various objects belonging to the world.
"From this very fact" means "from the mere opening of the eyes.
He states the etymological meaning of the word *kavi* (poet): "because of the absence of speech."
"Āsūtrayantī" means illuminating.
Having kept in mind the transition that is about to be described, he says: "consisting of intuition. In this context, "vision" (dṛṣṭi) refers to visual cognition.

"To savor flavors" means to prepare substances for drinks such as *ṣāḍava* that are endowed with sweet and other tastes; or alternatively, it means she is active in tasting the sweet and other flavors contained within the *ṣāḍava* and so forth.
He states that this is the figure of speech known as *virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction) because of the perception of a contradictory meaning, beginning with "her gaze there," etc.
To indicate the contradiction, he says, "for this very reason," etc.
The sense is that "not" (*na*) indicates a contradiction.
*Dhvani* refers to the *dhvani* in which the expressed meaning is transmuted into another meaning (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*).
It is not that [the expressed meaning] is entirely unintended (*atyantam avivakṣita*).
The meaning is that it is not "entirely set aside.

The phrase "because of the absence of impossibility" implies that even the visual cognition of the moon, gardens, and so forth occurring in the poet is useful for the production of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
"And not intended as something else" means that it is neither intended to convey a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) nor is it what was meant to be expressed; rather,
it has transferred into another meaning characterized by intuitive flash (*pratibhāna*).
The meaning is that here the word *pratibhā* (intuition) characterizes knowledge (*jñāna*) by way of its form as intuition.
Here, qualities such as the lack of clarity of the intuition are what is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
To demonstrate the connection with the primary meaning, he says: "perceptual," and so forth.

"Sensory consciousness" (*aindriyaka-vijñāna*) refers to worldly visual cognition regarding various objects; its "practice" (*abhyāsa*) is its repetition (*āvṛtti*), by which [the world] is "illumined," meaning made manifest.
He connects the stated meaning with the commentary, beginning with "he will say that," etc.:

"Relying upon both of those [the senses and the mind], we have been incessantly describing the universe, yet we are exhausted and have not obtained at all a happiness equal to devotion to You, O Lord who reclines upon the ocean."

And that vision which is such as this is the "locana" (eye); it is one whose opening (*unmeṣa*) is directed toward an object that has been fully established and is immovable—that is, toward an object to be ascertained.

Likewise, it is one whose opening is directed toward an object well-established in common worldly usage, but not toward a novel object like that of a poet; this [vision] of the wise is called *vaipaścitī*.
Regarding the phrase "having relied upon these":
by the expression "of poets" (*kavīnām*) and "of the wise" (*vaipaścitām*), he suggests his own lack of arrogance, implying, "I am neither a poet nor a scholar.
The meaning is that, like the utensils in a poor man's house, I have brought these two perspectives from elsewhere for the sake of utility, even though they do not belong to me.
"Those two as well"—
for a complete description of the entire universe (*viśvam*) without exception cannot be accomplished by means of a single vision alone.
"Aniśam" means repeatedly and without interruption; "nirvarṇayantaḥ" means by way of description.

Likewise, for those describing an object of certain meaning as "this is thus," there is the thorough examination by means of reflection, inference, and so forth, analyzing it to determine what the essence here might be, scrutinizing it bit by bit. And that which is thoroughly examined is indeed properly scrutinized by a steady gaze that operates in the middle [of the object] and which possesses a certain unfolding toward the specific details of the object within.
Thus we say.
The meaning is that they are addicted to seizing [objects] through false views of reality.
"Exhausted" means that not only was the essence not obtained, but on the contrary, weariness was instead acquired; this is the intended sense.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "tu" (but/however).
Regarding the term "abdhiśayana" (reclining on the ocean):
because of your yogic sleep, you are therefore a knower of the essential nature [of all things], meaning you remain established in your own true nature.
For one who is weary, there arises great respect toward that which is situated in the state of rest.
Regarding the phrase "devotion to you" (*tvadbhakti*):

you alone are the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the essence of the universe; devotion to you is the absorption (*āveśa*) born from the sequence of worship preceded by faith and so forth. Thus, for the sake of explaining the meaning of the phrase "the object of the child's affection," he says: "that which is to be ascertained."
And so forth.
He explains it otherwise as well, beginning with "tathā" (thus) and so on.
Having stated the meaning implied by the phrase "taking hold of those," he states the explicit meaning [of the verse] beginning with "anātmīyam" (not belonging to a self) and so on.
Regarding the phrase "as in a house":
the ellipsis is to be supplied as "adornment and so forth, which are non-existent.
He states the result of saying "both" with the words beginning "for not," and so on.
He states two meanings for the word *aniśam* with the words "again," and so forth.
He explains the act of gazing (*nirvarṇanam*) in two ways by means of the perspective of the poet: as "gazing while describing" (*nirvarṇayanto varṇanayā*) and as "likewise," and so forth.
Describing by means of verbal characterization (*varṇanayā*), they observe while scrutinizing (*nirvarṇayantaḥ*).
He explains the scrutiny (*nirvarṇanam*) by relying on the vision of Vipaścit: "This is thus," and so forth. Having analyzed it, he clarifies that very scrutiny: "What is here? and so forth.
The result of the description [is given] by means of the twofold objective support of views—namely, "not by one alone," and so forth.
He clarifies exactly what was stated previously with the words "and that which," and so forth.
He states the intended meaning of the word "we" with the words "false," and so forth.
"False view is the view of the poet; the view of reality is the view of the wise man.
Regarding these two, he states their essential meaning with the words "false," and so forth.
The meaning is that those who are addicted to these two—the false view of the poet and the view of reality of the wise man—are intent upon them.
Regarding the meaning of the word "tu" (but):
it means that which indicates a specific form of meaning.
He states the implied meaning of the term "abdhiśayana" (reclining on the ocean) with the words "by yogic sleep," and so forth.
"From this very reason" means: because there is no happiness equal to devotion to you.
"Sāra" [means]...
The meaning is that he is the knower of that which is his own essential nature, the essence of all.
And he demonstrates another suggested meaning with the words "of the one who has reached the end," and so forth;
[this refers to] "his immersion" (tadāveśa).
The meaning is an excess of love directed toward that [object].
Alternatively, the meaning is the state of the mental modification (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) being shaped into the form of that [object].
In the phrase "the essential nature of devotion," there is a fusion of the type of suggestion (dhvani) known as *arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya* with the figure of speech *virodha* (contradiction).
And the coexistence of verbal figures of speech (*vācyālaṅkāra*) occurs only with respect to individual words.
For where some words [are present], let it be that even something similar to them is not obtained;

nevertheless, this statement belongs to one who, from the very beginning a devotee of the Supreme Lord, having relied merely out of curiosity upon both the practices of poets and authorities, considers it proper that there should once again be a resting solely in devotion to the Supreme Lord.
The bliss that arises from the specific objects— both seen and unseen— ascertained by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

or even that which is supramundane and consists of the relishing of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), in both cases the bliss of resting in the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) excels; for it was stated by us previously that the tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*) is indeed the manifestation of a mere drop of that bliss.

The intended meaning is that worldly happiness is, for its part, almost inferior even to that [supramundane happiness] because it is accompanied by much greater suffering. In that very context, there may be the inclusion of a single word with respect to the term "view" (*dṛṣṭi*); or else, one may resort to the figure of speech known as *virodhālaṅkāra* (the ornament of contradiction), based on the description [of the world] while relying upon a [false] view.

There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determining one way or the other— whether the word "sight" (*dṛṣṭi*), by its placement like that of a blind man, is a case of extreme exclusion of the literal meaning (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*)—
because it is charming in both ways.
Nor should the same be asserted regarding the former [example].
By the word "new" (*nava*), because of the resonance of the power of the word (*śabda-śakti-anuraṇana*), contradiction (*virodha*) is supported in every respect.
Having thus illustrated the threefold *saṅkara* (blending), he illustrates *saṃsṛṣṭi* (collocation) with the words "vācye" and so on.

For if, throughout the entire sentence, both the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) and the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) are predominant, then there is *saṅkara* by way of the relationship between the assisted and the assister; in the absence of that [relationship], [there is *saṃsṛṣṭi*].
Its nature as supreme bliss is demonstrated in works such as the *Bhaktirasāyana*.
He provides the introduction to this verse with the words "Thus," and so forth;
the connection is that "this statement is thus."
He states the ultimate intended meaning of this verse with the words beginning "sakala" (with parts), etc.

By the term "intermingling" (*saṅkīrṇatva*) in the commentary, he shows that both the intermingling by way of the relationship between the recipient of grace and the bestower of grace, as well as the intermingling through the penetration into a single word, are intended; he demonstrates this with the words beginning "tatra," etc.
"Tatra" (there) refers to that very aforementioned verse.
Regarding the phrase "entry into a single word":

the remainder [of the sentence] is that this refers to the *dhvani* (suggested meaning) in which the expressed sense is transmuted (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*), occurring alongside the figure of speech *virodha* (contradiction).
Here he also demonstrates the "blending through doubt" (*sandehasaṅkara*) with the words beginning "having taken hold of her gaze," and so forth.
"Or else, it is the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction).

This means that in the phrase "they, having resorted to [it], gazed," the pronoun *te* (they) refers back to the object denoted by the word *dṛṣṭi* (gaze)—that is, the act of seeing. Thus, the meaning "they saw, having resorted to the act of seeing" results in the perception of a contradictory sense, and therefore it is the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra*.
The resolution of the contradiction here is based on the meaning that is about to be explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "blind" (*andha*), in expressions such as "blinded by sighs" (*niḥśvāsāndha*), when the word *dṛṣṭi* (vision) refers—by means of the word *andha* (blind), which is a case of complete concealment of the literal sense (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*)—to the implied meaning in the form of creative intuition (*pratibhā*), then it is indeed "Suggestive Poetry" (*dhvani*) characterized by the complete concealment of the literal sense. This is the meaning.
"In the previous case as well" means that this applies even to the view that "it is the faculty of sight which possesses the activity of tasting flavors.
"In the same way" refers to this.
The meaning is that there is a confusion of doubt. Regarding the phrase "not," and so forth:
the word "not" (na) is connected with the word "because of relying" (avalambanāt).
The meaning is: "because it is manifested by the word 'nava'.
The instrumental case is used in the qualifier *śabdaśaktyanuraṇanatayā* [meaning "by way of being an after-resonance of the power of the word"].
He provides an example (*udāharati*).
The meaning is "it shows.
Regarding the phrase "in the entire sentence," the meaning is "in a complete sentence."
Some [verses] possess verbal ornaments (*vācyālaṅkāra*), and some are endowed with varieties of suggestion (*dhvani*).
For example: "Lengthening the sharp, sweet warbling of the cranes at dawn, [the breeze] is perfumed by its friendship with the fragrance of blooming lotuses.

Regarding this, there are three varieties: that which is realized through *locana* (direct perception), through *dhvani* (suggestion), or through both in alternation or simultaneously, with the pause resting on the words. Thus, there are three divisions.
Having internalized this, he states with emphasis: "only in relation to the words.

He begins to provide an illustration of that third type, where even the suspicion of a relationship between the recipient of grace (*anugrāhya*) and the bestower of grace (*anugrāhaka*) does not arise, by saying: "for where...
because in some cases certain [words] possess poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), while others are endowed with suggestion (*dhvani*).

Just as in the phrase "making [it] long here," so too, by repeating the word, the connection with the preceding text must be made thus: "the state of being conjoined with a verbal figure of speech (vācyālaṅkāra) is to be understood only in relation to such a word. Regarding the phrase "for here":
The logical connection of the text is that the word *hi* (for/indeed) should be placed immediately after the phrase *maitrīpadam*.
Regarding the expression *dīrghīkurvan*:
for by the breeze from the Siprā river, this sound is carried even to a great distance.
Likewise, they warble for a long time, filled with joy born from the touch of the gentle breeze;
and that warbling becomes mingled with the sweet sound produced by the waves of the Siprā as they are tossed by the wind—this constitutes its length. "Sharp" (paṭu) means:
Likewise, that breeze is so delicate that the sound produced by it does not even overwhelm the warbling of the cranes; on the contrary, being a companion to them, it illuminates that very sound.
And this illumination is not useless, for it makes their cry sweet and melodious when heard in its intoxication at dawn.
Thus [it is said]: "at daybreaks."
The dawn possesses the quality of being an occasion for such service.
The plural number indicates that this [beauty] is always pleasing to the heart there.
They are blossomed by the abundance of nectar contained within.
"In the absence of that" means the absence of their commingling. "By way of synonyms" [means]:
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "one must rest upon the word.
Regarding the phrase "only the third":
the meaning is that it has already been stated that one must rest simultaneously upon both words. He connects the sentence beginning with "where" by saying "because," and so forth.
"Because" (*yasmāt*) explains the meaning of the word "for" (*hi*). Regarding "by repetition" (*āvṛttyā*):

since the nature of being conjoined with a verbal figure of speech depends precisely upon the words, there is a repetition of the words; the sense is that the phrase "depending upon the words" means "depending upon such words."
One should understand that "this" is an elliptical expression and that "therein" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

By the phrase "making it long," he explains that the lengthening of the cooing is threefold— caused by the wind from the Siprā river, spatial, and temporal— and produced by the blending of its own kind— as stated in the passage beginning with "with the wind" and ending with "lengthening."
Intending to explain that "making [the intention] long" is an adverbial modifier meaning "clever" or "capable," he says "tathā" and so forth.
"Sukumāraḥ" means "mild. The connection is as follows: because it illuminates—that is, nourishes—it is sweet; therefore, it is not useless.
"Service of such a kind" means service in the form of removing the exhaustion of the rainy season and so forth.
"Therein" [means]...
The meaning is "in Ujjayinī.
He "demonstrates" means he shows.
Having kept in mind that the word *sphuṭitāni* (burst open) means *truṭitāni* (broken), he shows the implied reason for that with the words beginning with *antara*.
He says "tathā" and so forth to indicate that another meaning is also intended by the word "sphuṭitāni" (blossomed):
"Where the breeze from the Siprā river, blowing favorably against the limbs, removes the fatigue of love-making for women, like a beloved lover offering flattering words of entreaty."

The eyes were thus blossomed and opened, captivating the gaze; the fragrance of those lotuses produced a sense of intimacy through the attainment of mutual compatibility and inseparable union resulting from practice, whereby they were stained with passion and rendered the color of a decoction by the nectar.
Regarding the phrase "of women":
he who acts in this manner removes the exhaustion and fatigue caused by sexual union for all such beings who constitute the very essence of the three worlds;
furthermore, he removes the weariness concerning that [union] by rekindling the desire for further enjoyment.
Moreover, even though it is abundant, this touch is indeed agreeable to her limbs and has entered within her heart;
O most beloved, she causes him to utter endearments for the sake of requesting that very object,
while the beloved, too, has his desire for union awakened by the touch of that breeze.

He performs flatteries for the sake of solicitation; thus, by him, it is made to happen in that way. This wind is the very essence of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), whose life-breath is mutual passion. And this is appropriate for him, because he is a wind familiar with the Siprā river; he is a refined city-dweller (*nāgarika*), not one who is unrefined. [The commentator] states the intended meaning of the word "eyes" (*nayana*): "Because the primary meaning of the term 'friendship' (*maitrīpada*) is contradicted here, he shows what is intended by that word through the phrase beginning with 'through close contact' (*abhyāsaṅga*). *Bālapriyā* (the commentary on the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*): He states the essential meaning—namely, "by the eyes. Since the primary sense of the word "friendship" is obstructed here, he indicates what is actually intended by that term through the words beginning with "through close contact."

The non-separation (*aviyoga*)—that is, the non-interruption—of the constant attachment (*abhyāsaṅga*), which is the close union (*saṃśleṣa*), means the attainment of mutual conformity and mutual assistance; in other words, it refers to an uninterrupted union. Here, the distinction is that "uninterrupted union" is the denoted meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), whereas "the attainment of mutual conformity" is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
"Uparaktaḥ" means connected.
He states another meaning with the words "by makaranda," and so forth. "Red mixed with yellow" refers to a tawny color; this is an explanation of the meaning of the plural form "sarvasya."
"Of such a woman" means one characterized by femininity.
The phrase "of the three worlds," etc., is a statement of the implied meaning (*gamyārtha*).

Regarding the term "exhaustion from sexual union" (*surataglānim*), he explains it in two ways—as exhaustion caused by sexual union and as exhaustion pertaining to the object of sexual union—by saying "caused by sexual union," and so forth.
"Tāntam" means bodily fatigue;
"glānim" means [physical exhaustion].
The meaning is "lack of enthusiasm.
As for the word "na" (not),
it is connected with the verb "harati" (takes away).
He states that the meaning "conducive to the heart" (*hṛdayasyānukūla*) is also intended by the phrase "contained within the heart" (*hṛdayāntarbhūta*).
This means "affectionate.

Furthermore, intending the word-division *priyatame* (dative), he also connects it as an adjective for the wind, namely *vātaviśeṣaṇatayā*, by saying "the supplication to the beloved and the flattery," beginning with the words "to the most beloved" (*priyatame*).
The analysis of "priyatama" ending in the locative case is "tadviṣaye" (in relation to that).
"For the purpose of prayer" means the production of a desire for sexual enjoyment in women.

Regarding the term *cāṭukāra*, he states that the suffix is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) from the causative form (*ṇyantāt*). Here, "flatteries" (*cāṭūni*) constitute the suggestive power (*dhvani*) where the literal meaning of the word "friendship" (*maitrīpada*) is not intended to be expressed. In other words, there are different figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) in the other words.
An example of a suggestive power (*dhvani*) mixed with other combined figures of speech is as follows: [Locana]—the meaning is "mostly vulgar."

Even the beloved lover, at the conclusion of lovemaking, removes the exhaustion of sexual union by massaging her limbs and other such means, and employs endearing flattery for the sake of further solicitation.
He prolongs her cooing—consisting of words of refusal and the like—which is a sweet-sounding murmur.

And on the occasion of his offering flattery, her face, which possesses the luster of a blooming lotus, becomes suffused with a fragrant scent through its friendship with that fragrance—the natural acquaintance with its innate perfume.
"Conducive to the sixty-four arts of love in its various parts;

likewise, where sounds, forms, scents, and touches are pleasing, and where the breeze is likewise so—such a place is truly urban (nāgarika), and you must certainly go there. This is the speech of a lover addressed to the cloud in the *Meghadūta*.
He applies the definition to the example with the words "the term *maitrī*.
It has already been stated that the word *hi* (for/indeed) is to be read immediately after;
[this refers to] "other figures of speech" (*alaṅkārāntarāṇi*).
The meaning is that these occur in sequence as *utprekṣā*, *svabhāvokti*, *rūpaka*, and *upamā*.

Thus, by this much, [the types of poetry] have been explained along with their own subdivisions— those where the suggested sense is subordinated (*saguṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) and those possessing ornaments (*sālaṅkāra*)—
as well as through the two modes of *saṅkara* (blending) and *saṃsṛṣṭi* (juxtaposition).

Having explained up to this point and having examined the examples, [the author] elucidates the meaning of the two words "punar api" (again) found in the portion of the verse by means of examples themselves—beginning with "saṃsṛṣṭā" and so on.

The meaning of the word "punar" is as follows: not only are *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) and *saṅkara* (conflation) intended for the *dhvani* itself along with its own subdivisions and so forth, but they are also intended for those [subdivisions] among themselves; [this is what] Bālapriyā [explains] by saying "priyatamo 'pi" and so on.
"By that" means by the wind;
"mutually," and so forth.
The sense is that [the mention of the river] serves to kindle the desire for sexual enjoyment in one who is most dear to women.
By the phrase "familiar with the Siprā," the river Siprā is understood to function as the heroine (nāyikā).
The word "iti" is used here in the sense of a reason.
He applies the qualifiers even to the beloved who serves as the point of comparison—namely, "even the beloved," and so forth.
The construction is: "one who is favorable toward the limbs through massaging and other such acts.
[The term] "cāṭukāra" means one who speaks flattering words.
The meaning is "one who utters flattering words.
"With words of non-acceptance" means with words such as "it is merely [a garland]," and so forth.
The explanation of "madakalam" (sweetly warbling) is "madhuradhvanitam" (sweet-sounding).
"Cāṭivat" and so forth means: at the occasion of hearing the affectionate, flattering words of one's beloved.
"Blown open" (vikasitam) means "by a smile produced from hearing flattering words"— this is the intended sense.
He states that the word *kamala* (lotus) refers to the face by means of a metaphorical indication (*sādhyavasāna-lakṣaṇā*)— thus he says "the lotus," and so forth.
Regarding the word "face," the term "of women" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
He explains the phrase "conforming to the limbs" in another way as well, beginning with the words "in the limbs," and so forth.
Showing the essential meaning of this verse, he concludes the commentary with the words "Thus," and so forth. "That region" means the region of Ujjayinī.
"Utprekṣā" and so forth:

in the phrase "making [the night] appear long and intense," there is a suggested *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), while in the description of the nature of dawn (*pratyūṣasvabhāvokti*), there is a direct description of the essence of the time.
The term "smooth" (*snigdha*) is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) because it is superimposed upon the wind as being favorable to the body;

alternatively, the meaning of "metaphor" here is "hyperbolic metaphor" (*rūpakātiśayokti*), since the face is understood through the word "lotus. Therefore, that [hyperbole] is to be understood there.
The meaning is that there is also a simile, "as if [he were] the beloved.
He introduces the passage beginning with "saṃsṛṣṭā" (intermingled) with the words "evam iyatā" (thus, by this much), etc.
[He says] "teṣām anyonyam api" (among those, even mutually).

The tooth-marks and the gashes torn by claws upon your body, where thick horripilation has burst forth, were bestowed by the lioness with a mind intent on blood; yet they were gazed upon even by sages who felt a surge of longing.

For here, there is the manifestation of a type of *dhvani*—in which the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is not the primary focus (*alakṣyakrama*)—which is intermingled with the figure of speech *virodha* (contradiction) that is itself commingled with *samāsokti* (condensed expression).
This is because, in the ultimate sense, the sentiment of compassion (*dayāvīra*) constitutes the very essence of the sentence-meaning.

The *Locana* [comments]: "The commingling of various types of *dhvani* occurs when they are either commingled or combined with other types of *dhvani*, whether through their own subdivisions or with *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion)."

Since the state of being "intermingled" (*saṃsṛṣṭatva*) is difficult to perceive, it does not serve as a clear example; with this intention, the commingling (*saṃkara*) and intermingling (*saṃsarga*) of one figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) with another within *dhvani* must be demonstrated.
Thus, among these four varieties, he first provides an illustration of the first variety: "dantakṣātanī... (She who whitens her teeth...).
Someone offers words of praise to the Bodhisattva who has offered his own body to a lion that had set upon devouring his own cub;
in that act, a dense thrill of horripilation arises from the abundance of bliss born of the fulfillment of the welfare of others—
[the lioness] whose desire was for blood red with [fresh] gore.

There is a contradiction in [the phrase] "whose mind is attached" and "men whose possession by passion has been awakened. Furthermore, the term "by those who have conceived longing" refers to those possessed by the royal dream of wishing: "When shall we too ascend the path of the compassionate, so that we may truly become sages?"
And there is *samāsokti* (synecdoche) because of the perception of the heroine's narrative.

Regarding "of the hero of compassion" (*dayāvīra*): since it is motivated by compassion, dharma here is referred to by the term "hero of compassion," as it is essentially the hero of dharma (*dharmavīra*).
And the sentiment (rasa) here is the heroic (vīra), because enthusiasm (utsāha) alone is the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva); this is the intended meaning.
Alternatively, one may designate the tranquil (śānta) by the term "compassionate hero" (dayāvīra).
The ellipsis here is that "the *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) and *saṅkara* (fusion) intended [by the author] are meant";

this meaning is connected with what precedes. Now, one might ask: "What is the reason for showing in the commentary merely the distinctions such as being mixed with other figures (*alaṅkāra*) in *saṃsṛṣṭi*? To this, he says: "Of its own sub-varieties," and so forth.
"By means of sound" (dhvaninā) means "together with sound.
"Difficult to perceive" (durlakṣam) means... [end of fragment].
The meaning is "because the reason is difficult to discern.
The word *vispaṣṭa* means "very clear" (*suspaṣṭa*).
"Capable of being demonstrated" means they can be shown.
"The first distinction" means the distinction consisting of the nature of being a mixture (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) or a blend (*saṅkīrṇa*) of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
"Born from the perfection of the welfare of others" means born from the protection of others;
and "not born from enjoyment with a female lead."
By the phrase "in your body," it is understood as "the body of a lustful man";
by the phrase "the consort of the king of beasts," it is understood as "the consort of a specific species of animal called a deer.

Regarding the phrase "even by sages who have conceived longing," he states "and the sages," etc., because there is an apparent contradiction in the sense that even those detached from sense objects would have their desire awakened.
He states the subject at hand with the words "by those whose longing has arisen," and so forth;
the construction is "by those possessed of [worldly] mental fantasies.
Since the Sage did not speak of the heroism of compassion (*dayāvīra*), he says "compassion," and so forth.

Since dharma is characterized by compassion, the connection here is that the term "compassionate hero" (*dayāvīra*) refers specifically to the "hero of dharma. He states another alternative interpretation with the words "by the term compassionate hero," and so forth.
He explains the passage beginning with "by means of the *samāsokti* [synecdoche] combined with," etc., with the words "he, in this case," and so forth.

That rasa may be the heroic (dharmavīra) or the tranquil (śānta); and as for the state of being a combination of figures of speech (alaṅkāra-saṃsṛṣṭatva) within a suggestive work (dhvani), it is as follows: "In these days, which have acquired a new charm through the arrival of travelers, the dancing of flocks of peacocks with outspread tails is beautiful."
The *locana* [commentary] states that the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is enhanced by the figure of speech of commingled ornament (*saṃsṛṣṭālaṅkāra*).

For this meaning is accomplished through the greatness of the figure of elliptical expression (*samāsokti*): just as someone experiences horripilation at the moment of union with a beloved long sought after through hundreds of desires, so too is your excellence of compassion—kindled by the abundance of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and ensuants (*anubhāva*)—manifested in the gift of your own body for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others.
In two days;
likewise, toward travelers, they have become "turned dark" (śyāmāyiteṣu), meaning they have assumed the nature of night because they produce delusion;
or else, they are those from whom the "darkening" (śyāmāyitam) of travelers arises through the power of their suffering.

The dance of flocks of peacocks with their necks outstretched is beautiful when there are travelers in the audience who delight in the performance of dramatic gestures; for the dance of these flocks of peacocks— whose songs follow excellent melodic strings (*sāraṇā*) as they stretch forth their songs, and whose necks are extended in the movement of their necks— is truly splendid.

The suffix *kyac* is applied in the sense that "they act like Śyāmās toward the travelers," thereby indicating an elided simile (*luptopamā*). Since the compound *pathikasāmājikeṣu* (among the assemblies of travelers) is clearly a *karmadhāraya*, it constitutes a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
The author’s intention is that there is a "conjunction" (*saṃsarga*) of these two with the word *dhvani*.
It is not provided that another example is given here, with the intention that within this very same example, two other varieties could be illustrated.

To explain: since [the term] *vyāghra* and others belong to a class of words (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the phrase "among travelers who are like members of an assembly" contains both simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*), which constitute the "essence" (*rasa*) dear to children.
"By means of a combined ornament (*saṃsṛṣṭālaṅkāra*)" means by means of the ornament of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*) combined with the ornament of implied metaphor (*samāsokti*).

Having considered that the fact that even sages look upon [the scene] with longing clearly demonstrates the subordination of the contradiction through the perception of the full development of the heroic sentiment of compassion (*dayāvīra*), he establishes that [development] by means of the implied metaphor, starting with "by the power of the implied metaphor," and so forth.
The word *iti* means "for this reason" (*ityarthāt*).
[The passage beginning with] *anubhāva*, etc., [is as follows].
The *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) is the manifestation of dense horripilation;
the *ālambana-vibhāva* (objective determinant) is the lioness;
and the *uddīpana-vibhāva* (excitant determinant) is the tooth-wound and so forth—this is how it should be understood.
"Second" means having the nature of being a combination of combined ornaments (*saṃsṛṣṭālaṅkāra*). "Abhinava," etc. [refers to this].
Description of the Rainy Season.
Here, at the outset, he explains the meaning of what is to be expressed, beginning with "fresh" (*abhinava*) and so forth;
[it refers to] travelers who are separated from their lovers.

Regarding the verse "iyāmāyitoṣu," he explains it with the words beginning "moha," intending that the suffix *kyac* is added to the word *śyāmā*, which denotes "night," in the sense of "acting like" (ācāra).
Intending that the meaning of *śyāmāyitam* is "darkness" (*śyāmikā*), he says "yadi vā," etc.;
*śyāmikā* refers to a particular color.
By showing another shadow (chāyā), he demonstrates the implied meaning here with the words "in the application of gestures" (*abhinayaprayoga*), and so forth.
The explanation of the phrase "of those who have stretched out their songs" (*prasāritagītānām*) is "excellent," and so forth.
He states "likewise," and so forth, indicating that in this interpretation, the phrase "of those who have stretched out their necks" (*prasāritagrīvāṇām*) should also be applied.
He explains the nature of the conjoined figures (*saṃsṛṣṭālaṅkāra*) in the sound (*dhvani*) with the verse beginning "O travelers" (*pathikān*), etc. Regarding the term "metaphor" (*rūpaka*):
the sense is that it is because the state of being a spectator (*sāmājikatva*) is superimposed upon the travelers.
"Of the resonance" (dhvaneḥ) means "of the suggested meaning" (vyaṅgya) as described in the passage beginning with "in the application of dramatic gesture" (abhinayaprayoga).
"Conjunction" (saṃsargaḥ) means "commingling" (saṃsṛṣṭiḥ).
"Another two varieties [of *saṃsṛṣṭi*]"—

for here, there is a commingling (*saṃsṛṣṭatva*) of *dhvani* whose suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), arising from the power of words (*śabdaśaktyudbhava*), takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) through both simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Thus, who is able to enumerate the primary divisions of *dhvani* and the sub-divisions of those divisions?
We have stated this merely as a general indication for the purpose of enumerating them.
Thus, by whom could the divisions of sound and the further subdivisions of those divisions be enumerated? We have stated this [merely] as a mere indication of their direction. (44)
For the varieties of suggestion (dhvani) are indeed infinite; only a mere indication of them has been stated for the instruction of those with aesthetic sensitivity.
Thus, that which is defined as *dhvani* should be diligently investigated by the virtuous who are earnestly devoted to either composing or correctly understanding excellent poetry. (Dhvanyāloka 3.45)

Thus, this *dhvani* whose characteristics have been described should be discerned with effort by the virtuous who are earnestly intent on either composing excellent poetry or understanding it correctly. (45)

For excellent poets and connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), who are skilled in defining the nature of *dhvani* as previously described, certainly [distinguish] between the two—metaphor (*upamā*) and metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*)—when they are mixed in dramatic performance (*abhinayaprayoga*) and in new compositions among connoisseurs.

Regarding the phrase "extended songs" (*prasāritagītānām*), that which arises from the power of words (*śabdaśaktyudbhava*) is merely a combination (*saṃsarga*), because there is no mutual subordination (*anugrāhyatva*).

However, in the verse containing the word *pahiasāmāiesu*, because those two—metaphor and metaphorical identification—are mixed, the *dhvani* rooted in the power of words is itself mixed through the "entry into a single manifestor" (*ekavyañjakānupraveśa*); thus, it is a case of the mixture of mixed figures of speech (*saṅkīrṇālaṅkārasaṃsṛṣṭa*).
One should also consider two further divisions: that which is mixed with other ornaments (saṅkīrṇālaṅkāra) and that which is itself mixed (saṅkīrṇa). // 43 //
He concludes this with the word "thus" (evam);
it is clear. // 44 //

Now, with the intention that what was previously indicated by the phrase "for the delight of the hearts of the sensitive" (sahṛdaya) is now not merely stated in words but fully accomplished, he says: "Thus it has been said.
That *dhvani*—which must be discerned through diligent effort and which possesses the characteristics we have described—is this very essence of poetry (*kāvyatattva*).

[This is so] because those who are unable to explain it through the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) and stylistic modes (*rīti*), despite their detailed descriptions as previously set forth, [resort to these]. The meaning is that there are two types of mixture: the mixture of ornaments (*alaṅkārasaṃsṛṣṭi*) and the mixture of ornaments with ornaments (*alaṅkārasaṅkīrṇatva*).
The connection is with "from the mixed metaphors and similes.

By showing that the word *ahiṇaa* can be interpreted in both ways—as *abhinaya* (acting) and as *abhinava* (new)—he demonstrates the *dhvani* (suggestive power) through the passage beginning with "abhinaya," etc.
[He says this] because there is an absence of anything to be further embellished (*anugrāhyatva*).
The phrase "of that" (tasya) is to be supplied with both the simile and the metaphor. // 43 //
"Etad" means the statement of its many divisions. // 44 //
The phrase beginning with "sahṛdaya" means:
"We shall describe its true nature for the pleasure of the hearts of sensitive readers," as has been stated;
[the term] "śabdamātra" means mere words or mere speech.
He states that the two verses beginning with "having the characteristics thus described" (*ityuktalakṣaṇa*) constitute a single syntactical unit by saying "he who," and so forth.
Regarding the word "stated" (*ukta*), he completes the sense by supplying "by us.
The word "this" (*etat*) is a reference back to the pronoun "he who" (*yaḥ*).

Showing that the phrase "as stated" (yathoditam) is connected with the word "to explain" (vyākartum), he explains [the passage] beginning with "as stated" (yathoditena) and so forth, and "others, however" (anye tu) and so forth.
The meaning is that they read [the text as]: "this is *dhvani* according to the definition thus stated."
According to this view, in the domain of poetry, they attain the highest state of excellence.
This essence of poetry, which has been described as manifesting in an indistinct manner, was unable to be fully articulated; therefore, the *rītis* were introduced. (Dhvanyāloka 3.46)
Because this essence of poetry, as it has been described, is not clearly manifested and cannot be fully articulated by those who lack proficiency, the *rītis* (styles) have been introduced. (46)

Having determined the true essence of poetry through this exposition of *dhvani*, those who were unable to demonstrate it clearly as it was only faintly manifest established the styles (*rītis*) known as Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, and Pāñcālī. For it appears that to those who formulated the definitions of these styles, this essence of poetry was only slightly manifest due to its lack of clarity; therefore, there is nothing to be gained here from any other definition of style that has been presented with such clarity.
When this definition of poetry is understood, certain functions (vṛtti) based on the essence of words and others joined with the essence of meaning also become manifest. (Dhvanyāloka 3.47)
When this definition of poetry is understood, certain functions (vṛtti) based on the essence of sound and others joined with the essence of meaning also become manifest. (47)

When this definition of poetry, which consists of an analysis of the relationship between the suggested and the suggester, is understood, whatever well-known modes (*vṛttis*) based on the essence of words— such as the *aupacchandasika* and others— and those connected to the essence of meaning— such as the *kaiśikī* and others—
all properly enter the path of the term "style" (*rīti*).
Otherwise, these functions would be as untrustworthy as those whose purpose is unseen (adṛṣṭārtha), and their status as established by experience would not exist.

Thus, the very nature of this *dhvani* must be clearly defined, wherein certain words and meanings are perceived by specific observers; this connects with the subsequent verse which states that "the eyes have been directed [toward them]."
Others, however, read "this" (*ayam*) in place of the word "which" (*yat*).
The meaning is that [it reaches] the state of excellence both in its manifestation and in its realization.
The reason why [the masters] were unable to provide a definitive explanation is stated as: "having made it unclear, it has flashed forth.
It is "perceived" because style (rīti) is indeed ultimately grounded in the poetic qualities (guṇas).

As he said: "The particular (viśeṣa) consists of the qualities (guṇas), and the qualities culminate in rasa alone"—for this was stated previously in the definition of the qualities [in the passage]: "Only the erotic (śṛṅgāra) is sweet. // 45-46 //
"Shine forth" means that they attain the status of being established by experience as the very lifeblood of poetry. "The path of *rīti*"— [refers to this].

It should be understood that "called *Bālapriyā*" and so forth constitutes one sentence, while "not clearly manifest" (*asphuṭa*) and so forth is another sentence; therein, by the word "this" (*etat*), there is a reference to *dhvani*.
Regarding the phrase "reaching the highest state of excellence," he completes the sense by saying "in its creation and in its comprehension.
By the commentary's statement "being [a state] where it is not clearly manifest yet shimmering," it is shown that the word "this" (*tat*) contains a reason within it.
He clarifies that very point with the words "to explain" (*vyākartum*), and so forth.
Since it was stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) that "[it] is characterized thus" (*iti lakṣyate*), he establishes how that is so with the words "the style (*rīti*)," and so forth.
Here, the connection is: "for it has been said thus. (45–46)

Having in mind the essential meaning that will be stated in the commentary—that [the nature of dhvani] is established through experience—he explains it with the words beginning "anubhava" and so forth.

As for the definition of *dhvani* stated by someone else—that in poetry, an indescribable beauty, like the generic quality (*jātyatva*) of specific jewels, manifests itself, and therein the term *dhvani* is employed—that is incorrect and does not deserve to be mentioned;
because, first of all, the nature of words consists in their being used in a manner that is unforced and not previously employed [in that specific sense].

The distinction [between the two types of suggestion] lies in the fact that [in the first case], clarity resides in the expressive words (*vācaka*), whereas [in the second], it consists in suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*). Furthermore, the distinction regarding meanings is that they appear with vividness, possess a focus on the suggested (*vyaṅgyaparatva*), and are characterized by the element of the suggested (*vyaṅgyāṃśaviśiṣṭatva*).
These two distinctions can be explained, and indeed have been explained in many ways.
However, the possibility of a specific quality that is distinct from those [other elements] and yet indescribable is rooted solely in the failure of discrimination.

This is because the state of being indescribable is, like the eye itself, ultimately nothing but aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Alternatively, there is a reading: "into the path of apprehension" (*pratītipadavīm*).

For the term "urbane" (*nāgarikā*), being a form of alliteration (*anuprāsa-vṛtti*), finds its rest in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others; "harsh" (*paruṣā*) [finds its rest] in the intense sentiments such as the furious (*raudra*); and "soft" (*komalā*) [finds its rest in the opposite].
In the case of laughter and so forth;
likewise, as for what was stated by the Sage [Bharata] that "the *vṛttis* are the mothers of poetry," therein a *vṛtti* is specifically a particular kind of physical action appropriate to the *rasa*.
As he said: "The *Kaiśikī* has smooth attire and arises from the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) *rasa*," and so on.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Others have declared its non-existence to this extent," among the various alternatives concerning non-existence, [the opponent asks]: "The poetic qualities (*vṛttis*) and styles (*rītis*) have come within the range of hearing; what then is this *dhvani* that is distinct from them?
To this, an acceptance has been made in one way and a refutation offered in another way by means of the statement "it is manifested indistinctly" (*asphuṭasphurita*).

Regarding what was said [previously], "now [poetry] resides in that which is beyond the scope of speech," although that was already refuted in the first chapter (uddyota), it is refuted here again with the intention that if one were to describe the entire manifold world (prapañca), its being "inexpressible" would be utterly impossible; thus,
the term "akliṣṭatva" means the absence of harshness of sound (śrutikaṣṭa) and so forth.
"The application of what has not been previously applied" is not a redundancy;
"just like that" means "just like *rīti*";
it should be stated that this is an explanation of the phrase "they manifest as they descend into the path of *rīti*."
And that is not possible, because those two have different meanings.

Furthermore, in the phrase "entering the path of *rīti*," it is difficult to establish that knowledge of the definition of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*) is the cause; therefore, he says "the path of comprehension" (*pratītipadavīm*) to indicate that the reading here must be otherwise.
He specifically demonstrates that the function (*vṛtti*) culminates in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by saying "by the *nāgarikā*," and so forth.

In the commentary—starting with "where," etc.—the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as the genuineness (*jātyatva*) of certain specific jewels is perceivable only by a qualified connoisseur, so too, in certain words and meanings, a beauty that is truly inexpressible manifests itself.
"[It is] improper" refers to this [objection].
The meaning is: "because of the lack of logical connection" (*ayuktatvāt*).
Intending to state that "beauty" (*cārutvam*) must be some kind of specific quality (*viśeṣa*), he explains why it does not deserve to be denotable by saying "since," and so forth.

The term "based on its own nature" (*svarūpāśraya*) is connected with the word "specific quality" (*viśeṣa*). In the *Locana*, he speaks following a restatement of what has occurred, beginning with "to this extent," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "dhvaniriti": the word "yadūce" (as was said) is to be understood as being drawn back [to apply] here. [The verb] "dūṣayati" (he refutes).
The meaning is that, having restated [the opponent's position] with the words beginning "yatra" (where), he refutes it with the passage beginning "tadayuktam" (that is incorrect).
The connection is that he refutes it according to his own intention.
He explains the phrase "akliṣṭatattve" (in the unafflicted reality) with the words beginning "śruti" (scripture).
The portion consisting of the state of being devoid of conceptual differentiation (*viveka*) and exhaustion (*avasāda*) cannot belong to anything by virtue of being beyond the scope of all words;

for, ultimately, it is possible to designate it even with the word "inexpressible" (*anākhyeya*). This is provided that it remains beyond the scope of conceptual words that touch upon universals (*sāmānya*).
Furthermore, that which is sometimes called "inexpressibility" (anākhyeyatva) regarding the state of being manifest— that too is impossible for specific poetic works, just as it is for specific gems;
for those [poems] have their forms explained by the authors of technical definitions (lakṣaṇakāra),
and because we observe that the determination of the value of specific gems occurs only through a general estimation of their possibility.
For both of these [categories], there is indeed the quality of being perceivable by a specific type of cognizer.
For who would dispute that only jewelers know the true nature of gems, and only those with aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya) are connoisseurs of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of poems?

As for that "indefinability" (*anirdeśyatva*) which is well-known among Buddhists as pertaining to all defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), we shall examine that in another work during our investigation of their doctrine.
However, in this context, we do not proceed with it, because explaining even a fragment of what is heard in another work would cause distress to those of refined sensibility (*sahṛdaya*).
Or rather, according to the Buddhist view, just as there is a definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, so too will there be our own definition of *dhvani*.

Therefore, because another defining characteristic cannot be established and because it is not the meaning of the word, [the author] explains "those two" as pertaining to both the word and the object.
"The state of non-discrimination" (*nirvivekatvam*) is the condition wherein there is a collapse of discrimination.

He shows that even in the case of the example, there is no "inexpressibility" regarding the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which touches upon the universal (*sāmānya*), by stating: "and of the specific jewels."
Anticipating the objection that "surely that is not experienced by everyone," he replies by way of admission: "of both.
[This refers to] gems and poetic works.
Now, one might object: "But words do not even touch upon the meaning."
If it is asked, "In the passage beginning with 'the knower of the inexpressible,' how is the inexpressibility of things stated?", he says here: "As for that which...

The sense is this: since sound (*dhvani*) would thus be exactly equal to the entire range of all entities, the definition that the nature of sound is inexpressible would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).
